stories.title: Ontario-backed High Art Capital pays $22.3-million for 43 unsold Toronto condo units
stories.summary: Bulk purchase at well below market rate is the fund’s first transaction and one of the few of its kind to be revealed publicly
stories.author: Rachelle Younglai
stories.content:
Ontario government-backed investment firm High Art Capital has paid $22.3-million for 43 unsold condo units at new towers in midtown Toronto, an amount well below the market rate.

The bulk purchase is the $1.3-billion fund’s first transaction. The firm bought the units in a condo complex called Line 5, which was named after the city’s new light-rail transit on Eglinton Avenue.

The purchase is one of the few of its kind to be revealed publicly. Large investors, such as real estate companies, have been bulk-buying unsold condo units at a discount to take advantage of the recent downturn.

But the deals are not typically public, nor are the precise locations or pricing per unit. The $22.3-million price tag works out to an average of $518,000 a unit, according to data from CoStar Group, a U.S.-based commercial real estate information provider that reviewed land transfer records for the transaction.

High Art, a privately owned fund, launched this year to buy up unsold inventory in the Toronto region and turn them into rentals. It is backed by $300-million in financing from the Ontario government through its Building Ontario Fund, which was formed in 2024 to invest with private investors in infrastructure deemed critical for the province.

Its Line 5 deal was initially announced in mid-August in a news release without information on the location, pricing or number of units. At the time, a High Art spokesperson said it would not disclose transaction details.

This week, spokesperson Laryssa Waler reiterated that the fund does not comment on details of confidential commercial transactions.

Developers lobby Ottawa for mortgage-interest tax changes on new homes

The Line 5 project was developed by Westdale Properties and Reserve Properties, which launched sales prior to the pandemic when there was strong demand for pre-construction condos. Now, there’s very little demand.

Westdale chief operating officer Mitchell Cohen said a lot of developers are sitting on inventory and the transaction with High Art helps get the units out on the market so people can live in them. “It was a perfect opportunity,” said Mr. Cohen.

High Art paid less than the average price of a pre-construction condo in Toronto and those on the resale market.

“Bulk buyers are acquiring at a notable discount to an individual buyer,” said Shaun Hildebrand, president with condo research firm Urbanation Inc.

High Art’s plan is to buy about 2,200 unsold condos and then sell most of them after a minimum of five years. Of that amount, 550 units are expected to be rented at below-market rates and remain affordable rentals in perpetuity.

Building Ontario Fund spokesperson Julia Sakas said High Art’s plan creates both market and affordable rental housing.

As part of its first deal, High Art has said it has an agreement with the Service Employees International Union to provide its members in health care, such as personal support workers, with rental units below market rates.

The union said the response has been overwhelming, with more than 500 members expressing interest.

“Some of our members have enormous commutes,” said John Klein, the union’s secretary treasurer, adding that the fund wanted to prioritize health care workers and first responders.

In depth: In downtown Toronto, the office is back

Rent would be 25 per cent below the going rate. For example, the Line 5 condos are near the heavily trafficked intersection of Yonge Street and Eglinton Avenue. There, the typical rent for a one-bedroom is about $2,400 per month, according to Mr. Klein. That means union members could rent a unit at around $1,800 per month, he said.

The real estate downturn has prompted the federal and Ontario governments to introduce a temporary tax break to help revive the condo market and spur homebuilding.

From April, 2026, through March, 2027, buyers are eligible for an HST rebate on the purchase of new homes, up to a maximum of $130,000 on homes priced up to $1.5-million.

So far, the tax break is mostly boosting purchases of new houses. But Westdale’s Mr. Cohen said the rebate has also helped condo sales.

In August, there were 215 purchases of new condos in the Toronto region, including condo apartments and stacked condo townhouses, according to a report from new-home research group Altus and trade group Building Industry and Land Development Association.

That’s 78 per cent below the 10-year average for that month, according to the report.
paragraphs: Ontario government-backed investment firm High Art Capital has paid $22.3-million for 43 unsold condo units at new towers in midtown Toronto, an amount well below the market rate.
The bulk purchase is the $1.3-billion fund’s first transaction. The firm bought the units in a condo complex called Line 5, which was named after the city’s new light-rail transit on Eglinton Avenue.

The purchase is one of the few of its kind to be revealed publicly. Large investors, such as real estate companies, have been bulk-buying unsold condo units at a discount to take advantage of the recent downturn.

But the deals are not typically public, nor are the precise locations or pricing per unit. The $22.3-million price tag works out to an average of $518,000 a unit, according to data from CoStar Group, a U.S.-based commercial real estate information provider that reviewed land transfer records for the transaction.

High Art, a privately owned fund, launched this year to buy up unsold inventory in the Toronto region and turn them into rentals. It is backed by $300-million in financing from the Ontario government through its Building Ontario Fund, which was formed in 2024 to invest with private investors in infrastructure deemed critical for the province.

Its Line 5 deal was initially announced in mid-August in a news release without information on the location, pricing or number of units. At the time, a High Art spokesperson said it would not disclose transaction details.
This week, spokesperson Laryssa Waler reiterated that the fund does not comment on details of confidential commercial transactions.
Developers lobby Ottawa for mortgage-interest tax changes on new homes

The Line 5 project was developed by Westdale Properties and Reserve Properties, which launched sales prior to the pandemic when there was strong demand for pre-construction condos. Now, there’s very little demand.

Westdale chief operating officer Mitchell Cohen said a lot of developers are sitting on inventory and the transaction with High Art helps get the units out on the market so people can live in them. “It was a perfect opportunity,” said Mr. Cohen.
High Art paid less than the average price of a pre-construction condo in Toronto and those on the resale market.
“Bulk buyers are acquiring at a notable discount to an individual buyer,” said Shaun Hildebrand, president with condo research firm Urbanation Inc.

High Art’s plan is to buy about 2,200 unsold condos and then sell most of them after a minimum of five years. Of that amount, 550 units are expected to be rented at below-market rates and remain affordable rentals in perpetuity.
Building Ontario Fund spokesperson Julia Sakas said High Art’s plan creates both market and affordable rental housing.

As part of its first deal, High Art has said it has an agreement with the Service Employees International Union to provide its members in health care, such as personal support workers, with rental units below market rates.
The union said the response has been overwhelming, with more than 500 members expressing interest.
“Some of our members have enormous commutes,” said John Klein, the union’s secretary treasurer, adding that the fund wanted to prioritize health care workers and first responders.
In depth: In downtown Toronto, the office is back

Rent would be 25 per cent below the going rate. For example, the Line 5 condos are near the heavily trafficked intersection of Yonge Street and Eglinton Avenue. There, the typical rent for a one-bedroom is about $2,400 per month, according to Mr. Klein. That means union members could rent a unit at around $1,800 per month, he said.
The real estate downturn has prompted the federal and Ontario governments to introduce a temporary tax break to help revive the condo market and spur homebuilding.
From April, 2026, through March, 2027, buyers are eligible for an HST rebate on the purchase of new homes, up to a maximum of $130,000 on homes priced up to $1.5-million.
So far, the tax break is mostly boosting purchases of new houses. But Westdale’s Mr. Cohen said the rebate has also helped condo sales.

In August, there were 215 purchases of new condos in the Toronto region, including condo apartments and stacked condo townhouses, according to a report from new-home research group Altus and trade group Building Industry and Land Development Association.
That’s 78 per cent below the 10-year average for that month, according to the report.

stories.title: Council rejects bid to increase density of Sarnia Road development
stories.summary: London city council has rejected a proposal to increase the height and density of a planned student housing development on Sarnia Road, despite a recommendation from city planning staff to approve the changes.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London city council has rejected a proposal to increase the height and density of a planned student housing development on Sarnia Road, despite a recommendation from city planning staff to approve the changes.
· Posted: Sep 22, 2026 7:20 PM EDT | Last Updated: 35 minutes ago

London city council has rejected a proposal to increase the height and density of a planned student housing development on Sarnia Road, despite the city's Planning and Environment Committee recommending approval earlier this month.
Councillors voted 13-2 against the proposed changes Tuesday, following strong opposition from neighbours who argued the increased density would be incompatible with the surrounding area.
The decision prompted applause from residents gathered in the council gallery.
"Everybody understands that there's going to be more student housing in the neighborhood," said Ward 6 Coun. Sam Trosow, who represents the area.
"I am satisfied that members of this neighborhood in good faith appreciate that. This is not an anti-student backlash. This is not NIMBYism. "
The development at 299-307 Sarnia Rd. was originally approved by council in June 2025 as a six-storey building with 150 residential units.
The developer later submitted an amended proposal calling for an eight-storey building with 204 units and 188 vehicle parking spaces. The building would step down toward the rear of the property.
This concept drawing shows an artistic rendering of the previously-approved six-storey version of the application. (Zelinka Priamo)
Several councillors who voted in favour of the original development, including Peter Cuddy and Steve Lehman, ultimately voted against the proposed increase.
Cuddy said his decision changed after he toured the area and spoke with residents.
"This was a difficult one because I know ... I approved it at committee, but after touring the area and speaking with residents I find it very difficult ... to support this," Cuddy said.
"It's very quiet. Its residents have been here for years."
Cuddy also said he was concerned about the potential impact of student housing on noise levels.

Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis, one of the two councillors who voted in favour of the proposed changes, cautioned his colleagues against making their decision based on who might eventually live in the building.
"I've heard some colleagues express concern that it's student housing," Lewis said.
"It's not up to us. In fact, it would be contrary to the law for us to discriminate on an application based on who was going to live there."
City planning staff recommended approval of the amended application, which raised the building from six to eight storeys.
Lewis urged council to consider that recommendation, saying councillors should rely on city staff's work on planning and transportation issues.

"We're not professional planners or traffic engineers. Our staff have evaluated this. They've said it meets the requirements under the Planning Act and under the London Plan and they're bringing forward as a recommendation," he said.
The city says the proposed eight-storey development conforms to its planning framework and includes 204 residential units, 188 vehicle parking spaces and 225 bicycle parking spaces.
Coun. Susan Stevenson said she was also concerned about how information about the amended proposal was communicated to residents.
Stevenson claimed information on the amended development plan was difficult to find on the city's website, and argued the city didn't do enough to directly notify residents who could be affected.
"In my opinion, it wasn't done in such a way that I can stand with the development process on this," Stevenson said.
Lewis and Mayor Josh Morgan disagreed with the suggestion that the process lacked transparency.
"There was a get involved piece on the London.CA website. There was transparency in this, regardless of how many people participated," Lewis said.
The decision means the developer cannot proceed with the proposed eight-storey version of the project as submitted.
The developer can still build the previously approved six-storey, 150-unit development, or it can challenge council's decision through the Ontario Land Tribunal.

stories.title: Tractors, horses and a combine derby: International Plowing Match plows into Walkerton, Ont.
stories.summary: Horses and wagons led the way as the International Plowing Match and Rural Expo got underway with a parade on the outskirts of Walkerton, Ont. The opening parade marks the start of a five-day competition, filled with county fair activities.
stories.author: John Vennavally-Rao
stories.content:
Walkerton, Ont. — Horses and wagons led the way as the International Plowing Match and Rural Expo got underway with a parade on the outskirts of Walkerton, Ont. The opening parade marks the start of a five-day competition, filled with county fair activities.

The celebration of agriculture — that’s expected to draw tens of thousands of visitors — is one of Ontario’s longest-running traditions. Matches have been held nearly every year in the town since 1913.

This year’s match included 113 participants, some of which came from overseas.

Seventeen of the competitors plowed with horses instead of tractors. The goal: cut a furrow that’s dead straight, with the soil turned over firm and even.

‘Does it cover our costs? No.’

Two-time winner Paul Robinson has been taking part in matches for 45 years. He explained that plowing runs in the family, as his father previously competed with his grandfather.

“I have five grandkids that I’m hoping will get up on the seat one day and try it,” Robinson said.

This year he’s competing in the vintage division, for tractors built at least 70 years ago. He says it’s less about the prize money — top payout is $100 a day — and more about bragging rights.

“Does it cover our costs? No. But what nowadays does?” he said with a chuckle.

What keeps him coming back, rain or shine, is the camaraderie.

A ‘dying art’ and global sport

As farmers turn to more modern ways to plow than with a tractor, some are calling competitive plowing a dying art. But for some in Walkerton, Ont, it’s a full-blown sport, one that even takes place in countries well beyond Canada.

Liam O’Reilly flew in from Ireland to compete, piloting a borrowed 1950 Massey Harris tractor in the vintage class. What struck him most wasn’t the machinery around him; it was who was driving it.

“I’m amazed at the amount of young people and young girls and young women and women in general that are plowing,” O’Reilly said. “Back at home there’d be very few.”

Stephanie Sanders knows how challenging a match can be. She’s chief steward of the Ontario Plowmen’s Association and started plowing in 2007, the same year she met her husband at a match.

“Every day is different,” she said. “Are you going to be plowing on a hill? Are there going to be lots of rocks? Is the ground going to be really hard?”

A ‘tented city’ springs up

The rest of the grounds has been transformed into what organizers call a “tented city” — 100 acres of vendors, exhibits and entertainment, along with a sprawling temporary RV park.

It’s by design, according to Gord Lang, chair of this year’s event. The International Plowing Match has no permanent home; it packs up and moves to a different Ontario community every year.

“It moves all over Ontario. They try to spread it all around and give different counties the chance to showcase their stuff,” Lang said.

“It’s about bringing the people from the city and the towns to the rural area — like, ‘come visit us, we’re farmers, and we’re putting on a show to show everybody what we do.’”

More than 500 exhibitors and 1,600 volunteers are keeping this year’s edition running.

Square dancing tractors and a derby

If watching farmers plow perfectly straight lines feels a little too genteel, organizers have another offering this weekend: a demolition derby fought with combines.

stories.title: Belleville gunman spouted COVID-19 conspiracies while in army, say sources
stories.summary: The Canadian Armed Forces confirmed Sean Ward served in the military until 2022.
stories.author: Jeff Semple, Stewart Bell
stories.content:
The gunman accused of opening fire at police outside an Ontario synagogue left the army after expressing conspiracy theories about COVID-19, according to military sources.

A member of the Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry when the pandemic hit, Sean Ward was discharged for refusing to be vaccinated, they told Global News.

Speaking on the condition they would not be identified, the sources said the former infantry soldier had voiced a wide range of falsehoods about the coronavirus.

One of the sources said that some of the conspiracies he spouted were antisemitic, blaming Jews for COVID-19 — a meme spread by extremists during the pandemic.

The 29-year-old was armed with a shotgun when he arrived near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont. at about 7 p.m. on Sunday, according to police .

Due to security concerns, an unmarked police vehicle was parked nearby, while worshippers were inside observing Yom Kippur, the holiest evening of the Jewish faith.

Wounded during an exchange of fire with police, Ward died in hospital on Monday night. Police have not said whether they suspect he was targeting the synagogue.

One of the police officers suffered gunshot wounds and remains in hospital. Ontario Solicitor General Michael Kerzner said police had prevented a “massacre in the making.”

Belleville Police were only assigned to the synagogue because congregants had reported a suspicious vehicle parked outside a week earlier, Global News has learned.

The Canadian Armed Forces said Ward joined the army in July 2017. He was a corporal when he was released in June 2022, without ever having deployed overseas.

A military spokesperson would not comment on the allegations he adhered to pandemic-related conspiracies, saying the circumstances of his release were protected by the Privacy Act.

Two national Jewish organizations said in a statement they were “profoundly grateful” to the wounded officer but that synagogues should not require armed police outside their doors.

“Canadians cannot accept a future, as now exists in Europe, in which synagogues and Jewish schools can only operate safely behind permanent armed police and soldiers with machine guns,” the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs and Jewish Federations of Canada said.

“With Parliament returning this week, governments at every level must turn their attention to the domestic situation and the growing threat of extremist violence here in Canada.”

On Saturday, Durham Police arrested a 19-year-old, Alexander Parfitt, following an investigation into alleged online posts about shooting a local synagogue.

Jewish institutions have been repeatedly targeted with violence in Canada since the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel , and the military response in Gaza.

Global News revealed in July that Canadian authorities had disrupted four “violent extremist attack plots against Jewish targets” since the latest Israel- Hamas conflict .

A June 29 report by the federal government’s Integrated Threat Assessment Centre said Canada’s Jewish population had been increasingly targeted since the U.S. and Israel began airstrikes in Iran on Feb. 28.

“There has been an uptick in harassment, threatening rhetoric, and criminal incidents—such as assault, arson and shooting firearms—against Jewish communities in Canada, primarily in the Greater Toronto Area since the Iran-U.S. conflict began in February 2026,” it said.

The intelligence report also pointed to a broader problem in which acts of antisemitism become so prevalent that they create a permissive atmosphere that further enables such violence.

“Over the longer term, an environment in which the targeting of the Jewish community as a group frequently occurs and becomes more normalized will likely influence some susceptible individuals towards violent extremist pathways.”

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA

stories.title: Rents in tariff-exposed cities fall faster than those least affected by trade war
stories.summary: Ten Canadian cities most vulnerable to U.S. tariffs saw average rents drop by 3% since last January
stories.author: Salmaan Farooqui
stories.content:
Rental rates are dropping nearly four times faster in cities that are the most exposed to U.S. tariffs than in the communities least affected by the trade war, according to new data from Rentals.CA and Urbanation .

Tariff-exposed cities, such as Oshawa, Ont., Kitchener-Waterloo, Ont., and Hamilton, face added headwinds to an already beleaguered rental market, Shaun Hildebrand, president of Urbanation, said in an e-mail. These three cities, hubs for auto manufacturing, steel and industrial exports, all rely on industries hit hard by U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

The 10 cities most vulnerable to U.S. tariffs, as determined by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce , saw average rents drop by 3 per cent since January, 2025, when Mr. Trump took office and launched his trade war.

In contrast, the 10 least tariff-exposed cities – which include Vancouver, St. John’s, Halifax and Saskatoon – have seen rents drop by only 0.8 per cent on average. The chamber created the ranking by quantifying how much Canadian cities depended on exports to the U.S.

Canada’s 100 best cities for renters

Mr. Hildebrand said rental markets are expected to decline more broadly if the trade war continues.

“Rents respond to the labour market with a lag of several quarters, so what we are seeing now reflects the first round of tariffs, not the most recent ones,” Mr. Hildebrand said.

“If the trade war persists, the effect widens from job losses in a handful of industries to a broader reluctance to form new households, and that impacts far more renters.”

Oshawa was the weakest market included in the study, with rents there dropping by 8.9 per cent since January, 2025.

“Oshawa stands out as it is a market where one industry sets the tone for the entire local economy, so when the auto sector cuts shifts and jobs, it shows up in rents faster than anywhere else,” Mr. Hildebrand said.

Bill Senyk, a realtor and property manager in Oshawa, agreed that tariffs have had a chilling impact on his area’s real estate market.

Average national prices for rental listings fall 4.7 per cent in May

He said properties that once took a month to fill with a tenant will now sit empty for two or three months because the market is so slow.

He pointed to General Motors’ decision to reduce shifts in response to the trade war, which in turn reduced operations at other manufacturing firms around Oshawa and created a downturn felt across the city.

“Restaurants that used to be jammed on a Friday or Saturday night will at most have eight tables sitting at one time,” said Mr. Senyk, who added that people’s ability to spend on housing has decreased, too.

“I don’t think we’ve even hit bottom yet.”

Not all tariff-affected cities saw values decline at the same pace. Rentals.CA data showed that Windsor (the second most exposed city) only saw rent decline by 2.4 per cent in the last year, which is half the national average of 4.8 per cent.

The report attributed the resilience of that city to its tight rental market, which has far fewer available listings than other communities.

The study also noted that the trade war will likely lead to supply shortages in cities such as Vancouver and Toronto in the coming years, as tariffs lead to increased building costs and fewer housing starts.

It found that steel framing costs have increased by 7.8 per cent since the onset of American tariffs and Canadian countertariffs.

“Tight supply will amplify rent increases when demand rises. Rental supply cannot respond quickly, and when demand grows, price is the only thing left that can adjust,” Mr. Hildebrand said.

stories.title: City council rejects 8-storey development after resident pushback
stories.summary: In an eleventh-hour reversal, London city council has rejected a proposal to increase an apartment complex near Western University from six to eight storeys, a decision met with relief by residents of the Orchard Park neighbourhood.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
In an eleventh-hour reversal, London city council has rejected a proposal to increase an apartment complex near Western University from six to eight storeys, a decision met with relief by residents of the Orchard Park neighbourhood.

The development, proposed for 299-307 Sarnia Road, initially involved a zoning change to permit an 8-storey apartment building stepping down to 4 storeys at the rear. The plan included 204 residential units,188 vehicle parking spaces, and 225 bicycle parking spaces.

Residents had largely resigned themselves to a six-storey student-oriented complex, a compromise reached after previous negotiations. However, when the developer pushed for two additional storeys, residents organized a campaign to oppose the revision.

“We felt betrayed,” said Bill Tsioros, who helped lead the opposition. The campaign faced an initial setback when the city’s Planning and Environment Committee approved the revision based on a city staff recommendation.

The tide turned Tuesday afternoon during the full council vote. Ward 3 Councillor Peter Cuddy, who had initially voted in favour of the change at committee, shifted his stance, stating, “I find it very difficult… to support this.”

Ultimately, the council defeated the additional storeys by a decisive vote of 13-2. Councillor Sam Trosow, representing the ward, explained that residents and council had already compromised once, allowing the project to grow from four to six floors. “I think in the end, the council really respected the compromise nature of what had been done over the last few years,” Trosow commented. “This just did not come up in the last few weeks. So I think it was a good vote.”

The previously approved six-storey development can still proceed based on approval granted by the city last year.

Neighbour Sharanne MacDonald told CTV News that residents understand the inevitability of higher density developments along Sarnia Road and are not opposed to student housing. “They are part of our community and that’s really important,” she stated.

While some councillors voiced concerns that reversing the committee’s recommendation could lead to an Ontario Municipal Board appeal, Trosow expressed confidence that the strong opposing vote would prevent such action.

stories.title: Trump 'no longer working' in best interest of Americans, Trudeau says in U.S. speech
stories.summary: Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said the U.S. is an "extremely unpredictable" partner.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Former prime minister Justin Trudeau said the U.S. is an “extremely unpredictable” partner because President Donald Trump’s administration is “no longer working” in the best interest of Americans.

The former prime minister shared his thoughts on the current Trump administration as part of a question and answer session with Brown University President Christina Paxson in Rhode Island on Tuesday.

Asked by Paxson where he sees the current “trade tensions” between Canada and the U.S. ending up, Trudeau said that there are differences between the current administration and when he negotiated with Trump during his first term.

One of them is the increased predictability as Trump seeks to sign “win-lose” deals, rather than “win-win” deals, with other countries, even if it has a negative impact on Americans.

“Suddenly, the unpredictability is the U.S. administration is no longer working in the best interest of the American people, and that makes it extremely unpredictable and difficult for countries to navigate through, for friends to rely on, but also for businesses to invest,” he added.

To prove his point, Trudeau cited Trump’s latest tariffs on Canadian aluminium and softwood lumber as self-harming policies by the U.S. administration.

The U.S. does not produce enough aluminium and has long relied on Canadian product to meet its domestic demand, Trudeau said. So, when Canadian aluminum costs more due to U.S. tariffs, a myriad of American products like beer cans become more expensive without local production increasing.

“So you have raised prices on the cost of your own beer and everything else, and you are substituting buying aluminum from Canada from buying aluminum from Bahrain,” he said.

“You’re making it more difficult for consumers and producers and manufacturers in America to get aluminum from a reliable supply.”

The same goes for Canadian softwood lumber, the former prime minister said. Since the U.S. can’t produce enough of it locally to support a major housing boom, it still needs to turn to Canadian product… which now costs more because of Trump’s new tariffs since 2025.

“That means home builders pay more for their wood in the United States than you would need to, just so that the few companies that actually make and harvest wood in the United States can charge higher prices,” he said.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers, and not necessarily making anything better for America by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said.

Trudeau told the crowd that they are not alone in staring into the unknown abyss that is the future in these tumultuous times.

“Over the past 10 years, leaders have been sort of trying to figure it out on the fly,” Trudeau said.

stories.title: Trump’s threat not a concern for Saskatchewan potash mining town, mayor says
stories.summary: The mayor of a Saskatchewan town said residents are not worried, or currently affected, by recent threats made by U.S. President Donald Trump to get potash from Belarus.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Despite a recent statement made by U.S. President Donald Trump that he plans on slowing U.S. imports of Canadian potash, those involved in the industry say they are not worried.

Trump said the U.S. is working with Belarus to purchase potash on Truth Social Monday. The U.S. president claimed the “pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada.”

He later walked back on that post at a meeting in New York Tuesday.

Regardless of where the president lands on the issue, Saskatchewanians said they aren’t concerned.

Potash sales in the province are up by approximately 21 per cent in its year to date for 2026 , when compared to last year, according to Saskatchewan’s mineral sales.

“Everyone needs (potash) if they want to grow food, so, I think it’s a commodity that is worth a lot to a lot of people,” Allan Mayor Jordan Hafichuk said. The town, approximately 60 kilometres southeast of Saskatoon, houses multiple potash mines.

Even with the U.S. threats, not much has changed in the town of Allan, according Hafichuk.

“A lot of our residents in Allan work at the mine, there is no two ways about it. But in terms of how they see the economic outlook, and anything like that, I don’t think it necessarily affects what we’re doing,” Hafichuk said, adding that “we’re looking so far beyond the U.S.”

“As a community, I think we’ll be just fine,” Hafichuk continued.

Devan Mescall, a professor at the University of Saskatchewan’s Edward School of Business, said Trump’s threats should not cause panic.

“Belarus May replace some of the Canadian potash in the U.S. market, but it can’t realistically replace Canada as a whole,” the professor said, pointing to the Belarusian president’s recent comments.

During a meeting, President Aleksandr Lukashenko told Vladimir Orlovsky, Belarus’ chairman of the state customs committee, that the country could not fulfill all of the United States’ potash needs for 2026, because this year’s output is already contracted.

“Potash is a global market. And so, it is a little bit like musical chairs. If some of our sales to the U.S. get replaced, if Belarus removes that from another customer, there will be a need, a demand in the market that we can replace,” Mescall told Global News in an interview.

Canadian potash producers would be more affected by Trump’s threat if a new supply was suddenly made available, he said.

Seventy-nine per cent of potash imported into the U.S. is Canadian, according to the U.S Geological Survey.

stories.title: RCMP tell victims’ families no investigative avenues left to pursue in bombing of Air India Flight 182
stories.summary: Families of the victims of the bombing of Air India Flight 182 have been told there are currently no more investigative avenues to pursue and the case will be moving to "inactive status."
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
By Rashmeen Rupal, Omni News and Meredith Bond

Posted September 22, 2026 6:31 pm.

Families of the victims of the bombing of Air India Flight 182 have been told there are currently no more investigative avenues to pursue and the case will be moving to “inactive status” in a recent meeting with the RCMP, raising new questions about the future of the probe.

For Deepak Khandelwal, who lost his two older sisters in the Air India Flight 182 bombing, the fight for justice has been ongoing for 41 years. He said he was shocked to hear the latest update from the RCMP when he and around 65 other victims’ families met with them.

“This is Canada’s largest mass murder, the worst act of aviation terrorism in the world, other than 9/11, and basically the RCMP is throwing their hands up and saying we can’t do anything about this,” said Khandelwal.

In a statement to Omni News, the RCMP say there are currently no persons of interest or suspects currently under consideration. The police service added the investigation remains open and if any new or credible information comes forward, it will be investigated.

However, for victims’ families like Khandelwal’s, simply keeping the investigation open is not enough. “By saying that it’s open doesn’t mean that there’s anybody actually working on it. There are no proactive investigative agents assigned to it. There’s no proactive work that’s being done on it,” explained Khandelwal.

On June 23, 1985, a bomb planted inside Air India Flight 182 exploded over the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of Ireland, killing all 329 people on board. Of the passengers on board, 286 were Canadian citizens with East Indian origin.

The plane was enroute from Toronto to India via London, carrying mostly Canadians passengers. Another related bombing simultaneously exploded at Japan’s Narita International Airport, instantly killing two baggage handlers.

The trial for two people accused of being apart of the bombing began nearly 18 years later in 2005 and served as the longest and most expensive investigation in Canadian history. The two accused, Ripudaman Singh Malik and Ajaib Singh Bagri, were both found not guilty. Malik was later shot and killed in 2022 outside his business in Surrey, B.C.

An update was also given about the individual, referred to as Mr. X, in connection to the investigation. The RCMP say while they have been identified, no definitive link to the bombing could be established.

The RCMP said last year the suspect died before facing charges, and police would not be releasing his name.

Khandelwal said the families asked for information on Mr. X back in June of 2025, but didn’t receive any update until the Sept. 12 meeting.

The roots of the terrorist attack are connected to the Sikh extremist movement in the aftermath of the 1984 attack on the Golden Temple and the assassination of Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.

Sikh extremist Talwinder Singh Parmar is known as the “mastermind” behind the Air India bombing. He was a high-profile leader of Babbar Khalsa, a listed terrorist entity both inside Canada and India. After the bombing, Parmar returned to India, and he was killed by Punjab police in 1992.

The only person ever convicted was Inderjit Singh Reyat, who pleaded guilty to one count of manslaughter and a charge linked to the creation of the bomb. He was initially sentenced to 10 years behind bars but later received nine more years for perjury.

Khandelwal states that the passage of time and the deaths of witnesses and potential suspects is further diminishing the chances of achieving justice.

“It’s very unclear that the RCMP has really done any investigative steps since 2005 going forward,” said Khandelwal. He added the families present at the meeting pushed them on what actions have been taken and “they really couldn’t answer the question.”

While the investigation remains open, the affected families argue that merely having an open file is not enough; rather, an active investigation must continue in order to secure answers and accountability in this matter.

“We, as the families, believe that this investigation should continue and be moved into an active status,” said Khandelwal. “We would like them to pursue all angles and there’s definitely investigative angles that are open for them to investigate both of the people responsible and also the broader organization responsible for killing 331 innocent people.”

With files from Dorsa Delara, Omni News

stories.title: ‘Absolutely infuriating’: $70K worth of Pokémon cards stolen from Winnipeg flea market owner
stories.summary: One Winnipeg vendor is in shock after tens of thousands of dollars worth of his Pokémon cards were stolen.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – One Winnipeg vendor is in shock after tens of thousands of dollars worth of his Pokémon cards were stolen.

Kenan Hyseni, who owns and operates Mulvey Market, said high-end, valuable products were stolen from his shop after a trading event he held last weekend.

He believes someone snuck in, hid inside the market, waited for staff to leave, then stole the merchandise before fleeing.

“I got a message from my building saying that someone was leaving the premises and tripped the alarm just 10 minutes before midnight,” he said. “We saw from the video that he had a massive blue backpack and as soon as I saw it, I knew that it had to have been Pokémon.”

He said sealed Pokémon products and specialty collection boxes were among the items stolen, totalling around $70,000 in losses.

“There’s some boxes that were worth $4 or $5,000 and then there were some cards that were $3 to $4,000, as well,” he said.

“I’m still going through all of my inventory when it comes to the cards, because the cards are the more important, the more expensive part of the whole collection.”

Unless the product is found, Hyseni says he won’t be able to recoup the costs that were lost in this theft.

He plans to bring in more security measures, including more surveillance and security staff, but in this circumstance the thief was already inside the building.

“There’s no way anyone can get into the market from the outside because there’s alarms and everything all over the building,” he said.

Terri Settle, owner of Terri’s Trinkets and Toys in Winnipeg, said her shop was ransacked by thieves who stole roughly 7,000 Pokémon cards, about 3,000 Yu-Gi-Oh cards, 7,000 sports cards, as well as action figures and Lego sets.

“I think I lost about $6,000 in merchandise, which for a big-box store wouldn’t be anything, but for a little store like mine, that’s substantial,” she told CTV News on Sept. 10.

“I absolutely think that I was targeted for the Pokémon cards.”

Pokémon heists occurring across Canada

The recent thefts in Winnipeg are just the latest in a string of Pokémon heists across Canada.

Surveillance footage caught a thief stealing thousands of dollars worth of Pokémon cards at a hobby shop in Nanaimo, B.C., last week.

A Vancouver trading card shop was targeted in early August, where the owners said between $60,000 and $80,000 worth of Pokémon cards were stolen, including at least one card valued at nearly $19,000.

Other thefts have been reported in Ontario and Quebec.

A thief stole thousands of dollars worth of Pokémon cards from a Vancouver Island collectibles shop in less than two minutes.

‘Gold for thieves’

Pokémon cards have skyrocketed in value, making them a desirable target for thieves.

“It’s literally become gold for thieves in the last little while,” said Bruce Winder, who is a retail analyst in Toronto.

“The collector market for Pokémon has absolutely surged from a price perspective, so would-be thieves are seeing an opportunity to steal from stores, even from people who are selling online.”

He says collectibles, like Pokémon products, are hot around the world right now, but trends like this change overtime.

“It’s really an equation, when you think about it. (Thieves) think, ‘what’s the value of the merchandise I can steal? How hard is it to steal it? What’s the consequences to steal? And can I move it quickly and easily to get cash?’” he said.

“Anything that falls within that equation, where it has a massively high value, coupled with the ease today of converting some of the stolen product into cash, makes it an attractive pastime, or I guess, career, unfortunately, for a number of people.”

The Retail Council of Canada (RCC) says retailers are enhancing protection by locking display cases, limiting sales-floor inventory and implementing new security technologies, including body-worn cameras.

“(The) RCC is also calling on the Manitoba government to strengthen transparency and accountability for illicit sales on online marketplaces, with nearly half of illicit sales now through online platforms,” said John Graham, Prairie region director of government relations for the RCC.

“The United States and European Union require greater transparency from high-volume online sellers and help marketplaces and authorities identify and address the resale of stolen goods.”

Hyseni says he will bounce back from this theft but says it’s frustrating to see a product, which is already so difficult to come by, disappear so quickly.

“Unfortunately, Pokémon has become a product that a lot of thieves, a lot of criminals are going to try and get their hands on and the best way to prevent this is to protect each other within the community,” he said.

“If you see something, if you hear something, speak up. Contact your local authorities. Contact the stores that were hit, that were affected, and that’s the best way to kind of help one another with this kind of climate right now.”

With files from CTV News Winnipeg’s Danton Unger

stories.title: London’s Jewish community reacts to Belleville shooting
stories.summary: London’s Jewish community is responding after a shooting outside a Belleville, Ont. synagogue over the weekend
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
London’s Jewish community is responding after a shooting outside a Belleville, Ont. synagogue over the weekend

“We are horrified,” said Dean Lavi with the London Jewish Federation. “We are grief stricken, and we are just thankful no one was killed.”

Sean Ward, a 29-year-old former Canadian armed forces member, allegedly opened fire on a police officer Sunday night.

Ward has since died.

“Our officers are out there every day putting their lives on the line to make the community feel safe,” said David Pratt with London Police Service.

Constable Jeff Smith with Belleville Police Service was shot at multiple times and remains in hospital.

“It is only because of heroes like him that we have not seen massive fatalities happen here in Canada,” said Lavi.

Police said the incident took place as congregants prepared to mark Yom Kippur.

“Yom Kippur is a fast day, a 24 hour fast,” said Lavi. “Observant Jews will go to synagogue and aim to make new promises and turn a new leaf.”

London police have increased visible police patrols at places of worship and community locations across our city.

“We work closely with our community,” said Pratt. “We pay attention to any attention that May come across and we respond accordingly.”

Pratt said everyone should be able to gather and worship without fear.

“It’s really sad that this is where we are in 2026,” said Lavi. “This is not just a potential threat that could potentially happen, this is the reality that we are living within Canada today.”

Members of London’s Jewish community say the incident is part of a larger concern that antisemitism is on the rise.

“It’s happening in a small town that is a fraction of the size of London which is a massive escalation,” said Lavi. “A really worrying escalation in the violence that we’ve seen.”

He said the message is clear.

“The Jews are becoming threats,” said Lavi. “How did we get here?”

Police have not yet commented on the motive behind the shooting.

stories.title: TD Bank, Cohere announce $25-million collaboration to support AI development
stories.summary: Organizations to explore how AI can be applied to improve productivity, strengthen decision-making and improve client experience
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TD Bank Group TD-T has announced a strategic relationship with Cohere to support artificial intelligence development and adoption.

The lender says the agreement includes an initial investment of up to $25-million over three years.

The relationship will see a collaboration between Layer 6, a Toronto-based AI company that was acquired by TD in 2018, and Canadian AI firm Cohere.

The organizations will explore how AI can be applied at the bank to improve productivity, strengthen decision-making and improve client experience.

As part of the agreement, a team from Cohere will work with Layer 6 at the MaRS Discovery District.

Earlier this month, TD announced a five-year $150-billion commitment to accelerate investment in the country in key sectors, which included AI.

stories.title: ‘It’s a death-trap’: Farmers demand traffic lights at Wonderland and Glanworth as harvest approaches
stories.summary: Harvest season is about to get underway in southwestern Ontario, and many farmers in south London and parts of Elgin County worry high traffic volumes along a north-south corridor will prevent their equipment from getting around.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Harvest season is about to get underway in southwestern Ontario, and many farmers in south London and parts of Elgin County worry high traffic volumes along a north-south corridor will prevent their equipment from getting around.

“My biggest fear is some innocent person is going to come through here and run into the side of one of our pieces of equipment, and be hurt badly, or possibly worse,” said farmer Richard Smibert, who farms land in south London close to the London and Elgin County border.

Smibert represents a group of area farmers raising safety concerns about the intersection of Wonderland Road South and Glanworth Drive. Nearby Colonel Talbot Road is closed at Glanworth for construction, with much of the traffic using Wonderland Road South instead.

Farmers gathered Tuesday at a property just south of London to voice their concerns.

“It’s not safe, it’s not easy, and it’s inefficient. As older people would say, it’s a death-trap,” expressed farmer John Ferguson.

“We don’t want to be on the road holding people up, being in the way, and making things unsafe. But sometimes it really does put us in an unsafe situation,” said Jason Rauhe, who farms in the area and serves as councillor in the municipality of Aylmer.

The intersection is controlled by a stop sign on Glanworth for traffic traveling east-west. There’s also a flashing light in the middle of the intersection. Vehicles wait at the corner for extended periods, and have mere seconds to cross when they do get the chance, said a dump truck driver who stopped during a late-day rush hour to vent his frustration.

“Sometimes I count, and it was 12 minutes set up at this stop-sign,” he exclaimed.

Farmers are calling for traffic signals to be installed.

“I would like to see a four-way set of stoplights put up here immediately,” said Smibert.

The intersection is located on the border of Ward 9 and Ward 12 in the city of London. It will occupy just one ward once council boundaries are redrawn for the next term of council. Councillor Elizabeth Peloza, whose ward currently takes in the east side of the intersection, says the corner is continually being assessed for potential changes or upgrades by city engineers.

“Traffic patterns are changing. We also have a lot of construction, including Wellington Gateway, which would also push some people onto Wonderland and surrounding areas, just adding to the issues this area’s already having,” explained Peloza.

In the meantime, Smibert says he wants other drivers to be mindful that farmers will be out there in force over the next couple of months.

“We can’t wait for a construction project to be completed over on Colonel Talbot Road. Things have to move. Fertilizer has to move. Grain has to move. Combines have to move. Our equipment’s four metres to six metres wide, travels at 30 to 40 kilometres per hour, and it has to mix in with this flow of traffic here. It is complete chaos,” he said.

stories.title: Avi Lewis defends 'despicable' Yom Kippur message, claims critics are after 'partisan points'
stories.summary: NDP Leader Avi Lewis said his critics are trying to "score partisan points" after he was he assailed for a social media post on Yom Kippur.
stories.author: Stuart Thomson
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

Liberal MP Ben Carr told reporters on Monday that the post was 'naive, it was miscalculated, irresponsible, and dangerous'

Last updated 23 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/politics/avi-lewis-defends-despicable-yom-kippur-message-claims-critics-are-after-partisan-points#comments-area)

New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis speaks during a press conference in the foyer of the House of Commons in Ottawa on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026.Photo by Hyungcheol Park /Postmedia

Ottawa — NDP Leader Avi Lewis defended his social media post made on Yom Kippur saying his fellow Jews had “failed” to do enough to stop a “genocide,” referencing the war between Israel and Hamas, and accused critics Tuesday of trying to “score partisan points” after he was assailed for the comments.

Lewis’s message was posted on Sunday evening, as the Jewish holiday was beginning and just before news broke that a police office had been critically injured when a gunman opened fire at a Belleville, Ont. synagogue where worshippers had gathered for the evening. The gunman, a 29-year-old former Canadian Armed Forces soldier, later died in hospital after an exchange of gunfire.

“Holding Canadian Jews and Jews across the world collectively responsible for events over which they have no control is despicable,” Liberal MP Anthony Housefather said on X in response to Lewis’s post.

Lewis, who like Housefather is Jewish, had posted: “This year I’m reflecting on the fact that we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name. There are many other fronts where I have to do the work of repair. But nothing on this scale.”

On Monday, Lewis accused them of his distorting his comments.

“I did not blame Jews for the actions of the Israeli government, that’s simply untrue,” said Lewis at a press conference on Monday. “Holding Jews collectively responsible for the actions of the State of Israel is antisemitic. I’ve never done it. I think it’s dangerous and that’s absolutely not what I did.”

“I think it’s pretty ugly to see this occasion being used to score partisan points. I won’t be doing that. It was a personal reflection that I know is shared by many people,” said Lewis.

Carr said he couldn’t comprehend how Lewis could offer that response, given what he had written.

“I didn’t quite understand how he was able to come to (that) conclusion that that’s in fact not what he was doing,” said Carr. “When … In fact, he was saying that we as Jews, had not done enough to prevent what was happening.”

stories.title: Most CentreBC MLAs rejoin Conservatives as snap provincial election called
stories.summary: B.C. Premier David Eby dropped the writ for a snap provincial election on Tuesday, citing U.S. President Donald Trump's attack on workers as a reason for the vote.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Seven legislators from the breakaway CentreBC party are rejoining the official Opposition B.C. Conservatives after NDP Leader David Eby called an early election for Oct. 24.

Eleanor Sturko says she is the sole CentreBC member who is not rejoining the Conservatives, who say interim leader Lorne Doerkson and CentreBC’s leader Peter Milobar “have come together to give British Columbians a viable governing alternative.”

The Conservatives say the election is “cynical” and not what British Columbians want, but it offers the province a hope for change.

The seven CentreBC legislators who are returning to the Conservative fold all resigned or were kicked out of the main Opposition caucus by former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who quit on Sunday.

But Sturko, who was ejected last year by former Conservative leader John Rustad, says she can’t go back to a party that previously supported the repeal of the human rights code.

Eby is framing the snap election as an urgent necessity to respond to the threat posed by U.S. President Donald Trump and his trade war, calling it an “existential moment” for the province

stories.title: ‘Agriculture is the backbone of our country’: Visitors revel in first day of International Plowing Match near Walkerton
stories.summary: Thousands of Ontarians are taking a tour through the Bruce County countryside on Day 1 of the International Plowing Match (IPM) near Walkerton.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Thousands of Ontarians are taking a tour through the Bruce County countryside on Day 1 of the International Plowing Match (IPM) near Walkerton. “We were two and a half years planning for this, and all the people have just taken a big sigh of relief, and yeah, it’s here. Beautiful weather. I don’t know how you get any better than this,” said 2026 IPM Bruce County Chair Gord Lang.

100 acres near Walkerton has been converted into a tent city showcasing Ontario agriculture, past and present. “Agriculture is the backbone of the country, if we didn’t have that, and running smoothly, we’d get pretty hungry. So yeah, it means a lot,” said Joe Benninger, visiting the IPM from nearby Formosa.

One in nine Canadian jobs are in the agri-food industry, so it’s timely that thousands of school kids will be a part of this year’s annual agricultural showcase, many of them with no connection to farming. “Having an appreciation for agriculture where our food, fibre, and fuel comes from is the only requirement.

Having that passion, and wanting to see a strong future for our agriculture, and our communities moving forward,” said Margaret Vincent, Ontario Federation of Agriculture representative for Bruce and Grey Counties. This is the fourth time in 50 years that the International Plowing Match has been held in Bruce County.

Three of those matches held on the exact plot of land, hosting it over the next 5 days. “We’ve got such a great agriculture industry. And certainly Brockton is at center of that. We had the highest farm gate receipts of any municipality in Bruce County last year, so we are very dependent, and very supportive of our farmers here in Brockton,” said Municipality of Brockton Mayor Chris Peabody.

Whether it’s a trip back in time, or to present day agriculture, Bruce County organizers are hoping attendance to this year’s edition of the International Plowing Match rebounds from recent ones, that have fallen below expectations. “Yeah, we’re really hoping for big crowds. Imagine the attendance May be down a little bit today, but we’re hoping as it warms up through the week here, it will get better and better.

We got a nice week coming. So come on, and see us,” said Lang. “It’s very important for people to see how important farm living is, and farm work is. And our land, it’s sad to seeing so much farm land being developed into houses when they could be growing crops on it. There’s such a shortage of food,” said IPM visitor, Cathy Benninger from Formosa.

“We know the value of agriculture and keeping things down to earth and protected. And we need to see all this stuff so it’s important to us,” said Theresa and Gord Coburn from Wiarton. The 2026 International Plowing Match near Walkerton runs Tuesday, Sept. 22 through Saturday, Sept. 26.

stories.title: Reptile preservation program makes record incubation numbers
stories.summary: The Southern Ontario At Risk Reptiles program recently celebrated its best incubation season to date, beating ...
stories.author: Kelly Nicol
stories.content:
Spiny softshell turtle hatchlings, courtesy of Scott Gillingwater

The Southern Ontario At Risk Reptiles program recently celebrated its best incubation season to date, beating last year’s record by about two-hundred more nests.

“Just like any wildlife or even plants that we have in nature, they’re all part of a larger ecosystem. You get rid of one, and you have a domino effect,” said Scott Gillingwater, director of the program. Spiny softshell turtles play a critical role in the environment, making their continued presence necessary for a healthy ecosystem. “The turtles themselves, they provide food for many predators. Their eggs are eaten by many predators. Raccoon, skunk, coyote, fox, etcetera. Turtles act as predators as well, so they will take a number of animals as food in the environment, and that keeps the environment healthy.” Gillingwater explained.

“We’ve done everything from surveying natural areas, that means the Thames river, and many other wetlands, woodlands, etcetera,”

For Gillingwater, the results show what is possible when people come together for the betterment of the environment. “I think a lot of people, when they think of endangered species, they think of pandas or whales, but in our own backyard we have a number of species at risk. In terms of reptiles, some of those include endangered queen snake, we have the spiny softshell turtle, and a number of other species not currently at risk.”

stories.title: Ford government stalls paying Taste of the Danforth full $200K premier promised
stories.summary: The popular street festival, which typically attracts up to a million people to Toronto's Greektown, took a three-year hiatus in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Isaac Callan
stories.content:
Months after Premier Doug Ford promised to revive the Taste of the Danforth with hundreds of thousands of dollars in provincial funding, the cash from Queen’s Park has been slow to arrive, leaving festival organizers facing pressure over unpaid bills.

The popular street festival, which typically attracts up to a million people to Toronto’s Greektown, took a three-year hiatus in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since then, it has struggled to regain its financial footing.

Faced with the potential permanent end of the festival, Ford promised to rescue the Taste of the Danforth earlier this year with taxpayer funding from Queen’s Park and City Hall.

“I’ve got an idea — I’m going off-script, I always get in trouble. Do you know what I miss? I miss the Taste of the Danforth,” Ford said in February in an off-the-cuff moment at an unrelated news conference.

“I will commit, and I’ll talk to our friend the boss there (Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy) to see if we can put money into revitalize Taste of the Danforth.”

In June, the government followed through on the funding commitment, offering $200,000 to the GreekTown on the Danforth Business Improvement Area, twinning the amount pledged by the City of Toronto.

“People were very happy. It’s a major event in this community, it’s a major event in this city and having the province come onside was a really good sign,” said Peter Tabuns, the NDP MPP representing the area.

The BIA received a funding agreement letter from the provincial government in April, paving the way for organizers to plan the event, book guests, and hire security for the festival over the weekend of Aug. 7.

Six weeks after the souvlaki was served, organizers are still awaiting the full funding amount from the province to arrive.

“The BIA has been saying to me, and I gather to the province, ‘Look, we have vendors who haven’t been paid. We need you to come forward with the money,'” Tabuns said.

“As of Friday, last week, the funds hadn’t arrived.”

While the BIA declined an interview request from Global News, Tabuns said they haven’t received a specific answer from the Ministry of Tourism on the reasons behind the delay, only that the funding has been stalled.

The Ministry of Tourism told Global News the government has been working with organizers to “resolve their several document issues” in order for the funding to be released.

“To date, our government has flowed over 60 per cent of the funding awarded to Taste of Danforth,” the ministry said in a statement.

“As with all public funding, there are strict guidelines in place to protect taxpayer dollars. As such, the entirety of the funding will be provided only once the organization submits their final reporting and audited financial statements.”

Tabuns said vendors have been increasingly flagging the payment issue to the BIA and suggested the delay risks trust built with suppliers.

“Vendors need money because it’s not the greatest economy. But if you’re going to have future events, they need to have confidence that they will get paid,” Tabuns said.

“So if you want to have a successful event next year, vendors this year need to know that money came in … that it’s not a risk getting involved next year.”

The government has yet to commit to funding the festival in 2027.

stories.title: Rower Archie MacKinnon helped usher in a golden age for his sport on Canada’s West Coast
stories.summary: He and his teammates shocked the sporting world when they won a gold medal at the 1956 Olympics in Australia and became known as the Cinderella Four
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
Though the teenager had never once sat in a racing shell, Archie MacKinnon, a freshman electrical engineering student, tried out for the varsity rowing team when he arrived on campus.

He later said he “thought it would be easy to make” the team, guided by Frank Read, the University of British Columbia’s legendary coach.

As it turned out, he failed to win a spot among the coxed eights, the sport’s glamour boat. He and three other cuts were encouraged to continue as spares with the possibility one or two might be used as a substitute in case of illness or injury.

The unheralded youths trained in a shell for four without a coxswain. A year later, the novices shocked the sporting world by winning a gold medal at the 1956 Olympics in Australia.

The first-ever Olympic rowing championship for Canada helped launch a golden age for the sport on the West Coast, the effects of which linger to this day.

Mr. MacKinnon, who has died at the age of 89, was the last surviving member of a student crew forever remembered in lore as the Cinderella Four.

“They are the pioneering Olympic champions of Canadian rowing, one of the most important crews ever assembled in our country’s history,” said Jason Beck, curator of the B.C. Sports Hall of Fame and Museum, who is completing a book on the province’s rowers from that era.

“As the bowman, he was responsible for steering the shell straight with his foot while stroking his oar in time with his crewmates for 2,000 metres at a pace that would bury most normal humans.”

Archibald Alan MacKinnon, who carried the name of his paternal grandfather, was born on Jan. 13, 1937, in Cranbrook, a small city in British Columbia’s East Kootenays region. He was the first of two sons born to the former Ivy Elsie Marshall and Charles Eric MacKinnon, an engineering graduate who took over the family’s foundry.

The father insisted his son study at the University of Toronto. A lean but muscular athlete, Archie, who stood six-foot-two (1.88 metres) and weighed 176 pounds (79.8 kilograms), instead chose Vancouver, where Mr. Read’s program showed great promise with an eights boat representing the university and the Vancouver Rowing Club. The coach’s eights had upset a heavily favoured Thames Rowing Club on the Vedder Canal in B.C.’s Fraser Valley to claim the gold medal at the 1954 British Empire and Commonwealth Games. That unexpected victory led Prince Philip, who was in attendance, to invite them to the famed Henley Royal Regatta in England the following year. The Canadians defeated the Soviets before narrowly losing the 1955 Grand Challenge Cup to an American crew.

The coach was a hard-nosed, tongue-lashing disciplinarian, a hotelier accustomed to barking orders to his staff. The rowers trained along Vancouver’s working waterfront, where driftwood and freighters were occasional hazards. Without a coxswain, it was Mr. MacKinnon’s duty in the bow to steer and avoid debris.

“It was a tremendous strain on him during our training sessions avoiding all the logs and drift in Coal Harbour,” assistant coach John Warren told a reporter in 1956.

Mr. Read only offered instruction to the eights boat, so those in the four boat often had to quickly row over to get within earshot.

Gruelling two-hour sessions on the water beginning at dawn in even the wettest weather were followed by studies on campus, and further rowing in the evening. The four lived in spartan quarters at the rowing club. The men eschewed dating and a social life to dedicate themselves to training.

In summer, the four young men worked as labourers, handling jackhammers and wielding axes to help cut a path through rugged terrain for a pipeline.

The crew showed such dedication to their training that Mr. Read decided to bring them along to the Canadian Olympic rowing trials in 1956. “They have worked terribly hard for months,” the coach said. When the unknown quartet arrived at the Royal Canadian Henley course at Port Dalhousie, Ont., an Ontario coach haughtily told Mr. MacKinnon not to interfere with the undefeated fours from the Brockville Rowing Club. After the Western upstarts humiliated the favourites by 10 lengths, Mr. MacKinnon sought out the rival coach to ask, “Did we give them enough space?”

In the final, the Vancouver boat crushed their opponents, completing the 2,000-metre course in 6 minutes, 23.1 seconds, nearly 13 seconds faster than the Olympic record set in 1928 by a British foursome. (One of those British rowers, John Lander, had been in Hong Kong on business when the Japanese invaded in 1941. He immediately volunteered and was killed in action on Christmas Day, the final day of the Battle of Hong Kong. He was 34.) In an earlier heat, the Vancouver four had performed even better, besting the Olympic mark by an astonishing 31 seconds in what was their first competitive race in Eastern Canada.

Both the fours and eights qualified for the Olympics to be held in Melbourne four months later. But the success of the four freshmen – Don Arnold at stroke, Walter d’Hondt at No. 3, Lorne Loomer at No. 2, and Mr. MacKinnon at bow – meant funds had to be raised to cover the cost of sending them overseas.

A last-minute appeal for money, led by popular Vancouver mayor Fred Hume, raised $6,000.

The Olympic regatta was held on windswept Lake Wendouree, a man-made basin about 120 kilometres west of the host city. The Canadian crew easily advanced to the finals only to have disaster strike as they washed out on their first stroke, a rookie mistake in which the oars pop out of the water before completing a stroke. In an instant, they were in last place.

They needed to call on their superb conditioning. They hunted down the other boats with each stroke, Mr. Arnold calling for a series of “hard 10s,” reaching a peak rate of 36 strokes a minute at the midway point when they overtook the French to grab the lead. They held off a late challenge from a U.S. crew from the Detroit Boat Club to win by five lengths.

The jubilant quartet then cheered on the Canadian eights boat, which took a silver medal after being defeated by an American boat.

After the disappointment of failing to make the eights months earlier, Mr. MacKinnon and his crew made history of their own.

The four returned to Vancouver as conquering heroes. At the airport, lieutenant-governor Frank Ross presented each with a signet ring, while the mayor gave each a gold watch with an inscription including their name, reading “from the citizens of British Columbia in tribute to a magnificent performance at the 16 th Olympiad.” The mayor raised funds for the gift after premier W.A.C. Bennett refused to pay for them.

After being whisked downtown from the airport, the athletes were paraded by a 50-vehicle procession led by university cheerleaders and the firefighters’ band to the Vancouver Rowing Club for a reception.

Later, when Mr. MacKinnon finally returned to his hometown, 500 well-wishers gathered at the arena as the mayor presented him with a travelling case and a gold plaque.

With several of the eights crew graduating, Mr. MacKinnon and his three mates at last won coveted spots in what is known in the sport as the heavyweight boat.

In 1958, he was part of the crew to win a British Empire and Commonwealth Games gold medal on windswept Llyn Padarn in Wales. The Canadians defeated the Australians by three-quarters of a length, followed by England and Scotland. They received their medals from Prince Philip and cheers from a small but hardy crowd of 1,500, who endured bone-chilling winds.

Two years later, ON Lake Albano near Rome, Mr. MacKinnon sat in the No. 3 seat with Mr. Arnold at No. 2 and Mr. d’Hondt at No. 7 (with Mr. Loomer serving as a spare) as the Canadians finished three-quarters of a length behind a German team. The Canadian boat also included future Canadian federal cabinet minister David Anderson. The silver was Canada’s only medal at the 1960 Summer Olympics.

After graduating with a degree in electrical engineering, Mr. MacKinnon later earned a master’s in business administration from York University’s Schulich School of Business. In Toronto, he worked for Ford and General Electric before becoming a vice-president of CDC Ventures Inc., a venture capital subsidiary of the Canada Development Corporation.

He moved to Calgary in 1983, where he built a career in venture capital and investment banking as president and CEO of Alta-Can Telecom Inc., followed by four decades as head of Sutter Hill Capital Corporation, which focused on the energy and telecommunications industries.

Mr. MacKinnon and his Cinderella crew have been inducted into Canada’s Sports Hall of Fame (1957), the Canadian Olympic Hall of Fame (1958), the B.C. Sports Hall of Fame (1966), UBC Sports Hall of Fame (1993) and the Canadian Rowing Hall of Fame (2018). He has also been additionally enshrined in the B.C. and UBC halls for his participation in the 1960 Olympics boat.

Mr. MacKinnon died of esophageal cancer at Foothills Hospital in Calgary on Aug. 28. He leaves Judy, his wife of 47 years. A first marriage ended in divorce. He was predeceased by a younger brother, Paul Marshall MacKinnon, who died in 2000 of melanoma. He was also predeceased by his former Cinderella Four crewmates, as Mr. Loomer died in 2017, while Mr. Arnold and Mr. d’Hondt both died in 2021.

Their unexpected Olympic gold medal helped to move the centre of Canadian rowing from Ontario to the West Coast, where generations of rowers have continued to find success on the world’s watery stages.

Mr. MacKinnon was humble about his sporting success. His résumé did not include his status as a two-time Olympian. His second wife had been with him for two years before learning of his achievements.

“His mother was visiting and asked about the status of his medals,” Judy MacKinnon said. “I thought, ‘Was he in the military?’”

Last year, Mr. MacKinnon had an emotional reunion when he visited the B.C. Sports Hall of Fame in Vancouver. His rowing shell from the 1956 Olympics is on permanent display in the Hall of Champions. Nearly seven decades had passed since Mr. MacKinnon and his friends had raced in the shell, crafted by the famed boatbuilder George Pocock.

The shell, which the team named the J.M. Warren after their assistant coach, is on its side on a wall so visitors can peer inside to see such features as the foot stretchers into which the oarsmen’s feet are strapped. It is stationary now, but four young men once sat inside it to glide with serene power toward Olympic glory.

stories.title: Manitoba’s Kinew throws down fitness challenge for province’s students
stories.summary: The program encourages students to set personal goals they can track throughout the year, like trying a new sport or increasing their daily steps.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Manitoba’s premier is challenging students in the province to get faster, stronger or even just walking more.

Wab Kinew says the fitness challenge he announced Tuesday is about encouraging all students to end the year more active than they started as part of building a healthier future.

The program encourages students to set personal goals they can track throughout the year, like trying a new sport or increasing their daily steps.

Kinew says the challenge is provincewide, and schools where students manage to improve will get a banner for the gym and a million dollars in funding.

He made the announcement at the groundbreaking for a $10-million gym and track for École Secondaire Kelvin High School in Winnipeg.

The province launched a pilot program just before the school year started to make in-person physical education mandatory for all students from kindergarten to Grade 12.
