stories.title: 'This is torture': Lives of Congolese people disrupted by Canada's Ebola travel ban
stories.summary: A wedding missed. A school semester deferred. The last several months have been marked by misses for people from the Democratic Republic of Congo with ties to Canada.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — A wedding missed. A school semester deferred. The last several months have been marked by misses for people from the Democratic Republic of Congo with ties to Canada. Visa holders from the DRC have been banned from entering the country since May, which Canada’s government has called a precautionary measure as an Ebola outbreak rapidly spreads predominantly in a concentrated area of northeastern Congo.

“This is torture for people, to be separated from their families,” Theodyle Kumpava said from Kinshasa, almost 3,000 kilometres from the outbreak in the country’s southwest, where no cases have been reported. Several people whose lives have been disrupted by the ban have shared their stories ahead of Sept.

28, when the restrictions are set to expire. They question why they can’t quarantine for 21 days, like Canadian citizens and permanent residents can, or take an Ebola test before boarding a flight, or self-monitor for symptoms, as is the case in Europe.

The government has not said whether it plans to extend the measures again. Last month, they were extended by 30 days at short notice. A ‘double standard’ Kumpava is praying the measures won’t be extended again. Her son Nathan Boongo, a permanent resident and civil engineer, is getting married on Oct.

2 at a venue near Ottawa, where he went to university and met his fiancée. Just the thought of not walking him down the aisle is suffocating, she said. “To not see the children while I’m alive, it feels like they’ve killed me already.

It’s like I can’t exist,” Kumpava said, speaking of being separated from Boongo and three other sons who live in Canada. Kumpava and her husband already missed their younger son’s graduation in June because of the restrictions.

At the time, the government characterized the measures as precautionary ahead of an increase in tourism tied to the World Cup, despite World Health Organization guidance against blanket travel bans. Mark Johnson, a spokesperson for the Public Health Agency of Canada, said the risk of Ebola to people in Canada is low, but “given the severity of Ebola disease and the evolving international situation” the travel restrictions remain in place.

Johnson said the government recognizes that border measures can place burdens on Canadians, their families and people coming to Canada. Health organizations including the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control have instead advised travellers returning from the DRC or Uganda to self-monitor for symptoms and only quarantine if they have a high-risk exposure.

Boongo questions why Canada’s rules differ. “I’m African,” said Boongo, before hesitating to add, “There is always a double standard.” His fiancé and partner of nine years, Claude-Dee Laguerre, chimed in with a case in point – cruise passengers who were on board a Dutch ship hit by hantavirus in May were allowed to quarantine in Canada.

“It almost feels like you treat people like second-class citizens because, and again, we hate to say that because we appreciate that the situation is dangerous, we understand, but make it fair for everyone,” Laguerre said.

Student visas After weeks of trying to reach Canadian immigration agents without success, David Isiyo had to defer his third year at a college in Quebec. “I fully have to postpone my semester. That’s what hurts me,” he said.

“I had planned to come back around August 10,” Isiyo said from his hometown of Kinshasa. His siblings and cousins could be heard in the background. “I wanted to make the most of the time with my family.” He called Canada’s immigration office right as it opened repeatedly to see if he could get an exemption from the restrictions to get back to school.

He wanted to ask if he could quarantine in Europe, or if there were any options that would prevent him from deferring the semester. stories.title: Feds call for students to choose the trades as government prepares to ‘Build Canada Strong’
stories.summary: With a wrench in hand, second-year Electric Vehicle Technician students at Ontario’s Durham College are hoping that all their hard work will help them fasten their future career choice.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Whitby, Ont. - With a wrench in hand, second-year Electric Vehicle Technician students at Ontario’s Durham College are hoping that all their hard work will help them fasten their future career choice.

The program is only in its second year, though its gaining plenty of buzz around campus and enrollment demand has risen year over year.

“It’s the direction that everything is going,” proclaims Durham College Hybrid Electric Vehicle Professor, Mike Frederick.

The Federal Government expects to reach a 75 per cent electric vehicle (EV) adoption rate by 2035, with hopes of reaching a goal 90 per cent by 2040.

“As an automotive technician, if we can’t repair EV’s there’s going to be serious consequences. There’s going to be increased demand for all automotive technicians in the near future, there’s more people retiring from the industry than graduates coming into the industry right now” says Frederick.

He tells CTV News he believes automotive technicians are just one of multiple trades soon to be in high demand across Canada.

“I believe the average age of a bricklayer right now is 59 years old, all of the old trades guys like me are starting to get out of it,” adds Frederick.

According to the federal government, by 2033, Canada will need more than 1.4 million new trades workers across the country, in-part due to a retirement rate of trades workers that’s sitting at about 21 per cent.

“With the number of people reaching their retirement age we do need to backfill all those jobs and if you look at anything happening with construction, anything happening in Ontario, or elsewhere in the country, we need trades workers, we need skilled professionals,” says Durham College Skilled Trades Associate Dean, Kara Woods.

The most recent data from Statistics Canada backs up the claim made by both Woods and Frederick. Stats Can says roughly 700,000 tradespeople are expected to retire by the end of this decade.

Trades as a viable career path

“I’m trying to follow the future that’s going to come” says second-year Electric Vehicle Technician student, Noman Shakeel.

Shakeel moved from Pakistan to Canada 20 years ago. For the larger part of the two decades, he was running a restaurant and working as a chef, until the pandemic hit and he watched as the spending habits of Canadians changed.

The second-year student believes working in the trades and specifically training to be an EV technician, will position him well in a future job market that’s become difficult to predict with the rise of AI technology.

“When it comes to working with electric vehicles, you’re not only looking into the EV industry, but you also have electric lawnmowers at home, delivery trucks you see on the road, trains and the wider transport sector, I have a whole field of industry right in front of me that needs workers,” says Shakeel.

Canadian families are increasingly looking at the trades as a viable option for their children, with one report finding that half of Canadians now see trade school as the best way to prepare their child for a career by 2050, compared to just 37 per cent feeling the same way about a university degree.

“Building Canada Strong,” has been a buzz term shared by the federal government. As part of the initiative, Ottawa has pledged $2 billion to recruit and train up to 100,000 new red-seal trades workers within the next five years.

“If you want to build a country, you need to get into the trades, you need to have the hands-on skills. The power of any nation is its ability to build their own industries, rather than getting it from somewhere else,” says Shakeel.

As Shakeel packs his school bag and heads to his next class for the day, the second-year college student shares that one day he hopes to have his own hybrid and electric vehicle mechanic shop. He believes it’s a dream that he’ll soon make a reality.

stories.title: AFN chief warns Carney against ‘abusing’ majority to pass major projects bill
stories.summary: Ottawa — The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations is warning Prime Minister Mark Carney against "abusing" his majority government powers to pass his new major projects bill, which she says could affect First Nations rights.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations is warning Prime Minister Mark Carney against “abusing” his majority government powers to pass his new major projects bill, which she says could affect First Nations rights.

The Building Canada Strong Act shifts the responsibility for reviewing many big projects, such as pipelines and power transmission lines, from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada to the Canada Energy Regulator.

It also proposes changes to the Canada Labour Code.

Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says Carney’s government risks dishonouring the Crown if it limits debate and consultations on the bill, as it did when it passed its major projects legislation in 2025.

She says Carney must let First Nations leaders bring forward amendments to the legislation and his government must be open to them.

Federal ministers say the legislation will speed up construction of major projects and boost employment as the country grapples with a changing trade relationship with the United States.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ottawa's plan for private airport investment likely to drive up costs: NDP leader
stories.summary: NDP Leader Avi Lewis says it’s “disingenuous” for the government not to use the word privatization to describe its plan to have investors take over operations of Canada’s four biggest airports.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — NDP Leader Avi Lewis says it’s “disingenuous” for the government not to use the word privatization to describe its plan to have investors take over operations of Canada’s four biggest airports.

Prime Minister Mark Carney made the pitch at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Sept. 15, arguing it would allow Ottawa to spend more on operations at smaller airports, reducing costs there.

But Lewis, flanked by his caucus and labour leaders outside the House of Commons on Tuesday, said private operations are likely to lead to higher traveller fees at airports in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver.

He said the government’s plan is clearly privatization because it is turning a public asset over to investor control for decades.

“Now we’ve heard the government say, ‘Don’t worry, it’s not actually privatization because the public will still own the land and the buildings.’ This is disingenuous. It’s a distinction without a difference,” Lewis said, comparing the idea to the Ontario government’s handling of Highway 407.

“The government of Ontario sold a 99-year lease for around $3 billion in 1999,” he said. “The road is worth $40 billion today and Ontario drivers have paid $25 billion in tolls over the intervening years, and there are still 72 years left in the lease. It makes absolutely no difference that the land is owned publicly.”

Tammy Moore, Unifor’s aviation council chair and an Air Canada worker out of Saint John, N.B., said union members are afraid private operators will increase precarious contract employment at airports. She said many airport workers, such as baggage handlers, work as subcontractors and their jobs are made vulnerable if an airport changes service providers.

“After all, profits do not appear out of thin air. In the case of airport privatization abroad, private investors squeeze through staffing cuts and fee increases for travellers and airlines,” Moore said.

“The investor doesn’t pay. You do and the workers do.”

The federal government maintains it will still own the land and the airports would still be subject to the same safety regulations.

NDP transport critic Heather McPherson said the government already makes $525 million annually from airports and could put that money back into regional hubs.

She called for an emergency debate in the House of Commons on Monday but was voted down.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Suspect in shooting outside Belleville synagogue has died, police watchdog says
stories.summary: Police have identified the man as 29-year-old Sean Ward of Quinte West
stories.author: Molly Hayes, Jill Mahoney
stories.content:
The suspect in Sunday’s shooting at a small synagogue in Belleville, Ont., has died.

Kristy Denette, a spokesperson for the province’s Special Investigations Unit, confirmed Tuesday that the suspect died Monday night.

The man had been identified by police as Sean Ward, 29, of Quinte West.

The SIU handles cases involving Ontario police that result in death or serious injury.

A post-mortem is scheduled to take place in Kingston on Wednesday, Ms. Denette said.

The suspect had allegedly opened fire with a shotgun on a police officer stationed outside the the Sons of Jacob synagogue as worshippers gathered to mark Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

The officer, Constable Jeff Smith of the Belleville Police Service, remains hospitalized in stable condition in Kingston.

Lauren Wilkinson, a spokesperson for the Belleville Police Service, referred questions about Mr. Ward’s death to the SIU.

stories.title: Latest polls show Brad Bradford catching up with Olivia Chow in Toronto mayoral race
stories.summary: With the Toronto mayoral election just over a month away, the polls suggest Bradford is catching up with Chow, after a drop in her support.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
The Toronto mayoral election is now just over a month away, and the latest polls show Councillor Brad Bradford closing the gap with Mayor Olivia Chow after a drop in her support.

A recent Liaison Strategies survey shows Chow currently leading Bradford by seven points, down from her 11-point lead in early September. She receives support from 47 per cent of voters, compared to 50 per cent earlier in the month, while Bradford’s share of support has increased from 39 per cent to 40 per cent.

This picture varies, however, across different parts of the city. The Liaison Strategies data reveals that the most competitive areas in Toronto are North York and Scarborough, where Chow leads Bradford 46 per cent to 41 per cent and 46 per cent to 43 per cent respectively.

Those are much closer results than Etobicoke, where Bradford leads 54 per cent to 33 per cent, or Downtown, where Chow leads 60 per cent to 27 per cent.

Meanwhile, there is also a sharp age divide among younger age groups. Bradford has 47 per cent among decided and leaning voters aged 18 to 34, compared with 41 per cent for Chow. Among those aged 35 to 49, however, Chow leads 57 per cent to 33 per cent.

Despite Chow’s smaller cushion compared to previous polls, David Valentin, principal at Liaison Strategies, said the latest survey results are “not enough to establish a new trend.”

“ Bradford has gained some ground without overtaking the mayor,” he said.

Though Valentin doesn’t make suggestions about the reasons for the closing gap between Chow and Bradford, the survey did ask voters about the issues that matter most to them in the mayoral race.

Cost of living came first at 23 per cent, followed by housing affordability at 19 per cent, crime and public safety at 17 per cent, and traffic and congestion at 13 per cent. Together, cost of living and housing account for 42 per cent of responses.

Meanwhile, the latest Mainstreet Research survey also reveals what it calls “a tighter race” post-Labour Day and following the first mayoral debate, which took place on Sept. 14.

Among those surveyed, 38.8 per cent said they would vote for Chow, while 31.4 per cent said they would vote for Bradford. But 13.5 per cent said they might change their vote before election day and 16.8 per cent remain undecided.

In contrast to Valentin’s assessment, Quito Maggi, president & CEO of Mainstreet Research, said the latter two figures make the Toronto mayoral race “too close to call.”

Elsewhere, Chris Alexander, who was once Canada’s ambassador to Afghanistan and an immigration minister under former prime minister Stephen Harper, comes in third in both polls, with 10 per cent support in the Liaison Strategies survey and 8 per cent support according to Mainstreet Research.

Alexander joined the mayoral race on July 29 and, at the time, Valentin noted this might pose a problem for Bradford, because he “no longer has the centre-right lane entirely to himself.”

However, Alexander’s support remains unchanged from the previous Liaison strategies survey.

Instead, Valentin suggests Bradford’s main challenge lies in his personal approval ratings. Though the share of voters who view him favourably has increased from 31 per cent to 33 per cent, so has the share who view him unfavourably, which is now 37 per cent, up from 34 per cent.

It comes as the share unfamiliar with him has fallen from 24 per cent to 19 per cent, with another 11 per cent unsure.

Meanwhile, the latest polls coincide with Ontario Premier Doug Ford appearing to endorse Chow last week, before taking back his comments a day later.

At a press event in North York on Sept. 17, a reporter asked Ford for his thoughts on the mayoral race, to which he responded that he had “a phenomenal relationship” with Chow. “We’re going to continue supporting the mayor. She’s doing an incredible job,” he said. “So, read between the lines.”

The Bradford campaign, having positioned itself as the conservative alternative to the left-wing Chow, later released a statement to the media which said “of course the premier endorsed Olivia Chow” because “she’s the easiest negotiation he has ever had.” It went on to say that she “handed over on a silver platter” things she had vowed to oppose.

Then, ON the evening of Sept. 18, the Premier’s Office released a statement of its own, which read: “We would like to clarify that Premier Ford did not endorse Olivia Chow and will not endorse any candidate in the Toronto mayoral race.”

Ford explained during an appearance on Newstalk 1010 the following morning that “read between the lines” was meant as a message to say, “we’re going to work things out” and “get through this.”

“When I endorse someone, which I’m not, you come out and fully endorse them. You don’t say, ‘read between the lines,'” he said.

Liaison surveyed a random sample of Toronto residents from September 19 to September 20, 2026, and the resulting data was weighted to match targets based on the 2021 Census. For the total sample, the margin of error is +/- 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

The Mainstreet Research poll was conducted between September 14 and 17, 2026 and also has a margin of error of +/- 3.1 per cent, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: New out-of-control wildfire growing near Sooke, B.C.
stories.summary: Crews are responding to the Mount Jack wildfire
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
BC Wildfire Service says a new fire is burning out of control on southern Vancouver Island.

The service says in a social media post that crews are responding to the Mount Jack wildfire, which is burning about four kilometres west of Sooke River and south of Mount Jack.

It says the fire was discovered late Sunday and has grown to a 1/2 square kilometre amid warm and dry conditions.

The service says smoke from the fire can be seen as far north as Shawnigan Lake and in Greater Victoria.

Crews are working to contain the flames, but the service says further growth of the fire can be expected.

The service says the wildfire does not currently pose a threat to public safety nor critical infrastructure.

While the wildfire season is winding down, there are still more than 100 fires burning across the province and four of them are considered out of control.

stories.title: Search for Parker Wells was delayed by 911 issues: Calgary police
stories.summary: Parker's disappearance in July sparked a massive search in Calgary that went on for two weeks until his body was found in a system of pipes under the city's Deerfoot freeway.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
The City of Calgary says 911 operators broke rules leading to a delay of almost an hour before the alert went out for Parker Wells, a missing 11-year-old with autism who was non-verbal.

The boy’s disappearance in July sparked a massive search that went on for two weeks until his body was found in a system of pipes under a city freeway.

Foul play is not suspected.

Iain Bushell, the city’s head of emergency management, said in a statement Tuesday that 911 operators had the information they needed to alert police right away that July morning, but did not.

“Established procedures were not followed, resulting in a delay in how certain information was acted on,” Bushell said.

“That delay did not meet the standard of service we expect.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That delay did not meet the standard of service we expect."

He said disciplinary action has been taken against those involved, but declined to provide details due to privacy rules.

“Calgary 911 employees are deeply committed to public safety,” he added. “When an event has a tragic outcome such as this, they feel the weight of that responsibility.”

The city said it has made changes after a review on the 911 response that day — more supervisors, more checks, and more spot reviews, along with updated training reviews.

“We are committed to strengthening our processes and ensuring our employees have the support, training and tools they need to serve Calgarians effectively,” Bushell said.

Parker walked away from his day home in north Calgary on the morning of July 16.

A city review cited by Bushell found that when the initial call came in from the day home at 10:53 a.m., the 911 operator did not flag it as an emergency because the day home did not want to officially list Parker as missing.

The review found that regardless of what the day home wanted, the 911 operator had enough information to alert police, which would have triggered other emergency search procedures and notifications in those crucial early minutes.

Soon after, the review said, a 911 supervisor reviewed the call and didn’t take action.

“The supervisor should have more fully considered the totality of available information, specifically the child’s age and the inability of day home staff to locate the child,” the review said.

A half-hour after the first call, the day home called back to report the child missing. The alert then went out to police, but not until 11:41 a.m. — a total of 48 minutes after the first call.

The search for the boy captured the attention and emotion of the city. Hundreds of police and volunteers checked and rechecked homes, boats, sheds, garages and waterways trying to find the child.

It was a complex undertaking complicated by Parker’s neurological condition.

Police cautioned that the boy could become more scared if confronted by strangers. Searchers played some of Parker’s favourite Disney songs from patrol vehicles to try to draw him out. Some left out Goldfish crackers.

After two weeks, the search was called off.

A day later, Parker’s shoe was found near a culvert.

His body was found a short distance away in a network of pipes under the north end portion of the Deerfoot Trail expressway. The spot was about three kilometres from the day home.

In the days that followed, a makeshift memorial of flowers, stuffed toys and candles grew by a footbridge near where his body was found.

Parker’s plight has also prompted petitions to change Amber Alerts. Such alerts are broadly disseminated warnings for children believed to have been abducted and in serious danger. In Parker’s case, an Amber Alert was issued as a special exemption but not until the second day of the search.

The Alberta government is now reviewing criteria for Amber Alerts.

stories.title: 10/3 podcast: Treatment or prison? What happens when a killer is found mentally ill
stories.summary: About 20 homicide cases every year in Canada wind up with the killer being found not criminally responsible, and sentenced to mental health treatment instead of jail.
stories.author: Shawn Knox
stories.content:
On average, about 20 homicide cases every year in Canada wind up with the killer being found not criminally responsible, and sentenced to mental health treatment instead of jail.

But how are these cases decided, and what is the fallout for families of the victims when the perpetrator isn’t sent to prison?

Emma Jarratt, a reporter with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, joins me to discuss key factors that are frequently present in cases where an accused is designated NCR, why the designation is seen as controversial, and what changes people are proposing.

Background reading: Not Criminally Responsible: The broken system behind the killers who don’t go to jail

stories.title: Mistakes found in handling of missing Calgary boy, city says
stories.summary: Parker Wells, 11, was found dead in late July after a two-week search
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The City of Calgary says 911 operators broke rules leading to a delay of almost an hour before the alert went out for missing 11-year-old Parker Wells.

The boy’s disappearance in July sparked a massive search that went on for two weeks until his body was found in a system of pipes under a city freeway. Foul play was ruled out.

Iain Bushell, the city’s head of emergency management, told reporters Tuesday that a review of the 911 handling of the call led to disciplinary action and one person “is no longer with the city.” He declined to provide details.

The review, also released Tuesday, concluded that 911 operators had the information they needed to alert police to their highest priority call right away that July morning, but did not.

“We discovered that some mistakes were made, that procedure was not followed correctly,” Bushell said. “At 911, I can tell you that whole room feels awful that this has happened.

“We take it to heart that the public expects excellence from us.”

The city said it has made changes: more supervisors and more checks along with updated training reviews.

Parker walked away from his day home in north Calgary on the morning of July 16.

The City of Calgary says 911 operators broke rules leading to a delay before the police started a search for missing 11-year-old Parker Wells.

The Canadian Press

The review determined that when the initial call came in from the day home at 10:53 a.m., the 911 operator did not flag it as an emergency because the day home did not want to officially list Parker as missing.

The review found that regardless of what the day home wanted, the 911 operator had enough information to alert police, which would have triggered other emergency search procedures and notifications in those crucial early minutes.

Soon after, the review said, a 911 supervisor reviewed the call and didn’t take action.

“The supervisor should have more fully considered the totality of available information, specifically the child’s age and the inability of day home staff to locate the child,” the review said.

A half-hour after the first call, the day home called back to officially report the child missing. The alert then went out to police but not until 11:41 a.m. – a total of 48 minutes after the first call.

The search for the boy captured the attention and emotion of the city. Hundreds of police and volunteers checked and rechecked homes, boats, sheds, garages and waterways trying to find the child.

The search was complicated by Parker’s neurological condition. Police cautioned that the boy could become more scared if confronted by strangers. Searchers played some of Parker’s favourite Disney songs from patrol vehicles to try to draw him out. Some left out Goldfish crackers.

After two weeks, the search was called off. A day later, Parker’s shoe was found near a culvert. His body was found a short distance away in a network of pipes under the north end portion of the Deerfoot Trail expressway. The spot was about three kilometres from the day home.

In the days that followed, a makeshift memorial of flowers, stuffed toys and candles grew by a footbridge near where his body was found.

The tragedy has also prompted petitions to change Amber Alerts.

Such alerts are broadly disseminated warnings for children believed to have been abducted and in serious danger. In Parker’s case, an Amber Alert was issued as a special exemption but not until the second day of the search.

The Alberta government is now reviewing criteria for Amber Alerts.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said he supports calls from advocates for the creation of an Indigo Alert – an advisory specifically for vulnerable youth.

“This is an incredible tragedy and how we find the silver lining is through improving processes,” Farkas said.

The boy’s disappearance in July sparked a massive search that went on for two weeks until his body was found in a system of pipes under a city freeway. Foul play was ruled out.

“We discovered that some mistakes were made, that procedure was not followed correctly,” Bushell said. “At 911, I can tell you that whole room feels awful that this has happened.
“We take it to heart that the public expects excellence from us.”
The city said it has made changes: more supervisors and more checks along with updated training reviews.

stories.title: Canadian whisky lottery draws thousands as trade war shifts buying habits
stories.summary: Wyatt Cooper-Brown, manager of Okanagan Spirits' Kelowna location, says the company has seen increased sales as more Canadians look toward homegrown spirits amid the trade war.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
What if winning the lottery didn’t mean millions of dollars, but a chance to buy a bottle of whisky?

That’s what thousands of Canadians are hoping for as Okanagan Spirits prepares to release 5,000 bottles of its Laird of Fintry single malt whisky through a draw.

The Okanagan Spirit distillery received more than 42,000 entries.

Wyatt Cooper-Brown, manager of Okanagan Spirits’ Kelowna location, says the company has seen increased sales as more Canadians look toward homegrown spirits amid the Canada-U.S. trade war.

“The trade war for us is almost a silver lining,” Cooper-Brown said. “Massive increase in our sales.”

He says the company’s bourbon-style whisky has seen particularly strong interest, bringing more customers to its other products.

The changing buying habits extend beyond the distillery.

A recent TD survey found 79 per cent of Canadians plan to support local or Canadian businesses, while 48 per cent said supporting Canadian businesses is a stronger priority than it was last summer.

For some Kelowna residents, the trade dispute has changed where they choose to spend their money.

Hubert, a local resident, said buying Canadian products is a way of supporting the country.

“For us it just means that we’re defending home and kind of trying to uphold Canadian culture,” he said.

Another resident, Cindy, said she has become more deliberate about checking where products are made.

“I don’t think a lot of people realise what was produced in Canada,” she said. “But everyone that I know now, they look at were things are made.”

The increased interest in Canadian whisky comes with a catch for Okanagan Spirits: the company can’t simply increase production overnight.

Its Laird of Fintry whisky is finished in specialized wine barrels from local wineries, which give the whisky its distinct flavour. The distillery says there are only a limited number of those barrels available.

Cooper-Brown says the boost in sales also needs to be viewed in the broader context of the trade war.

“The trade war can be beneficial for some and quite negative for others,” he said. “Although we are seeing increase in sales and what not, it’s still an uphill battle.”

For Okanagan Spirits, the trade war has brought more attention to Canadian-made spirits. For other businesses, the economic impact has been very different.

stories.title: Mount Jack wildfire burning out of control on southern Vancouver Island
stories.summary: While the wildfire season is winding down, there are still more than 100 fires burning across the province and four of them are considered out of control.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
BC Wildfire Service says a new fire is burning out of control on southern Vancouver Island.

The service says in a social media post that crews are responding to the Mount Jack wildfire , which is burning about four kilometres west of Sooke River and south of Mount Jack.

It says the fire was discovered late Sunday and has grown to a 1/2 square kilometre amid warm and dry conditions.

The service says smoke from the fire can be seen as far north as Shawnigan Lake and in Greater Victoria.

Crews are working to contain the flames, but the service says further growth of the fire can be expected.

The service says the wildfire does not currently pose a threat to public safety nor critical infrastructure.

While the wildfire season is winding down, there are still more than 100 fires burning across the province and four of them are considered out of control.

stories.title: CBC journalist says protesters tried to 'taunt and intimidate' him from attending Yom Kippur service
stories.summary: Neil Herland says he got an Austrian passport "in case Canada becomes unsafe for me as a Jew. I fear that moment is approaching."
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
CBC National Radio News Reader Neil Herland recounts the intimidation he faced when trying to enter a building to attend Yom Kippur service in Toronto on Monday night, adding that he May have to leave Canada amid rising antisemitism.

“On Yom Kippur I went to a synagogue service in Toronto and was met by protesters trying to taunt and intimidate me from entering the building,” wrote Herland in a post on X, where he identifies himself as a journalist and a Jew. His post came a day after a synagogue came under attack in Belleville, Ont., a city about two hours to the east.

Video taken by Herland shows a group of about 20 people milling about, blowing horns and waving Palestinian flags in front of the Meridian Arts Centre at Yonge and Sheppard, where The Song Shul holds annual events to mark Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, and Yom Kippur, known as the Day of Atonement. The synagogue doesn’t have its own building but rents different locations to hold services.

“My late father was an Austrian Jew who survived the Holocaust in Romania. And came to Canada as a refugee. This year I got an Austrian passport, in case Canada becomes unsafe for me as a Jew. I fear that moment is approaching, here in Canada and elsewhere.”

In the video by Herland, the shouts of the group are hard to make out, but at one point someone yells: “Palestine will be free.” As Herland moves through the crowd, someone shouts in his face several times with a megaphone: “You’re going to hell!”

At another point he turns to look behind him — some distance away are two individuals with a placard that says “Where’s your humanity?” One of them shouts “Zionist alert” through a megaphone before waving at the camera.

He added that the cantor (singer) at the event revealed that his nephew had been murdered on Rosh Hashana in Ukraine, in a suspected hate crime. The event listed Simon Spiro as the cantor.

“And this morning the Toronto synagogue announced there had been an attack outside a synagogue in Belleville,” Herland continued.

The Belleville shooting happened Sunday night outside a synagogue in the city of 55,000 where worshipers had gathered to mark Yom Kippur. Const. Jeff Smith, a nearly 13-year veteran of the Belleville Police Service, was in critical but stable condition after exchanging gunfire with a shooter outside the building. No one else was injured in the attack.

“Jewish Canadians are living in a parallel world,” Herland wrote in his post. “Where police stand guard with guns outside synagogues. And Jewish schools, religious sites and businesses are targeted with bullets. And most Canadians have no awareness or understanding.” Dedicated police protection has become commonplace at synagogues across Canada, particularly during Jewish holidays, in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attacks in Israel. Multiple synagogues in Ontario, and specifically the Greater Toronto Area, have been targeted in shooting attacks in recent years. In March, three GTA synagogues were struck by gunfire in the space of five days — Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto in Thornhill, and Temle Emanu-el and Shaarei Shomayim in North York. York Regional Police have charged three suspects in connection with two of the shootings. Toronto police were present at Monday’s protest, and kept protesters about five metres away from the door. Herland noted that the guest speaker was an Australian-born university teacher who lives in Israel, identified by the Song Shul as Mark Regev, former Israeli ambassador to the U.K. A Canadian group called Just Peace Advocates had submitted a complaint demanding that Regev be barred from entering Canada. National Post has reached out to the group for more information. “His speech was about making peace in the Middle East. Let’s hope that happens this year,” Herland wrote.

stories.title: Exclusive: Suspect in Belleville synagogue shooting dead
stories.summary: A suspect who allegedly opened fire on a police officer outside a Belleville, Ont. synagogue over the weekend has died, sources confirm to CP24.
stories.author: Chris Fox
stories.content:
A former Canadian Armed Forces soldier who allegedly opened fire on a police officer outside a Belleville, Ont., synagogue over the weekend has died.

Sean Ward, a 29-year-old Quinte West resident, was shot during an exchange of gunfire with police outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday night as congregants inside prepared to mark Yom Kippur.

Ward was initially without vital signs at the scene of the shooting but was revived and rushed to the hospital in life-threatening condition.

He died in hospital on Monday night, and an autopsy has been scheduled for Wednesday in Kingston, Ont., the Special Investigations Unit confirmed to CP24.

Investigators have previously said that Ward was armed with a shotgun and opened fire on a police officer stationed outside, shortly after arriving in the area in a truck.

A 13-year veteran of the Belleville Police Service—Const. Jeff Smith—was critically injured in the shooting.

Sources tell CP24 that Smith was shot multiple times, including in the neck, and remained in hospital in stable condition as of Tuesday.

While police have not commented on the motive behind the shooting, SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette did agree with a reporter’s suggestion on Monday that it could fit the description of a terrorist attack.

“I think that common sense would say that probably was the case,” she said.

Individual matching gunman’s description served with CAF

In a statement provided to CTV News on Tuesday, a spokesperson for the Canadian Armed Forces confirmed that a former member matches the description of the shooting suspect.

The spokesperson said that Ward enrolled in the military in July 2017 and was released in June 2022 at the rank of corporal.

“He served as an infantry soldier with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry and did not deploy during his service,” the spokesperson said. “We remain ready to provide assistance to the investigation if required.”

Police identified Ward on Monday but have not provided any further details, citing the ongoing investigation being conducted by Ontario’s police watchdog.

The SIU has estimated that 20 to 30 shots were fired at the scene.

Congregation members at Sons of Jacob Synagogue have said that some of those shots shattered stained-glass windows in the building.

Consul general visits synagogue

Nadav Zysblat, the consul general of Israel to Toronto and Western Canada, visited the synagogue on Tuesday and talked to the members of the community.

He said people are concerned and frightened in the wake of the shooting.

“They’re seeing levels of antisemitism in Canada that we haven’t seen before, and this is extremely concerning. And again, we call upon the Canadian government to take all the measures to make sure that any Canadian feels safe; that includes, of course, the Jewish community in Canada,” Zysblat said in an interview with CP24.

“I think we really have to make sure that this really is the last time and that that is a call for action, not for words, but for actual decisive action.”

Seeing the bullet holes in the stained glass felt “surreal” for the president of the congregation, who returned to the synagogue for the first time since the shooting.

“It’s kind of strange actually coming back in. But we are glad to be back in,” said Norm Weddum.

He recounted hearing loud bangs and closing the wooden doors once he realized they were gunshots. Weddum said he crouched down and did not move until the shooting had stopped.

He also remembered the congregation being taken to the police station and doing service in there.

“We moved the tables and chairs over together there, and we all sat there, and we had a bit of a service with the rabbi and did some hymns and songs and just kind of put things like back in place, what we were here to do,” Weedum said.

“It kind of brought people closer together after a traumatic event.”

Weedum said he is still in shock but cannot wait to hold service at the synagogue again.

“Let’s get back to what we do and running services and programs and teaching, and that’s what we want to do, and so we’re going to get started again,” he said.

Reacting to news of the shooting on Monday, Premier Doug Ford called Smith a “hero” and said that he “stopped a tragedy in its footsteps.”

In an interview with CP24 on Tuesday, Richard Marceau, who is the Senior Vice President Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, said the incident further underscores the need for resources to protect synagogues and other Jewish institutions amid an increase in violent act targeting the community.

“Words are not enough and there are things that need to happen. So we need to convene a a meeting of federal, provincial, and territorial and municipal leaders to make sure that there’s intelligence sharing, that the law is properly enforced and there needs to be an expedited way to get Jewish institutions like synagogues, community centres and schools to have access to off-duty armed police officers to protect our institutions because imagine if those two heroes, those two police officers, had not been there in Belleville,” he said.

With files from CP24’s Beatrice Vaisman

stories.title: Anyone with a cellphone can help track monarch butterflies tagged in New Brunswick
stories.summary: Earlier this month, Nature New Brunswick and the Point Lepreau Bird Observatory attached tiny Bluetooth tracking tags to 22 monarchs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Researchers in New Brunswick say they are using new Bluetooth tags to track monarch butterflies on their long journey from Canada to Mexico.

Employees and volunteers from two New Brunswick-based conservation groups attached the tiny tracking tags to 22 monarchs in early September.

The solar-powered tags emit signals that can be picked up by any Bluetooth-enabled cellphones within 100 metres.

The location of the insect is then automatically posted on the Project Monarch map, helping researchers track the monarch’s annual 4,000-to-5,000-kilometre migration to its overwintering grounds in Mexico.

Francie Morgan, a program coordinator with Nature NB, said much of the monarch migration remains a mystery and this data will help scientists better understand where the insects are stopping along their route and where they are finding shelter from storms.

Nature NB partnered with the Point Lepreau Bird Observatory on the project, which could also help the provincial government craft its plan to protect the species, which was designated as an endangered species in the province in 2022.

“If we can get a better understanding of the areas that monarchs are taking refuge … we can better protect them to be more resilient in the face of climate change,” she said.

Morgan said traditional tracking methods involve attaching visual tags to monarchs and recapturing them along their migration to record their location.

Now, researchers can see a monarch’s location more frequently, which helps fill in gaps along their lengthy journey south.

Each tag costs about $300, Morgan said, adding that the project received funding the New Brunswick Environmental Trust Fund, NB Power and Environment and Climate Change Canada.

Jim Wilson has been tagging monarch butterflies at Point Lepreau for 20 years and he said the new technology is a significant improvement.

“It’s light-years ahead because in real time, we can see where our butterflies are going,” he said. “Everybody who is following this literally is mesmerized by what we’re seeing.”

Wilson says the group has already learned something new about the monarchs they tagged.

He said the map showed that several butterflies went from Point Lepreau to Nova Scotia instead of flying south.

Wilson believes strong westerly winds May have blown the monarchs off course for a few days, but he said that they have since started making their way south again.

Morgan said they attached the tags to each monarch’s back with eyelash glue, adding that the antennas are about the length of the insect’s abdomen.

She said the tags weigh as much as a few grains of rice but are still a “notable portion” of a monarch’s body weight, which is about half a gram.

These tags are more invasive for monarchs than the traditional visual tags, but Morgan said the butterflies have responded well.

“They are incredibly resilient, and they’re using the technology like champions,” she said.

The data from the tags will also be available to scientists and conservation groups across Canada, the U.S. and Mexico, which will help them make conservation decisions moving forward, she said.

But the data isn’t just for researchers, anyone who wants to learn more about the monarch migration can track the butterflies using the Project Monarch app.

Wilson said watching each monarch’s progress is “amazing.”

“What you see here as this is unfolding is this fragile little butterfly battling the elements,” he said. “And you’re just rooting for it … you’re hoping that this little butterfly will make it.”

stories.title: Man, 19, arrested in Ontario after threats to shoot up synagogue: police
stories.summary: The Whitby resident, 19, is accused of posting about carrying out a shooting on an online message board.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A 19-year-old man in Durham Region was arrested for threatening to shoot a synagogue. He was charged just a day before a gunman opened fire outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., injuring Const. Jeff Smith stationed outside.

Alexander Parfitt, a resident of Whitby, is accused of posting about carrying out a shooting on an online message board, according to Durham Regional Police . Officers received information about the threats from a law enforcement partner.

Police were able to identify the user and executed a search warrant at the man’s Whitby home on Sept. 19.

He was charged with threats motivated by hate.

The shooting in Belleville, roughly 140 kilometres west of Whitby, took place around 7 p.m. on Sunday evening, when a 29-year-old suspect Sean Ward fired shots at the synagogue.

At the time, there were roughly 25 congregants inside the building for evening prayers on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for the Jewish community. None of the congregants were injured. Smith was rushed to Kingston General Hospital where he remains in critical but stable condition.

Meanwhile, the suspect is in life-threatening condition.

Durham police said it had increased patrol during the Jewish high holidays at community centres and places of worship.

Synagogues across Canada have become the target of antisemitic attacks.

In January, a synagogue in Winnipeg was graffitied with swastikas . In March, three synagogues in the Greater Toronto Area were hit with bullets. In June, a suspect was arrested after an attempted arson at a synagogue in Montreal.

stories.title: Ottawa’s airports plan will mean higher costs, NDP Leader says
stories.summary: The government’s plan is clearly privatization, says Avi Lewis
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
NDP Leader Avi Lewis says it’s “disingenuous” for the government not to use the word privatization to describe its plan to have investors take over operations of Canada’s four biggest airports.

Prime Minister Mark Carney made the pitch at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Sept. 15, arguing it would allow Ottawa to spend more on operations at smaller airports, reducing costs there.

But Lewis, flanked by his caucus and labour leaders outside the House of Commons on Tuesday, said private operations are likely to lead to higher traveller fees at airports in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver.

He said the government’s plan is clearly privatization because it is turning a public asset over to investor control for decades.

“Now we’ve heard the government say, ‘Don’t worry, it’s not actually privatization because the public will still own the land and the buildings.’ This is disingenuous. It’s a distinction without a difference,” Lewis said, comparing the idea to the Ontario government’s handling of Highway 407.

“The government of Ontario sold a 99-year lease for around $3-billion in 1999,” he said. “The road is worth $40-billion today and Ontario drivers have paid $25-billion in tolls over the intervening years, and there are still 72 years left in the lease. It makes absolutely no difference that the land is owned publicly.”

Carney details plans to open up Canada’s four largest airports to private investment

Tammy Moore, Unifor’s aviation council chair and an Air Canada worker out of Saint John, N.B., said union members are afraid private operators will increase precarious contract employment at airports. She said many airport workers, such as baggage handlers, work as subcontractors and their jobs are made vulnerable if an airport changes service providers.

“After all, profits do not appear out of thin air. In the case of airport privatization abroad, private investors squeeze through staffing cuts and fee increases for travellers and airlines,” Moore said.

“The investor doesn’t pay. You do and the workers do.”

The federal government maintains it will still own the land and the airports would still be subject to the same safety regulations.

NDP transport critic Heather McPherson said the government already makes $525-million annually from airports and could put that money back into regional hubs.

She called for an emergency debate in the House of Commons on Monday but was voted down.

By David Baxter, The Canadian Press
Posted September 22, 2026 12:23 pm.
Last Updated September 22, 2026 1:33 pm.

Ottawa — NDP Leader Avi Lewis says it’s “disingenuous” for the government not to use the word privatization to describe its plan to have investors take over operations of Canada’s four biggest airports.
Prime Minister Mark Carney made the pitch at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Sept. 15, arguing it would allow Ottawa to spend more on operations at smaller airports, reducing costs there.

But Lewis, flanked by his caucus and labour leaders outside the House of Commons on Tuesday, said private operations are likely to lead to higher traveller fees at airports in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver.
He said the government’s plan is clearly privatization because it is turning a public asset over to investor control for decades.

“Now we’ve heard the government say, ‘Don’t worry, it’s not actually privatization because the public will still own the land and the buildings.’ This is disingenuous. It’s a distinction without a difference,” Lewis said, comparing the idea to the Ontario government’s handling of Highway 407.

“The government of Ontario sold a 99-year lease for around $3 billion in 1999,” he said. “The road is worth $40 billion today and Ontario drivers have paid $25 billion in tolls over the intervening years, and there are still 72 years left in the lease. It makes absolutely no difference that the land is owned publicly.”

Tammy Moore, Unifor’s aviation council chair and an Air Canada worker out of Saint John, N.B., said union members are afraid private operators will increase precarious contract employment at airports. She said many airport workers, such as baggage handlers, work as subcontractors and their jobs are made vulnerable if an airport changes service providers.

“After all, profits do not appear out of thin air. In the case of airport privatization abroad, private investors squeeze through staffing cuts and fee increases for travellers and airlines,” Moore said.
“The investor doesn’t pay. You do and the workers do.”
The federal government maintains it will still own the land and the airports would still be subject to the same safety regulations.
NDP transport critic Heather McPherson said the government already makes $525 million annually from airports and could put that money back into regional hubs.
She called for an emergency debate in the House of Commons on Monday but was voted down.

stories.title: At Charli xcx’s electric spectacle in Toronto, a Canadian filmmaking legend had a lasting presence
stories.summary: The British superstar began with a shout-out to ‘Mr. David Cronenberg’
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
At the end of her 90-minute spectacle of pulsing hyper-pop and industrialized, rave-ready rock experimentations at Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena on Monday, the British superstar Charli xcx spoke to the audience before the final song, No One Lasts Forever .

She began with a shout-out to a Canadian octogenarian filmmaker, “Mr. David Cronenberg,” whose voiceover is featured prominently on the track that also closes her new album, Music, Fashion, Film . In 2025, she travelled to Toronto to record a conversation with the shock auteur.

“It’s the last thing I did for this album, it kind of completed the whole thing,” she explained, describing No One Lasts Forever as the most important song on the album and a “mission statement of how I feel.”

The song and the album are the 34-year-old’s reaction to the zeitgeist level of fame caused by the success of her 2024 LP Brat. Transcending the music world, brat was a flash cultural movement officially deemed by Collins English Dictionary as 2024’s word of the year, redefined as someone with an independent and hedonistic attitude.

“I don’t wanna go home, now I’m more confident than ever,” she sang on the synth-popped No One Lasts Forever in front of the electrified crowd. “Since everyone knows my name, all the parties got better.”

Charli xcx’s choreographer Eric Christison on leaving pointe shoes for fashion and music

Parties and fame end. Even concerts have curfews. The Scotiabank show closed with the recorded words of Cronenberg on legacies repeated like a mantra: “They are dead, they are gone, no one lasts forever.”

Charli and her troupe of female dancers posed as a bunch, frozen in place as Cronenberg’s phrase “Oblivion is freedom” was shown on the large video screens flanking the stage. The idea is that there is liberation in the acceptance that we’ll all be unremembered eventually.

Which doesn’t mean this concert will be forgotten anytime soon. Banger after banger, relentless visually and sonically, in front a largely female audience, dressed like their idol in short skirts or shorts with fancy stockings. There hasn’t been this much fishnet in one place since Canada’s cod fishing collapse in 1992.

The star attraction initially appeared all in black leather. The motocore fashion gave way to other self-confident styles that were more trashy than flashy. The stage was stark, dark and blocky, with diminishing tiers stacked toward the rafters. The lighting was minimalist.

Despite the last name xcx, the singer is not Roman. She was born Charlotte Emma Aitchison, the daughter of a Scottish businessman and a Gujarati Indian nurse and flight attendant. Her first (and highest) charting single in Canada was Boom Clap in 2014. The name of her 2022 album Crash was inspired by the 1996 Cronenberg film of the same name.

In this month’s Rolling Stone magazine, the often breathless music critic Rob Sheffield declared Olivia Rodrigo the “best arena rock act in years.” The assertion already seems dated. Brat has entered the chat.

The show began with the jagged Rock Music , a winking − sarcastic, even − jump into the genre. Charli’s take on rock could be described as post-Strokes. Her three-piece band at least looked the part.

The line “I’m really banging my head, I’m really hurting my neck, the nerve damage is real” is authentic. Charli’s energetic stage performances take a toll. As for the chorus – “I think the dance floor is dead, so now we’re making rock music” – that is cheeky and not to be taken literally.

The band appeared off and on throughout the evening, replaced by Charli’s more familiar modus operandi: auto-tuned vocals accompanied by backing tracks. The 2013 song Grins was performed live for the first time in years. During the Brat -era electroclash hit Guess, canons flung underwear into the air instead of confetti.

Cronenberg once said that we’re all mad scientists with life as our labs: “We’re all trying to experiment to find a way to live, to solve problems, to fend off madness and chaos.”

Some experiments are more interesting than others. Like visionaries Madonna and Lady Gaga, Charli xcx wets her finger, sticks it in the air − and ignores the wind’s direction. Her brash sounds, charismatic audacity and controlled chaos are state of the art.

stories.title: TD Bank closure worries some Cherryhill seniors who rely on nearby branch
stories.summary: TD Bank's Platt's Lane branch at 215 Oxford St. W. will close Nov. 6. Customers are being redirected to the bank's Oakridge branch, about a 10-minute drive west, but some seniors in the Cherryhill neighbourhood say the new location will be difficult to access.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: TD Bank's Platt's Lane branch at 215 Oxford St. W. will close Nov. 6. Customers are being redirected to the bank's Oakridge branch, about a 10-minute drive west, but some seniors in the Cherryhill neighbourhood say the new location will be difficult to access.
· Posted: Sep 22, 2026 12:17 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Some seniors in London's Cherryhill neighbourhood say they're worried about how they'll access their banking after a nearby TD branch closes its doors in November.
TD Bank's Platt's Lane Branch at 215 Oxford St. W. will close Nov. 6. Customers are being redirected to the bank's Oakridge branch at 1213 Oxford Street West, about a 10-minute drive west.
For seniors who walk to the Platt's Lane branch, however, the trip to Oakridge can be much more complicated.
"Where they're going is too far, " said Cherryhill resident Maria-Teresa Vicencio. "You can't get there with your walker. You have to take a bus or drive. How many people can drive in the winter?"
Cherryhill Village is home to 12 residential buildings, and Vicencio says many of the residents are seniors who rely on being able to walk to nearby businesses and services.
She said she believes TD did not fully consider the needs of older customers when it made the decision to close the branch.
"I know most young people do banking online, but this is not an area of very young people," she said.
Residents forced to travel out of town after closure of only bank in their rural Ontario town
Another bricks and mortar bank to close in northwestern Ontario amid region-wide trend

In an emailed statement to CBC News, TD spokesperson Natasha Ferrari said the decision to close the Platt's Lane location was made as the building's lease came to an end and the company reviewed client demand.
"Following a detailed review of client activity patterns, number of transactions and accessibility, we determined that Oakridge is well positioned to serve our clients' needs," Ferrari said.
She said the Oakridge branch offers the same services and hours of operation as Platt's Lane, with enhanced staffing levels.
Vicencio said her concern is not about the quality of service, but how she will get to the new branch.

"Transit is fine, but then you have to be there on a schedule. You do your banking, then you have to wait for the transport to bring you back. That's a whole day of activity. Here, people can come do their banking and go home."
Vicencio has been a TD customer at the Platt's Lane branch for 22 years, ever since she moved to the Cherryhill neighbourhood from Vancouver.
She walks from her residence to the bank every two weeks. She keeps a safety deposit box there and prefers to do all of her banking in-person.
"If you have questions, a person can answer to you," Vicencio said. "I think the problem is that they assume everybody uses a computer. Most seniors cannot."
Vicencio said she doesn't yet have a plan for how she'll get to her new branch, adding that she prefers not to drive at this point in her life and that transit is not convenient.
"If it's too difficult, maybe I'll have to stop going to the bank."

Betty Noble said she's been a TD customer since the 1970s, and has been at the Platt's Lane branch for about 14 years. It takes her less than 10 minutes to walk to the bank, and she often builds it into her day's routine.
"I was very taken back that they were proposing to move or close down," said Noble, who lives in the Cherryhill area.
Another N.B. town will lose its only bank, leaving residents ‘devastated’
BMO branch closure brings anxiety for some seniors in Prince Rupert, B.C.
Noble said she does most of her banking online, but visits the brick-and-mortar building monthly to pick up cash. She said she plans to drive to Oakridge, but said it is not ideal.
"It's the stress of driving. The traffic is so heavy and there's a lot of construction in London to go anywhere," she said. "For an older person, I don't think that's healthy."
She said she's more worried about her future.
"If it came to the point where I couldn't drive anymore, then I don't know how I'm going to do my banking at TD" she said.

Other seniors told CBC News they're unsure how they will get to the new branch. Some are considering switching to Scotiabank, which is located inside Cherryhill Mall. Vicencio said that option doesn't make sense for her.
"It's so complicated to change banks. You have all your accounts and a payment schedule. It's big work to do that," she said.
Both Noble and Vicencio said they hope TD at least puts a bank machine inside Cherryhill Village mall so they can continue to withdraw cash close to home.

In an emailed statement to CBC News, TD spokesperson Natasha Ferrari said the decision to close the Platt's Lane location was made as the building's lease came to an end and the company reviewed client demand.

"Following a detailed review of client activity patterns, number of transactions and accessibility, we determined that Oakridge is well positioned to serve our clients' needs," Ferrari said.

She said the Oakridge branch offers the same services and hours of operation as Platt's Lane, with enhanced staffing levels.

Vicencio said her concern is not about the quality of service, but how she will get to the new branch.

"Transit is fine, but then you have to be there on a schedule. You do your banking, then you have to wait for the transport to bring you back. That's a whole day of activity. Here, people can come do their banking and go home."

Vicencio has been a TD customer at the Platt's Lane branch for 22 years, ever since she moved to the Cherryhill neighbourhood from Vancouver.

She walks from her residence to the bank every two weeks. She keeps a safety deposit box there and prefers to do all of her banking in-person.

"If you have questions, a person can answer to you," Vicencio said. "I think the problem is that they assume everybody uses a computer. Most seniors cannot."

Vicencio said she doesn't yet have a plan for how she'll get to her new branch, adding that she prefers not to drive at this point in her life and that transit is not convenient.

"If it's too difficult, maybe I'll have to stop going to the bank."

Betty Noble said she's been a TD customer since the 1970s, and has been at the Platt's Lane branch for about 14 years. It takes her less than 10 minutes to walk to the bank, and she often builds it into her day's routine.

"I was very taken back that they were proposing to move or close down," said Noble, who lives in the Cherryhill area.

Another N.B. town will lose its only bank, leaving residents ‘devastated’

BMO branch closure brings anxiety for some seniors in Prince Rupert, B.C.

Noble said she does most of her banking online, but visits the brick-and-mortar building monthly to pick up cash. She said she plans to drive to Oakridge, but said it is not ideal.

"It's the stress of driving. The traffic is so heavy and there's a lot of construction in London to go anywhere," she said. "For an older person, I don't think that's healthy."

She said she's more worried about her future.

"If it came to the point where I couldn't drive anymore, then I don't know how I'm going to do my banking at TD" she said.

Other seniors told CBC News they're unsure how they will get to the new branch. Some are considering switching to Scotiabank, which is located inside Cherryhill Mall. Vicencio said that option doesn't make sense for her.

"It's so complicated to change banks. You have all your accounts and a payment schedule. It's big work to do that," she said.

Both Noble and Vicencio said they hope TD at least puts a bank machine inside Cherryhill Village mall so they can continue to withdraw cash close to home.

stories.title: Competition Bureau, Empire reach deal on grocer’s property control commitments
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Competition Bureau says it has reached a deal with Empire Co. Ltd. regarding its use of property controls, formalizing commitments made by the grocer earlier this year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
People enter a FreshCo store in Mission, B.C. on Thursday, April 25, 2019. THE Canadian Press/Jonathan Hayward THE Canadian Press

By The Canadian Press

Posted September 22, 2026 12:13 pm.

Last Updated September 22, 2026 1:38 pm.

Ottawa — The competition watchdog says Sobeys’ parent company Empire Co. Ltd. has formalized its commitment to winding down property controls, which can limit rival grocers from setting up shop nearby.

The Competition Bureau said Tuesday the grocer has agreed to officially stop using so-called restrictive covenants, which many retailers have used to prevent rivals from opening a store on their former site after moving away.

Empire is the parent company of multiple grocery banners including Sobeys, Safeway, IGA, Foodland and FreshCo.

Under a consent agreement registered with the Competition Tribunal, Empire will no longer use or enforce land restrictions. It will also limit its use of exclusivity clauses, which prohibit landlords from leasing space to another tenant that competes with an existing tenant.

The commitments will be legally binding and enforceable, the bureau said.

Empire spokesperson Sarah Dawson said the grocer is pleased to have “resolved the matter of property controls with the Competition Bureau.”

Empire pledged in July to stop using such measures, shortly after the competition watchdog broadened its probe into Empire’s use of property controls countrywide through a Federal Court order.

The court order granted the bureau access to additional information at a national level, such as how the grocer negotiates property controls and their effects on competition.

Property controls have drawn attention from regulators, politicians and the public in recent years as high food prices have increased scrutiny of competition in the grocery industry.

The Competition Bureau began investigating various grocers for their use of property controls in 2024, after a report on the sector described property controls as a tool that retailers May be using to curb competition in local markets across Canada.

Some major grocers, including Walmart Canada and Loblaw Cos. Ltd., have previously pledged to axe property controls relating to retail competition.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Jim Balsillie’s food bank donation spurred by soaring demand in prosperous Waterloo region
stories.summary: Tech executive-turned-philanthropist announces $1.5-million gift, plus $1-million each to Cambridge, Fergus and Guelph
stories.author: Olivia Grandy
stories.content:
In the past decade, the Food Bank of Waterloo Region has undergone a drastic transformation: The number of staff has more than doubled to 54, the storage square footage has shot up to accommodate millions of pounds of food annually and the trucks that transport that food have gotten even larger.

Although based in one of Canada’s most prosperous regions, the food bank’s growth has been a response to a surge in demand for emergency food support.

Data released last year from the Kitchener, Ont.-based food bank, which serves dozens of smaller agencies in the area, found that food hamper visits, the largest regular program the bank runs with its partners, were up by 205 per cent since 2019. That translated to more than 621,000 visits between July, 2024, and July, 2025, the highest recorded number ever.

Tech executive-turned-philanthropist Jim Balsillie has taken notice. On Tuesday, he announced a donation of $1.5-million to the Food Bank of Waterloo Region as well as $1-million each to other Ontario food banks in Cambridge, Fergus and Guelph.

Mr. Balsillie, who has been vocal about Canada lagging behind the U.S. in gross domestic product per capita , is the former co-CEO of Research in Motion, the company famous for creating BlackBerry mobile devices, which helped put the Waterloo-Kitchener corridor on the map as an innovation and academic hub.

“The prosperity doesn’t spread uniformly,” Mr. Balsillie said.

The food bank’s chief executive, Kim Wilhelm, said growing food bank demand is a reflection of the overall high cost of living that those in her community are facing, including rising housing costs, which have become especially challenging for those with unstable employment. As wages have not kept up with inflation, food is increasingly becoming a discretionary item for many Canadians, she said.

This year, her organization’s budget for food purchases is more than $3-million, compared to about $200,000 before the pandemic.

“We are a high-tech community,” said Ms. Wilhelm. Yet, those who rely on food support come from all backgrounds, she said.

She believes the rising need is an economic warning sign that Canada should no longer treat the issue of hunger as charity.

“While we’re so deeply grateful for the investment, philanthropy alone cannot solve food insecurity,” she said.

Mr. Balsillie is also a proponent of policy changes to address the challenge. However, the urgent “here and now” compelled him to take action, he said.

Opinion: Canada’s new Food Security Strategy won’t end food insecurity

The philanthropist, who has previously made large donations to Wilfrid Laurier University and the University of Waterloo, said he began anonymously contributing to food banks after the initial economic shock of the pandemic.

Now, he hopes the public gift will inspire people to learn more about this issue as many food banks are facing a harsh choice: Expand or leave those seeking the necessities to feed their families empty-handed and hungry.

“At the end of the day, people still need to eat, and if they have to choose between rent and food, somehow some kind of support’s got to come,” he said.

The rise in demand signals that pay cheques are not keeping up with the cost of living, Mr. Balsillie said. “That’s a natural consequence of inattention to these issues.”

The entrepreneur often speaks about the importance of nations owning their intangible assets, such as intellectual-property and data, to thrive in today’s global economy. He argues that Canada didn’t take advantage of the shift in value from tangible to intangible assets, resulting in a relatively lower GDP per-capita. Mr. Balsillie has stated that poverty and food insecurity are outcomes of this.

On the potential for the federal government to reverse course on patterns that put food out of reach for Canadians, Mr. Balsillie sounded somewhat optimistic. “Maybe we’ll see the pressure on this food insecurity ease up because we’re paying attention to prosperity drivers.”

For the Food Bank of Waterloo Region, Mr. Balsillie’s gift will act as a bridge through a transitional period where the food bank is working at capacity, while also looking for a new building to call home. Currently, the food bank is leaning on some off-site storage to manage the overflow.

“What’s especially meaningful is that it allows us to think beyond our immediate needs and help us plan for the future,” Ms. Wilhelm said.

The money will also help the Guelph Food Bank process more local food, the Cambridge Food Bank complete its new facility and the Centre Wellington Food Bank, located in Fergus, expand its network.

Mr. Balsillie is confident he will see the value of his investment come to fruition, adding that food bank operators are lean, hard-working and adaptive.

“The demand for what they do is growing, but, my goodness, do they put your money to good use.”

stories.title: No ‘blanket answer’ on when Ottawa would end strikes under proposed changes, Hajdu says
stories.summary: Canadian Labour Congress argues proposed changes to Section 107 would weaken the position of workers in collective bargaining
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
The federal jobs minister says she can’t give a “blanket answer” on when the federal government would move to end a strike or lockout under the new labour legislation tabled Monday.

According to the proposed Building Canada Strong Act, a work stoppage must be affecting the “national interest” before the minister can trigger Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end a labour disruption.

The existing tool allows a minister to refer two deadlocked parties to the Canada Industrial Relations Board to declare an impasse, end the work stoppage and move talks into binding arbitration.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu said in an interview there’s no set timeline for federal government intervention in a strike affecting a critical industry.

“It is a high bar to establish a national interest,” she said. “What I would say is that each strike in each industry is different and so it’s very hard to answer that with a blanket answer.”

Labour code changes will threaten workers’ right to strike, unions warn

The federal government has leaned on Section 107 in recent years to end walkouts at Canada Post, the CN and Cpkc railways, and at the B.C. and Montreal ports. Air Canada flight attendants defied an attempt to use the measure to end their strike in 2025.

The Canadian Labour Congress argues the proposed changes to Section 107 would weaken the position of workers in collective bargaining.

The organization plans to respond to the government’s proposals in a press conference on Tuesday.

Hajdu said strikes could still happen under the proposed legislation and acknowledged the point of a work stoppage is to inflict economic pressure in a labour dispute.

But she said that pressure can mount quickly when, for example, a work stoppage hits the transportation sector and puts perishable goods at risk. She said the government will be evaluating each strike individually.

Other proposed changes to the labour code include the introduction of a special mediator to publish a report outlining both sides’ positions in an impasse. The act would also require pre-emptive relationship repair work with the federal mediation service in cases where there has been a history of acrimony between the union and employer.

Hajdu said these changes are intended to reduce the number of work stoppages by boosting transparency and reducing “bad blood” between the parties.

“Hopefully, this sharpens both employers’ minds and unions’ minds to the task at hand, which is to really, really get that deal,” she said.

According to the proposed Building Canada Strong Act, a work stoppage must be affecting the “national interest” before the minister can trigger Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end a labour disruption.
The existing tool allows a minister to refer two deadlocked parties to the Canada Industrial Relations Board to declare an impasse, end the work stoppage and move talks into binding arbitration.
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu said in an interview there’s no set timeline for federal government intervention in a strike affecting a critical industry.
“It is a high bar to establish a national interest,” she said. “What I would say is that each strike in each industry is different and so it’s very hard to answer that with a blanket answer.”
