stories.title: Quebec election campaign enters 27th day as final debate nears
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec's party leaders are expected to be back out on the campaign trail today, with less than two weeks to go before the provincial election vote.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - With less than two weeks to go in the Quebec election campaign, party leaders are gearing up for a third and final debate that could see Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon at the centre of attention.

“Everyone is taking aim at the Parti Québécois,” said André Lamoureux, political scientist and professor at Université du Québec à Montréal.

The Radio-Canada debate on Wednesday will be the last opportunity for leaders to spar before the vote on Oct. 5. They met twice already on the debate stage last week.

But in the last few days, Lamoureux has noted how the PQ has become a frequent target of attacks by other parties, with public opinion polls suggesting it is leading in the campaign.

But the political analyst noted how some of the criticism can backfire.

For example, last week, when Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said that 70 per cent of Quebecers did not want a referendum, St-Pierre Plamondon responded by saying that 80 per cent of the province did not want the Quebec Liberals in government.

“That’s what I’m looking forward to seeing. Will it be effective against the Parti Québécois? Or will Paul St-Pierre Plamondon take those attacks and redirect them with even more efficiency?” he said.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette is struggling to position her party as an alternative to the Parti Québecois, said Lamoureux. He noted how she is also trying to distance herself from the track record of her predecessor, François Legault who led the province as premier for close to eight years.

“Quebecers don’t trust this party,” he said.

Lamoureux expects Fréchette to try to regain momentum in this last debate.

“She is going to try to give it her all. That’s where we’ll see if her leadership … can give mass appeal to her message and turn the tide,” he said.

Anne-Marie Gingras, retired political science professor, still expects a close battle between the Coalition Avenir Québec and the Parti Québécois in many ridings, while also warning that some voters are tuning out.

“People don’t know where to turn to find a solution. And that is at the core of the Coalition Avenir Québec’s decline over the last few days, because (people feel like) everything is going wrong,” she said.

She also said the Coalition Avenir Québec has not managed to get voters to focus on any of its achievements while in government.

“With everything that has happened over the past eight years, there have been successes and there have been mistakes, but the successes aren’t really being highlighted,” she said.

The Quebec Liberal Party is currently the official Opposition, but its support is concentrated in urban ridings in Montreal and the English-speaking community, and Lamoureux said he does not expect them to make headway among French-speaking voters.

“For francophones, right now, the Quebec Liberal Party is going through the worst period in its history,” he said.

Lamoureux described the Conservative party as a “surprise” and May win seats in the election, he said, which would be a first in its history.

At the last general elections, the conservatives won close to 13 per cent of the popular vote but elected no candidates. Before the legislature dissolved, the Conservatives had one member who had crossed the floor from the Coalition Avenir Québec.

Lamoureux sees Québec solidaire as failing to convince voters of their message and losing support with francophone voters.

The party leaders have faced questions in recent days about potential alliances if no party succeeds in forming a majority.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Monday that an alliance was out of the question, after his rivals suggested his ideas are similar to those of Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Trump to address UN General Assembly as Carney becomes voice of multilateralism
stories.summary: United Nations - U.S. President Donald Trump is set to address the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, despite his administration's efforts to undermine multilateralism and to target allies with threats and tariffs.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
United Nations - U.S. President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday he has a choice to make on Iran: negotiate a deal or “annihilate the Islamic Republic.”

In a wide-ranging speech, Trump defended his war on Iran and boasted of American strength, claiming that “while others have talked, I have acted.”

He celebrated the U.S. military operation to oust Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year and a new agreement to expand the American military presence in Greenland, which came after his threats of annexation.

But those actions have upended U.S. relationships with other nations, including traditional allies. Many of those allies have used the United Nations forum to call for a return to international law.

This 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly is taking place as the world grapples with oil supply shocks and rising prices driven by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and under the shadow of Trump’s constant attacks on multilateralism.

Canada, like most countries, has not been able to escape the geopolitical effects of Trump’s erratic deployment of military force and tariffs.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said one of the shared challenges of the moment is a multilateral system that doesn’t reflect the times and cannot respond to them.

“But at the same time, the need for multilateral co-operation is very much alive,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday.

Carney — who has emerged in recent weeks as a key global champion of multilateralism and alliances in the face of Trump’s repeated attacks — said no one country, no matter how powerful, can manage the world’s challenges alone.

“Co-operation, therefore, is not an act of idealism. It is a practical necessity,” he said. “And the question is not whether multilateralism can survive but how it must evolve to meet the challenges of the moment.”

Trump has demanded massive reforms at the UN and has held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil. The Trump administration has withdrawn from multiple UN organizations, including the World Health Organization.

Carney, meanwhile, has been making the case for continued global collaboration to address crises like climate change, financial instability and war.

For nearly a year now, Carney has been travelling the globe calling on middle powers to band together in defence of what he has called “shared interests, and occasionally shared values, rather than shared institutions.”

Carney has sought to build a bridge between the European Union and a Pacific Rim trading bloc called Cptpp so middle powers can better resist economic coercion by the United States and China.

The prime minister’s efforts have caught the attention of the Trump administration, especially since trade negotiations between Canada and the United States ended acrimoniously last month.

After European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last week opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the European Union, Trump said it could be a “hostile act.”

Carney did not hold any official meetings with Trump or members of the U.S. administration while in New York this week — his first return to the United States since trade negotiations fell apart last month.

The prime minister said during a gathering of global leaders “it’s most valuable to meet those who you don’t normally see.”

Carney held bilateral meetings with Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast and Angola President Joao Lourenco on the sidelines of the assembly. He also met with King of Jordan Abdullah II and a delegation from the United Arab Emirates.

Earlier Tuesday, Carney was quickly greeted by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese when he arrived for the opening of the General Assembly. He also walked across the floor to speak with Crown Prince of the State of Kuwait Sabah Al-Khalid Al-Sabah before formal speeches began.

Carney co-hosted with France and the United Kingdom an event on the two-state solution — one year after the three countries recognized an independent Palestinian state at the General Assembly. More than 150 countries followed the move to recognize Palestinian statehood.

At the General Assembly last year, Trump said recognizing a Palestinian state would amount to rewarding Hamas for the “horrible atrocities” of the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Trump also claimed the move could hinder Canada’s ability to make a trade deal with the United States.

Canada and the United States now seem further than ever from reaching that deal. Bilateral relations have continued to deteriorate as the trade war has escalated.

Trump, meanwhile, partially walked back remarks he’d made on social media about getting potash from Belarus instead of Canada. During a bilateral meeting on Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said “we’ll continue to go with Canada (for potash), but Belarus would like to sell it for a much lower price.”

Asked about Trump’s change of tone, Carney said “the Canadian potash industry is one of admiration.”

“I think that there is a real opportunity, if we so choose, and it’s one of many, many opportunities that Canada and the United States have to co-operate and to become fertilizer-independent,” Carney said.

“Not just potash, but across all ammonia and other fertilizers. That would be good for Canadian farmers, it would be great for American farmers.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Trump defends Iran war in address to UN General Assembly
stories.summary: United Nations — U.S. President Donald Trump defended his war against Iran before the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, claiming that "while others have talked, I have acted.”
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
United Nations — U.S. President Donald Trump defended his war against Iran before the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, claiming that “while others have talked, I have acted.”

“While others have promised strength, I have used it to make America the most powerful country in the world,” Trump said in his speech.

The theme of the General Assembly this year is “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.”

It’s taking place as the world grapples with oil supply shocks and rising prices driven by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and under the shadow of Trump’s constant attacks on multilateralism.

Prime Minister Mark Carney — who has emerged in recent weeks as a key global defender of multilateralism and alliances in the face of Trump’s repeated attacks — arrived Tuesday morning for the opening of the General Assembly, where he was quickly greeted by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Carney, who is not addressing the assembly, also walked across the floor to speak with Crown Prince of the State of Kuwait Sabah Al-Khalid Al-Sabah before formal speeches began.

Trump has demanded massive reforms at the UN and has held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil. The Trump administration has withdrawn from multiple UN organizations, including the World Health Organization and the cultural agency Unesco.

Carney, meanwhile, has been making the case for continued global collaboration to address crises like climate change, financial instability and war.

For nearly a year now, Carney has been travelling the globe calling on middle powers to band together in defence of what he has called “shared interests, and occasionally shared values, rather than shared institutions.”

Carney has sought to build a bridge between the European Union and a Pacific Rim trading bloc called Cptpp so middle powers can better resist economic coercion by the United States and China.

The prime minister’s efforts have caught the attention of the Trump administration, especially since trade negotiations ended acrimoniously last month.

After European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last week opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the European Union, Trump said it could be a “hostile act.”

stories.title: Angine de Poitrine among 10 Canadian acts vying for $30,000 Polaris Music Prize
stories.summary: Toronto — A mysterious Quebec rock duo that's gained worldwide fame over the past year is among the acts competing tonight for the prestigious Polaris Music Prize.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Rock duo Angine de Poitrine perform at The Mod Club in Toronto on Tuesday, July 14, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Arlyn McAdorey

By Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

Posted September 22, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 22, 2026 7:13 am.

Toronto — A mysterious Quebec rock duo that’s gained worldwide fame over the past year is among the acts competing tonight for the prestigious Polaris Music Prize.

Angine de Poitrine, the masked musicians known for their microtonal sound with Klek on drums and Khn playing a double-necked guitar, are also performing tonight at a gala at Toronto’s Massey Hall.

Another prominent artist up for the $30,000 award is folk singer Charlotte Cornfield with her sixth album “Hurts Like Hell,” which explores themes of personal growth and renewal.

And there’s singer-songwriter Beverly Glenn-Copeland, nominated for the album “Laughter in Summer,” which was recorded with his wife and longtime collaborator Elizabeth Copeland and blends new music with reimagined old songs.

A change to the voting process means this year’s winner will be picked by about 200 music industry experts instead of an 11-person jury, as was the case in previous years.

The contenders are still evaluated based on artistic merit, without regard to commercial popularity or genre.

Also among the nominees are Halifax R&B and soul artist Aquakultre, Winnipeg alt-pop singer-songwriter Begonia, Montreal indie pop duo Bibi Club, and Toronto-born electronic rocker Peaches.

Rounding out the contenders are Nunavut-raised throat singer and 2014 Polaris winner Tanya Tagaq, Toronto-raised R&B and electronic-dance artist Rochelle Jordan and Montreal-based indie artist Les Louanges.

Eight of the 10 nominees are set to perform at the gala hosted by musician and broadcaster Odario Williams. Two-time Polaris winner Jeremy Dutcher will be a special guest presenter.

Organizers will also hand out a $10,000 Polaris Song Prize, with the winner to be revealed shortly before the album of the year prize.

Last year’s Polaris Music Prize went to Montreal-based rocker Yves Jarvis for his album “All Cylinders” while Toronto-born folk artist Mustafa took home the song prize for “Gaza is Calling.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 22, 2026.

Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

Public Service Announcement

[](http://london.ca/newsroom/public-service-announcement/fall-love-forest-city-season)

Tuesday, September 22, 2026

The City of London is excited to bring back the much-loved fall tradition, Fall in Love with the Forest City! We are once again opening our doors and inviting Londoners to City Hall’s top floor observation deck at no cost. Starting Thursday, September 24 until Sunday, October 25, join us and take in a view of the forest city as we welcome in the fall colours.

While taking in the views from the Top of the Hall, guests are invited to enjoy seasonal treats and hot drinks available by donation. All proceeds will go towards this year’s United Way Elgin Middlesex campaign on behalf of the City of London. Last year’s donations totalled over $4,000!

The observation deck will be accessible to the public from September 24 to October 25, 2026 during the following times:

Thursdays and Fridays from 5 p.m. to sunset

Saturdays and Sundays from 12 p.m. to 4 p.m.

The observation deck will be closed on Sunday, October 11

For more information, please visit london.ca/FallintheForestCity.

Tuesday, September 22, 2026

The City of London is excited to bring back the much-loved fall tradition, Fall in Love with the Forest City! We are once again opening our doors and inviting Londoners to City Hall’s top floor observation deck at no cost. Starting Thursday, September 24 until Sunday, October 25, join us and take in a view of the forest city as we welcome in the fall colours.

While taking in the views from the Top of the Hall, guests are invited to enjoy seasonal treats and hot drinks available by donation. All proceeds will go towards this year’s United Way Elgin Middlesex campaign on behalf of the City of London. Last year’s donations totalled over $4,000!
The observation deck will be accessible to the public from September 24 to October 25, 2026 during the following times:
Thursdays and Fridays from 5 p.m. to sunset
Saturdays and Sundays from 12 p.m. to 4 p.m.
The observation deck will be closed on Sunday, October 11
For more information, please visit london.ca/FallintheForestCity.

stories.title: Fatal motor vehicle collision
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (September 22, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Frontline Division and Road Safety Section are investigating a serious motor vehicle collision that took place yesterday in the city’s northwest end.

On Monday, September 21, 2026, at approximately 8 p.m., emergency crews responded to a collision involving a motorcycle and a motor vehicle in the area of Sarnia Road and Castlegrove Boulevard. Roads in the area were closed while emergency crews were on scene and have since reopened.

The motorcyclist was transported to hospital by paramedic services with critical injuries and has since succumbed to those injuries.

All involved drivers remained on scene.

The investigation has been reassigned to members of the London Police Service Road Safety Section and remains ongoing.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area on Monday, September 21, 2026, between 7:45 p.m. – 8:20 p.m., and May have witnessed the collision, or who has dashcam, residential, or business surveillance footage, to please contact the London Police Service.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Ice unit investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (September 22, 2026) – A London man was arrested late last week by members of the London Police Service (LPS) Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit in relation to possession of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem).
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (September 22, 2026)– A London man was arrested late last week by members of the London Police Service (LPS) Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit in relation to possession of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem).

In March of 2025, LPS members commenced an investigation after the RCMP National Child Exploitation Crime Centre (Ncecc) made them aware of information involving a London man.

On Friday, September 18, 2026, a search warrant was executed at a residence near Monsarrat Avenue and Delphi Road.

A suspect male was arrested, and electronic devices were seized. Evidence of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem) was located.

As a result of the investigation, Kole West, 27, of London, has been charged with one count of possess child sexual abuse and exploitation material.

The accused was released from custody and is scheduled to appear in London court on December 17, 2026, in relation to the charges.

London Police Service is a member of the Provincial Strategy to Protect Children from Sexual Abuse and Exploitation on the Internet. The Strategy has been made possible by a grant from the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously toLondon Middlesex Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Family remembers Darius MacDougall one year after disappearance
stories.summary: A year after his disappearance, the family of Darius MacDougall still returns to the campsite where he was last seen, hoping answers will one day come to light.
stories.author: Justin Sibbet
stories.content:
On Sept. 21, 2025, six-year-old Darius MacDougall vanished from a public camping area near the Alberta-British Columbia border in the Crowsnest Pass.

Almost at once, police, search and rescue crews and other first responders began a full-scale search of the mountainous terrain in an effort to find Darius.

Now, one year later, with no answers, Darius’ family has returned to that camping spot, holding out hope that he is still out there, somewhere.

“Darius, we still love you, miss you. We’re never going to stop searching for you, buddy,” said Leslie Tallmadge, Darius’ grandfather. “I come here and I walk and I look, (I’d) look anywhere for you.”

The search effort was extensive, with drones, dogs, helicopters and hundreds of crew members, including specialized teams such as underwater divers, all taking part in the hopes of finding Darius.

After more than a week, RCMP called the search off.

On Monday, one year after Darius went missing, officers released a statement saying they haven’t stopped their investigation.

“The Alberta RCMP recognizes that Darius’ disappearance continues to weigh heavily on his family and those who know and love him. The passage of time does not lessen the importance of finding answers, and investigators remain committed to pursuing information that May help bring clarity to what happened to Darius.”

They say investigators remain focused on reviewing information, pursuing viable leads and identifying any information that May help provide answers about Darius’ disappearance.

“To date, RCMP has received just over 70 tips from the public regarding this investigation, and every tip was fully investigated. Unfortunately, none have led to finding Darius. However, we will continue to investigate.”

For Darius’ family, the concern is that he was never lost in the mountains, but kidnapped instead.

“Somebody had to have taken him. There’s just been too many people out here, too many searches not to find anything. To me, somebody as come and taken him,” said Tina Herron, Darius’ grandmother.

Tallmadge agrees, believing search crews exhausting all efforts should have yielded results.

“11 days straight with 200 plus searchers every day — there’s no way we missed anything,” said Tallmadge.

At the time, RCMP said there was no evidence of a kidnapping and an Amber Alert was never issued, something that has never sat well with Herron.

“No matter who it is, it’s a child. They should have an Amber Alert, whether it meets the criteria or not, he should have it.”

A few days after Darius went missing, a Change.org petition was started to change how Amber Alerts are issued.

As of Monday, it has more than 20,000 signatures.

Darius would be seven years old now and his family is still urging anyone with any information to contact RCMP.

“If you see something or you know something, call the police. He’s out there somewhere. If you see him, call the police,” said Tallmadge.

RCMP have the same public message.

“The Alberta RCMP continues to encourage anyone who May have information about Darius’ disappearance or whereabouts to come forward. You can contact the Crowsnest Pass RCMP at 403-562-2866. Information that May seem insignificant could be important to the investigation, and investigators will assess any new information provided.”

On Tuesday evening, a candlelight vigil will be held at Lethbridge City Hall to bring greater awareness to the ongoing search efforts for Darius MacDougall.

stories.title: RCMP has pulled resources from Air India bombing investigation, victims’ families say
stories.summary: Only one person was ever convicted in connection with the 1985 terrorist attack, which remains the deadliest in Canadian history
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
The head of the group that represents the families of the victims of the 1985 Air India bombing says the RCMP has pulled back resources dedicated to investigating the deadliest terrorist attack in Canadian history.

Deepak Khandelwal, whose two siblings, Chandra and Manju, died in the bombing, said the RCMP told victims’ families in a Sept. 12 meeting in Toronto that investigators had exhausted all angles, and the investigation is considered “inactive.”

Only one person was ever convicted in connection with the bombing, bomb maker Inderjit Singh Reyat, who pleaded guilty to manslaughter in 2003. Trials for two British Columbia men allegedly tied to the explosion ended in acquittals.

Families of Air India victims still waiting for Ottawa to release the wreckage

Mr. Khandelwal said in an interview that he is “disappointed, angry, upset.”

“But not surprised, because they have let us down for 41 years, and this is just the next step in it.”

Federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said in a statement to The Globe and Mail that the RCMP have told Ottawa that the investigation “remains open.”

“This is not a closed matter. Should new, credible information or evidence come forward, it will be assessed and investigated and May lead to further investigative steps,” Mr. Anandasangaree said. His office did not immediately respond to follow-up questions asking for specifics on what resources remain actively committed to the investigation.

The RCMP did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Khandelwal was a first-year university student from Saskatoon when he flew across the Atlantic with his father to identify the bodies of his older sisters. He is now head of the Air India Flight 182 Victims Families Association. “They don’t close a file, but inactive means there’s no resources assigned to it,” he said of the RCMP.

Since the meeting with police earlier this month, families of some victims have sent letters to Prime Minister Mark Carney and the RCMP accusing investigators of failing to look into every possibility.

Sudha Berry, whose 16-year-old brother was killed on the flight, wrote in her letter to Mr. Carney and the RCMP that the trust victims’ families placed in Canadian institutions has been “betrayed repeatedly.”

“While we acknowledge that there are many activities that you undertake that we will never be aware of and that there are many dedicated officers who have devoted their careers to the investigation, the fact remains that the results have been less than satisfactory,” Ms. Berry wrote.

It has been more than 41 years since Air India Flight 182 departed Montreal’s international airport en route to Delhi and was destroyed by a bomb in midair as it flew near the coast of Ireland. All 329 passengers, most of them Canadian, were killed in the June 23, 1985, bombing.

Authorities believe Sikh extremists fighting for independence from India planted the bomb on the plane, which crashed in the Atlantic Ocean near Ireland’s southern coast.

Four decades later, police say suspect known as ‘Mr. X’ in 1985 Air India bombing is dead

A public inquiry into the subsequent investigation found “a cascading series of errors” by the RCMP, Csis and the federal government, according to the inquiry’s 2010 final report.

Recently, families of victims have been waiting for Ottawa to release the scattered pieces of airplane fuselage from storage in B.C., held under lock-and-key because of the investigation.

Many of the families living in Canada have received the belongings of victims that were collected in the wreckage, Mr. Khandelwal said. But only some of the families in the U.S. and India have received the belongings of their loved ones, he said.

Mr. Khandelwal said he and the families were blindsided by the RCMP’s decision. The RCMP’s invitation to the Sept. 12 meeting, reviewed by The Globe, said it would be providing an update on the status of the investigation, “including an outline of future steps.”

The RCMP’s communication with families in recent years has slowed to a drip, Mr. Khandelwal said.

He said families requested a meeting with RCMP investigators in June 2025 when, days before the attack’s 40th anniversary, Mounties told media that a suspect known as “Mr. X” had died before facing charges . RCMP said the individual was believed to have helped test a bomb before the attack.

Mr. Khandelwal said families learned of the revelations through media reports and requested a meeting shortly after. He said the meeting didn’t happen until the RCMP summoned families for the update earlier this month in Toronto.

His message to the RCMP is simple: continue the investigation.

“I just think they need to keep the investigation going. They need to be transparent with the family members in whatever confidential way, and they have to commit to being a little bit more regular in communicating with families,” he said.

The RCMP did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Khandelwal was a first-year university student from Saskatoon when he flew across the Atlantic with his father to identify the bodies of his older sisters. He is now head of the Air India Flight 182 Victims Families Association. “They don’t close a file, but inactive means there’s no resources assigned to it,” he said of the RCMP.

Since the meeting with police earlier this month, families of some victims have sent letters to Prime Minister Mark Carney and the RCMP accusing investigators of failing to look into every possibility.

Sudha Berry, whose 16-year-old brother was killed on the flight, wrote in her letter to Mr. Carney and the RCMP that the trust victims’ families placed in Canadian institutions has been “betrayed repeatedly.”

“While we acknowledge that there are many activities that you undertake that we will never be aware of and that there are many dedicated officers who have devoted their careers to the investigation, the fact remains that the results have been less than satisfactory,” Ms. Berry wrote.

It has been more than 41 years since Air India Flight 182 departed Montreal’s international airport en route to Delhi and was destroyed by a bomb in midair as it flew near the coast of Ireland. All 329 passengers, most of them Canadian, were killed in the June 23, 1985, bombing.
Authorities believe Sikh extremists fighting for independence from India planted the bomb on the plane, which crashed in the Atlantic Ocean near Ireland’s southern coast.
Four decades later, police say suspect known as ‘Mr. X’ in 1985 Air India bombing is dead
A public inquiry into the subsequent investigation found “a cascading series of errors” by the RCMP, Csis and the federal government, according to the inquiry’s 2010 final report.
Recently, families of victims have been waiting for Ottawa to release the scattered pieces of airplane fuselage from storage in B.C., held under lock-and-key because of the investigation.

Many of the families living in Canada have received the belongings of victims that were collected in the wreckage, Mr. Khandelwal said. But only some of the families in the U.S. and India have received the belongings of their loved ones, he said.

Mr. Khandelwal said he and the families were blindsided by the RCMP’s decision. The RCMP’s invitation to the Sept. 12 meeting, reviewed by The Globe, said it would be providing an update on the status of the investigation, “including an outline of future steps.”
The RCMP’s communication with families in recent years has slowed to a drip, Mr. Khandelwal said.

He said families requested a meeting with RCMP investigators in June 2025 when, days before the attack’s 40th anniversary, Mounties told media that a suspect known as “Mr. X” had died before facing charges . RCMP said the individual was believed to have helped test a bomb before the attack.

Mr. Khandelwal said families learned of the revelations through media reports and requested a meeting shortly after. He said the meeting didn’t happen until the RCMP summoned families for the update earlier this month in Toronto.
His message to the RCMP is simple: continue the investigation.

“I just think they need to keep the investigation going. They need to be transparent with the family members in whatever confidential way, and they have to commit to being a little bit more regular in communicating with families,” he said.

stories.title: BC Conservatives regroup as several ex-MLAs return to caucus in wake of leader’s resignation
stories.summary: Opposition party attempts to bolster its ranks ahead of possible snap election
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Some dissident MLAs are rejoining the BC Conservatives as the province’s Opposition attempts to bolster its ranks ahead of a possible snap election and just a day after its leader resigned.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s announcement Sunday that she was stepping down as leader because of “infighting” prompted the return of some party members who had left the caucus over her leadership. On Monday, the party announced that Scott McInnis, Trevor Halford, Claire Rattée, John Rustad and Linda Hepner are once again Conservatives.

Speculation that NDP Premier David Eby would call an election two years early dramatically ramped up last week. Mr. Eby has said he has warned Elections BC and his caucus to be “election ready” amid disruptions posed by the U.S. trade war.

His government has made a flurry of announcements in recent days, including last week pausing an expansion to the provincial sales tax and on Monday reversing an earlier halt to long-promised expanded services at Burnaby Hospital.

On Monday, Vancouver Mayor Ken Sim urged the NDP government not to call an early vote until after provincewide municipal elections on Oct. 17, which he said deserve the “full, undivided attention” of residents.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigns as B.C. Conservative leader after weeks of party turmoil

Mr. Rustad, who returned to the Conservatives Monday after being expelled from caucus last Friday, said they have had unity talks with CentreBC, a party of eight MLAs who were formerly Conservatives. He himself is a long-time MLA who led the Conservatives from a fringe party to within a hair of winning the previous provincial election in 2024 before being ousted as leader.

“The province cannot afford two opposition parties while [Premier] David Eby measures the timing of an election,” he said in a news release.

He stated the chances of a merger are high, but neither the Conservatives nor CentreBC would confirm any efforts to coalesce centre-right politicians into one party.

Mr. Rustad said he would not impose his vision on the renewed party, and he advised former BC Liberal premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell to follow his example. He identified both of them as among the ”players" trying to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and said they should realize that “their time is over.”

The caucus of B.C.’s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election after Ms. Findlay’s resignation, raising the prospect of the vote happening while the Opposition has no permanent leader.

Rustad invited back to B.C. Opposition after being expelled by ex-leader Findlay

Mr. Rustad said he accepted an offer to rejoin the Conservatives because he believes in Lorne Doerkson, their new interim leader. Mr. Doerkson was first elected to represent a riding in the Interior in 2020 for the BC Liberal Party, which later rebranded itself as BC United, before he crossed the floor to join the Conservatives and was re-elected in 2024.

Mr. Doerkson is expected to speak to reporters for his first time as party leader on Tuesday.

Ms. Findlay said Sunday that she would remain the Conservative candidate for a by-election this Saturday in Abbotsford-Mission. But a snap provincial election called before then would override that.

Her resignation as leader followed weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, with the defection or expulsion of 13 MLAs, including Mr. Rustad.

He said Monday that he asked Ms. Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was “emotion and frustration around the table.”

The next day, he said, he got a text from her expelling him, but 15 minutes later that was rescinded. On Friday, he was once again told he was out.

B.C. NDP caucus meets to discuss potential early election after Findlay resignation

Ms. Findlay’s departure prompted the NDP caucus to meet on Sunday night, according to an e-mail from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators on Sunday, instead of just those on the government benches.

“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the e-mail obtained by The Canadian Press said.

The message said the meeting was to “discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Mr. Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

In a question-and-answer period with Union of BC Municipalities conference delegates after Mr. Eby’s keynote address last week, the Premier ducked questions about an early election call.

Conference delegates on Wednesday had passed an emergency resolution urging Mr. Eby to hold off on calling an election until after October’s municipal votes, to avoid interfering with local campaigns.

Gary Mason: Is David Eby about to gamble away his government?

Mr. Eby told the crowd he understood the anxiety that duelling elections could create and that he would take the resolution and its concerns seriously.

B.C. Attorney-General Niki Sharma was asked at an unrelated news conference Monday whether it was ethical to call an election with the Opposition in such disarray. She declined to answer the question directly after being asked twice.

“If the Premier decided to do an election call, he will do so by recommending that to the Lieutenant-Governor in accordance with our Constitution and all the laws,” she said.

Ross Pink, a professor of political science at Kwantlen Polytechnic University, said the Opposition should appoint a new leader as soon as possible, adding campaign debates have frequently catapulted lesser-known political leaders toward wider electoral victories.

The professor, who has run a mentorship program for the past five years pairing Kwantlen students with provincial and federal politicians for four-month stints, said Mr. Eby’s election calculus could reap huge rewards or backfire immensely.

“Politics really is always about opportunity and timing,” Prof. Pink said.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ontario to standardize trucker training after audit flagged widespread issues
stories.summary: Large trucks accounted for 12 per cent of all fatal collisions between 2019 and 2023, according to Auditor-General’s report
stories.author: Sara Mojtehedzadeh
stories.content:
The Ontario government says it will standardize commercial truck driver training in the wake of a scathing Auditor-General report that identified widespread issues with instruction and licensing in the province.

The province will work with industry stakeholders to develop a new curriculum aimed at strengthening road safety, Minister of Transportation Prabmeet Sarkaria said on Monday. But some representatives of the trucking industry say additional measures are required to address their concerns with training and oversight of commercial truck drivers.

The announcement follows a May report from provincial Auditor-General Shelley Spence, which found some private career colleges in Ontario were accrediting drivers without the minimum training requirements, and in some cases had altered student records to falsify their qualifications.

Trucking association calls for overhaul of commercial truck driving school inspections in Ontario

Currently, aspiring commercial truck drivers in Ontario must complete mandatory entry-level training, which consists of a minimum of 103.5 hours of instruction. Private career colleges must submit their curriculum details for approval to the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security to ensure they meet provincial standards.

The Transport Ministry said that under the new approach schools will be required to follow a standardized curriculum that will include “more than 103 hours of clear, robust and consistent training.” The plan is expected to be implemented by early 2027, after consultation with industry stakeholders.

While large trucks represent about 3 per cent of all vehicles on provincial roads, they accounted for 12 per cent of all fatal collisions between 2019 and 2023, Ms. Spence’s report noted. Truck driver violations in Ontario have also spiked in recent years. For example, between 2020 and 2024, the percentage of truck drivers found in violation of rules requiring them to keep daily vehicle inspection logs increased by 135 per cent.

It is not clear how the new curriculum proposals will differ from the province’s existing practices, but the province said it is considering additional training subjects such as fatigue management and rural driving.

Rolf VanderZwaag, one of the architects of Ontario’s mandatory entry-level training standards, which were implemented in 2017, said the essential driving skills program he helped develop is “effectively a standardized curriculum.”

“Most Ontario schools already use it,” said Mr. VanderZwaag, who is the CEO of Techni-Com Inc., which produces compliance and training products for the trucking industry.

Mike Millian, president of the Private Motor Truck Council of Canada, a national association representing companies with in-house commercial trucking fleets, said any improvement in training standards are welcome.

However, additional reforms are urgently needed to address industry’s concerns around training and oversight, he said.

“Having a standardized curriculum is not what our key issue is. Our key issue is people aren’t following the curriculums that they’re submitting,” he said.

Around one quarter of the 216 private colleges offering truck driver training in the province had never been inspected by the provincial colleges ministry, the report found – noting the ministry employed just eight inspectors to audit all 595 private colleges in Ontario.

As part of the research conducted for the May report, Ms. Spence’s office sent students undercover to five unnamed private colleges and found that some students were not taught the required elements of truck driving, including reverse parking and emergency stopping.

As previously reported by The Globe, industry groups have called on the province to overhaul training and licensing procedures, and for the Transport Ministry to take full carriage of the file from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities.

The Private Motor Truck Council of Canada has called for more inspections at private career colleges and heftier fines for those who fail to meet provincial training standards for truck drivers.

Currently, private career colleges face fines of between $250 and $1,000 for first offences, according to the Auditor-General report.

In its statement Monday, the Transport Ministry said it was introducing a dedicated integrity manager for truck driver testing across the province and weekly reviews of commercial driver training schools.

Alberta mulls restrictions on new truck drivers but industry groups urge caution

The Professional Truck Training Alliance of Canada (Pttac), which advocates for progress in education and training in the transportation sector, has also called for numerous reforms, including stricter screening of aspiring drivers’ criminal record and driver abstracts. The organization has also advocated for testing instructors to be equipped with body cameras as a fraud prevention tactic, and has called for dual-facing cameras to be required in training vehicles.

“We want to continue to see improvement, but at the end of the day, regulation and compliance without any enforcement falls on deaf ears,” said Kim Richardson, a senior adviser to Pttac.

The Private Motor Truck Council’s Mr. Millian said any improvements to the provincial curriculum must include more one-on-one training time for drivers.

“The key area that we see as an issue in the industry is people’s ability to back up the vehicle and operate the truck safely up and down the highway,” he said.

After completing entry-level training, aspiring drivers must take road exams at DriveTest centres. These are run by a third-party provider, Serco, for the Transport Ministry.

As previously reported by The Globe, five employees of driver-licensing centres in Ontario were also charged earlier this year with allegedly accepting bribes to manipulate the results of commercial truck-driving tests.

Mr. Millian says Serco’s Brampton, Ont. testing campus already employs two integrity officers to prevent cheating on road tests.

“We have seen some increases in enforcement, which is welcome,” he said. “But we need to go further.”

Around one quarter of the 216 private colleges offering truck driver training in the province had never been inspected by the provincial colleges ministry, the report found – noting the ministry employed just eight inspectors to audit all 595 private colleges in Ontario.

As part of the research conducted for the May report, Ms. Spence’s office sent students undercover to five unnamed private colleges and found that some students were not taught the required elements of truck driving, including reverse parking and emergency stopping.

As previously reported by The Globe, industry groups have called on the province to overhaul training and licensing procedures, and for the Transport Ministry to take full carriage of the file from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities.
The Private Motor Truck Council of Canada has called for more inspections at private career colleges and heftier fines for those who fail to meet provincial training standards for truck drivers.
Currently, private career colleges face fines of between $250 and $1,000 for first offences, according to the Auditor-General report.

In its statement Monday, the Transport Ministry said it was introducing a dedicated integrity manager for truck driver testing across the province and weekly reviews of commercial driver training schools.
Alberta mulls restrictions on new truck drivers but industry groups urge caution

The Professional Truck Training Alliance of Canada (Pttac), which advocates for progress in education and training in the transportation sector, has also called for numerous reforms, including stricter screening of aspiring drivers’ criminal record and driver abstracts. The organization has also advocated for testing instructors to be equipped with body cameras as a fraud prevention tactic, and has called for dual-facing cameras to be required in training vehicles.
“We want to continue to see improvement, but at the end of the day, regulation and compliance without any enforcement falls on deaf ears,” said Kim Richardson, a senior adviser to Pttac.
The Private Motor Truck Council’s Mr. Millian said any improvements to the provincial curriculum must include more one-on-one training time for drivers.
“The key area that we see as an issue in the industry is people’s ability to back up the vehicle and operate the truck safely up and down the highway,” he said.
After completing entry-level training, aspiring drivers must take road exams at DriveTest centres. These are run by a third-party provider, Serco, for the Transport Ministry.

As previously reported by The Globe, five employees of driver-licensing centres in Ontario were also charged earlier this year with allegedly accepting bribes to manipulate the results of commercial truck-driving tests.
Mr. Millian says Serco’s Brampton, Ont. testing campus already employs two integrity officers to prevent cheating on road tests.
“We have seen some increases in enforcement, which is welcome,” he said. “But we need to go further.”

stories.title: After Belleville, Ont., shooting, a look at recent violent incidents near synagogues
stories.summary: Ontario’s police watchdog is investigating after a 29-year-old man allegedly opened fire at a constable stationed outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Sunday night. The resulting shootout left both the suspect and the officer with serious injuries and sparked widespread condemnation from political leaders. Police have declined to comment on a possibl…
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario’s police watchdog is investigating after a 29-year-old man allegedly opened fire at a constable stationed outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Sunday night. The resulting shootout left both the suspect and the officer with serious injuries and sparked widespread condemnation from political leaders. Police have declined to comment on a possible motive in the attack.

Here are some other violent incidents that have taken place at or near Canadian synagogues and Jewish institutions in the last few years.

June 2026: Police are called for a fire at Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom in Westmount, Que., ON the island of Montreal. The synagogue’s rabbi said at the time the fire appeared to have been triggered by a Molotov cocktail tossed at a window. A 38-year-old man is arrested and was expected to face charges.

April and May 2026: A man in Toronto allegedly carries out two assaults against members of the Jewish community using a gel blaster imitation gun. One of the incidents takes place outside the Congregation Chasidei Bobov synagogue. The 18-year-old suspect is charged with assault with a weapon and possessing a weapon for a dangerous purpose.

March 2026: Two Toronto-area synagogues, the Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto synagogue in Vaughan, Ont., and Shaarei Shomayim synagogue in Toronto’s north end, are damaged by gunfire overnight. No injuries are reported. Over the following months, police arrest three suspects aged 17, 18 and 23 and charge them with several offences. York regional police said last month they are no longer seeking suspects, but the investigation is ongoing.

December 2024: A Montreal-area synagogue, Congregation Beth Tikvah in Dollard-des-Ormeaux, Que., is firebombed, causing minor damage to the building and the nearby offices of a Jewish community group. Months later, police arrest a 19-year-old man and charge him with arson and other offences.

December 2024: A Jewish girls’ school in Toronto’s north end is damaged in an overnight shooting. Police said the suspects were allegedly seen shooting from inside a vehicle before fleeing. They said Bais Chaya Mushka in North York had also been the target of two similar shootings in October and May of that year.

May 2024: The front door of the Schara Tzedeck synagogue in Vancouver is charred in an alleged arson. No one is injured.

May 2024: Bullet holes are found in the front of a Montreal building housing a Jewish school, Belz, and the Young Israel of Montreal synagogue.

November 2023: Montreal police find bullet holes in the door of the Yeshiva Gedola school and bullet casings on the ground. Police said a suspect had been seen firing a weapon at the school before taking off in a vehicle. A 20-year-old man is arrested months later and charged with offences including discharging a firearm and vehicle theft.

November 2023: The front door of the Congregation Beth Tikvah synagogue and the back door of the nearby Jewish organization Federation CJA office in a Montreal suburb are damaged in two overnight firebombings. The buildings were empty at the time.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Danielle Smith denies watering down government messaging on independence question
stories.summary: Alberta Premier disputes social media post by UCP president which claims she is trying to appear neutral
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Monday reiterated her position that the province should remain in Canada, even as her United Conservative Party grapples with an internal fight over separatism and a constituency association openly called for a leadership review.

On Monday, Ms. Smith disputed a social media post by UCP president Rob Smith, in which he claimed that she watered down the government’s messaging around the upcoming independence question in a bid to appear neutral.

On Oct. 19, Alberta voters will pick between two options: remain in Canada, or begin working toward holding a second, binding secession vote.

Ms. Smith made her comments days after the Ucp’s Highwood constituency association – her former riding – voted to challenge her leadership, with one prominent separatist citing the Premier’s pro-Canada position as the motivating factor.

“The fact of the matter is, you always do have alternative voices in every political party. You’ve got to listen to them, you’ve got to respect them – but in the end, we make decisions based on the things that we can agree on,” Ms. Smith said at an unrelated news conference.

The Alberta premier told a virtual assembly discussing the province's future in Canada that a lot of Albertans are angry, but it would be a mistake to separate now that progress is being made with Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sept. 19.

The Canadian Press

The Premier referenced Alberta’s long-standing grievances with Ottawa, but stood by her support for a “sovereign Alberta within a united Canada,” nodding to the Ucp’s founding principles that pledged a commitment to the federation. At a public forum on separation over the weekend, Ms. Smith choked back tears while recounting a historic list of frustrations with Ottawa.

“I’m not a neutral party, and I believe that we should remain, and I believe that we should do everything we can to address the things that are causing grievances,” she said on Monday.

Support for separation in Alberta, estimated to be between 25 and 30 per cent, has remained steady for years. But a large segment of UCP members, pegged by some pollsters to make up about half the party’s membership, support independence.

The Highwood constituency association’s vote is the first time since becoming UCP Leader in 2022 that Ms. Smith has faced formal dissatisfaction over her leadership from within party ranks. At her last leadership review in November, 2024, Ms. Smith received 91 per cent support from party members.

A leadership review would only be triggered if at least 21 of the party’s 87 constituency associations vote for holding a special meeting on Ms. Smith’s future.

Opinion: Danielle Smith is no separatist – she’s something even more dangerous

The Highwood association’s president, Helen Holder, also sits on the UCP provincial board as vice-president of fundraising. Ms. Holder declined to comment.

RJ Sigurdson, the party’s MLA for Highwood, pledged his support to Ms. Smith in an e-mailed statement, writing that the constituency association “does not reflect the views of my constituents broadly.”

Ms. Smith’s office did not respond to e-mailed questions, including whether the Premier feels it’s appropriate for Ms. Holder to remain on the party board.

UCP spokesperson Dave Prisco, in a statement, pointed to Ms. Smith’s 2024 leadership review and the party’s fundraising strength as evidence that most UCP members support her. Mr. Prisco did not address Ms. Holder’s involvement in the vote.

“You only see results like that when you have a strong leader with overwhelming support,” Mr. Prisco wrote.

Tanya Clemens, a leader with the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide and a Highwood UCP member, linked her endorsement of a leadership review to what she described as Ms. Smith’s “adversarial role” toward independence.

But her vote doesn’t mean she wants Ms. Smith “gone,” she said in a video posted to social media.

Opinion: Why we should stop taking Alberta separatism seriously

Divisions around separatism have wrought tensions within the UCP and, at times, put party leadership at odds with the Premier. On Monday night, UCP board members Samantha Steinke and Brad LaForge were scheduled to appear at a Calgary event with prominent separatist leaders Mitch Sylvestre, Jeffrey Rath and Cory Morgan. Neither Ms. Steinke nor Mr. LaForge responded to a request for comment.

Ms. Smith’s government has budgeted $4-million to advertise ahead of the referendum, prompting questions around fairness from both separatist and federalist groups hamstrung by strict spending limits.

Mr. Smith, the party president, attempted to address those concerns to party members over the weekend in a social media post where he claimed that the Premier “assured” him that the government’s advertising around the independence question would be “as Neutral as possible.”

“I’ve heard some of these ads, and I believe what the Premier told me,” wrote Mr. Smith, who has no relation to the Premier.

Asked at the Monday news conference whether she told him the government would be neutral on the separation question, the Premier said: “That’s not true.”

The two have previously clashed over the Ucp’s stance on separatism. In May, Mr. Smith told The Globe and Mail that the party would be neutral on the issue ahead of the referendum , and he believed the majority of UCP members will vote against remaining in Canada.

The next day, Ms. Smith said the party supports Alberta staying in Canada, saying she holds the final word on the Ucp’s stance.

stories.title: Bear cub rescued from Okanagan Lake faces uncertain future
stories.summary: However, at an estimated 30 pounds, wildlife experts say the young bear faces significant challenges heading into winter with the odds of survival not in its favour.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik, Amy Judd
stories.content:
A dramatic rescue unfolded in the middle of Okanagan Lake when a family boating near Vernon came across a young bear struggling to stay afloat.

Christina Zamniuk and her family jumped into action after spotting the cub in the water on Saturday, Sept. 12.

“He was struggling to stay above the water,” Zamniuk said. “His little nose was going under, he was blowing bubbles, his back legs were not moving anymore.”

The family managed to get the bear onto their boat and safely out of the water.

They affectionately named the cub Boo Boo.

But what happened after the rescue has raised concerns for Zamniuk.

She says the family was surprised when conservation officers did not attend in person. Instead, they were advised over the phone to push the bear off the boat once they reached shore.

“They told us just to shove him off the boat. We didn’t want to do it,” Zamniuk said. “The fact that the conservation officers were just like, well, you know, we have to trap him, and we don’t know if we can do anything, and just let him go. He’ll be fine.”

Reluctantly, the family followed the advice and released Boo Boo near the shoreline.

The cub was seen heading into the woods.

However, at an estimated 30 pounds, wildlife experts say the young bear faces significant challenges heading into winter with the odds of survival not in its favour.

“Very slim,” said Angelika Langen of the Northern Lights Wildlife Society.

“There’s still some time for it to gain weight for the winter, but normally we say they should have at least 50 pounds. If it’s a small cub, 50 pounds can sustain them through hibernation. Thirty pounds will not be able to do that.”

The Northern Lights Wildlife Society has sent a team to the area where the cub was released near the Chief Saddlemen Road in the Parker Cove area off of Westside Road near Vernon.

They are hoping to capture it and bring it into shelter for the winter before releasing it.

When asked why conservation officers did not pick up the cub after it was rescued from the water, the ministry responsible said it wasn’t a public safety issue.

However, Zamniuk says she feels conflicted about pushing the bear cub off the boat and hoping he makes it on his own.

“I don’t know if that doesn’t sit that well with me,” she said.

“And I can’t stop thinking about him.”

content_blocks.text: A dramatic rescue unfolded in the middle of Okanagan Lake when a family boating near Vernon came across a young bear struggling to stay afloat.
content_blocks.html: A dramatic rescue unfolded in the middle of Okanagan Lake when a family boating near Vernon came across a young bear struggling to stay afloat.

content_blocks.text: Christina Zamniuk and her family jumped into action after spotting the cub in the water on Saturday, Sept. 12.
content_blocks.html: Christina Zamniuk and her family jumped into action after spotting the cub in the water on Saturday, Sept. 12.

content_blocks.text: “He was struggling to stay above the water,” Zamniuk said. “His little nose was going under, he was blowing bubbles, his back legs were not moving anymore.”
The family managed to get the bear onto their boat and safely out of the water.
They affectionately named the cub Boo Boo.
But what happened after the rescue has raised concerns for Zamniuk.
She says the family was surprised when conservation officers did not attend in person. Instead, they were advised over the phone to push the bear off the boat once they reached shore.

“They told us just to shove him off the boat. We didn’t want to do it,” Zamniuk said. “The fact that the conservation officers were just like, well, you know, we have to trap him, and we don’t know if we can do anything, and just let him go. He’ll be fine.”
Reluctantly, the family followed the advice and released Boo Boo near the shoreline.
The cub was seen heading into the woods.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Bear rescued from Okanagan Lake'

content_blocks.text: However, at an estimated 30 pounds, wildlife experts say the young bear faces significant challenges heading into winter with the odds of survival not in its favour.
“Very slim,” said Angelika Langen of the Northern Lights Wildlife Society.

“There’s still some time for it to gain weight for the winter, but normally we say they should have at least 50 pounds. If it’s a small cub, 50 pounds can sustain them through hibernation. Thirty pounds will not be able to do that.”
The Northern Lights Wildlife Society has sent a team to the area where the cub was released near the Chief Saddlemen Road in the Parker Cove area off of Westside Road near Vernon.
They are hoping to capture it and bring it into shelter for the winter before releasing it.
When asked why conservation officers did not pick up the cub after it was rescued from the water, the ministry responsible said it wasn’t a public safety issue.
However, Zamniuk says she feels conflicted about pushing the bear cub off the boat and hoping he makes it on his own.
“I don’t know if that doesn’t sit that well with me,” she said.
“And I can’t stop thinking about him.”

stories.title: Major language school Ilac closes abruptly after filing for bankruptcy, stranding hundreds of students
stories.summary: Sudden shutdown leaves at least 1,362 students in limbo, with some at risk of losing thousands of dollars in prepaid fees and accommodations
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
When Berta Alonso received an e-mail on Friday from the International Language Academy of Canada telling her the school had filed for bankruptcy and was closing immediately, she figured she had been hacked.

The 18-year-old student from Barcelona was two weeks away from completing a marketing diploma at Ilac’s Vancouver campus. She couldn’t fathom that Ilac, one of the largest private language-instruction schools in the country, would file for bankruptcy and shutter without warning, stranding at least 1,362 students studying in Toronto and Vancouver. Some are at risk of losing accommodations and work permits tied to Ilac.

“Everybody thought that it was fake because it was, like, a crazy thing that no one expected,” Ms. Alonso said. “I was so scared and frustrated.”

The sudden closing of Ilac is the most recent fallout from the federal government’s U-turn on international student policy, even though many of Ilac’s students were in Canada on visitor’s visas, rather than study permits, according to Languages Canada. The organization represents private English and French language schools nationwide.

When the federal government began imposing restrictions on student visas and postgraduate work permits in early 2024, private schools that taught Canada’s two official languages to people from overseas saw demand dwindle. The number of students learning English or French as a second language at a private school has fallen nearly in half since 2019, down to 81,636 students last year from 150,112 in 2019, according to Languages Canada .

Less than a week before Ilac closed, EC English, an international language school with campuses in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, abruptly shut its doors as well. That closing affected 471 students across the country.

“Canada’s linguistic infrastructure is disappearing, and without it, we actually can’t build,” said Gonzalo Peralta, executive director of Languages Canada. “It should be part of the talent strategy for Canada’s future.”

Mr. Peralta said other language schools have closed since Ottawa reined in the international student program. It did so in response to public concerns that a surge in temporary residents had made housing, entry-level jobs and other resources harder for Canadians to access.

But previous shutdowns were orderly, he added. “What is really concerning right now is that we have these two large schools that have closed in a disorderly fashion, without assuming the responsibility for the students.”

Bankruptcy documents obtained by The Globe and Mail show Ilac had just over $1-million in cash on hand, plus $6.9-million in securities. The company had just over $135-million in liabilities when it filed for bankruptcy on Friday.

Ilac chief executive officer John DeFranco informed staff of the closing in a brief video call at 4:15 p.m. ET on Friday, according to a student-services worker who had been with the company for four years.

The Globe has agreed not to name the former employee because he hopes to keep working at language schools and fears that speaking out will hurt his career prospects.

Before their e-mail and internal messaging access was cut off, Ilac staff scrambled to share personal phone numbers with co-workers who had become like family, he said. Teachers who had developed curriculum rushed to print copies before the printers were shut off.

“Everybody who worked at Ilac did not know this was going to happen, and are horrified that it did,” he said, adding staff had just welcomed a fresh crop of overseas students to an Ilac high school in Toronto a few weeks ago. Friday was parent-teacher interview day.

Before the shutdown, Ilac ran traditional language classes in person and online, a diploma-granting career college and private high schools in Vancouver and Toronto. It also had long-standing partnerships, known as pathways programs , with dozens of publicly funded colleges and universities that helped students improve their French or English before starting postsecondary programs.

In 2019, Oncap, the mid-market private equity platform of Onex Corp., acquired a majority stake in Ilac Education Group in partnership with Ilac’s founders and management.

One of those founders, Jonathan Kolber, wrote on LinkedIn on Monday that he left Ilac’s board a year and a half ago because of differences with the company’s new CEO.

He wrote that the closing was a surprise to everyone at Ilac, “and the hardest part is the sales team are being accused of knowing. Please know they were lied to until the last moment. They were promised Ilac would never go bankrupt. They were told to sell to clients right until the end.”

Mr. Kolber did not respond to an interview request.

Mr. DeFranco, the CEO of Ilac, told The Globe by e-mail: “Limits on international students mean fewer people can access the education and opportunities we were built to provide. We know how difficult this is for our students and staff. We are working closely with regulators to ensure students receive the support they need during this transition, and are doing everything we can to minimize impacts on our students, employees, and partners.”

Adam Shantz, a managing partner at Oncap, added in a separate e-mailed statement that “sector-wide limits on admissions for international students have negatively impacted every language school in the country, including Ilac.”

Mr. Peralta said Languages Canada and its other member schools have promised to place every student whose education was disrupted by the EC Canada and Ilac closings in a Canadian language program as soon as possible at no charge.

But some students risk losing the thousands of dollars they paid to Ilac for accommodations and other services beyond tuition.

Annabel Wittan, a 19-year-old student from Berlin, said she paid Ilac about $11,000 for three months of English classes plus shared accommodations in residence in Burnaby, B.C. She moved in less than a week before receiving the same e-mail as Ms. Alonso informing her that Ilac was closing immediately.

“I have to move out or pay again because we don’t get the money back,” she said.

stories.title: London Airport offers sunny destinations for winter travellers, including stops in U.S. despite trade war
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/1HUUGAxpz08 As the seasons change and the temperature decreases, birds flying south for the w...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
As the seasons change and the temperature decreases, birds flying south for the winter will become a common sight for people in and around London. Some people even follow them down as well, flying off to somewhere warm and sunny to wait out the cold and return for the spring.

But for some, the choice of where they might go May have changed.

The London International Airport released its winter sun flight schedule on Friday, Sept. 18, featuring a large list of destinations including Cancun, Mexico, Orlando, Fla. and Montego Bay, Jamaica, as well as locales in the Dominican Republic, among others.

“We’ve been [to Jamaica] before and it’s a nice place,” said John Smith, a resident of Comox, B.C. who was flying out of London to Toronto. “We would like to go back.”

Janet Benoit from Calgary and Sarah Mann from Edmonton, respectively, both considered Mexico to be their destination of choice if they were to fly south for the winter.

The locations that Londoners wanted to go to weren’t the only ones on their mind. When asked about where they’d want to travel, Smith, Benoit and Mann all had the same answer, one that speaks to the larger ongoing trend of Canadian tourism to the United States declining because of the ongoing trade war: “Anywhere but the U.S.”

“I don’t feel safe leaving Canada going to the United States,” said Benoit, with Mann adding that she had stopped flights to the United States that she was supposed to be on.

A copy of the London Airport’s winter sun flight schedule. Airport staff expect all of the venues to be popular, even with the trade war causing a decline in Canada-U.S. tourism. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

The winter sun flight list has two American destinations on its list: Orlando and Fort Lauterdale, both in Fla.

“They’re both booked fully going and coming,” said ACE (Airport Comfort Enhancer) staff member Corinna Rogers, adding that every option on the winter flight schedule is equally popular. “I find it goes on right up until the very end.”

Rogers said that in her experience, flights to the United States out of London have declined on a casual basis, but that American holiday destinations still have things that travellers find appealing.

“Fort Lauterdale for the kids,” she said. “They like to go to Orlando, they want the beaches and stuff like that.”

Rogers also said that even while people May think about the trade war, they will take flights to the United States for the benefit of their friends and families.

Wendy Joanasie, a Londoner waiting on a flight to Toronto, cited Hawaii as her travel destination of choice.

“I haven’t thought about it, but if I was going to [fly south], I would go,” she said.

Ultimately, Rogers highlighted that the Orlando and Fort Lauterdale destinations are still just two of several options for Londoners to choose from.

“It just gives them an opportunity to make the decision for themselves.”

The flights are offered in partnership with with Porter Airlines, Air Transat, WestJet and Sunwing Vacations, and the travel destinations are:

Nine flights weekly to Cancun, Mexico

Three flights weekly to Orlando, Fla.

Four flights weekly to Fort Lauderdale, Fla.

Three flights weekly to Montego Bay, Jamaica

Two flights weekly to Punta Cana, Dominican Republic

Weekly service to Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic

stories.title: Forever Canadian officially becomes third-party advertiser in upcoming Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Forever Canadian will officially participate in the campaign as a third-party advertiser despite being registered as one with Elections Alberta since June.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Forever Canadian has announced it will shift direction with just weeks until Albertans head to the polls, and encourage voters to choose to remain in Canada, despite criticism that the group has been campaigning this entire time.

The group’s founder and former deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk said Monday that Forever Canadian will pivot from promoting national unity to officially become a third-party advertiser to campaign for Alberta remaining in Canada.

“We will be imploring that every eligible voter votes in this particular election, and checks off option 1, that is option A, ON question 10 for Alberta to remain in Canada,” Lukaszuk said.

Question 10 on the upcoming referendum ballot asks if Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or if the Government of Alberta should commence the legal process to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

The move comes as the group has been crisscrossing the province for more than than a year handing out more than 80,000 lawn signs and hosting events, including a weekend concert in Calgary to support Canadian unity.

Lukaszuk formed Forever Canadian in July 2025 to petition Albertans to remain in Canada, which gathered 404,293 verified signatures.

However, Lukaszuk has maintained he wanted MLAs to vote on the matter in the legislature rather than a referendum.

With weeks to go until Albertans head to the polls, Lukaszuk said the group had to “shift gears” due to concerns around voter apathy.

“This is not the time for complacency. Voter turnout is the most important thing at this time and we have learned what happens when voters are complacent,” he told reporters. “It is imperative during this most important vote, that I think any of us will participate in our lifetime, to not assume anything and come out and vote.”

To do that, Lukaszuk said, Forever Canadian must act as a third-party advertiser despite being registered as one with Elections Alberta since June 8.

“The difference between what they have been doing and what they’re about to do is probably going to be difficult for most people to discern,” said Lori Williams, an associate professor of policy studies at Mount-Royal University in Calgary.

Third party advertisers are subject to stringent regulations like a $607,000 spending limit as well as weekly donation disclosures.

Lukaszuk told reporters Forever Canadian will be filing its financials “moving forward,” but not since it registered as a third-party advertiser.

Cory Morgan, who founded the pro-separation third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, has accused Forever Canadian of not following the regulations since the campaign period began.

“Mr Lukaszuk has been playing pretty cute with the wordage of the legislation and definitely at the least has been violating the spirit of the legislation of disclosure and campaign limits throughout this thing,” Morgan told Global News. “Claiming he’s not campaigning while he has a campaign office, while he has a campaign bus and while he puts out campaign signs.”

According to Elections Alberta, Forever Canadian “had not engaged in referendum advertising,” which it said “must relate to a specific referendum question, must be advertising (meaning paid) and must attempt to persuade an elector to vote in a particular way with respect to that referendum question.”

Forever Canadian has raised $0 as of Sept. 17, according to the Elections Alberta website.

“We’ve gotta know how much did you raise and where did it come from because, let’s quit pretending, he’s been participating in a campaign for months,” Morgan said.

In an interview with Global News, Stephen Carter, the founder of Alberta’s Voice, welcomed Forever Canadian into the pro-federalist campaign.

However, Carter noted the importance that all third-party advertisers follow the regulations laid out in the legislation.

“We don’t want to give that excuse to Danielle Smith, the second that this campaign becomes something that wasn’t official or where the rules weren’t followed, it gives her the opportunity to open this door again and have another referendum,” Carter said.

According to Lukaszuk, Forever Canadian has complied with the legislation as the campaign “up to now was not a referendum campaign in the view of Elections Alberta.”
