stories.title: Massive 30-foot basking shark stuns onlookers in Nova Scotia
stories.summary: A massive 30-foot basking shark, one of the world's largest fish, cruised among boats in Halifax's Bedford Basin Friday and Saturday, drawing crowds of astonished spectators.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Ella Macdonald
stories.content:
A rare visit from one of the ocean’s largest fish turned heads in Nova Scotia over the weekend, as a basking shark estimated to be about 30 feet long cruised among boats and drew dozens of onlookers to the waterfront in Halifax’s Bedford Basin.

Video shared on social media Friday and Saturday showed the massive shark swimming near the surface, its dorsal and tail fins breaking the water as it moved through the northwestern end of the Halifax harbour.

The sighting quickly became the talk of the area, attracting spectators to the Bedford Basin Yacht Club in hopes of catching a glimpse of the giant fish.

“As we were driving along the shoreline we saw a fin. I screamed ‘Shark!’ to the girls and we pulled over and we ran down to the dock to get a closer look,” said Christie Wisener, who witnessed the animal Friday evening.

Her daughter, Sydney Wisener, described the encounter as exciting. “It was splashing me. I was very excited to see it,” she told Global News.

David Hamilton, a member of the Bedford Basin Yacht Club, said he and his son went to the marina hoping to spot the shark after hearing reports about it. About 10 minutes after arriving, Hamilton said he noticed the animal’s large dorsal fin cutting through the water.

“All of a sudden we had 30 kids and adults at the end of the dock watching this shark swim around,” he said. “It was three or four feet away from us. It was pretty daunting to see something that large.”

Hamilton said the shark spent time weaving among boats in the marina. “It had come right up and it was doing loops,” he said. “And then you just see the thing come by, and it was super ominous as it just cruised by. There’s the head, there’s the dorsal fin, there’s the tail.”

“This thing is massive.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "This thing is massive."

Another witness, David Rankin, compared the animal to the famous shark from the movie Jaws . “The shark is so big-looking, like the mechanical shark in Jaws,” he said. “It almost seemed to want to play with us. It seemed like it knew we were there and kept coming in.”

Despite its imposing size, experts say basking sharks pose no threat to humans.

“They’re a filter-feeder,” said Fred Whoriskey, a biology professor at Dalhousie University. “In many respects, you could consider them a gentle giant. There’s no reason to panic when you see one of these.”

The basking shark is the second-largest fish in the world, reaching lengths of up to 12 metres. It feeds on plankton and is commonly found along Atlantic Canada’s coastline during the summer months.

Tonya Wimmer, co-executive director and conservation director with the Marine Animal Response Society, said the organization received a call about the shark through its incident reporting hotline on Friday.

While basking sharks are native to Atlantic Canadian waters, she said seeing one so deep inside Bedford Basin is exceptionally rare.

“We certainly do get reports of basking sharks around Nova Scotia and even in some coastal areas, but in the very back of the Bedford Basin? That was a new one for us,” Wimmer said.

Whoriskey said it is uncommon to find a basking shark inside a harbour and suggested the animal May have entered the area while searching for food or had become disoriented in shallow waters.

“My guess is that this is a very lost basking shark,” he said. “It somehow got itself into a constricted area and it is really confused and doesn’t know how to get out.”

Wimmer called the encounter a “pretty spectacular sight” and said it was encouraging to see people observing the shark from a safe distance. “It was great to see people were watching from shore, they were watching from the wharf and no one was in the water trying to approach,” she told Global News.

The Atlantic population of basking sharks has been listed as a species of special concern by the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada since 2009. Scientists say much remains unknown about the species, including where the sharks spend the winter after leaving coastal waters.

For many of the people who gathered along the basin this weekend, however, the encounter was simply a memorable reminder of the marine life found off Nova Scotia’s shores.

“It just made us really appreciate Nova Scotia and all that we have in this beautiful province and in our oceans here,” said Christie Wisener.

–with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Schwarzkopf Professional mousse recalled over packaging risk
stories.summary: More than 90,000 units of Schwarzkopf Professional Osis Grip Mousse have been recalled in Canada over a packaging issue that could cause the container to burst.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
More than 90,000 units of a popular hair product have been recalled in Canada.

According to a Health Canada notice on September 21, the recall affects the 6.76-fluid-ounce (200-millilitre) Schwarzkopf Professional Osis Grip Mousse, sold between November 2023 and June 2026. The product was manufactured in Hungary.

The notice says the recalled product has packaging issues that can cause it to leak when the container is under pressure.

“The leakage and resulting pressure May cause the package to burst, which could result in injury or property damage,” it adds.

As of Sept. 18, the company had received one report of an incident in Canada, but Health Canada said there had been no reports of injuries.

The recall affects the following 25 batches:

2901x4577n, 2901x4578n, 290265p91o, 290665q30o, 290855n31o, 290866r38p, 290994281n, 291046l06p, 291174w17n, 291435h76o, 291435h77o, 291455n33o, 291515a59o, 291515a99o, 291515b01o, 291555n33o, 291615b01o, 291616b68p, 291716b69p, 291825e960, 291925e96o, 292015b73o, 2928y538bo, 2928y539bo and 293066u32p.

Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and return it to the place of purchase for a refund.

Consumers can also contact the company’s consumer support at skpcanada-support@henkel.com . Health Canada also advises consumers to report any health or safety incidents involving the product through its Consumer Product Incident Report Form .

The recall follows a similar action by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Aug. 11, where the product was distributed across 12 states.

stories.title: How B.C. Conservatives went from 44 seats to a party in turmoil
stories.summary: Just two years ago, B.C.’s Conservatives appeared to be on the verge of taking power. Now, it's fighting for political survival after a damaging exodus.
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
Vancouver – Just two years ago, B.C.’s Conservatives appeared to be on the verge of taking power.

John Rustad led the party to 44 seats in the 2024 provincial election, just three seats short of the Ndp’s 47 seat majority. It was the Conservatives’ strongest showing in decades, a coalition of moderates and the more socially conservative, moving the party from the political fringe into the province’s official opposition.

Now, the party is fighting for its political survival after a damaging exodus.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned as Conservative leader Sunday after less than four months on the job, following weeks of defections, expulsions and internal fighting that have divided the right.

MLA Lorne Doerkson was appointed interim leader Monday with Premier David Eby’s NDP poised to call an early election.

The turmoil is not simply the result of Findlay’s divisive leadership.

University of British Columbia political scientist Stewart Prest says the Conservatives are dealing with a deeper debate over what the party should actually represent.

“There is more that divides these two groups in many ways on some crucial questions than what brings them together,” Prest told CTV News Monday.

The Conservatives’ rise and the first cracks

The modern Conservative resurgence in B.C. began under Rustad, who joined the party in 2023 and helped turn it into the primary alternative to the NDP.

The party absorbed much of the vote that for decades went to the B.C. Liberals, who had unsuccessfully rebranded as B.C. United, then suspended its campaign during the 2024 election.

Leader Kevin Falcon urged supporters to back the Conservatives as several B.C. United MLAs crossed the floor to run for Rustad’s party.

Despite its stunning success, the patchwork Conservative caucus contained a wide range of political views and the tension became too difficult for Rustad to manage.

By December 2025, several Conservative MLAs had signed a letter calling for Rustad to resign. The party’s board attempted to remove Rustad after he initially refused to leave.

Rustad resigned the following day saying he wanted to avoid a civil war within the party.

Findlay takes the reins post-Rustad

The party chose Findlay as its new leader in May 2026, but just barely. She won after a four-round leadership contest, receiving 51 per cent of the vote.

Findlay appealed to the right, promising a government guided by faith, family, and freedom.

But the new leader quickly faced resistance from members of her caucus. Beginning in August, MLAs announced they were leaving, with several citing concerns about Findlay’s leadership and the direction of the party.

“She said it’s my way or the highway. And a lot of members of her caucus chose the highway,” said University of British Columbia political scientist Hamish Telford.

By the middle of September, a total of 13 MLAs had exited or been kicked out of caucus.

Eight of them joined CentreBC, a party formed in 2025 that is now being led by Kamloops Centre MLA Peter Milobar, who left the Conservatives in mid-August.

CentreBC is now the B.C. legislature’s third-largest party. Milobar has said it intends to run candidates in all 93 ridings if an early election is called.

The divide May be bigger than Findlay

In the wake of Findlay’s departure, politicians on both sides say the door is open to a dialogue on reuniting the right.

Prest describes the current Conservative movement as two distinct factions: a more centrist group represented by CentreBC and a Conservative Party that has moved further to the right.

For more moderate voters, he said, some of the positions associated with Findlay and her supporters May be difficult to reconcile with their own political views.

“It would take a special kind of politician to find a way to bring those two groups together,” Prest said.

Telford doesn’t see the two merging. “I think in the short term at least, we’re going to have sort of two centre-right parties, competing against each other. And that’s why the NDP wants to call this election and take advantage of it.”

That creates a new political problem for the right: voters who once had essentially one major alternative to the NDP could soon have two.

That division could have immediate consequences if Eby calls an election.

The premier has repeatedly said his government and Elections B.C. need to be ready for an election, while declining to announce when or if one will happen. The NDP currently holds a one-seat majority.

A provincial election would also overlap with B.C.’s municipal election campaign, which is already underway ahead of voting Oct. 17. Local government representatives have criticized the possibility of an early provincial vote.

For the Conservatives, an election would come with the party still led on an interim basis and without a permanent leader.

For that reason, Telford says an election call could be seen as dirty pool. “There’s long been a sort of a gentlemen’s understanding or agreement in Canadian politics that you don’t call an election when the official opposition party is without a leader,” he said.

Prest said the government could benefit from Conservative disorganization, but an early election could also remind voters that the NDP has chosen to seek a new mandate only two years after winning one.

“The NDP could run the risk of looking very much focused on their own interests, rather than voters’ interests,” Prest said.

stories.title: Fourth Marineland whale dies after relocation from Niagara Falls park
stories.summary: Osiris, a 26-year-old beluga, has died at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died.

Shedd Aquarium in Chicago says Osiris was a 26-year-old beluga that was part of a pod of 30 that experts moved out of the closed Niagara Falls, Ont., tourist attraction over the course of six weeks in the summer.

Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its animals.

Third Marineland beluga dies after being moved

Shedd took in 10 Marineland belugas, but three have since died along with a longtime resident at the Chicago park.

Another Marineland beluga died at Oceanografic Valencia last week.

Shedd says Osiris had issues eating since arriving from Marineland, but it does not know what caused the death.

stories.title: Funeral for London woman at the centre of second-degree murder investigation to be held Saturday
stories.summary: Near a seasonal scarecrow out front of a townhome at 685 Chelton Road in London sits several floral bouquets.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Near a seasonal scarecrow out front of a townhome at 685 Chelton Road in London sits several floral bouquets.

Each was placed by passersby, wanting to express grief for a mother who died in what police called a “violent incident” last week.

Authorities have not named the victim, but multiple social media posts and online fundraisers confirmed she is Raman Devi, a mother of two young children.

London Police began a femicide investigation after the arrest of 41-year-old Mandeep Singh at the home in the Summerside neighbourhood on Sept. 15.

Officers arrived to find a woman with life-threatening injuries. She was rushed to hospital, where she died.

Off camera Monday, a neighbour recalled a disturbing scene, telling CTV News they witnessed children being hurriedly carried out of the family home by a grandmother moments after the incident.

Singh faces a second-degree murder count .

But should the police femicide investigation lead to an automatic first-degree murder charge, there would also be a minimum 25-year sentence if convicted.

Police have said there are “indications that it (the investigation) could meet the threshold” for femicide.

Meanwhile, two separate online fundraisers in Raman Devi’s name have already raised more than $30,000.

One of the fundraisers is endorsed by the London Sikh Society.

In a telephone call, its president Hakikat Singh Gill said he is grateful for the support offered by the local community.

He also stated his organization is working with Raman Devi’s family members, including her children.

Gill added a funeral for her will be held on Saturday, Sept. 26 at 1 p.m. at Forest Lawn Funeral Chapel on Dundas Street East.

stories.title: Punk Rock Flea Market celebrates 10th anniversary
stories.summary: London's Punk Rock Flea Market (Prfm) is celebrating its 10th anniversary. The event, which runs from this Thu...
stories.author: Kelly Nicol
stories.content:
London’s Punk Rock Flea Market (Prfm) is celebrating its 10th anniversary. The event, which runs from this Thursday to Saturday, is expected to take over Dundas Place and Downtown London with live music, vendors, and skateboarders. But for the organizers, it’s more than just punk rock.

“We’re really talking about the local arts and culture, but the name Punk Rock Flea Market, that’s our roots, that kind of DIY ethos, but we kind of wrapped our arms around any of the local artists and community members and musicians.” Said Julie and Shayna, two of the co-organizers of Prfm. “We started in 2016, when we saw a gap in events of this sort, to gather alternative makers and small businesses, that didn’t really have a place to sell their wares at traditional pop-up markets.”

London is itself recognized as a Unesco City of Music. The organizers say they’re proud to be apart of London’s rich history of music. “[We] think that the designation really helps to uplift artists in terms of export opportunities, and it also helps put us on the map as a city of importance, musically in Canada.”

“London has a pretty vibrant punk culture, it has a history of punk culture”, said Adi Berardini, editor-in-chief of Femme Art Review, a publication providing space for Lgbtq+ and women’s voices to reflect on art. She went on to emphasize the importance of events like Prfm. “In a more conservative city like London, I think it’s important to have these events, because we have to continue to work against the grain as well, and create space for those who are alternative and part of the punk scene.”

Punk Rock Flea Market begins Thursday night and runs until Saturday. You can find more info on their Instagram .

stories.title: Pharmacy treatments for Lyme disease cut N.S. emergency visits in half: study
stories.summary: Blacklegged tick bites can lead to Lyme disease, as well as Anaplasmosis, Babesiosis and Powassan virus though Nova Scotia has not seen Powassan cases so far.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The number of Nova Scotians visiting the emergency department for treatment of tick bites dropped by about half after the province gave pharmacists permission in 2021 to assess and provide preventative Lyme disease treatment, a new study has found.

The study, published Monday in the Canadian Pharmacies Journal, showed pharmacists are able to examine a suspected bite and if confirmed to be from a tick that can transmit Lyme disease , prescribe the standard oral treatment called doxycycline to limit the risk of it developing.

Emily Black, lead supervising author of the study and acting director of the College of Pharmacy at Dalhousie University, said it’s a sign of improvements in the system.

“It really shows that people want other options for access for things like tick bites. They really don’t want to be sitting in the emergency department,” she said. “But I also think it suggests or shows that they really value the care that pharmacists can provide and really trust their assessment and ability to do that.”

The study looked at patient cases of tick bites reported at three Nova Scotia emergency departments in the 16 months before and 16 months after the August 2021 change.

Before implementation, there were a total of 617 visits for tick bites. Once pharmacists could assess the bites, the study found 402 people visited an emergency department during a period of 16 months after the change. When compared to the overall emergency department volume in each 16-month period, the study showed the rate of tick-bite visits was cut roughly in half.

By expanding tick treatments to pharmacies, the Pharmacy Association of Nova Scotia says people can get help faster.

“We really don’t want people with minor ailments, things that they categorize in the ER as level four or level five, we don’t want those in the ER, we want them being taken care of in the community,” said Allison Bodnar, CEO of the association.

In the latest quarter, from April to June, Bodnar said pharmacists in the province assessed more than 8,000 tick bites. She stressed it shows how prevalent the issue of tick bites has become in Nova Scotia.

Nova Scotians can typically book a same-day or following day appointment online as opposed to driving to the hospital and waiting hours to be seen. Treatment for tickborne illnesses must be administered within 72 hours to limit the risk of their development.

“Their community pharmacy May be a lot closer for them to their home and a lot easier to access than, say, driving to an emergency department,” Black said. “It gives them more timely accesss as well, where they May not be able to get in to see their primary care provider.”

Pharmacists are becoming a primary source for Lyme disease treatment in Nova Scotia, a separate study showed.

A 2024 study in the Canadian Pharmacists Journal, which Black was also a part of, found pharmacists prescribed 61.3 per cent of all single-dose doxycycline prescriptions following the province giving them prescribing authority.

Even though a high number of people are turning to pharmacists for Lyme disease treatment, Black said more work can still be done.

“There’s still a lot of people out there who maybe don’t know about the service,” Black said. “I think there’s work to do in terms of increasing awareness around what can be offered in community settings and the different health-care providers that can offer that.”

Nova Scotia has high rates of Lyme disease, the provincial government said in a bulletin last year. It said the province is also seeing more cases of Anaplasmosis and a few cases of Babesiosis, two other tick-borne illnesses. While Powassan virus is another known tick-borne illness, there are no known cases in the province.
paragraphs: The number of Nova Scotians visiting the emergency department for treatment of tick bites dropped by about half after the province gave pharmacists permission in 2021 to assess and provide preventative Lyme disease treatment, a new study has found.

The study, published Monday in the Canadian Pharmacies Journal, showed pharmacists are able to examine a suspected bite and if confirmed to be from a tick that can transmit Lyme disease , prescribe the standard oral treatment called doxycycline to limit the risk of it developing.
Emily Black, lead supervising author of the study and acting director of the College of Pharmacy at Dalhousie University, said it’s a sign of improvements in the system.

“It really shows that people want other options for access for things like tick bites. They really don’t want to be sitting in the emergency department,” she said. “But I also think it suggests or shows that they really value the care that pharmacists can provide and really trust their assessment and ability to do that.”
The study looked at patient cases of tick bites reported at three Nova Scotia emergency departments in the 16 months before and 16 months after the August 2021 change.

Before implementation, there were a total of 617 visits for tick bites. Once pharmacists could assess the bites, the study found 402 people visited an emergency department during a period of 16 months after the change. When compared to the overall emergency department volume in each 16-month period, the study showed the rate of tick-bite visits was cut roughly in half.
By expanding tick treatments to pharmacies, the Pharmacy Association of Nova Scotia says people can get help faster.

“We really don’t want people with minor ailments, things that they categorize in the ER as level four or level five, we don’t want those in the ER, we want them being taken care of in the community,” said Allison Bodnar, CEO of the association.

In the latest quarter, from April to June, Bodnar said pharmacists in the province assessed more than 8,000 tick bites. She stressed it shows how prevalent the issue of tick bites has become in Nova Scotia.

Nova Scotians can typically book a same-day or following day appointment online as opposed to driving to the hospital and waiting hours to be seen. Treatment for tickborne illnesses must be administered within 72 hours to limit the risk of their development.

“Their community pharmacy May be a lot closer for them to their home and a lot easier to access than, say, driving to an emergency department,” Black said. “It gives them more timely accesss as well, where they May not be able to get in to see their primary care provider.”
Pharmacists are becoming a primary source for Lyme disease treatment in Nova Scotia, a separate study showed.

A 2024 study in the Canadian Pharmacists Journal, which Black was also a part of, found pharmacists prescribed 61.3 per cent of all single-dose doxycycline prescriptions following the province giving them prescribing authority.
Even though a high number of people are turning to pharmacists for Lyme disease treatment, Black said more work can still be done.

“There’s still a lot of people out there who maybe don’t know about the service,” Black said. “I think there’s work to do in terms of increasing awareness around what can be offered in community settings and the different health-care providers that can offer that.”

Nova Scotia has high rates of Lyme disease, the provincial government said in a bulletin last year. It said the province is also seeing more cases of Anaplasmosis and a few cases of Babesiosis, two other tick-borne illnesses. While Powassan virus is another known tick-borne illness, there are no known cases in the province.

stories.title: Civilian schools are training the air force’s next generation of technicians for the first time
stories.summary: Demand for professionals who certify whether an aircraft is fit to fly surges as Ottawa focuses its defence modernization efforts
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
The Royal Canadian Air Force is outsourcing its aircraft technician training for the first time, as demand for the professionals who certify whether an aircraft is fit to fly surges amid modernization efforts.

Nearly 200 Rcaf members are learning how to be aircraft technicians at civilian schools while the air force’s own academy in Borden, Ont., runs at full capacity. The inaugural students under this initiative began classes in July.

It’s a first for the air force, after the Canadian Forces , more broadly, has been outsourcing training for decades with professions such as construction engineers.

“We have a number of new and extremely modern and complex aircraft coming online, and we need to stand ready and have our technicians ready when these platforms arrive at the operational units,” said Lieutenant-Colonel Meagan McGrath, a staff officer who leads the outsourced training initiative for the Rcaf’s Air Maintenance Branch. “There’s no time to waste here.”

The air force has secured standing offers from 10 civilian schools across the country to train aircraft technicians, allowing it to increase its pace of graduation as it experiences a growth in enrolment. Not all 10 currently have Rcaf members studying at them. One of the busier schools is the British Columbia Institute for Technology (Bcit), where 84 of the approximately 190 Rcaf members in the Force’s program are enrolled.

On a Monday afternoon in early September, students in uniform stood attentively, listening to their professor talk about aircraft wiring at Bcit’s aerospace campus near the Vancouver International Airport. In a classroom close by, their civilian colleagues did much the same, learning everything from how to repair fuselages made with composite materials to what the inside of an airplane wheel looks like.

The two cohorts will study the same Transport Canada-certified curriculum over the next several months, but with two very different outcomes. One will finish their program and enter the job market, likely looking for work in the commercial aviation sector. The other will either finish and travel to their posted unit to learn more about the military aircraft fleets they’ve been assigned to or return to base for further training.

The air force began looking into outsourcing training for these technicians in the fall of 2024, shortly after publishing its training modernization strategy in the spring.

This was also around the time when the military branch decided it would aim to train its aircraft technicians to national standards, such as Transport Canada’s, and work with schools whose curriculum abides by these standards, Lt.-Col. McGrath said.

“It’s part of the modernization effort. There’s a standard that exists. Let’s reach towards it,” she said.

Aircraft technicians are critical to an aircraft being deemed safe to fly. It’s their name on the line if anything goes wrong, said Gerry Egan, associate dean of aerospace at Bcit.

“The buck stops with that individual and the team of individuals making that aircraft safe for flight, and then they hand it off to the flight crew and say, ‘Here’s your aircraft,’” said Mr. Egan, a former aircraft maintenance engineer himself.

There are three main categories that aircraft technicians can specialize in at Bcit: structures, electronics – also called avionics – and maintenance. Those specializing in structures are responsible for maintaining and repairing parts of the aircraft such as the fuselage, wings and tail. Those specializing in avionics are responsible for all of the electrical systems, including navigation and communication. And those specializing in maintenance are the “jack or jill of all trades,” said Mr. Egan, meaning they’re the ones responsible for the certification of an aircraft after it has undergone any type of repair or routine maintenance. Thus, they have to know a little bit of everything.

While the Rcaf has different professional titles for each of the three aforementioned technician categories, they’re consistent with what the military employs.

The maintenance, repair and overhaul work these technicians perform is highlighted as a key capability by Ottawa’s new Defence Industrial Strategy, which was released earlier this year, as well as the Department of National Defence’s 2026-27 departmental plan. In this plan, Ottawa highlights the modernization of aerospace maintenance technician training as one of the air force’s priorities for the current fiscal year.

Across the country from Bcit, Nova Scotia Community College has a heavy military presence on its campus too. The school has been working with the Forces for decades, including on its outsourced training for construction-related courses.

The college is also training aircraft technicians for the Rcaf, but this time through a different military education program called the Non-Commissioned Member Subsidized Training and Education Plan. This program offers full-time paid education at certain Canadian schools to either civilians looking to join the Forces, or non-commissioned members who are already enrolled but want to become experts in their field.

Andrew Lafford, vice-president of academics at the college, said he’s noticed an increase recently in the number of students in uniform on campus in tandem with an increase in the number of training contracts the school is working with the Forces on.

Back at Bcit, the school is preparing to launch its first 18-week full-time program in May dedicated to teaching people how to build, repair, fly and collect data with drones. Through informal discussions, Mr. Egan said he’s gleaned the military is keen to learn more about it, as they, too, are having to navigate new training for autonomous systems.

The scope of the modernization effort that the air force is currently undertaking is the greatest since the Second World War, said Lt.-Col. McGrath.

“It’s really a moment in time, and I think we’ve grasped very quickly that we need to adjust to accommodate this moment and to find solutions.”

stories.title: $16 million housing project unveiled in Walkerton for low to moderate income earners
stories.summary: Ground has officially been broken on a new housing project in Bruce County.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Ground has officially been broken on a new housing project in Bruce County.

“This fills a really important piece of the housing puzzle, that subsidized county housing provided by the Bruce County Housing Corporation. It meets the needs of some people who really need help finding homes in our community,” said Bruce County Warden Luke Charbonneau.

The $16 million project, located in Walkerton, will be a mix of 41 affordable and market rate units. Tenants will be selected from Bruce County’s community housing waitlist, which is more than 800 people long.

“41 units isn’t solving that problem, but it’s one project at a time, one unit at a time, until we meet that need,” said Charbonneau.

Brockton’s Mayor calls the new housing project “workforce” housing, geared towards existing, and possibly new, low to middle income earners.

“For example, there is great demand at our hospitals and long term care homes, for personal support workers (PSW). They might make a salary in the range of $28 an hour. If that’s the only source of income they have, they are definitely under stress with rent. And this type of project will be geared towards that person. So, a PSW who lands a job at Bruce Lea Haven Long Term Care Home for example, could apply to the county to be on the waiting list, and at that income level, they could qualify for a subsidized rent in this building,” said Brockton Mayor Chris Peabody.

The mix of tenants concerns Walkerton business owner, Darren Holm. He believes those already on Bruce County’s nearly 1000 person community housing waitlist, should be first in line, for the new Bruce County housing project, expected to be completed by the end of 2027.

“What happens to the people that are indeed challenged and are vulnerable, that have been on the list for multiple years? Are they passed over for this new population of residents?” questioned Holm.

Bruce County didn’t provide the break down of how many units in the new Eastridge Community Housing Project would be affordable, and how many would be market-rate, or how tenants would be selected.

Peabody says nearby this new project, 70 housing units are currently being constructed, a portion of which will be affordable, and a handful of units in the existing apartments in the Eastridge development are subsidized by the county as well.

“We know there’s the need, and this isn’t the only solution. There have been other solutions we’re working on,” he said.

“We’re a growing community. Every one of the municipalities in Bruce County is slated to grow. So, we have more and more people moving here wanting to live here. And we need to find places for them to be. Ultimately, we want this county to be a place where anybody can find a place to live,” said Charbonneau.

Bruce Power has contributed $1 million towards the Eastridge Community Housing project. The Ontario government is also covering a multimillion-dollar portion of the construction costs. Brockton donated the land. Bruce County will build, and operate the housing complex.

“It would just be really nice to have some clear cut answers on who’s paying for it, who’s going to live there, and how the whole economics of it works out. How much we as taxpayers are going to be on the hook for the initial buildout, and the ongoing operations of it,” said Holm.

“What happens to the people that are indeed challenged and are vulnerable, that have been on the list for multiple years? Are they passed over for this new population of residents?” questioned Holm.
Bruce County didn’t provide the break down of how many units in the new Eastridge Community Housing Project would be affordable, and how many would be market-rate, or how tenants would be selected.

stories.title: As costs climb, more P.E.I. families seek help with baby basics
stories.summary: A P.E.I. pregnancy centre is seeing rising demand for free diapers, formula, clothing and other baby essentials as families struggle with the high cost of living.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Summerside, P.E.I. - With a reusable bag slung over her shoulder and her baby in one arm, new mother Katie Murray uses the other to flip through clothing racks at the Island Pregnancy Centre. Everything she chooses is free.

Eight-month-old Teddy is Murray’s first child. Not entirely sure where to begin, she turned to the centre for help. Inside the Summerside Baby Boutique, she found a list of necessities and welcoming staff members offering guidance on what to take home.

“It means that he always has what he needs,” Murray said.

The non-profit organization, which operates a second site in Charlottetown, provides emotional and practical support to those facing pregnancy-related challenges and early family life.

Demand for its services has surged in recent years, with its two locations logging about 2,500 visits in 2025, a figure executive director Tammy MacKinnon expects will rise.

“The cost of living is so high…We just have a lot of people who are pregnant and who are in need,” she said. “The more people that move to P.E.I. from other countries also are coming here with very little to start with.”

The baby boutiques rely entirely on community donations. Volunteers sort, wash and display what comes in. To stretch the inventory, shopping visits have been reduced from once a week to once a month.

Diapers in sizes three and up are some of the hardest items to keep stocked. On Monday morning, the Charlottetown location was completely out, while the Summerside donation room had no size four diapers and fewer than 10 tins of baby formula.

Other programs for families facing financial hardship are under pressure as well, MacKinnon said. There are waiting lists for infant car seats and hospital-grade breast pumps, while more mothers are seeking free professional counselling.

“It has been really difficult to keep up,” she added, calling the centre the only service of its kind on the Island.

For mother of three Rebecca Smith, access to the boutique offers comfort, and one less thing to worry about, during difficult periods.

When her children, aged 10 months, two and 13, outgrow their clothes, she brings them back, swapping for replacements.

“Being a low-income family, this really helps us to be able to feel more in control, and to be able to provide for our family,” she said.

In a statement, the Department of Social Development and Seniors told CTV News social assistance rates have risen steadily since 2018 to help Islanders meet the cost of living. It also pointed to the P.E.I. Child Benefit for low and moderate-income households, as well as the Island Essentials Benefit, adding the province continues to review its supports.

Donations can be dropped off at the Island Pregnancy Centre’s Summerside location on Mondays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and in Charlottetown from Tuesday to Thursday during the same hours. People can also donate online .

stories.title: Could these pills help people with anorexia? New London, Ont. study aims to find out
stories.summary: Researchers at Western University and London hospitals are starting a clinical trial testing fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) for anorexia.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
A new clinical trial is recruiting people diagnosed with anorexia nervosa as researchers hope to discover if fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) capsules could help better manage this eating disorder.

Led by researchers at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri), Lawson Research Institute of St. Joseph’s Health Care London and Western University, the novel study will investigate whether these capsules can restore healthy gut bacteria (the microbiome), improve nutrition and modify how people make food choices.

Anorexia nervosa is a severe and sometimes life-threatening condition that leads a person to perceive themselves as overweight and believe they must restrict food consumption or exercise continuously to reduce their weight.

Researchers have noticed patients with anorexia nervosa also have a disturbance in their gut microbiome which could be linked to how they think about food and their body.

“There appears to be a direct link between the gut microbiome and how the brain functions,” said study co-lead Dr. Elizabeth Osuch, a professor of psychiatry and medical biophysics, researcher at Lhscri and psychiatrist at London Health Sciences Centre.

“This connection is thought to occur through chemical processes that convey information from the gut to the brain. Since we take the FMT capsules from healthy donors, we think we can enhance the microbiome of people with anorexia nervosa, which in turn could also signal the brain to develop a healthier emotional process, improve nutrition and positively impact self-perception.”

Researchers at Western, Lawson Research Institute and London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute are exploring whether fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) capsules – tasteless, odourless pills made from stool samples given by healthy donors – could help manage anorexia. (L to R) Microbiologist Jeremy Burton and psychiatrist Dr. Elizabeth Osuch. (Lhscri)

The research would not be possible without the pioneering work of the Lawson Research Institute (Lawson) FMT team, collaborators on the study process who have customized the capsules specifically for this study. The Lawson team – under the leadership of scientist Dr. Michael Silverman, medical director of the Infectious Diseases Program at St. Joseph’s, and Seema Nair Parvathy, scientific director of the FMT program at Lawson – screens stool donors, ensuring only healthy stool without harmful bacteria or other issues is used, and processes samples into tasteless, odorless pills.

“Eating disorders can be stubbornly difficult to treat, even with a combination of psychological therapy, nutritional counselling and medical monitoring,” said microbiologist Jeremy Burton, interim vice-president research of St Joseph’s, scientific director of Lawson and co-leader of the study with Dr. Osuch.

### “As unconventional as the FMT approach May seem, it could give hope to struggling patients and their families – while also supporting evidence that mental health and physical health are often linked through the gut microbiome.” – Dr. Jeremy Burton, microbiologist and study co-lead

Participants will ingest capsules and complete questionnaires as well as provide stool samples before and several times after the intervention. They will be followed carefully to examine the effects of the procedure.

Both Lawson and Lhscri are leaders in FMT research and have conducted world-first studies also showing promise in the field of cancer. It also is an approved treatment for patients with Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), which is a condition where bacterium produces toxins and infects the colon causing inflammation.

The study is being funded by the Academic Medical Organization of Southwestern Ontario(Amoso).

“Our hope is that the clinical trial shows positive outcomes for individuals with anorexia nervosa and it becomes a standard treatment option for those whom there are currently very few treatment choices,” said Osuch.

The study is seeking to recruit 20 research participants. To be eligible, participants must be:

Ages 16 – 35

Diagnosed with anorexia nervosa, restricting type and not in active cognitive behavioural therapy(and not in hospital)

Able to travel to London Health Sciences Centre at 54 Riverview Avenue and St. Joseph’s Hospital at 268 Grosvenor Street

See full eligibility criteriahere

For more information or to express interest, please contactmichael.wammes@LHSC.on.CA%20Study%20for%20Anorexia%20Nervosa) or 519-646-6000 ext. 65196.

stories.title: Snowbirds base gets a glimpse at aircraft expected to replace Tutor jets
stories.summary: Four CT-157 Siskin II turboprop aircraft landed in Moose Jaw, Sask., Monday. They are expected to be the model that will replace the Snowbirds retiring fleet.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Royal Canadian Air Force (Rcaf) members in Moose Jaw, Sask. got a first look at the type of trainer aircraft that will replace the retiring Snowbirds fleet.

Four new CT-157 Siskin II turboprop advanced training aircraft arrived at 15 Wing in the southern Saskatchewan city Monday, after two landed in Gatineau, Que. last Thursday . These specific aircraft will be used for training, but they are the same model as the ones expected to replace the Canadian Forces Snowbirds aging CT-114 Tutor jets after their final showing at the Grey Cup in Calgary’s McMahon Stadium Nov. 15 .

“This is very exciting. Having new aircraft reinvigorates our training streams, but more importantly, it provides our young students and young aviators with the opportunity to learn new technologies,” said acting commander of 15 Wing Moose Jaw, Lt.-Col. Craig Cloete. He spoke with reporters at an event commemorating the Battle of Britain Sunday, prior to the Siskin IIs arriving.

The Snowbirds have called Moose Jaw home since the performance fleet was founded in 1971.

Two flight schools are also housed at 15 Wing Moose Jaw. Ensuring students at the base have access to modern equipment will help prepare them for future flights and gives them a leg up as technology continues to evolve, Cloete said.

“We cannot remain stagnant in our training methodologies or the tools that we use for training,” he continued.

A total of 19 Siskin II aircraft are expected to be stationed in the Saskatchewan city.

Maj. Zacharie Charbonneau said a lot the technology in the training aircraft, such as the fully digital cockpit, ensures trainees are ready for the future of aviation.

“We’re very happy and excited to start flying them,” Charbonneau told Global News.

“Information management is the new way of flying. So, teaching people how to gather the information, how to perceive it, how to comprehend what’s coming at them and protect ahead of the aircraft. It’s a bit of a different change in the paradigm and the way that we teach flying.”

He had the opportunity to fly a Siskin II while undergoing training in Switzerland, where the aircraft are manufactured, this summer. Students will have the chance to fly them after the other instructors are adequately trained, Charbonneau said.

“It’s an amazing aircraft, rolls incredibly fast,” the major continued, adding that it is “kind of the F-1 of trainers.”

The advanced trainer has a maximum speed of 685 km/h , which is slightly slower than the Tutor jets’ 763 km/h max speed , according to the Rcaf website. The four that arrived Monday will be used for advanced flying training and as a step towards jet training while stationed in Moose Jaw.

stories.title: Fanshawe students weigh the costs of college
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/BZyWSXm3AZ8 With the cost of tuition, textbooks, transportation and everyday expenses ...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
With the cost of tuition, textbooks, transportation and everyday expenses adding up, affordability is an ongoing concern for students at Fanshawe College.

For some students, balancing the cost of education with other living expenses can make attending college more difficult. Especially today, September 21 being the 10 day which means that students must pay their balance of fees for fall term today.

Micheal Demelo, a Fanshawe student in the human service foundation, said “It makes it a lot harder to get job interviews and jobs because you go into the interview and tell her your availability, and they’re like well how are you going to manage that with a full-time job? I’m going to have to. and then they just don’t hire you.”

Micheal Demelo, human service foundation, year 1

The cost of attending college goes beyond tuition. Students May also have to budget for textbooks, course materials, food, and other expenses.

Luckily, there are discounts available to help students afford college. Fanshawe Student Union President, Shade Dias, said “Currently we have – after 7 at The Nest we have discounts for students who have late-night classes, as well as on Fridays we have discounts for students which we launch just at the start of term. 10 per cent discounts for students every Friday.. and then Outback Shack we have a thing called 12 minutes in, 12 minutes out for students. All of this in place helps students afford meals on campus… I launched the breakfast program for students. This will help your affordability as well.”

Shade Dias, FSU president

The Nest is Fanshawe Colleges convenient store located at (L1001). Fanshawe Student Union, (FSU) promotes these discounts through their social media and website .

Jason Yabes, a Fanshawe student in the business marketing program, says his advice for students is “Start budgeting. If you can see your expenses, you know what’s coming in, coming out, you’re able to see the future kind of, and budget that way.”

The financial assistance resources that are available at Fanshawe College are Osap, Work Study Bursury, scholarships and awards, entrance bursaries, first generation bursary, and the financial aid department located in room (E2020).

Jason Yabes, business marketing, year 2

Starting in fall 2026, the maximum share of provincial Osap funding available as non-repayable grants has been reduced from 85 per cent to 25 per cent. The remaining funding is provided as loans, which students must repay 6 months after you finish or leave your studies. The change means students who previously relied more heavily on grants May now have ti take on more repayable financial aid to help cover the cost of college.

As students continue to balance education with the cost of everyday life, affordability remains an important issue on campus.

stories.title: Twin 10-storey high-rises proposed for Elgin Centre parking lot
stories.summary: The Elgin Centre has seen a massive resurgence over the past decade. After bringing in big box retailers and a hotel, the owners now have plans to take the development much further by proposing a pair of 10-storey high-rise apartments with retail space at street level.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Elgin Centre has seen a massive resurgence over the past decade. After bringing in big box retailers and a hotel, the owners now have plans to take the development much further by proposing a pair of 10-storey high-rise apartments with retail space at street level.

One will be located at the south end of the parking lot along Wellington Street with another in the southwest corner along Highview Avenue and will be at the current site of the Denny’s restaurant.

The mixed-use buildings would have a total of 232 residential units with underground parking, commercial space and outdoor courtyard.

“From the time we purchased the property ten years ago to now, we did envision some of this,” said Jay Burnstein, owner of Elgin Centre. “We didn’t think hotel in the very beginning and that kind of came as things went along but our main goal at the beginning was to try to fill up the vacant spaces.”

St. Thomas City Council held a public meeting on Sept. 14 as they are being asked to change the zoning from a five-storey building in an original proposal years ago, to 10.

“We had approved a couple of apartment buildings on that pad around the same time as we approved the original of the Holiday Inn, but it’s taken them a while to come back with what it might look like,” said Joe Preston, mayor of St. Thomas.

“The buildings have gotten taller as is happening in a lot of market rent apartments. You need the extra floors to pay for what it costs to build an apartment building, and they’ve added a couple of levels of one floor commercial out along the edge of the parking lot.”

With industry coming to the area, Preston believes more housing is key in the city.

“I live right across the road from the Metro and I found it a pretty convenient place to live and shop and play,” said Preston.

“It’s great to see the Elgin Centre kind of finding its second life. We talked about the old mall and how empty it got and now it’s filled back in to a point where they’re building extra buildings to go with it. Pretty positive in our community, especially to get that market rent apartment in time for new employees coming to Saint Thomas.”

CTV spoke with a few neighbours who expressed concerns about the proposed height and potential privacy issues.

Trent Vindasius lives nearby and called into the recent public zoning meeting.

“Increasing to 10 stories…is really aggressive for this area,” Vindasius told council.

“It’s asking a lot of the area and the people that are that reside here. I mean, we just had a hotel built at five (storey’s)but to double that seems very aggressive. I have a five story building looking into my backyard already, and now you’re asking to double that for high density residential building. My concern is that ten stories is double the existing bylaw.”

Burnstein points to the eight-storey buildings just south of the mall.

“I believe those were built back in the early 70s and those were eight storeys back then,” said Burnstein.

“I think a developer probably like nowadays, if you’re going to apply, you’d probably be going for 15-to-17 stories, maybe 18, because it’s different today. Cities are getting more dense, and they’re getting the cities are more open to having higher buildings these days.”

Burnstein added that many cities in the province are seeing high-density buildings going onto the property of shopping centres.

Another detail to be ironed out is the flight path from the St. Thomas Airport. The maximum building height can only be 37.16 metres or the maximum allowable height in the airport zooming bylaw.

“As we build anything in Saint Thomas, we have to be careful about what’s in the flight path from the airport,” said Preston.

“I don’t remember seeing a lot of airplanes flying over the mall, but it is in the flight path for one of the runways, so they have to adjust the angles and see whether it works or not.”

Burnstein said the original plans were to build much higher, but the location of the airport just won’t allow it.

“We looked at what was happening over by the Walmart site and there’s that 14-storey building. We were looking at maybe 15, 16 storeys, but 10 is a good scale.”

Owners have completed a parking study and believe with the addition of underground parking, there will still be a lot of parking spaces for shoppers.

“We’re hoping to get started by sometime next year,” said Burnstein, who estimates about 18 months to two years for completion.

“We still need to serve certain approvals, but hopefully by the fall of next year we can get started. With that Volkswagen plant and the feeder plants that are expected to be built, studies have been done that show there will be a demand for this. We’re really excited about it.”

stories.title: Trial begins for Alberta RCMP officer accused of helping Rwanda
stories.summary: Const. Eli Ndatuje faces charges for alleged illegal use of the police database
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
A Mountie accused of misusing the police database to help a foreign country did nothing of the sort and is, in fact, a “Canadian success story,” his lawyer told court Monday.

RCMP Const. Eli Ndatuje faces charges under the Criminal Code and the Security of Information Act for alleged illegal use of the police database.

But his lawyer, Robb Beeman, told the court in his opening statement his client was simply trying to help out a friend on a missing person’s case in Canada.

Beeman said the 39-year-old Ndatuje and his family fled war-torn Uganda and moved to Ottawa when Ndatuje was a teenager.

“We anticipate that you will be able to conclude that (the law-breaking) did not happen,” Beeman told Justice Jason Wilkins.

“You will be able to conclude that Const. Ndatuje is a Canadian success story.

“He is utterly a credit to himself and to the RCMP.”

Alberta Mountie charged with accessing police records system to aid Rwandan agent

Ndatuje was arrested in February 2024 by the RCMP’s federal policing team. It identified Rwanda as the alleged “foreign actor” involved in the case.

Mounties at the time did not provide details on Ndatuje’s duties or the type of information allegedly accessed, but said the records involved were not top secret.

Crown prosecutor Kent Brown delivered a brief summary Monday of what he hopes to prove at trial.

“This will primarily be a paper case,” Brown told court. “This is really a matter of a police officer who is alleged to have engaged in a search on (the police database) and is alleged to have divulged information as a result of that search.”

Beeman told court his client was in touch with the Rwandan High Commission twice and both times for innocent purposes.

The first time, he said was in April 2022. He said it was for Ndatuje to clear up some confusion over his wife’s travel documents.

“I have no doubt there’s going to be some suggestion that the communication was nefarious,” Beeman said.

On the second occasion, he said, Ndatuje was contacted by a friend at the Rwandan High Commission who was worried about the disappearance of a housekeeper who worked at the Ottawa residence of the Rwandan ambassador.

Beeman said his client told the friend to report the disappearance to police in Ottawa. He said Ndatuje, ON his own initiative, then checked the police database to see if anyone had reported the housekeeper missing.

There was no record of the housekeeper being missing, and the man was later found unharmed.

“He did the search because he cared about a missing person,” Beeman told court. “One would hope that every police officer in this country would share that attitude.”

Beeman told the judge he will not find any evidence Ndatuje discussed the database search with anyone.

Bill McCrimmon, a foreign service officer from Global Affairs Canada, testified the department got a call from the Rwandan high commissioner about the missing housekeeper.

The trial is scheduled to conclude early next month.

“He is utterly a credit to himself and to the RCMP.”
Alberta Mountie charged with accessing police records system to aid Rwandan agent
Ndatuje was arrested in February 2024 by the RCMP’s federal policing team. It identified Rwanda as the alleged “foreign actor” involved in the case.
Mounties at the time did not provide details on Ndatuje’s duties or the type of information allegedly accessed, but said the records involved were not top secret.
Crown prosecutor Kent Brown delivered a brief summary Monday of what he hopes to prove at trial.

“This will primarily be a paper case,” Brown told court. “This is really a matter of a police officer who is alleged to have engaged in a search on (the police database) and is alleged to have divulged information as a result of that search.”
Beeman told court his client was in touch with the Rwandan High Commission twice and both times for innocent purposes.
The first time, he said was in April 2022. He said it was for Ndatuje to clear up some confusion over his wife’s travel documents.
“I have no doubt there’s going to be some suggestion that the communication was nefarious,” Beeman said.

On the second occasion, he said, Ndatuje was contacted by a friend at the Rwandan High Commission who was worried about the disappearance of a housekeeper who worked at the Ottawa residence of the Rwandan ambassador.

Beeman said his client told the friend to report the disappearance to police in Ottawa. He said Ndatuje, ON his own initiative, then checked the police database to see if anyone had reported the housekeeper missing.
There was no record of the housekeeper being missing, and the man was later found unharmed.
“He did the search because he cared about a missing person,” Beeman told court. “One would hope that every police officer in this country would share that attitude.”
Beeman told the judge he will not find any evidence Ndatuje discussed the database search with anyone.
Bill McCrimmon, a foreign service officer from Global Affairs Canada, testified the department got a call from the Rwandan high commissioner about the missing housekeeper.
The trial is scheduled to conclude early next month.

stories.title: 'It is fantastic news': With PQ set to take power in Quebec, the Bloc dreams of separation while Liberals stay quiet
stories.summary: Two weeks away from the Quebec election, the separatist Parti Québécois is well on its way to form government and is asking for a majority.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Quebec election is two weeks away and the separatist Parti Québécois is well on its way to form government, with new polling showing they remain in the lead.

While the Liberals either remain mum on the issue or claim that the situation can still change, Bloc Québécois MPs are already cherishing the idea of working with their provincial cousins to hold a third referendum for Quebec to separate from Canada.

“The election of the Parti Québécois will bring us closer to Quebec’s independence. And in that sense, for me, it is fantastic news, because it is a way to move toward our goal,” said Bloc MP Alexis Deschênes in an interview with National Post.

The PQ has promised to hold a referendum on separation in a first mandate, but only after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029. That means that the party would have a small window to hold one if it stays in power for a four-year term.

Deschênes said the last time the PQ took power with a promise to hold a referendum in the first mandate was in 1994 under Jacques Parizeau. He ended up holding a vote on separation a year later and nearly succeeded in Quebec seceding from Canada.

But for the moment, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is not campaigning on independence, instead insisting on good governance and slashing taxes. He even refused to say the word “referendum” in the first debate of the campaign.

Despite support for Quebec independence being at historical lows, Deschênes believes the PQ will respect its commitment to hold another referendum in a first mandate.

“What we see coming is the election of a Parti Québécois government with a mandate to achieve independence. So, it is a vitally important mandate,” he said.

How the desire for change and the threat of a referendum are shaping the Quebec election

Marc-Olivier Fortin: The Caq's fear-of-Trump campaign starts to crumble

Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet has been busy campaigning this summer with some PQ candidates in the suburbs of Montreal. His MPs have been doing the same, giving a helping hand to their local candidates in events and meeting stakeholders.

“It’s an organic relationship, I’d say. We’re part of the same family,” said Deschênes, who represents the riding of Gaspésie—Les Îles-de-la-Madeleine—Listuguj.

The federal Liberals are carefully not endorsing any of the provincial parties in the Quebec election to avoid any accusations of political interference from Ottawa.

Whilst there was speculation Prime Minister Mark Carney was backing incumbent premier Christine Fréchette because of their many joint announcements in the lead-up to the election, he has refrained from interacting with her since the writ dropped.

On Friday, Carney’s Quebec lieutenant Joël Lightbound said he was closely following the election in Quebec, but he said it is “too early to speculate on the election result” because there is still lots of time left and a large portion of voters are undecided.

“We will see what Quebecers decide, and then we will act in Quebec’s interest with the Quebec government,” he said.

But two more polls published on Monday are cementing the PQ’s lead as the frontrunner in Quebec, as has been the case for the last three years. Fréchette’s Coalition Avenir Québec and the provincial Liberals are still several points behind.

St-Pierre Plamondon is well on track to form a minority government as things stand right now, but he is now calling on voters to give him a majority mandate on Oct. 5.

Many federal Liberals questioned by the National Post would not comment on the scenario of another separatist threat looming in Canada, adding to the referendum in Alberta that could pave the way to another vote to secede from the rest of the country.

“My focus is here in Ottawa,” said Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, ON his way to the first question period of the fall session on Monday. “There are so many things to do. It will be a very busy session,” he added.

Liberal MP Sameer Zuberi, from Montreal, simply said he will be casting his vote in the Quebec election and is encouraging every Quebecer to do the same.

The PQ has vowed to pull out of federal priorities, such as the Alto high-speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City, and possibly review others, like the Churchill Falls energy deal between Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador.

His Liberal colleague Jean-Yves Duclos, from Quebec City, said that the federal government will do everything in its power to work collaboratively with the party that will form government in Quebec on Oct. 5, including working on those two priorities.

But he admits that, depending on the colour of the next government in the National Assembly, the federal level might have to “work harder” than with others.

On Monday, the federal Liberals were cheering in the House of Commons as they welcomed one of their newest additions to caucus, Chicoutimi—Le Fjord MP Daniel Gobeil, who won the byelection in Quebec with more than 50 per cent of the vote.

In the coming months, three more federal seats in Quebec will be up for grabs. And with Carney’s popularity in the province, Lightbound already sees more room for growth.

“I never take anything for granted, but you can see that people are satisfied.”

National Post calevesque@postmedia.com

stories.title: 48% of northern Canadians say Trump’s U.S. is biggest threat to Arctic
stories.summary: Northerners want the federal government to take a firm line on any disputes in the Arctic over borders or resources, according to new polling.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Nearly half of those in Canada’s North see the U.S. under President Donald Trump as the greatest threat to Arctic security, new polling data suggests.

The polling, conducted for researchers at Quebec’s Observatoire de la politique et la sécurité de l’Arctique (Opsa), asked residents in Nunavut, Northwest Territories, Yukon and Nunavik for their views on which countries pose the biggest threat, and suggests “heightened anxiety.”

Close to half of respondents (48 per cent) saw the U.S. as the greatest threat to the region, followed distantly by countries more traditionally seen as Canadian adversaries like Russia (30 per cent) and China (12 per cent).

That’s up from 37 per cent who said the U.S. posed the greatest threat last September , followed by Moscow (35 per cent) and Beijing (17 per cent).

“It’s really surprising to see that number so high,” said Mathieu Landriault, Opsa’s director, in an interview with Global News on Monday.

“I think it really supports this vision that we need to develop (Arctic) capabilities and, if push comes to shove, without the U.S. involved or with as little involvement by the U.S. as possible.”

That Canada’s erstwhile closest ally was viewed as the most significant security threat was both surprising and not, Landriault said. For generations, Canada and the U.S. have closely cooperated on northern security and continental defence, with the former Soviet Union as their main adversary.

But despite Russia’s willingness to wage war on neighbouring Ukraine, Trump’s rhetoric around the annexation of Canada and threats over Greenland have clearly rattled citizens in the North. It also might explain why northerners told Opsa that they want the federal government to take a hard line on any border or resource ownership disputes with other countries.

A clear majority, 60 per cent, of respondents said that Canada should take a “firm line” in defending its sections of the Arctic, compared to just 26 per cent that felt its better to “negotiate a compromise.”

The polling was released at a time when the federal government has renewed its focus on Canada’s North, both in terms of infrastructure investments and the possibility of expanded resource extraction.

It also comes as Canada explores greater cooperation with the European Union, including in the Arctic. In her state of the union speech last week, EU President Ursula von der Leyen suggested the Arctic would become a “flagship joint project” between the EU and Canada.

“Globally … northerners have a positive perception of European countries,” Landriault said.

“What we see, however, from northern respondents when we asked them what would be the preferred approach if there are disputes in the Arctic … compromise, or let’s negotiate and strike a compromise in the Arctic region, is not the first reflex, it’s not what (northerners) want Ottawa to do.”

“That being said, I think most people see partnerships as desirable if there are no disputes,” Landriault added.

The possibility of a conventional military threat to Canada’s Arctic remains remote, experts have told Global News — although troubling reports out of Europe over the weekend raised the spectre of Russian aggression towards Nato member states.

The Guardian newspaper, citing three European intelligence officials, reported on Sunday that the continent’s spy agencies have considered the possibility of “imminent” action by Russia to test the Nato alliance.

The newspaper pointed to recent comments by Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, that a Russian incursion on allied territory could seek to prove that Article 5 — Nato’s assurance of mutual assistance if a member is attacked — is “more theoretical than practical.”

On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters that the threat of Russia “hybrid attacks” on France and European countries has intensified in recent weeks.

“The intention behind it is to intimidate us and to derail the effort to support the Ukrainians. The consequence will be the opposite,” Macron told reporters, according to the France 24 news outlet.

“We are not intimidated, because we know that what is at stake today in Ukraine is our security.”

That Canada’s erstwhile closest ally was viewed as the most significant security threat was both surprising and not, Landriault said. For generations, Canada and the U.S. have closely cooperated on northern security and continental defence, with the former Soviet Union as their main adversary.

But despite Russia’s willingness to wage war on neighbouring Ukraine, Trump’s rhetoric around the annexation of Canada and threats over Greenland have clearly rattled citizens in the North. It also might explain why northerners told Opsa that they want the federal government to take a hard line on any border or resource ownership disputes with other countries.

A clear majority, 60 per cent, of respondents said that Canada should take a “firm line” in defending its sections of the Arctic, compared to just 26 per cent that felt its better to “negotiate a compromise.”

The polling was released at a time when the federal government has renewed its focus on Canada’s North, both in terms of infrastructure investments and the possibility of expanded resource extraction.

It also comes as Canada explores greater cooperation with the European Union, including in the Arctic. In her state of the union speech last week, EU President Ursula von der Leyen suggested the Arctic would become a “flagship joint project” between the EU and Canada.
“Globally … northerners have a positive perception of European countries,” Landriault said.

“What we see, however, from northern respondents when we asked them what would be the preferred approach if there are disputes in the Arctic … compromise, or let’s negotiate and strike a compromise in the Arctic region, is not the first reflex, it’s not what (northerners) want Ottawa to do.”
“That being said, I think most people see partnerships as desirable if there are no disputes,” Landriault added.

The possibility of a conventional military threat to Canada’s Arctic remains remote, experts have told Global News — although troubling reports out of Europe over the weekend raised the spectre of Russian aggression towards Nato member states.

The Guardian newspaper, citing three European intelligence officials, reported on Sunday that the continent’s spy agencies have considered the possibility of “imminent” action by Russia to test the Nato alliance.

The newspaper pointed to recent comments by Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, that a Russian incursion on allied territory could seek to prove that Article 5 — Nato’s assurance of mutual assistance if a member is attacked — is “more theoretical than practical.”
On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters that the threat of Russia “hybrid attacks” on France and European countries has intensified in recent weeks.
“The intention behind it is to intimidate us and to derail the effort to support the Ukrainians. The consequence will be the opposite,” Macron told reporters, according to the France 24 news outlet.
“We are not intimidated, because we know that what is at stake today in Ukraine is our security.”

stories.title: Vancouver Mayor Ken Sim urges province against election amid municipal campaign
stories.summary: Premier David Eby told NDP legislators last week they need to be "election ready," and there's rampant speculation an early vote could be called soon.
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
is urging the British Columbia government not to call an early election until after municipal voting on Oct. 17 that he says deserves the “full, undivided attention” of residents.

Premier David Eby told NDP legislators last week they need to be “election ready,” and there’s rampant speculation an early vote could be called soon.

Sim says time and attention need to be devoted to municipal issues and his views are consistent with the Union of B.C. Municipalities, which passed a motion last week asking the provincial government to preserve the integrity of local elections by avoiding overlapping campaigns.

Sim was speaking at a press conference on Monday to launch his ABC Vancouver party’s platform.

ABC says it’s three “anchor commitments” involve addressing public safety and street disorder, affordability and accountability at City Hall, and jobs and the economy.

It says it would ban open-air hard drug use in public spaces, commit to a zero-per-cent property tax increase in 2027, and rebuild the Vancouver Aquatic Centre and revitalize the Granville Street entertainment district.

Businessman Sim first ran for mayor in 2018 with the Non-Partisan Association and narrowly lost to Kennedy Stewart, before reversing the result with ABC in 2022.

stories.title: Oil prices and bond yields give back some of last week’s jumps
stories.summary: Oil prices are swinging as some crude from the Middle East is able to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, though nowhere nearly as much as the industry and customers would like.
stories.author: Chan Ho-him And Michelle Chapman
stories.content:
U.S. stocks are climbing with markets worldwide on Monday after oil prices and yields in the bond market gave back some of their jumps from last week.

The S&P 500 rose 1.5 per cent and pulled within 0.4 per cent of its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 348 points, or 0.7 per cent, as of 2:20 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.2 per cent higher.

They got help from the price for a barrel of Brent oil falling 3.4 per cent to $100.29 USD.

While that’s still much higher than its roughly $72 price from earlier this summer, it’s down from the nearly $110 it touched last week.

Oil prices are swinging up and down as some crude from the Middle East is able to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, though nowhere nearly as much as the industry and customers would like because of the war with Iran.

Morgan Stanley’s Michael Wilson said another leg higher in prices for oil, gasoline and other refined products is the main risk he sees in the near term that could keep the U.S. stock market from rising to his forecasted target for the year’s end.

The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline across the United States has already climbed to nearly $4.48 USD, according to AAA. That’s up from less than $4.32 USD just a week earlier and from $3.18 USD a year ago.

Monday’s pullback in oil prices helped lower the pressure coming from the bond market.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.97 per cent from 5.01 per cent late Friday after it crossed above the five per cent threshold last week for the first time in three years.

Yields have been on the rise because of worries about inflation, big debt loads for governments worldwide and other factors. That hurts the economy because high yields make it more expensive not only for the U.S. government to borrow money to pay its bills but also for households and businesses.

Worries remain about how much oil is available for customers worldwide, ING commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson wrote in a commentary on Monday.

However, they said profit-taking by investors after the recent jump in oil prices, together with hopes for constructive discussions at this week’s UN General Assembly and at a meeting between China’s and the United States’ leaders, helped improve optimism.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters following talks Sunday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York that the U.S. had “a very successful engagement” with the Chinese side. Bessent said talks with China touched on trade and AI. China and the United States have been discussing reciprocal tariff reductions on $30 billion worth of goods from each side. In Beijing, China’s Foreign Ministry on Monday confirmed that Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States between Sept. 23 and 25. Experts and policymakers believe trade, tariffs, and AI safety are likely among the topics to be on the agenda. The war in Iran and developments in the Middle East and ties between China and Iran could also be discussed.

On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry continued to stabilize following their worldwide slide at the start of last week. Leaders of the AI industry have recently warned a slowdown is needed in the industry’s development for the safety of humanity.

Stocks enmeshed in the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, rallied after bitcoin’s price rose back above $85,000 and returned to where it was in January.

Stock indexes around the world also climbed thanks to the easing of oil prices and bond yields.

Indexes gained 0.9 per cent in France, 1.2 per cent in Hong Kong and 1.6 per cent in South Korea.
