stories.title: The Canadian Opera Company’s unmissable La Traviata features a world-class Violetta
stories.summary: American coloratura soprano Kathryn Lewek is enchanting in the role, as expressive an actor as singer in Arin Arbus’s excellent staging
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Title: La Traviata

Written by: Giuseppe Verdi

Conductor: Paolo Carignani

Director: Arin Arbus

Company: Canadian Opera Company, co-produced with Houston Grand Opera and Lyric Opera of Chicago

Venue: Four Seasons Centre for the Performing Arts

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until Oct. 17

Audiences love a gilded cage. Succession ’s Kendall Roy, the strung-out heir to an all-powerful media company, makes contemptible choices; he’s also among TV’s most pitiable characters. The Great Gatsby ’s Daisy Buchanan, glossed with money, wants for nothing; and yet, by the novel’s shattering denouement, she wants for everything.

Giuseppe Verdi’s La Traviata , adapted from Alexandre Dumas fils’s La Dame aux Camélias and staged by director Arin Arbus with a profound sensitivity toward the suffering at the opera’s core, explores this idea at length. Courtesan Violetta (American coloratura soprano Kathryn Lewek) lives a life of opulent parties, in which each meal concludes in a symphony of cakes and croquembouches. Even her fellow guests look like pastries, dressed in layered gowns and towering headpieces as they chatter and groove. Life is sweet at the fringes of 19th-century France’s aristocracy, we can surmise.

Small problem, however: Violetta is dying of consumption.

La Traviata hits all the emotional beats you’d want from a melodrama of its musical scope. When Alfredo (Long Long), a visitor from the French countryside, convinces her to abandon her world of urban abundance to live with him, there’s a moment of hope – perhaps she’ll survive her disease, and craft a more meaningful future for herself away from Paris.

But Violetta can’t outrun her social standing as a courtesan. When Alfredo’s father (Russell Braun) catches wind of the relationship, he orders her to leave his son, demanding she must not tell him why. Soon enough, she’s back on the scene in Paris, with friend Flora (Ariana Maubach) and maid Annina (Emma Pennell) by her side as she schmoozes.

When Violetta and Alfredo finally reunite at her death bed, her disappearance at once forgiven, there’s that familiar whisper of possibility: Maybe she really will overcome the tuberculosis ravaging her chest. But instead, she dies in her lover’s arms, yet another casualty of the era’s vicious reputational politics.

Lewek, as expressive an actor as a singer, brings overflowing subtlety and depth to Violetta. Her eyes sparkle such that they’re likely visible from any of the Four Seasons Centre for the Performing Arts’ 2,071 seats; her high notes, even the high E-flat at the end of Sempre Libera, glimmer with elegant poise.

In a role performed by thousands of sopranos since the mid-19th century, Lewek threatens to eclipse a good percentage of them, including in the second act’s more robust vocal passages: At the conclusion of Friday night’s opening performance, the audience was appropriately rapturous, showering Lewek in a chorus of brava s and whistles.

Long, meanwhile, offers a more grounding presence to Alfredo, intentional in how he doles out the young nobleman’s inner angst. The tenor’s smooth voice pairs perfectly with Lewek’s, and their duet Un dì, felice, eterea in La Traviata ’s first act is enchanting – and achingly melancholy – in its parallel musings on the budding romance. In his early attempts to woo Violetta, Alfredo calls his love the “pulse of the universe, the whole universe,” the orchestra’s strings ebbing like a heartbeat underneath.

“I don’t know how to love,” responds Violetta in return – simply, playfully. Surely, she intimates, she has time for such coyness in her attraction to her unexpected suitor. Consumption be damned.

Director Arbus conjures a carnivalesque world in which ornate walls extend well into the heavens, cage-like in their containment of Violetta and her innermost dreams. Animals infiltrate a party gone wrong through out-of-this-world puppets by costume designer Cait O’Connor, whose structured frocks and suits suggest an almost Eyes Wide Shut -like absurdism to Violetta’s final days.

Set designer Ricardo Hernandez, meanwhile, takes “let them eat cake” rather literally: His attractive tablescapes are bursting with them, slick with frosting and visibly devoid of nutritional substance. Long shadows from Marcus Doshi’s clever lighting design further amp up the production’s surrealist edge.

It’s not often an operatic production of La Traviata ’s scale so entirely comes together in directorial vision, aesthetic experimentation and musical performance. Not only does this one have a point of view – there’s no guessing at its thesis on the futility of glamour – but as conducted by Paolo Carignani, La Traviata is a well-balanced gift for the ears, and hardly feels its three-hour runtime.

Spare a thought for the upper crust? Yeah, right. But La Traviata intimately conveys the sort of pity that transcends social class – and the sort of world-class singing you’d be foolish to miss hearing on a Canadian stage.

stories.title: B.C. government sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge mass shooting
stories.summary: Province seeking accountability from AI company and to recover costs, says Attorney General Niki Sharma
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
British Columbia Attorney General Niki Sharma says the government has filed a lawsuit against artificial intelligence company OpenAI in California over the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.

Sharma says the province is seeking accountability from the company and to recover costs associated with the shootings in February in which eight victims died.

She says OpenAI failed to warn police of interactions between the shooter and OpenAI’s chatbot ChatGP, and although she has not read the conversations, the province has asked for them.

Survivors and witnesses, including pupils and staff at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where six victims and the shooter died, are already privately suing OpenAI.

Sharma says laws and safety frameworks have not kept pace with AI technology and companies cannot be left to regulate themselves.

She says she has written to federal officials asking for changes to Canada’s Criminal Code to ensure AI companies can be held accountable for criminal conduct arising from their technologies.

stories.title: Conservatives criticized over appointment of candidate to run in Ontario byelection
stories.summary: Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is facing criticism from within his own party after choosing to appoint a candidate to run in an upcoming byelection in southern Ontario, instead of holding a nomination contest.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is facing criticism from within his own party after choosing to appoint a candidate to run in an upcoming byelection in southern Ontario, instead of holding a nomination contest.

Poilievre announced at a rally on Sunday the party chose outgoing Brantford, Ont., mayor Kevin Davis to carry the Tory banner in the byelection. The news prompted the two former members of Parliament for the area to walk out of the event.

The seat in Brantford-Brant South became vacant on Friday, when Larry Brock stepped down to return to his former role as a Crown prosecutor.

On Saturday, Brock appeared in a video on social media with Dave Carrol, the man he wanted to “hand over the baton to” as the Conservative candidate.

Carrol, a local pastor and longtime member of the Conservative party, shared the video, in which Brock said Carrol was “well poised to take over” and credited him with helping win the riding in 2021 and 2025.

A day later, Poilievre surprised many — including Carrol — when he announced Davis’s name will be on the ballot.

“We need someone who can fight for Brantford-Brant South the way that Larry Brock has for the last five years,” Poilievre said at the rally in Brantford.

“We need someone who will fight for Canada and fight for you, who will fight to save you money, save your job, keep you safe, fix immigration and put Canada first. And that person is your mayor, Kevin Davis.”

Brock, who was seated behind Poilievre at the event, left his seat seconds after the announcement was made. He did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Phil McColeman, who represented the seat for the Conservatives for 13 years before Brock, also stood up and walked out. He told the Brantford Expositor he was upset about the decision not to hold an open nomination.

A byelection has not yet been called in Brantford-Brant South. It must be called within six months of the seat becoming vacant.

A spokesperson for the Conservative party said Poilievre exercised his authority to choose Davis “to ensure a candidate was in place and ready to hit the ground running.”

“Kevin Davis was overwhelmingly endorsed by local grassroots Conservatives at the rally (Sunday), including the riding association president Caine Chapman, Larry Brock’s former campaign manager Phil Gillies, nomination opponent Josh Wall, and two candidates for mayor,” said Sarah Fischer in a statement.

Carrol said he had been working for six weeks to secure the nomination, and that he had the support of both Brock and McColeman.

“I wish Kevin Davis well, but I would be less than honest if I said I wasn’t deeply disappointed,” he posted on social media on Sunday.

Carrol said the party’s grassroots tradition is what drew him to the Conservatives, and noted that he has been active in fundraising, door-knocking and supporting local candidates.

“I think an open nomination process is a good thing. It tests the candidates to prove they have the support of party members and the community,” he wrote.

Poilievre, as party leader, has the ability to appoint candidates in up to eight ridings between elections.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Summer May be over, but London's construction season isn't
stories.summary: If it seems like there's a lot of roadwork going on right now, “It’s because there is,” said Jennie Dann, the city’s director of construction and infrastructure.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: If it seems like there's a lot of roadwork going on right now, “It’s because there is,” said Jennie Dann, the city’s director of construction and infrastructure.
· Posted: Sep 21, 2026 3:00 PM EDT | Last Updated: 6 hours ago

The summer season May be coming to a close, but the construction continues across London, with several major roadwork projects finally entering the homestretch, and others still a long way from completion.
The traffic troubles include spots such as Commissioners Road at Highbury Avenue, Queens Avenue over the Thames River, and Wellington Road through Base Line and Commissioners Roads, to name a few.

“This is the biggest construction season we’ve ever seen, and there are a number of factors that are driving that. We’re a rapidly growing city … We also have a lot of projects that are receiving federal and provincial funding to support housing, and those projects come with timelines."
Old South neighbours fed up with traffic, trucks cutting through residential streets
Here's what you need to know about London's new centre-running bus lanes
The city also has to ensure existing infrastructure at the end of its life, including sewers and watermains built decades ago, gets replaced before an emergency break forces the city’s hand.
City officials are already looking ahead to next year, Dann said.

“We have a map-based system that lays out the projects folks are thinking about doing. We talk to project managers about their readiness, about the impacts — is it lane reduction, or is it a full closure — so we can understand how we’re going to … minimize overlapping impacts, ” she said.
“But sometimes we have work that just is necessary; it can’t be deferred any further.”

The ongoing build-out of London’s bus rapid transit system has been a particular thorn in the side of drivers. A portion of the Wellington Gateway route’s centre-running lanes opened earlier this month, but more intensive work continues south of the Thames River.

In east London, work on the East London Link continues to cause headaches for motorists along Highbury Avenue, Dundas Street and Oxford Street, compounded by a major development taking shape on the old London Psychiatric Hospital grounds.
A rendering of what an operational East London Link is expected to look like outside of Fanshawe College. (City of London)
Among the firms working on the multi-year project is Bre-Ex Construction, a London-based company which specializes in heavy civil construction projects, such as roads and sewers.
The company is working on both the East London Link and the Wellington Gateway, and is in a good position to close out for the end of the season, said Cory Brekelmans, Bre-Ex’s president.

“What I mean by that is getting surface works, curb and asphalt, and getting it open for the winter. (There’s) usually a big push come fall, just because of weather and the minimizing amount of hours in the day,” Brekelmans said.

“The only one that’s been a little behind is Dundas Street. There was some unforeseen infrastructure that had to be moved before we could continue. But even with that delay, we’re still on pace to get it concluded for the winter to get things mobile and keep things moving.”
City transportation head says delays will be worth it as Highbury overhaul begins
More construction begins on Wellington as end of southern BRT project inches closer
Brekelmans understands the public’s frustration around roadwork, and how it can sometimes feel like road cones and lane closures are everywhere to be found, but not construction workers.
Some work May require a longer lead time, or specialized contractors who May be in high demand but short supply, but whose work is necessary to complete other components.

“The bus shelters, some of the line painting … some of the bus rapid transit lanes and stuff like that, that all takes time and is very very weather sensitive,” Brekelmans said. Recent heavy rains have also posed a challenge in completing necessary concrete flat work, which needs to cure.

“I can assure you there’s consistent work, and sometimes there’s lag time. Like some of these bus shelters are specialty parts … traffic, street lights, like the aluminum poles and stuff like that, there’s some time lag. And it depends on factories, (which) sometimes have issues with supply.”
Here’s where some major construction projects are at heading into the fall:

The eastern leg of the bus rapid transit network, connecting downtown to the Fanshawe College, is in its final third, fourth and fifth phases, the city says. A closure on Dundas Street between Ashland and Highbury avenues will go into the fall, while the Highbury bridge will be fully operational in the spring.
City of London map showing the multiple phases of the East London Link project. (City of London)

Major work has finished on Clark’s Bridge and on phase three, from Wilkins Street to Southdale Road. Phase four, from Southdale to Exeter Road, will see paving this fall. Phase two, from Watson to Wilkins streets, will continue through 2029.
City of London map showing the multiple phases of the Wellington Gateway project. The city says major work on Clark's Bridge and Phase 3 is finished. (City of London)

Rehabilitation work began in June from Adelaide Street to North Centre Road. Work on the south side of Fanshawe is set to finish in early October, shift to the north side, and finish by the end of the month. Overnight closures are expected late this month for watermain work, with milling and paving work in early November, the city says.

Part of a larger project to upgrade the concrete expressway from the Thames River to Hwy. 401, and carry out bridge work at Bradley Avenue and Commissioners Road. Crews are working on the northbound lanes from Commissioners to the river, and northbound ramps at Commissioners are closed. Work south to Hwy. 401 will start next year, the city says.
A city map showing the scope of the project's four phases. (City of London)

A key link connecting downtown to west London, work on the 53-year-old span began in the spring to replace and widen the deck, and improve pedestrian and cycling connections. Work on the north half of the bridge is finished, and is underway on the south half, with completion set for the spring.
City of London map showing the extent of work to rehabilitate the Queen's Bridge. (City of London)

York Street has reopened from Wellington to Waterloo streets, and will see final paving from Clarence Street to Wellington in early October, the city says. The intersection of York and Colborne streets will reopen in mid-October, and top asphalt from Wellington to Colborne will finish next year.
Map from the City of London showing work along York Street. (City of London)

stories.title: NDP leader Lewis criticized for saying Jews ‘failed to do our part’ to stop Gaza war
stories.summary: Ottawa — Critics are calling out NDP Leader Avi Lewis for suggesting online that he and his fellow Jews have failed to do their part to stop Israel's carnage in the Gaza Strip.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis poses for a photograph in Montreal on Tuesday, July 28, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Christopher Katsarov

By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted September 21, 2026 2:57 pm.

Last Updated September 21, 2026 4:57 pm.

Ottawa — Critics are calling out NDP Leader Avi Lewis for suggesting online that he and his fellow Jews have “failed” to do their part to stop Israel’s violence in the Gaza Strip.

Lewis posted Sunday that he is marking the holiest day on the Jewish calendar, Yom Kippur, by reflecting on geopolitics.

“For Jewish people, the personal has always been political and the political always personal. This year I’m reflecting on the fact that we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name,” Lewis posted Sunday evening on the platform X.

Lewis’s post did not directly mention the war that started in October 2023, when Hamas killed 1,200 people in a gruesome surprise attack on Israel.

Since then, tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed by Israeli strikes that frequently hit civilian areas, and by Israeli policies that led to an international declaration of famine.

Liberal MPs Anthony Housefather and Ben Carr, who are Jewish, both pushed back on Lewis’s comments, saying it’s wrong to collectively hold Jews responsible for the actions of Israel.

When asked whether Lewis’s comment was antisemitic, Carr called it “naive.”

“That’s an irresponsible thing for a leader to say,” the Winnipeg MP said.

“It’s dangerous and it’s the type of narrative that is actually contributing to the type of threats that we’re seeing levied against the Jewish community.”

Housefather wrote on X that Lewis’s post was “despicable.”

Lewis made the post before a shooting on Sunday outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., while worshippers were inside to mark Yom Kippur.

His office said he plans to speak about the matter on Parliament Hill on Monday.

The federal government’s official definition of antisemitism cautions against holding Jews collectively accountable for Israel’s actions because it can fuel anti-Jewish hate.

Advocates have linked that notion of collective responsibility to multiple attacks on Jewish institutions, including Sunday’s attack in Belleville.

Lewis condemned that attack Monday.

“The shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville is deeply upsetting, and has traumatized a community that gathered to pray,” he wrote on the platform X.

“I am sending love and solidarity to the Jewish community in Belleville and across the country on this Yom Kippur, the most solemn and holiest day of the year.”

Some — including former Canadian ambassador to Israel Jon Allen — argue that major Jewish groups in Canada are creating the false impression that they support Israel’s actions against Palestinians by not calling out the Israeli government.

“By not calling out what’s happening in the West Bank and Gaza, there is a complicity of silence,” Allen told a Senate committee this past June, adding that he himself is Jewish.

“The failure sometimes, frankly, of the Jewish community” to speak out against Israeli government actions “makes people in Canada say, ‘Well, do they support everything Israel does? Do they support what happened in Gaza?’” he testified.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

— With files from David Baxter

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

paragraphs: Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis poses for a photograph in Montreal on Tuesday, July 28, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Christopher Katsarov
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press
Posted September 21, 2026 2:57 pm.
Last Updated September 21, 2026 4:57 pm.
Ottawa — Critics are calling out NDP Leader Avi Lewis for suggesting online that he and his fellow Jews have “failed” to do their part to stop Israel’s violence in the Gaza Strip.
Lewis posted Sunday that he is marking the holiest day on the Jewish calendar, Yom Kippur, by reflecting on geopolitics.

“For Jewish people, the personal has always been political and the political always personal. This year I’m reflecting on the fact that we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name,” Lewis posted Sunday evening on the platform X.
Lewis’s post did not directly mention the war that started in October 2023, when Hamas killed 1,200 people in a gruesome surprise attack on Israel.
Since then, tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed by Israeli strikes that frequently hit civilian areas, and by Israeli policies that led to an international declaration of famine.
Liberal MPs Anthony Housefather and Ben Carr, who are Jewish, both pushed back on Lewis’s comments, saying it’s wrong to collectively hold Jews responsible for the actions of Israel.
When asked whether Lewis’s comment was antisemitic, Carr called it “naive.”
“That’s an irresponsible thing for a leader to say,” the Winnipeg MP said.
“It’s dangerous and it’s the type of narrative that is actually contributing to the type of threats that we’re seeing levied against the Jewish community.”
Housefather wrote on X that Lewis’s post was “despicable.”
Lewis made the post before a shooting on Sunday outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., while worshippers were inside to mark Yom Kippur.
His office said he plans to speak about the matter on Parliament Hill on Monday.
The federal government’s official definition of antisemitism cautions against holding Jews collectively accountable for Israel’s actions because it can fuel anti-Jewish hate.
Advocates have linked that notion of collective responsibility to multiple attacks on Jewish institutions, including Sunday’s attack in Belleville.
Lewis condemned that attack Monday.
“The shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville is deeply upsetting, and has traumatized a community that gathered to pray,” he wrote on the platform X.
“I am sending love and solidarity to the Jewish community in Belleville and across the country on this Yom Kippur, the most solemn and holiest day of the year.”

Some — including former Canadian ambassador to Israel Jon Allen — argue that major Jewish groups in Canada are creating the false impression that they support Israel’s actions against Palestinians by not calling out the Israeli government.
“By not calling out what’s happening in the West Bank and Gaza, there is a complicity of silence,” Allen told a Senate committee this past June, adding that he himself is Jewish.

“The failure sometimes, frankly, of the Jewish community” to speak out against Israeli government actions “makes people in Canada say, ‘Well, do they support everything Israel does? Do they support what happened in Gaza?’” he testified.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.
— With files from David Baxter
Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.summary: Ontario's police watchdog is investigating after a 29-year-old man allegedly opened fire at a constable stationed outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Sunday night. stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Pedestrians pass by a police car parked outside Shaarei Shomayim synagogue in Toronto, ON Sunday, March 8, 2026. The synagogue was struck with gunfire overnight. THE Canadian Press/Sammy Kogan The Canadian Press

By The Canadian Press

Posted September 21, 2026 2:57 pm.

Last Updated September 22, 2026 1:47 pm.

Ontario’s police watchdog is investigating after a 29-year-old man allegedly opened fire at a constable stationed outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Sunday night. The resulting shootout left both the suspect and the officer with serious injuries and sparked widespread condemnation from political leaders. Police have declined to comment on a possible motive in the attack.

Here are some other violent incidents that have taken place at or near Canadian synagogues and Jewish institutions in the last few years.

June 2026: Police are called for a fire at Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom in Westmount, Que., ON the island of Montreal. The synagogue’s rabbi said at the time the fire appeared to have been triggered by a Molotov cocktail tossed at a window. A 38-year-old man is arrested and was expected to face charges.

April and May 2026:A man in Toronto allegedly carries out two assaults against members of the Jewish community using a gel blaster imitation gun. One of the incidents takes place outside the Congregation Chasidei Bobov synagogue. The 18-year-old suspect is charged with assault with a weapon and possessing a weapon for a dangerous purpose.

March 2026:Two Toronto-area synagogues, the Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto synagogue in Vaughan, Ont., and Shaarei Shomayim synagogue in Toronto’s north end, are damaged by gunfire overnight. No injuries are reported. Over the following months, police arrest three suspects aged 17, 18 and 23 and charge them with several offences. York regional police said last month they are no longer seeking suspects, but the investigation is ongoing.

December 2024:A Montreal-area synagogue, Congregation Beth Tikvah in Dollard-des-Ormeaux, Que., is firebombed, causing minor damage to the building and the nearby offices of a Jewish community group. Months later, police arrest a 19-year-old man and charge him with arson and other offences.

December 2024:A Jewish girls’ school in Toronto’s north end is damaged in an overnight shooting. Police said the suspects were allegedly seen shooting from inside a vehicle before fleeing. They said Bais Chaya Mushka in North York had also been the target of two similar shootings in October and May of that year.

May 2024: The front door of the Schara Tzedeck synagogue in Vancouver is charred in an alleged arson. No one is injured.

May 2024: Bullet holes are found in the front of a Montreal building housing a Jewish school, Belz, and the Young Israel of Montreal synagogue.

November 2023:Montreal police find bullet holes in the door of the Yeshiva Gedola school and bullet casings on the ground. Police said a suspect had been seen firing a weapon at the school before taking off in a vehicle. A 20-year-old man is arrested months later and charged with offences including discharging a firearm and vehicle theft.

November 2023:The front door of the Congregation Beth Tikvah synagogue and the back door of the nearby Jewish organization Federation CJA office in a Montreal suburb are damaged in two overnight firebombings. The buildings were empty at the time.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: National Indigenous Scholarship recipient inspired by lacrosse and community
stories.summary: Brooke Macdonald brings a lifelong passion for lacrosse and sports medicine aspirations to Western.
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
Just two days before training camp began, Brooke Macdonald was medically cleared to play lacrosse after being out of the game for more than a year. The National Indigenous Scholarship recipient worked her way back from a serious knee injury to try out for the Mustangs women’s lacrosse team in late August.

She brings her passion for the sport, commitment to Indigenous community leadership and aspirations in sports medicine to London, Ont. this fall, as a first-year kinesiology student at Western University.

Returning to the field after reconstructive surgery and 12 months of physiotherapy proved challenging. Macdonald battled muscle pain, shin splints, exhaustion and rainy, sweltering weather throughout the Mustangs tryouts.

“All that just goes away once I get on the field. My head is in the playing zone,” she said.

It’s a familiar headspace after nine years of playing lacrosse competitively, capturing three provincial championships with Six Nations youth teams and competing internationally for two seasons with the Haudenosaunee Nationals. Macdonald’s athleticism also led her to basketball, volleyball, hockey and track, but lacrosse always calls her back. At Western, she found the 36 other aspiring Mustangs vying for one of 20 spots on the playing roster to be highly competitive, yet collegial, no matter how intense the game.

National Indigenous Scholarship recipient, Brooke Macdonald (right), was one of 37 aspiring Western Mustangs trying out for the women’s lacrosse team. (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

“I love the sisterhood in lacrosse and I love the coaching that pushes us really hard to get better.I’ve grown already through tryouts for Western’s lacrosse team,”she said.

Though Macdonald didn’t end up on the final roster, she plans to keep playing recreationally while training for the next opportunity. She credits her parents with instilling the work ethic that carried her through a demanding tryout camp – five practices a week plus weekend games – and the discipline to maintain a 94 per cent average in high school.

Macdonald’s academic achievement helped her earn aNational Indigenous Scholarship at Western,awarded not just for high grades, but for creative thinking and contributions to Indigenous communities.She put that into practice by organizing lacrosse games to support campaigns such asEvery Child Matters.Her community-mindedness traces back toSix Nations of the Grand River, where her grandmother was raised, and where she acquired a love for the game that runs deeper than sport.

National Indigenous Scholarship recipient Brooke Macdonald (second from left) with her mother, Ilana, father, John, and brother, Will, at the Hamilton Tiger-Cat stadium, where the CFL team honoured John as an alumnus. (Submitted)

Lacrosse carriescenturies of history rooted in Indigenous traditions. Known as Baggataway or Tewaarathon, among other names,the game was played long before French settlers called it “la crosse”. The Haudenosaunee call it the Medicine Game, a gift from the Creator played to heal communities, honour Elders and settle disputes. Its enduring heritage on Six Nations territory fostered Macdonald’s feeling of belonging.

“Growing up in Brantford,Ont.,I felt a little less connected to my family’s community, but playing lacrosse on Six Nations closed that gap.I really bonded with the girls there,” she said.

The experience drew her to coaching younger girls on Six Nations and in theHamilton Lacrosse Association. Her dad was her inspiration. The retired professional football player is now a teacher and coach at the high school she attended, where he coached her hockey team. He also coached her lacrosse team on Six Nations.

Macdonald’s own commitment to younger players is reflected in the influence of those who’ve helped her along the way.

“My dad’s a great role model, alongside other wonderful coaches and teammates who supported me in life and lacrosse. And my mom is my best friend.”

Her family and mentors have anchored not only how Macdonald approaches lacrosse, but how she sees her future. She’s studying kinesiology in Western’sFaculty of Health Sciences,with plans to build a career in rehabilitation therapy and improve access to specialized care in Indigenous communities.She believes her own positive experience with rehabilitation will provide a foundation for the compassionate care she hopes to offer others.

National Indigenous Scholarship recipient Brooke Macdonald. (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

“My doctors and physiotherapists were just so amazing, I want to contribute in the same way to help people recover, especially in Indigenous communities where specialties like sports medicine aren’t very common,”she said.

Macdonald envisions a future that allows her to remain connected to the sport that has shaped her. She hopes to continue coaching children’s lacrosse, sharing the guidance she received with the next generation.

“I’m very lucky to have had so many people contributing to develop every piece of me. I want to pay it forward through mentorship and future work in sports medicine.”

Learn more about how Western ispreparing future leaders and global citizens.

Though Macdonald didn’t end up on the final roster, she plans to keep playing recreationally while training for the next opportunity. She credits her parents with instilling the work ethic that carried her through a demanding tryout camp – five practices a week plus weekend games – and the discipline to maintain a 94 per cent average in high school.

content_blocks.alt: National Indigenous Scholarship recipient Brooke MacDonald with her parents and brother, wearing Hamilton Tiger-Cats jerseys

content_blocks.text: National Indigenous Scholarship recipient finds connection through lacrosse

Macdonald’s academic achievement helped her earn aNational Indigenous Scholarship at Western,awarded not just for high grades, but for creative thinking and contributions to Indigenous communities.She put that into practice by organizing lacrosse games to support campaigns such asEvery Child Matters.Her community-mindedness traces back toSix Nations of the Grand River, where her grandmother was raised, and where she acquired a love for the game that runs deeper than sport.

National Indigenous Scholarship recipient Brooke Macdonald (second from left) with her mother, Ilana, father, John, and brother, Will, at the Hamilton Tiger-Cat stadium, where the CFL team honoured John as an alumnus. (Submitted)

Lacrosse carriescenturies of history rooted in Indigenous traditions. Known as Baggataway or Tewaarathon, among other names,the game was played long before French settlers called it “la crosse”. The Haudenosaunee call it the Medicine Game, a gift from the Creator played to heal communities, honour Elders and settle disputes. Its enduring heritage on Six Nations territory fostered Macdonald’s feeling of belonging.
“Growing up in Brantford,Ont.,I felt a little less connected to my family’s community, but playing lacrosse on Six Nations closed that gap.I really bonded with the girls there,” she said.

The experience drew her to coaching younger girls on Six Nations and in theHamilton Lacrosse Association. Her dad was her inspiration. The retired professional football player is now a teacher and coach at the high school she attended, where he coached her hockey team. He also coached her lacrosse team on Six Nations.
Macdonald’s own commitment to younger players is reflected in the influence of those who’ve helped her along the way.
“My dad’s a great role model, alongside other wonderful coaches and teammates who supported me in life and lacrosse. And my mom is my best friend.”
From injury recovery to a career in rehabilitation therapy

Her family and mentors have anchored not only how Macdonald approaches lacrosse, but how she sees her future. She’s studying kinesiology in Western’sFaculty of Health Sciences,with plans to build a career in rehabilitation therapy and improve access to specialized care in Indigenous communities.She believes her own positive experience with rehabilitation will provide a foundation for the compassionate care she hopes to offer others.

content_blocks.alt: National Indigenous Scholarship recipient Brooke Macdonald in the library at Western University

content_blocks.text: National Indigenous Scholarship recipient Brooke Macdonald. (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

“My doctors and physiotherapists were just so amazing, I want to contribute in the same way to help people recover, especially in Indigenous communities where specialties like sports medicine aren’t very common,”she said.

Macdonald envisions a future that allows her to remain connected to the sport that has shaped her. She hopes to continue coaching children’s lacrosse, sharing the guidance she received with the next generation.
“I’m very lucky to have had so many people contributing to develop every piece of me. I want to pay it forward through mentorship and future work in sports medicine.”

stories.title: Below seasonal temperature to begin the week
stories.summary: Temperatures are below seasonal to begin the week in and around London.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Temperatures are below seasonal to begin the week in and around London.

According to CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison, Monday’s temperatures are about four to five degrees below average.

“A bit of cloud cover, a low-pressure system to the south is kicking up some cloud and a little bit of moisture pushing through Ohio and Pennsylvania that will stay south of us as we head into tonight,” she said.

“Partly cloudy conditions. High pressure will be building into the Great Lakes basin and that will lead to some beautiful weather.”

Temperatures overnight will drop to 7 C, 5 C closer to Kitchener-Waterloo.

“Your forecast highs for your Tuesday anywhere between 16 to 19 C,” said Atchison.

“So, still cool and a bit below normal. Lots of sunshine in the extended forecast and mix of sun and cloud Tuesday and Wednesday.”

Here’s a full look at your forecast:

Monday night: Partly cloudy. Wind northeast 20 km/h, gusting to 40 becoming light this evening. Low 7 C.

Tuesday: A mix of sun and cloud. Wind becoming northeast 30 km/h, gusting to 50 in the morning. High 17 C.

Wednesday: A mix of sun and cloud. High 20 C.

Thursday: Sunny. High 20 C.

Friday: Sunny. High 20 C.

stories.title: U.S. working on deal to buy potash from Belarus for lower price than Canada, Trump says
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.
stories.author: Kayla Thompson
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.

“The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers,” he posted to Truth Social on Monday .

Canada is the leading exporter of potash, shipping about 22.9 million tonnes in 2024, accounting for over 39 per cent of global exports according to the Government of Canada.

The leading destination of Canadian exports of potash is the United States. The U.S. imports nearly 85 per cent of its potash from Canada.

Belarus ranks third in potash production behind Russia and Canada.

According to Belarusian media reports Monday , President Alexander Lukashenko said even if there was a desire to enter Western markets, there is nothing left to supply.

According to reporting from Reuters, potash from Belarus remains under EU sanctions , and the landlocked country has been barred from exporting via the Lithuanian port of Klaipeda since February 2022.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe, whose province provides the U.S. with more than 86 per cent of its potash supply from Canada, said Trump’s tentative deal is “wrong and it doesn’t make sense.”

“More than 40 countries - Canada and its allies - have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression” he posted to X Monday afternoon.

“Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan - right here in North America?”

More than 40 countries - Canada and its allies - have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression. It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense. All of that potash has to be… pic.twitter.com/Omat5YxNOq — Scott Moe (@PremierScottMoe) September 21, 2026

Potash leverage in U.S.-Canada trade war

In June, Trump told reporters that there is nothing the U.S. needs from Canada. However, U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said America needs a “tremendous amount of things” including Canadian potash, since there are “not lots of other places that you can get it.”

Canada’s premiers have been at odds about whether to leverage the critical mineral against the U.S. amid trade war tensions.

While Ontario Premier Doug Ford has previously pushed to retaliate against Trump’s tariffs by cutting U.S. access to electricity, oil and other minerals, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Moe said they were concerned about the long-term consequences for those industries.

Canada’s 10 active potash mines are located in Saskatchewan.

Moe has said the province would not support any kind of export taxes or withholding supply for the U.S., as losing its biggest customer would cause job losses, price hikes and a tremendous hit to the local economy.

“The United States of America, most assuredly, would switch to buying potash from other nations around the world. We would lose a long-term customer to some degree,” Moe said during trade talks.

Smith also echoed Moe in July, when she told reporters oil and potash being used as retaliatory measures is “not going to happen.”

Canadian potash has remained exempt from Trump’s tariffs amid the ongoing trade war. However, the U.S. looking to Belarus for potash supply signifies the latest escalation.

The move comes after Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the “ambition” to become the European Union’s first associate member, which Trump said he’ll retaliate against if he deems it to be a “hostile act.”

The U.S., Canada and EU have all imposed sanctions on Belarus for its crackdown on human rights and for allowing its territory to be used by Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

However, in December 2025, the U.S. agreed to lift sanctions on Belarusian potash, after Lukashenko freed 123 prisoners with the help of Trump’s envoy.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Man charged in assault with a weapon investigation: LPS
stories.summary: A man has been charged in connection with an assault with a weapon investigation.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A man has been charged in connection with an assault with a weapon investigation.

On Saturday around 3:45 a.m., officers said a man was asleep in a structure in a wooded area near Clarke Road and Oxford Street, when a suspect woke him up. The suspect allegedly hit the man with a sword, causing serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The victim ran and called 911.

A police drone was launched to help find the suspect. They were arrested without incident. The LPS confirmed both the victim and suspect were known to each other.

A 36-year-old man from London has been charged with assault with a weapon and assault causing bodily harm.

stories.title: Edmontonians gather for clothing repair event: ‘Quiet act of rebellion’
stories.summary: Pearce Carpenter says fixing the holes in the black balloon bottoms they bought from an Edmonton thrift store is their way of tackling fast fashion.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
Pearce Carpenter says fixing the holes in the black balloon bottoms they bought from an Edmonton thrift store is their way of tackling fast fashion.

“There is so much textile waste in the world. So if we just fix old clothes, like holes in the crotch areas of pants, it’s one little quiet act of rebellion,” said Carpenter, who uses they and them pronouns, while stitching over the part of the pants where two holes once were.

“Crotches wear out so quickly in pants just from rubbing your thighs.”

Before they started stitching, they lengthened the pants by cutting them near the ankles, adding a blue-coloured fabric with yellow squares and threading the ends back on.

“It’s such a fun way to add creativity to your wardrobe.”

Carpenter was among dozens who spent a part of their Saturday fixing old and beloved items at a clothing mending event at the University of Alberta called Human Ecology Clothing Repair Café.

Samantha Barrios Mendoza, a psychology student and event coordinator, said the gathering has been happening monthly during the school year for the last five years.

But the number of attendees has grown in the last year or so, likely due to the affordability crisis.

“I think people are starting to become more interested in learning how to mend because things are a little tight right now,” said Barrios Mendoza, as the sound of sewing machines and classical music hummed behind her.

“Why buy something new with hard-earned money when you can just repair something you love?”

Barrios Mendoza said many attendees believe repairing clothes can also reduce the environmental impact of fast fashion.

Fast fashion describes clothing produced quickly with cheap materials that copies popular styles from major fashion labels and designers. In recent years, fast fashion manufacturers have come under intensifying pressure to reduce their contributions to climate change.

The United Nations Environment Programme estimates that each year the world generates fabric waste at a rate equivalent to a garbage truck’s worth being dumped or incinerated every second.

“There are new items and fabrics being pumped out every day in the fashion industry,” Barrios Mendoza said.

“So not buying new clothes and repairing is taking action for sustainability.”

Barrios Mendoza said that while repairing clothing does not reverse the climate crisis, it means a lot to the people who do it.

She said a woman once added floral trinkets to her wedding dress, and a mother used fabric she had kept since her kids were infants to make aprons for them after they grew up and moved away.

“People have made memories through mending,” Barrios Mendoza said.

Attendees are provided with needles, thread, fabrics and ribbons, as well as drinks and snacks.

Experts also attend some events to teach new repair methods.

Most of the mending consists of fixing holes.

“We also do a little bit of resizing. People will bring in their skirts or their shirts, and they’ll bring them down a size or up a size, or they’ll turn some fabric into a bag,” Barrios Mendoza said.

She said she got into mending when she was a teen.

“I have a bag that I’ve had for 15 years, and hole after hole, straps falling down, I’ve just stitched it back together,” she said.

The stitches remind her of how much she has improved her mending skills over the years.

“Now it has patches and little stitch marks, and I can see where I started learning how to sew and then how the stitch marks got more even.

“The bag is now a piece of me.”

Tacjana Maj-Pfleger, another event attendee, said she takes pride in the things she has fixed.

“I have this ethos where good clothing doesn’t have to be new clothing,” she said, while sewing fabrics onto the back of an old denim jacket to make it thicker.

“I’m fairly poor, honestly, but also, fast fashion is terrible.”

— With files from The Associated Press

She said a woman once added floral trinkets to her wedding dress, and a mother used fabric she had kept since her kids were infants to make aprons for them after they grew up and moved away.
“People have made memories through mending,” Barrios Mendoza said.
Attendees are provided with needles, thread, fabrics and ribbons, as well as drinks and snacks.
Experts also attend some events to teach new repair methods.
Most of the mending consists of fixing holes.

“We also do a little bit of resizing. People will bring in their skirts or their shirts, and they’ll bring them down a size or up a size, or they’ll turn some fabric into a bag,” Barrios Mendoza said.
She said she got into mending when she was a teen.
“I have a bag that I’ve had for 15 years, and hole after hole, straps falling down, I’ve just stitched it back together,” she said.
The stitches remind her of how much she has improved her mending skills over the years.
“Now it has patches and little stitch marks, and I can see where I started learning how to sew and then how the stitch marks got more even.
“The bag is now a piece of me.”
Tacjana Maj-Pfleger, another event attendee, said she takes pride in the things she has fixed.
“I have this ethos where good clothing doesn’t have to be new clothing,” she said, while sewing fabrics onto the back of an old denim jacket to make it thicker.
“I’m fairly poor, honestly, but also, fast fashion is terrible.”
— With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: A look back at Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s 4 months as BC Conservative leader
stories.summary: The B.C. NDP caucus met late Sunday to discuss Kerry-Lynne Findlay's resignation amid the ongoing speculation of an early election call.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned as the leader of the BC Conservatives on Sunday, stepping down after just 113 days in the role following the membership vote in May.

Her decision to resign came after mounting calls from MLAs who left party caucus and several decisions she herself said she would have made differently “with the benefit of hindsight.”

But how did the party that elected her get to the point it has no party leader? As the prospect of a snap election looms over the province, here is what led to Findlay’s resignation.

May 30, 2026: Kerry-Lynne Findlay is voted in as the new leader, receiving 51 per cent of the vote after four rounds of voting. Caroline Elliott comes in second with 49 per cent.

June 30: Findlay appoints several loyalists to key positions, naming Heather Maahs as interim leader of the Official Opposition, replacing Trevor Halford. She also appoints Steve Kooner and Anna Kindy, who endorsed Findlay during the leadership race, as “lieutenant” positions for stakeholder relations and Vancouver Island respectively.

July: Several high-profile Conservative staff depart or are let go from the party, including Dion Weisner as director of research, and the BC Conservatives’ executive director Angelo Isidorou, who resigned. The former said he was let go by the caucus chief of staff, but that “ultimately everything” was at Findlay’s direction. He also claimed there had been a 50 per cent turnover of caucus staff since Findlay came to power. Isidorou said he was leaving on “amicable and mutual terms.”

July 29: Rosalyn Bird, MLA for Prince George-Valemount, says she was asked to step down to give Findlay the chance to run for a seat in the B.C. legislature. West-Vancouver Capilano MLA Lynne Block and Delta South MLA Ian Paton say they also rejected requests.

Aug. 14: Peter Milobar announces he is quitting the BC Conservative caucus to sit as an independent and cites a lack of alignment with Findlay.

Aug. 22: Reann Gasper resigns from the party caucus to give Findlay the chance to run for a seat. Questions are raised when Findlay says Gasper will become her deputy chief of staff.

Aug. 24: Ian Paton leaves caucus to sit as an independent, but also announces he plans to form a new centre-right political party with Milobar.

Aug. 25: Rosalyn Bird says she will sit as an independent, saying the party was moving too far to the right than she would like.

Aug. 26: Teresa Wat and Brennan Day both announce they will sit as independents. Wat accused Findlay of reneging on a promise to apologize over “serious and unfounded accusations” made by the leader about Wat, calling her “CCP” in reference to the Chinese Communist Party. Wat said she could not stay in a party whose leader questioned her loyalty to Canada. Day said he had lost confidence in the judgment, conduct and ethical standards of Findlay’s leadership and those around her.

Aug. 27: Bruce Banman becomes the seventh MLA to resign from caucus, and sixth to criticize Findlay in their departure. He said Findlay was “unelectable” and urged other MLAs to join him.

Aug. 28: Audio recording surfaces on social media of Findlay allegedly offering “senior advisor” role to any MLA who would resign so she can run to enter legislature. Findlay called it “preposterous.” The B.C. RCMP say they’re aware of the purported recording. It is illegal under the Criminal Code to negotiate a reward or benefit related to resignation from political office. Findlay said a caucus meeting would be held Aug. 30.

Aug. 29: A byelection is called for Reann Gasper’s now vacant seat of Abbotsford-Mission. Findlay said she would run for the party in the vote.

Aug. 30: Findlay cancels the caucus meeting and the planned news conference set for Aug. 31.

Aug. 31: Áʼa꞉líya Warbus leaves caucus , saying she’s lost confidence in the party under Findlay. She cited the cancellation of the caucus meeting and Gasper’s resignation to make way for Findlay among her reasons.

Sept. 1: Ian Paton says he’s been asked to speak to the RCMP. He said he suspects it’s about his allegation chief of staff Chris Delaney allegedly said if Paton stepped down so Findlay could run, he’d be given an advisory position.

Sept. 2, 2026: Donegal Wilson and Scott McInnis leave the party , both citing Findlay’s leadership. The BC Conservative leader says Chris Delaney has resigned as her chief of staff and has appointed Reann Gasper as his replacement. She also says she’s the victim of a “co-ordinated political attack.”

Sept. 4: Rosalyn Bird, Bruce Banman and Áʼa꞉líya Warbus all announce they are joining Peter Milobar and Ian Paton in the new provincial party. Teresa Wat has also joined.

Sept. 14: Donegal Wilson says she’s joining Milobar’s party.

Sept. 15 : A new poll by Ipsos finds support for the BC Conservatives under Findlay sitting at 35 per cent, down eight points from the 2024 provincial election and 10 points behind the BC NDP.

Sept. 17: BC Conservative MLAs and former executives, along with a Victoria reporter, confirm they have been informed they were the subject of a private investigator hired by a former senior Conservative party official. The same day, Findlay says in a speech she is not going anywhere.

Sept. 18: Former BC Conservative member Peter Milobar is named new leader of the CentreBC party, with six other former Conservative MLAs who have left in the past two months joining him. The same day, Findlay says she’s removed former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford, and MLA Claire Rattee from the party caucus.

Sept. 20: The removal of three MLAs prompts Linda Hepner, MLA for Surrey-Serpentine River, to leave the caucus.

A few hours after Hepner leaves caucus, Findlay resigns as Conservative leader, saying “too much of our time and attention has been consumed by internal conflict.” She says she will still run for the party in the Abbotsford-Mission byelection. MLA Lorne Doerkson is named as interim leader.

The B.C. NDP caucus met late Sunday to discuss Findlay’s resignation amid the ongoing speculation of an early election call.

— with files from Global News’ Amy Judd and The Canadian Press

stories.title: As rivals China and U.S. prepare for AI meeting, here are the top concerns
stories.summary: The hopes for finding common ground on concerns around global AI safety are clouded by competition between the United States and China.
stories.author: Chan Ho-him
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, leaders of rival nations in a race to dominate artificial intelligence , are expected to meet this week against a backdrop of rising concerns about the threats that rogue AI could pose to humanity.

The hopes for finding common ground on concerns around global AI safety are clouded by competition between the two countries. As China narrows the technology gap with the U.S., each country has expressed concern over how AI in the other’s hands could hurt them.

“The U.S.-China conversation in AI is getting caught in the ups and downs in the broader U.S.-China relationship,” said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said after talks in New York with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of the meeting between Trump and Xi that the two countries discussed the setting up of a mechanism on AI dialogue and proposed a new “notification mechanism” for AI incidents that could impact national security.

Here is a look at some topics that May — or May not — come up for discussion around AI.

The agenda could focus on AI risks that could harm both countries, such as AI-enabled cyberattacks, biological misuse, major model failures or loss of human control, said Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

In that case, “there is still meaningful room for cooperation,” Sun said.

“It would be a mistake to dismiss the entire safety debate as geopolitical competition,” Sun said. “China itself is paying growing attention to loss-of-control risks, malicious use, cyber threats and the safety of AI agents.”

Bessent said after his meeting with He that the U.S. proposed a notification mechanism between the United States and China, such as when there are incidents that rises up to the national security level from AI. “We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats,” he told reporters.

Michael Kratsios, Trump’s science and technology adviser, told Fox News Sunday it’s important to have conversations with China about AI.

“The key thing that we want to talk to them about is avoiding shared risks, and that’s something that I think we can have a fruitful conversation on,” Kratsios said.

Both governments are concerned about how AI could be used to attack critical infrastructure. In China, AI governance documents identify finance, electricity, telecommunications and transportation as areas potentially exposed to frontier-AI risks, Sun said.

The Chinese side has shown real interest in discussing issues like AI and cyber incident information sharing with U.S. experts, said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Institute for America, China, and the Future of Global Affairs.

If the two countries can discuss how to report and communicate in the event of an AI-related emergency, said Xiao Qian, vice dean of the Institute for AI International Governance at Tsinghua University, “it can help the two countries to build technical confidence over time.”

Trump has repeatedly said “whoever wins AI, wins.”

He has insisted the U.S. needs to keep a technological edge over China and downplayed calls by American tech leaders to slow AI’s development over safety concerns. Beijing, in turn, has accused the U.S. of pursuing an AI monopoly as it curbs China’s AI growth including in restricting its access to the world’s most advanced chips.

At the meeting, any loosening of U.S. export controls on advanced technologies related to AI is likely to be off the table, said Alfredo Montufar-Helu with the consultancy Ankura.

With each country seeking competitive advantages in so many areas, Montufar-Helu said the room for U.S. and China to collaborate on AI is “quite narrow.”

In his essay this month calling for an AI slowdown, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the U.S. to continue seeking ways to limit Chinese AI development.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Amodei’s warnings about China were confrontational and a form of “fearmongering” and that all parties should work together on AI.

Despite the restrictions, Chinese AI models increasingly challenge American frontier models. Chinese AI models led by Moonshot AI and DeepSeek this year have shown they can be, by some measures, as powerful as those of U.S. rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI, often at a lower cost. Many of them are making inroads globally, including in the U.S.

“Export controls have not stopped China from developing frontier-competitive models, but they slow its rate of expansion by limiting the compute it can use to serve users,” said professor Will Cong of Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.

Despite the constraints, China’s chip developers have been catching up with the U.S., and companies in China are turning more to domestic chips. That’s giving Xi more confidence in his talks with Trump, George Chen with The Asia Group said.

U.S. claims that China is ripping off American AI technology are another sore spot in the relationship.

The U.S. government and AI companies have stepped up allegations of “malicious” extraction of capabilities, or “distillation,” from top American AI models, claims that Chinese officials have rejected.

Anthropic has accused Chinese AI models of DeepSeek and Moonshot of routing a number of their user requests to its Claude AI models. Chinese labs are likely attempting to “piggyback on the massive training and inference infrastructure of their U.S. rivals” given how U.S. restrictions are limiting China’s compute power, Rebecca Arcesati, with the Mercator Institute for China Studies, said.

Chinese officials and some technology analysts have argued that distillation is not uncommon across the AI industry and is not the main explanation behind Chinese models’ improving capabilities and ability to innovate.

Beijing, meanwhile, has expressed worries over threats to China’s critical infrastructure from American AI, including Anthropic’s powerful Claude Mythos, and more broadly, the risk of AI’s aiding of spreading of political misinformation and potentially challenging its governance.

“We cannot expect meaningful cooperation on AI safety if one side increasingly treats the other side’s technological progress as a national security threat,” Xiao said. Disagreements between the U.S. and China “make dialogue even more necessary,” she added.

stories.title: New Indigenous mural at Western recognizes Truth and Reconciliation
stories.summary: A new Indigenous mural at Western University helps tell the creation story.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
A new Indigenous mural at Western University helps tell the creation story.

“And it’s important for us to take care of the water and the earth because she can’t speak for herself. And so, we always honour the water,” said Western Indigenous Elder in Residence, Mary Lou Smoke.

She was addressing a group gathered at the Thames Hall Jeff and Shelley Parr Family Atrium for the unveiling of a new Anishinabek mural by Saugeen First Nation Indigenous artist Jeanette Ladd.

“So, it’s about how the earth came to be on the back of a turtle shell,” Ladd explained.

The mural is a row of seven paintings hanging over the atrium, which tells the story of Turtle Island.

“And the thought was that it was going to be about the creation story. And from there, I wanted to fit within the atrium space. So, with the living wall, the wood panels, the skylights, I wanted that to reflect in my piece as well,” Ladd said.

The event is part of the leadup to Truth and Reconciliation Day, Sept. 30.

“They call upon us to learn from the past, to confront the ongoing impacts of colonialism, and to work together toward a more equitable future. This mural stands as a reminder of that responsibility, and of the work that remains ahead,” said Dr. Shaun Boe, Dean of Health Sciences.

As for Ladd, she hopes her work sends a positive message.

“The animals, the land, the water. The moon, the sun, the sky. All of those things are connected. And you can’t have one without the others,” she said.

stories.title: Police officer shot outside Belleville synagogue identified, faces 'significant road to recovery'
stories.summary: "While he continues to face a significant road to recovery, his condition has stabilized," said Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
'When members of a vulnerable community needed protection, he put himself in harm’s way,' it says in the description of the fundraiser

A GoFundMe for the police officer who was injured while stationed outside of a Belleville, Ont. synagogue on Sunday has raised more than $75,000.

Const. Jeff Smith was critically injured after a 19-year-old gunman opened fire on the place of worship on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year in the Jewish faith. Smith was stationed outside. He remains in stable condition at Kingston General Hospital.

The fundraiser was started on behalf of the Jewish community in Toronto. Organizer Derek Kreindler said the initial goal of $18,000 was reached within 12 hours.

The fundraiser was set up for the Jewish community to express its “profound gratitude to Const. Smith and to support him and his family during what May be a long and difficult recovery.”

The fundraiser is also intended to convey a message to those who protect the Jewish community, the description said. “We will not forget what he did outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue.”

In a post on X, former Bay of Quinte MP Ryan Williams shared a photo of Smith and called him a hero. Belleville police confirmed to National Post that the picture in Williams’ post was Smith.

Jeff Smith is a real hero. A Belleville Police officer who put himself in harm’s way protecting our community. Please pray for Jeff, his family and his fellow officers. Our community is behind you, Jeff. Stay strong. Keep fighting. Come home to your family. pic.twitter.com/7tBeWH0C4T — Ryan Williams 🇨🇦 | The Competition Guy (@Ryan_r_Williams) September 21, 2026

“While he continues to face a significant road to recovery, his condition has stabilized, and we remain hopeful and encouraged by his progress,” said Belleville Police Service’s Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks, who spoke to media on Monday.

“Our thoughts are with Const. Smith, his family, his friends, and his colleagues. Supporting them has been our top priority.”

Smith was stationed outside the synagogue because of safety concerns, especially on a night where there would be many congregants in attendance, the synagogue’s president Norman Weddum told National Post.

Belleville Police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks says the shooting suspect has been identified as Sean Ward, 29, of Quinte West. Belleville Police Constable Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue, sustained serious injuries. His condition has since stabilized. pic.twitter.com/qZxiGSe76R — Toronto Crime Watch (@CrimewatchTO) September 21, 2026

Weddum said that before entering the building, he thanked Smith for being there. Soon after the evening prayer service started, around 7 p.m., dozens of shots rang out.

A 29-year-old suspect armed with a shotgun opened fire at Smith, who then is believed to have shot back, said Kristy Denette on Monday. She is a spokesperson for the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), the province’s police watchdog that is leading the investigation.

Denette said it is currently believed that the man drove to the area in a truck. A second officer got to the scene shortly after and fired back at the suspected shooter before more officers arrived.

stories.title: Rustad invited back to B.C. Opposition after being expelled by ex-leader Findlay
stories.summary: British Columbia Conservatives’ interim leader reached out by text, Rustad says
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
Former British Columbia Conservative leader John Rustad says he has been invited to rejoin the party’s caucus, just days after he was expelled by Kerry-Lynne Findlay in the dying days of her own tenure as leader.

Findlay quit on Sunday , with Lorne Doerkson appointed interim leader of the Opposition, and Rustad says Doerkson has reached out to him by text message and asked him to return.

The development comes after the caucus of B.C.’s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election after Findlay’s resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.

Doerkson is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis.

Rustad says there are “obviously lots of people” in B.C. who don’t know the Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but Doerkson is a “quality individual” and Rustad is happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wants.

Rustad says of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell need to “let politics go,” and realize that “their time is over.”

stories.title: Unions bracing as Liberals to table major economic and labour bill
stories.summary: Carney's government will table a major review of the Canada Labour Code as part of major legislation.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government tabled legislation that fundamentally reorganizes how it approves major projects, promising a “one project, one review, one year” process all the while implementing sweeping changes to Canadian labour rules around collective bargaining and work stoppages.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government tabled a new omnibus Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, ON Monday afternoon.

“Today we introduced our most significant piece of economic legislation yet,” Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said in a press conference with other federal ministers after the bill was tabled. “This legislation will give our country the tools we need to build more, better, and more efficiently.”

“Our objective today is straightforward: to make it easier for Canadian businesses to build, invest, grow, and get their products to market, while creating an economy that delivers certainty, prosperity, and opportunity for all Canadians,” MacKinnon added.

The bill aims to designate yet-unspecified areas as “regions of national interest” in which major infrastructure projects would receive the same fast-track approval process as those deemed to be “projects of national interest” under legislation (Bill C-5) passed last year.

It also removes the responsibility of conducting impact assessments for major energy and nuclear projects away from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada and puts it into the hands of specialized bodies: either the Canada Energy Regulator or the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission.

“This will provide a better look at the project as a whole, and lead to more efficiency and less consultation fatigue in the consultation process,” said one senior public servant during a background technical briefing for reporters.

Parliament returns with a big agenda and a fight brewing between Carney and labour unions

Federal ministers slam NHL player Alex Ovechkin’s pro-Putin ad, but won’t say if he should be sanctioned

One Canadian Economy Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the government held nationwide engagement with Indigenous peoples, provinces and territories, investors, municipal leaders, and Canadians over the past few months.

“While we are working quickly, Canada’s government is also doing its part to listen to Canadians,” he said.

The bill also proposes significant changes to how federally-regulated industries — transportation, telecommunications and banking, for example — negotiate union contracts, mediate disputes and resolve work stoppages.

The bill would mandate parties to begin renegotiating a union contract six months before it expires if the previous negotiations were acrimonious or if the expiring deal lasted five years or more.

It also proposes yet-undefined monetary penalties for parties found to be negotiating in bad faith by a labour arbitrator, and compels union and employer representatives to attend the labour version of couples therapy (“relationship development work”) at the end of negotiations that included work stoppage or binding arbitration.

Unions have been vocally opposed to how the Carney Liberals wielded a controversial section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to prematurely end multiple strikes in the transportation sector, including one by Air Canada flight attendants in the summer of 2025.

The government looks to address that criticism by proposing two new “guardrails” to when it can invoke section 107’s power to order a federal labour arbitrator to end a work stoppage and resolve the dispute between employer and union.

“First, the consideration of a report from a special mediator, and second, the minister has to be of the opinion that a strike or lockout would adversely affect the national interest based on a national impact assessment,” said a senior government official during the briefing. The assessment would be conducted by the labour program at Employment and Social Development Canada (Esdc).

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu said any suggestion that the government is weakening the right to strike is “incorrect.”

“In fact, what it does is put a guardrail around a very contentious tool, Section 107, that many unions had said was used without transparency by the minister. And so, in terms of workers’ rights, we’re actually strengthening their rights,” she said.

With Bill C-39, the government also looks to reorganize the administration of Canada’s biggest ports and create “national trade corridors” and a new “corridor council.” Its goal will be to “identify what’s causing delays and bottlenecks in our supply chains and propose remedies,” the officials said during the briefing.

Speaking to reporters Sunday alongside Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Carney described the upcoming bill as “the most consequential economic legislation certainly of this parliamentary session, arguably over the course of the next few years.”

NDP Leader Avi Lewis said it is precisely for that reason that he is making a public appearance on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish calendar, for the first time in 36 years of public life to respond to that consequential legislation.

“Prime Minister Carney is using our fear and disorientation around the trade war to push through a series of unpopular measures that he did not run on, has no mandate for, and would never get away with under normal circumstances,” Lewis said.

“This approach will create crises, not solve them. It will cause labour unrest, not bring peace to workplaces, and it will create a Canada where Indigenous rights, workers’ rights, and the protection of our precious natural environment will all be sacrificed on the altar of corporate profit.”

Union leaders said they were very worried about the new legislation introduced in Parliament.

“If this government thinks that they’re going to take away our fundamental rights, they’re in for a very big wake-up call,” said Mark Hancock, the national president of the Canadian Union of Public Employees, who joined Lewis at his press conference.

Bea Bruske, the President of the Canadian Labour Congress, said her organization has had a first look at the changes to the Canada Labour Code and while there are measures that are welcome in terms of protections for workers, she said the government broke its promise to workers on the right to strike.

“This bill gives government the new and expanded power to end a legal strike when it decides the strike is, or could be, against the national interest,” she said.

“We reject the idea that workers’ bargaining power is somehow contrary to the national interest.”

Before the bill was tabled, Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet denounced any move by the Liberals to curb workers’ right to strike or mandate binding arbitration to parties in a labour conflict.

He said it was much better that the government be forced to “grow a spine” and table special back-to-work legislation if it wants to end a strike and face the music in Parliament.

“The State must be an mediator between the interests of the workers and large industry. What we fear is that the government will abandon that responsibility in one direction, to the benefit of industries that know that, in general, arbitrators… generally rule in favour of employers,” he said.

Asked whether the government is “flooding the zone” in a similar fashion to U.S. President Donald Trump, Hajdu said the government is making all these consequential changes to respond to the crisis of the trade war.

“We’re doing exactly what Canadians have asked us to, which is to stand up for them, to stand up for their families, to stand up for their jobs. We’re fighting every single day to save jobs, to grow jobs, and to make sure that we can actually build big things in this country and get our goods to market,” she said.

Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said Canadians want to come together and build Canada in a time of uncertainty.

“That’s what Canadians expect us to do.”
