stories.title: Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor Maya Gebala turns 13 as her recovery continues
stories.summary: Images posted by her mom show Maya Gebala bowling, playing air hockey and blowing out candles on her birthday cake.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Maya Gebala, the Tumbler Ridge shooting victim who was so critically injured it was thought she might never see another birthday, has just turned 13 years old.

In her latest post to Facebook, Maya’s mom, Cia Edmonds, included numerous photos of Maya celebrating the big day.

They include the little girl bowling, playing air hockey and blowing out candles on her birthday cake (with a little help from mom).

In other pictures she is smiling at the camera and making rock-and-roll hand signs with her mom.

“Happy Birthday, my biggest baby girl,” Edmonds wrote in the post. “13 looks different, but you wear it well.”

She continued: “I am forever grateful for the time we get to share. I am constantly proud at all the new things you are learning to do. I am watching you become someone new, again and again. Thank you baby. Thank you for staying with us. Thank you for your strength, your courage, and your determination.”

Edmonds said that a year ago, Maya’s big birthday wish was to go with her best friend to visit “galaxy land,” an apparent reference to the theme park in West Edmonton Mall.

“This year is different, but we make it worth it,” Edmonds wrote, adding: “Many more to come my Maya Moon. All the stars in the sky, forever and always.”

The Tumbler Ridge shooting took place on Feb. 10, when 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar went on a murderous rampage that left eight other people dead, most of them at the secondary school in the small British Columbia town. Maya was shot three times in the head, cheek and neck.

Maya, who was just 12 years old when the shooting occurred, was taken to B.C. Children’s Hospital in Vancouver.

She has undergone at least five complex surgeries but has made remarkable progress since the shooting, which left her with severe brain damage.

Her mother, who posts on social media under the name “Cia Later,” and her father, David Gebala, have released regular updates over the months with news of her continued recovery.

Earlier this month Edmonds posted a brief video clip of Maya saying “mom” to her.

“Setbacks and victories,” she wrote in the post. “Her level of awareness is incredible and devastating at the same time. She still lives in a hospital, she cries because she wants to go home. Soon baby, soon.”

In July, Edmonds changed her Facebook cover photo and profile picture to include images of a small French bulldog, along with the sad news that their dog had died after being hit by a car.

stories.title: Nearly 1 in 4 Canadian households live in unaffordable housing, StatCan says
stories.summary: Nearly one in four (23.2 per cent) Canadian households were living in unaffordable housing in 2024, compared to 22 per cent in 2022, Statistics Canada said in a report on Monday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Housing affordability just worsened for a growing share of Canadians, new data from Statistics Canada shows.

Nearly one in four (23.2 per cent) Canadian households were living in unaffordable housing in 2024, compared to 22 per cent in 2022, Statistics Canada said in a report on Monday.

Statistics Canada defined households living in “unaffordable” housing as those that spent 30 per cent or more of their income on shelter costs.

Renters (33.7 per cent) were more likely than homeowners (17.4 per cent) to live in unaffordable housing, the report said.

In 2024, more than one -third (36.6 per cent) of all households in Canada were homeowners with a mortgage, while 27.8 per cent were homeowners without a mortgage.

Another 31.3 per cent were renters in the private market.

Affordability worsened for homeowners with a mortgage as well, with more than one-quarter (26.1 per cent) of living in unaffordable housing, up from 23.6 per cent in 2022.

Higher mortgage rates following the lows during COVID-19 pandemic meant many homeowners renewed their mortgages at high rates in 2024, with more than one in three (36.2 per cent) of homeowners with a mortgage reporting financial difficulty due to mortgage costs.

This was up 7.9 per cent compared to 2022.

Among renters, those who moved houses faced higher costs compared to those who stay put. The average monthly rent for those who had moved within the past two years was $1,740 a month in 2024, compared to $1,290 for those who had lived in their current home for more than two years.

Those who moved recently were more likely to face unaffordable housing, with 40 per cent living in unaffordable housing compared to 32.2 per cent among sitting tenants.
paragraphs: Housing affordability just worsened for a growing share of Canadians, new data from Statistics Canada shows.
Nearly one in four (23.2 per cent) Canadian households were living in unaffordable housing in 2024, compared to 22 per cent in 2022, Statistics Canada said in a report on Monday.
Statistics Canada defined households living in “unaffordable” housing as those that spent 30 per cent or more of their income on shelter costs.
Renters (33.7 per cent) were more likely than homeowners (17.4 per cent) to live in unaffordable housing, the report said.
In 2024, more than one -third (36.6 per cent) of all households in Canada were homeowners with a mortgage, while 27.8 per cent were homeowners without a mortgage.
Another 31.3 per cent were renters in the private market.
Affordability worsened for homeowners with a mortgage as well, with more than one-quarter (26.1 per cent) of living in unaffordable housing, up from 23.6 per cent in 2022.

Higher mortgage rates following the lows during COVID-19 pandemic meant many homeowners renewed their mortgages at high rates in 2024, with more than one in three (36.2 per cent) of homeowners with a mortgage reporting financial difficulty due to mortgage costs.
This was up 7.9 per cent compared to 2022.

Among renters, those who moved houses faced higher costs compared to those who stay put. The average monthly rent for those who had moved within the past two years was $1,740 a month in 2024, compared to $1,290 for those who had lived in their current home for more than two years.
Those who moved recently were more likely to face unaffordable housing, with 40 per cent living in unaffordable housing compared to 32.2 per cent among sitting tenants.

stories.title: Could these pills help people with anorexia?
stories.summary: Researchers in London, Ont., are recruiting people with anorexia nervosa for a clinical trial investigating whether fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) capsules can help treat the eating disorder by restoring healthy gut bacteria.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Researchers in London, Ont., are recruiting people with anorexia nervosa for a clinical trial investigating whether fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) capsules can help treat the eating disorder by restoring healthy gut bacteria.

The study is being led by researchers at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute, Lawson Research Institute of St. Joseph’s Health Care London and Western University.

“There appears to be a direct link between the gut microbiome and how the brain functions,” said Dr. Elizabeth Osuch, a psychiatrist at London Health Sciences Centre, researcher at Lhscri and professor at Western University.

The trial will examine whether FMT capsules can improve the gut microbiome, nutritional health and food-related decision-making in people living with anorexia nervosa.

Researchers say anorexia nervosa is a serious and potentially life-threatening condition that causes people to have a distorted perception of their body weight and can lead to severe food restriction and excessive exercise.

Researchers have also found that people with anorexia nervosa often experience disruptions in their gut microbiome, which they believe May be linked to how individuals think about food and body image.

“Some of the first early studies done with microbiome were when they took a microbiome from an obese mouse and put it in a lean mouse,” said microbiologist Jeremy Burton. “The lean mouse put on a lot of weight so we know the microbiome plays a really important role.”

Burton said they’ve noticed patients with Anorexia have “abnormal gut microbiome” which could be linked to their relationship with food

“There’s lots of links now between the gut and the brain,” said Burton.

Participants in the trial will take the capsules, complete questionnaires and provide stool samples before and after treatment. Researchers will monitor them over time to assess the effects of the intervention.

FMT is already an approved treatment for recurrent Clostridioides difficile, commonly known as C. difficile, an infection that affects the colon. Researchers have also been involved in studies exploring its potential use in cancer care.

The study is seeking to recruit 20 research participants. To be eligible, participants must be:

Diagnosed with anorexia nervosa, restricting type and not in active cognitive behavioural therapy (and not in hospital)

Able to travel to London Health Sciences Centre at 54 Riverview Ave. and St. Joseph’s Hospital at 268 Grosvenor St.

stories.title: Carney welcomes Norwegian Prime Minister to Ottawa
stories.summary: Two countries signed agreements on Arctic and Antarctic science and research, space-based capabilities and joint critical minerals mapping, PMO says
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his focus on building international relationships, including with Norway, is part of the answer to renewed threats from Russia.

During a news conference with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Ottawa, both leaders were asked about warnings from the Polish prime minister that Russia May be planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries that support Ukraine.

Store said those warnings should be taken seriously and that Norway’s intelligence has concluded there are “real threats coming from hybrid activity, ranging all the way to potential sabotage.’

Carney didn’t comment on the credibility of the threats, but said he agreed with Store’s statements.

“One of the advantages of this relationship and deepening across a broad range of relationships is, yes, greater intelligence sharing, greater perspective, greater capacities that are built together,” he said.

He said accomplishing that requires submarine and space capabilities, as well as the “right partners” among Arctic nations working together.

“The phrase that always sticks with me... is ‘High North, low tension,’” he said.

Canada calls for Nato strategy to secure Arctic as northern flank of military alliance

In July, Carney chose to buy a dozen submarines from a European shipbuilder instead of a Korean firm, after a months-long, hotly contested bidding process. The chosen partnership involves a German company but partners with Norway, with the three nations collaborating to produce and maintain the submarines.

Before meeting with Store in Ottawa on Sunday, Carney travelled to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon earlier in the day to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron.

Carney said the “time spent whether it’s in the high north in Norway, a meeting with the French president who’s directly implicated in a number of these decisions, our meeting today and beyond, it’s all connected,” Carney said.

In a statement released later Sunday, the Prime Minister’s Office said Canada and Norway signed a number of agreements, including on Arctic and Antarctic science and research, space-based capabilities and joint critical minerals mapping.

The statement said the two also intend to “advance an enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement in the new year.”

In a joint statement, the two countries said they “continue to work together to bolster deterrence and defence in the Arctic: Arctic security is national security for both countries.”

Store’s visit comes as Carney looks for closer ties with Europe, including potential “associate membership” in the EU.

Norway is not a member of the EU, but for three decades the country has had a deal with the EU that gives both sides free access to each other’s markets for goods and services – and gives Norway access to most EU programs.

Carney is courting deeper defence ties with the Norway, as well as investment from its massive, petroleum-based sovereign wealth fund.

Carney was in Norway in March – the first sitting prime minister since 1980 to visit the Nordic country.

During that visit, the two leaders pledged to advance collaboration in fields ranging from Arctic security to space, critical minerals and energy. Carney and Store also touted their reputations as low-risk global oil producers, amid supply shocks emanating from conflicts like U.S. President Donald Trump’s war on Iran.

Norwegian officials have often described Canada as a similar country, given that both seek to balance a large oil sector with a push for green energy and respect for Indigenous Peoples.

They both put an emphasis on using multilateral institutions to resolve disputes while identifying as strong proponents of Nato and deeply tied with the European Union, without being EU members.

Both countries have put support for Ukraine at the forefront of foreign policy, amid Russia’s 2014 and 2022 full-scale invasion.

Since late 2024, Canada has had an Arctic foreign policy that calls for more intense ties with Nordic countries in defence, strategic sectors and environmental issues.

stories.title: U.S. in talks to buy potash from Belarus at lower cost than what Canada charges, Trump says
stories.summary: Minsk confirms deal, but says most of the country’s exports are already destined for other markets
stories.author: Adrian Morrow, Kate Helmore
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to import potash from Belarus, an Eastern European dictatorship closely allied with Russia, in a bid to undercut Canada amid a continental trade war.

Mr. Trump announced the prospective deal in a social media post on Monday but provided no details on what exactly the agreement would entail, how much potash it would involve or what the pricing would be.

“The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus. The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko confirmed the deal but said Belarus doesn’t have much fertilizer to export to the U.S. because it is already destined for other markets.

“Even if we wanted to supply [potash] to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes — everything is contracted,” a Monday press release from his office quoted him as saying.

The largest export market for Belarus’s potash is China, which, according to figures from the U.S. Geological Survey, imported 29 per cent of Minsk’s product in 2024.

Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada has been repeatedly hamstrung by the fact that the United States depends heavily on its neighbour to the north for many goods, including potash. The U.S. imports much of the fertilizer from Saskatchewan and the President has granted it partial exemptions from his tariffs.

Belarus, which has been ruled since 1994 by Alexander Lukashenko, has helped Russian President Vladimir Putin with his invasion of Ukraine . Mr. Lukashenko allowed Russian troops to use Belarusian territory to launch the February, 2022, attack against Kyiv.

Belarus, like Russia, has been sanctioned by the U.S., the European Union and Canada over its role in the war against Ukraine.

In March, Mr. Trump lifted sanctions on Belarusian potash companies after Minsk promised to release political prisoners. The deal was struck as Mr. Trump tried to push down fertilizer prices after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, cutting down the world’s supply of nitrogen from the Middle East.

stories.title: Trump says he wants potash from Belarus for ‘subtantially less’ than Canada
stories.summary: European officials call Belarus an 'accomplice' to Russia's war in Ukraine and earlier this year, Belarus let Russia practice the use of nuclear weapons Moscow stations there.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The U.S. is working on a deal with Belarus to replace the potash it receives from Canada for “substantially less,” U.S. President Donald Trump said.

“The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said on his social media platform Truth Social.

“The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers. Thank you for your attention to this matter!” Trump added.

European officials have called Belarus an “accomplice” to Russia’s war in Ukraine and earlier this year, Belarus launched joint drills with Russia to practice the use of nuclear weapons that Moscow has stationed in the territory of its neighbor and ally.

Potash consists of minerals and chemicals that contain potassium and is a vital input used for manufacturing fertilizers. It is used to support plant growth, increase crop yield and disease resistance, and enhance water preservation.

Canada is the leading exporter of potash in the world.

The U.S. imports 79 per cent of its potash from Canada, according to the U.S Geological Survey. Russia, accounting for 11 per cent of U.S. potash imports, is a distant second while Belarus is in fourth place with three per cent.

“No substitutes exist” for potash in the agriculture industry, the Usgs says, making it a critical implement for food security.

pic.twitter.com/9An1HqtfBT — Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) September 21, 2026

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said more than 40 countries, including Canada and allies, currently sanction Belarus for supporting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

“Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression. It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense. All of that potash has to be shipped first through Russia, then across the ocean, then across the US to mid-Western farmers,” said Moe.

“Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan – right here in North America?”

More than 40 countries – Canada and its allies – have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression. It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense. All of that potash has to be… pic.twitter.com/Omat5YxNOq — Scott Moe (@PremierScottMoe) September 21, 2026

Fertilizer Canada on Monday said in a statement that Canada has been a reliable supplier to North American farmers for decades.

“Supported by geography and a highly integrated supply chain, Canadian potash helps ensure growers have access to the nutrients they need, when and where they need them,” the industry group said.

“Reliability, proximity, transportation infrastructure, product availability and the ability to deliver during critical application windows all matter. A strong and integrated North American fertilizer supply chain helps support farm productivity, affordability and food security on both sides of the border.”

Pam Schwann, president of the Saskatchewan Mining Association, said there will likely be challenges for Belarus to ramp up production to meet increased demand.

“Right now, most of the Belarusian supply goes to China. I’m not sure if they have any extra latent supply that they’re able to ramp up production with. They have a very complicated supply chain,” Schwann said in an interview with Global News.

“They are landlocked, much like Saskatchewan, but they would require to load onto ships and get their product landed into the United States and then they would require infrastructure built out to do what we already have in Canada in terms of an integrated supply chain. And so, I’m not sure what the capacity Belarus has for additional potash .”

Schwann said Canadian producers have deep and longstanding relationships with U.S. farmers.

“Obviously the U.S. market is very important to our Saskatchewan mining companies. Moving forward, it does speak to the importance of diversification of trade and the building out of trade-enabling infrastructure and diversifying markets. stories.title: Arrest made in St. Thomas vehicle break-in, fraud investigation
stories.summary: According to police, a 32-year-old St. Thomas man is facing multiple charges following an investigation into the fraudulent use of stolen bank cards.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
An arrest has been made in one of four vehicle break ins in St. Thomas over the weekend.

According to police, a 32-year-old St. Thomas man is facing multiple charges following an investigation into the fraudulent use of stolen bank cards.

St. Thomas police said officers were contacted Sunday after a wallet, bank cards, cash, a backpack and sporting equipment were stolen from a vehicle parked on Elizabeth Street.

Investigators determined the stolen bank cards were later used to make several purchases at a business on Talbot Street. After reviewing surveillance footage, officers identified a suspect and later arrested him.

Police said they recovered the stolen backpack, along with several other items believed to be stolen or obtained through criminal activity.

The accused is charged with possession of property obtained by crime, theft under $5,000, unauthorized use of a credit card, disguise with intent and failure to comply with an undertaking.

Meanwhile, St. Thomas police are investigating three other vehicle entries reported over the weekend.

In one case, four pairs of sunglasses were reported stolen from a vehicle on Rice Road after the passenger door was found ajar. Police believe the theft occurred Sept. 14.

In a separate incident, about $300 worth of personal property was reported stolen from a vehicle parked in a Talbot Street parking lot. Officers observed pry marks on the passenger-side door.

Police are also investigating the theft of a wallet containing identification and bank cards, prescription medication and cigarettes from a vehicle parked on Ross Street.

Anyone with information about the incidents is asked to contact St. Thomas police.

stories.title: 'Jewish people must be able to worship safely': Carney, Poilievre and others condemn Belleville synagogue shooting
stories.summary: Politicians and police forces across Canada have shared statements condemning a shooting that took place outside a synagogue in Belleville.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Two people, including a police officer, were wounded in the incident that occurred as worshippers gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish calendar

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, along with other politicians and police forces across Canada, have condemned antisemitic violence following a shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Sunday night.

Two people, including a police officer, were wounded in the incident that occurred as worshippers gathered for Yom Kippur , the holiest day of the Jewish calendar. No one inside the synagogue was hurt, according to a social media statement by the Sons of Jacob Congregation . A police officer and suspected gunmen were injured and taken to Kingston General Hospital after exchanging gunfire outside the synagogue.

To live free, open, proud Jewish lives,” Carney wrote in a statement on X . “Canada’s government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law. My thoughts are with the injured officer and his family, and the entire Jewish community.”

Poilievre echoed Carney’s support for the Jewish community, but called on the government to take action. “This vile antisemitic violence in Canada must end, and this Liberal government must act now to protect our people,” the opposition leader wrote in a statement on X.

“Jewish Canadians must once again be able to live in their communities and pray in their places of worship without fear of being shot at or attacked.”

On the holiest day of the Jewish year, a police officer was injured, a man suffered life-threatening injuries, and worshippers at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville were forced to take cover as gunfire erupted outside. This vile antisemitic violence in Canada must end,… — Pierre Poilievre (@PierrePoilievre) September 21, 2026

Belleville Police said on social media that one of their officers “encountered an individual in the area at about 7:10 p.m.” and “the officer and the individual sustained injuries and were transported to hospital,” adding that there was no further threat to public safety.

Police officer injured after Yom Kippur shooting at Belleville synagogue

'Bang! Bang! Bang!': Confusion, gunshots during Yom Kippur service at Belleville synagogue

The province’s Special Investigations Unit said the “exchange of gunfire” involved a 29-year-old man “armed with a shotgun” who is now in life-threatening condition. The officer is listed as critical but stable.

Other political leaders have expressed sorrow and support for the Jewish community following the shooting. Tyler Allsopp, Progressive Conservative MPP for the Bay of Quinte riding, representing Belleville, said in a statement on X that he is “heartbroken” by news of the incident.

“My thoughts go out to all members of our Jewish community, and to the police officer who was wounded and his family,” he said. “This attack was a disgusting act and it has no place in our society. It is my sincerest hope that the individual responsible feels the full weight of justice.”

My statement on the senseless shooting attack last night at Belleville's Sons of Jacob Synagogue. pic.twitter.com/TJPrS8tEIq — Tyler Allsopp (@tylerallsoppPC) September 21, 2026

And Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he is “disgusted” by the shooting.

In a statement shared on X , Ford wrote: “My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear. I expect that all those responsible are arrested and prosecuted to the full extent of the law.”

He added: “My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones. We owe an immense debt of gratitude to this brave officer and to all the first responders who acted so quickly to keep the community safe.”

The Ontario Liberal Party released a statement in which the party’s interim leader, John Fraser, called the shooting “a horrific act of antisemitic violence.”

“For years, we have seen a growing number of Jewish centres targeted by gunfire,” he said. “In most cases, they were empty, but these attacks have instilled fear and dread in the Jewish community. It was only a matter of time before someone was brazen enough to do something like this.”

Please read the Ontario Liberal Party’s Statement on Yom Kippur and the shooting at the Belleville synagogue this weekend. pic.twitter.com/GMmxQvpLZD — Ontario Liberal Party | Parti Libéral de l'Ontario (@OntLiberal) September 21, 2026

Ontario Liberal Party leadership candidates Lee Fairclough and Eric Lombardi also commented on the shooting.

Fairclough called it “horrifying” and said her thoughts are with the Jewish community and the injured police officer in a post on X , while Lombardi said the incident “comes amid an alarming rise in antisemitism and threats against Jewish institutions across Canada.”

He added : “Jewish Canadians deserve to live without fear and to gather and worship in safety and peace. We must stand unequivocally against antisemitism and ensure our Jewish communities are protected from rising hate.”

Elsewhere, Toronto mayor Olivia Chow wrote in a statement : “My thoughts are with the Jewish community and the injured officer in Belleville,” adding, “The Jewish community will see an increased police presence as we take precautions to keep people safe.”

She said: “Jewish Torontonians should not need police presence to observe Yom Kippur, or to simply live their day-to-day lives. As long as we contend with rising antisemitism and hate, we will spare no expense keeping the community safe.”

Brad Bradford, a Toronto city councillor and Chow’s main contender in the upcoming mayoral race, also shared a statement on social media. “Gunfire outside a synagogue hurts a community that has already carried far too much this year, in Toronto, in Montreal, and across Canada. No community in this country should have to live like this,” he wrote.

Bradford added: “An attack on a place of worship is an attack on all of us.”

Tonight, ON Yom Kippur, shots were fired outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, and early reports indicate a police officer was shot responding. Kathryn and I are keeping Belleville’s Jewish community, first responders, the officer who was injured, and everyone near… — Brad Bradford (@BradMBradford) September 21, 2026

Meanwhile, former Conservative Party leader Erin O’Toole called the incident “horrific” in a social media post , adding: “A reminder that the troubling rise in antisemitism leads to real risks to the Jewish community & our entire society.”

And Senator Leo Housakos, who serves as the leader of the Opposition in the Senate, said he is “horrified and beyond angry” by the shooting in a post on social media , adding: “We are failing Jewish Canadians. This violence persists and escalates because we allow it to. Governments in Canada can no longer pretend that antisemitism is anything less than an emergency.”

Conservative MP Shelby Kramp-Neuman said she is “deeply concerned” by the incident, Liberal MP Evan Solomon called it “horrific and despicable,” and fellow Toronto MP Leslie Church said : “A police presence should never be necessary to gather for worship in Canada, yet this is a terrible daily reality for Jewish Canadians.”

Elsewhere, Mark Baxter, president of the Police Association of Ontario, called the act of violence “deeply troubling” in a statement shared on social media.

“I am outraged by this attack on the Jewish community and their sacred space,” he added. “Those responsible must be brought to justice and held fully accountable.”

Absolutely appalling news out of Belleville. A Belleville Police Service officer was shot while bravely guarding the Sons of Jacob Synagogue and the Jewish community during Yom Kippur. Our thoughts are with the officer, their loved ones, and everyone affected by this horrific… pic.twitter.com/akdE8TEUuF — Mark Baxter (@PresidentPAO) September 21, 2026

The Durham Regional Police also released a statement on social media in which it said its membership is “saddened by the senseless violence” that took place in Belleville. “We join all in condemning senseless acts of violence,” it said.

Police services that have commented on the shooting include York Regional Police, which said in a message to the community that “officers will continue to be visible in the areas where people gather to worship, and we remain in close contact with community and faith partners.”

And Winnipeg Police said it will be increasing its presence at gathering spaces and places of worship as a precaustion, adding: “Our thoughts are with the Jewish community across Canada during this time, as well as with the officer in Belleville who remains in hospital.”

The Bay of Quinte’s pro hockey team, Belleville Senators, also shared a statement on social media, writing: “The Belleville Senators family is deeply saddened to learn about the shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday evening. Our thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville, as well as the injured officer and first responders and who attended the scene.”

The Belleville Senators family is deeply saddened to learn about the shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday evening. Our thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville, as well as the injured officer and first responders and who attended the scene. pic.twitter.com/xCn6lMzf0T — Belleville Senators (@BellevilleSens) September 21, 2026

Multiple synagogues in Ontario, specifically the Greater Toronto Area, have been targeted in shooting attacks in recent years as antisemitism grows in Canada. This March, three separate GTA synagogues were hit by gunfire within a five-day span — Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto in Thornhill, North York’s Temle Emanu-el and Shaarei Shomayim. York Regional Police have charged three suspects in connection with a pair of the shootings.

The shooting comes two months after Statistics Canada data showed that Jews were targeted in 71 per cent of religious hate crimes in Canada last year. While this represented a 16 per cent decline from the previous year, it remained 50 per cent higher than in 2022.

No one inside the synagogue was hurt, according to a social media statement by the Sons of Jacob Congregation . A police officer and suspected gunmen were injured and taken to Kingston General Hospital after exchanging gunfire outside the synagogue.

To live free, open, proud Jewish lives,” Carney wrote in a statement on X . “Canada’s government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law. My thoughts are with the injured officer and his family, and the entire Jewish community.”

Poilievre echoed Carney’s support for the Jewish community, but called on the government to take action. “This vile antisemitic violence in Canada must end, and this Liberal government must act now to protect our people,” the opposition leader wrote in a statement on X.
“Jewish Canadians must once again be able to live in their communities and pray in their places of worship without fear of being shot at or attacked.”

Belleville Police said on social media that one of their officers “encountered an individual in the area at about 7:10 p.m.” and “the officer and the individual sustained injuries and were transported to hospital,” adding that there was no further threat to public safety.

The province’s Special Investigations Unit said the “exchange of gunfire” involved a 29-year-old man “armed with a shotgun” who is now in life-threatening condition. The officer is listed as critical but stable.

Other political leaders have expressed sorrow and support for the Jewish community following the shooting. Tyler Allsopp, Progressive Conservative MPP for the Bay of Quinte riding, representing Belleville, said in a statement on X that he is “heartbroken” by news of the incident.

“My thoughts go out to all members of our Jewish community, and to the police officer who was wounded and his family,” he said. “This attack was a disgusting act and it has no place in our society. It is my sincerest hope that the individual responsible feels the full weight of justice.”
My statement on the senseless shooting attack last night at Belleville's Sons of Jacob Synagogue. pic.twitter.com/TJPrS8tEIq — Tyler Allsopp (@tylerallsoppPC) September 21, 2026
And Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he is “disgusted” by the shooting.

In a statement shared on X , Ford wrote: “My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear. I expect that all those responsible are arrested and prosecuted to the full extent of the law.”

He added: “My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones. We owe an immense debt of gratitude to this brave officer and to all the first responders who acted so quickly to keep the community safe.”
The Ontario Liberal Party released a statement in which the party’s interim leader, John Fraser, called the shooting “a horrific act of antisemitic violence.”

“For years, we have seen a growing number of Jewish centres targeted by gunfire,” he said. “In most cases, they were empty, but these attacks have instilled fear and dread in the Jewish community. It was only a matter of time before someone was brazen enough to do something like this.”

Ontario Liberal Party leadership candidates Lee Fairclough and Eric Lombardi also commented on the shooting.

Fairclough called it “horrifying” and said her thoughts are with the Jewish community and the injured police officer in a post on X , while Lombardi said the incident “comes amid an alarming rise in antisemitism and threats against Jewish institutions across Canada.”

He added : “Jewish Canadians deserve to live without fear and to gather and worship in safety and peace. We must stand unequivocally against antisemitism and ensure our Jewish communities are protected from rising hate.”

Elsewhere, Toronto mayor Olivia Chow wrote in a statement : “My thoughts are with the Jewish community and the injured officer in Belleville,” adding, “The Jewish community will see an increased police presence as we take precautions to keep people safe.”

She said: “Jewish Torontonians should not need police presence to observe Yom Kippur, or to simply live their day-to-day lives. As long as we contend with rising antisemitism and hate, we will spare no expense keeping the community safe.”

Brad Bradford, a Toronto city councillor and Chow’s main contender in the upcoming mayoral race, also shared a statement on social media. “Gunfire outside a synagogue hurts a community that has already carried far too much this year, in Toronto, in Montreal, and across Canada. No community in this country should have to live like this,” he wrote.
Bradford added: “An attack on a place of worship is an attack on all of us.”

Meanwhile, former Conservative Party leader Erin O’Toole called the incident “horrific” in a social media post , adding: “A reminder that the troubling rise in antisemitism leads to real risks to the Jewish community & our entire society.”

And Senator Leo Housakos, who serves as the leader of the Opposition in the Senate, said he is “horrified and beyond angry” by the shooting in a post on social media , adding: “We are failing Jewish Canadians. This violence persists and escalates because we allow it to. Governments in Canada can no longer pretend that antisemitism is anything less than an emergency.”

Conservative MP Shelby Kramp-Neuman said she is “deeply concerned” by the incident, Liberal MP Evan Solomon called it “horrific and despicable,” and fellow Toronto MP Leslie Church said : “A police presence should never be necessary to gather for worship in Canada, yet this is a terrible daily reality for Jewish Canadians.”
Elsewhere, Mark Baxter, president of the Police Association of Ontario, called the act of violence “deeply troubling” in a statement shared on social media.
“I am outraged by this attack on the Jewish community and their sacred space,” he added. “Those responsible must be brought to justice and held fully accountable.”

Absolutely appalling news out of Belleville. A Belleville Police Service officer was shot while bravely guarding the Sons of Jacob Synagogue and the Jewish community during Yom Kippur. Our thoughts are with the officer, their loved ones, and everyone affected by this horrific… pic.twitter.com/akdE8TEUuF — Mark Baxter (@PresidentPAO) September 21, 2026

The Durham Regional Police also released a statement on social media in which it said its membership is “saddened by the senseless violence” that took place in Belleville. “We join all in condemning senseless acts of violence,” it said.

Police services that have commented on the shooting include York Regional Police, which said in a message to the community that “officers will continue to be visible in the areas where people gather to worship, and we remain in close contact with community and faith partners.”

And Winnipeg Police said it will be increasing its presence at gathering spaces and places of worship as a precaustion, adding: “Our thoughts are with the Jewish community across Canada during this time, as well as with the officer in Belleville who remains in hospital.”

The Bay of Quinte’s pro hockey team, Belleville Senators, also shared a statement on social media, writing: “The Belleville Senators family is deeply saddened to learn about the shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday evening. Our thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville, as well as the injured officer and first responders and who attended the scene.”

The Belleville Senators family is deeply saddened to learn about the shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on Sunday evening. Our thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville, as well as the injured officer and first responders and who attended the scene. pic.twitter.com/xCn6lMzf0T — Belleville Senators (@BellevilleSens) September 21, 2026

Multiple synagogues in Ontario, specifically the Greater Toronto Area, have been targeted in shooting attacks in recent years as antisemitism grows in Canada. This March, three separate GTA synagogues were hit by gunfire within a five-day span — Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto in Thornhill, North York’s Temle Emanu-el and Shaarei Shomayim. York Regional Police have charged three suspects in connection with a pair of the shootings.

The shooting comes two months after Statistics Canada data showed that Jews were targeted in 71 per cent of religious hate crimes in Canada last year. While this represented a 16 per cent decline from the previous year, it remained 50 per cent higher than in 2022.

stories.title: Ontario fines StubHub $20,000 under new law capping ticket resale prices
stories.summary: Provincial website does not specify what events the penalties were linked to
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
The Ontario government has fined ticket reseller StubHub Canada Ltd. $20,000 under a recent law that caps the sale of seats at face value.

The province’s Consumer Beware List on Monday showed a $10,000 fine for allegedly making a ticket available for sale above face value and another $10,000 for allegedly facilitating a transaction without having proof of the original price.

The website said both fines were issued to StubHub on Sept. 9 but did not say what events the penalties were linked to.

StubHub would not provide any specifics about the fine but said it will push for the penalty to be overturned.

“The fact is we are upholding our responsibility as best we can despite the law’s silence on some core issues, like how a marketplace should verify the original price of a ticket,” spokesperson Jack Sterne said in an e-mail.

He claimed the government has acknowledged this gap and will fix it through regulation, but in the meantime, said the company will “continue to engage in productive conversation to address these matters, while we defend our rights through the appeals process.”

Giulia Paikin, a spokesperson for the Ontario Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery Stephen Crawford, did not answer questions about the nature of StubHub’s fines.

She sent a statement that repeated verbatim what the province has previously said about price cap violations.

“All ticket sellers in Ontario must comply with our legislation that prohibits the resale of tickets above face value,” the statement said. “Any seller who breaks those rules could face fines of up to $250,000 and be publicly identified on the Consumer Beware List. We will not hesitate to hold bad actors who break the rules accountable.”

StubHub has been on notice since the spring, when the province sent 27 ticket resale websites letters announcing the businesses would be inspected for non-compliance with the new law.

It later added StubHub and SeatGeek Canada to the consumer beware list, fining SeatGeek Canada $25,000 in August for allegedly flouting the price cap law.

The legislation was implemented earlier this year, ahead of World Cup soccer matches being held in Toronto. It was meant to tackle soaring resale ticket prices and scalpers profiting off their ability to score seats to the hottest concerts and games. Along with the World Cup, last year’s playoff run by the Toronto Blue Jays and Taylor Swift concerts in 2024 became flashpoints in the debate over resale prices.

But since the legislation came into effect, fans have complained tickets are still selling for above face value and resale websites have framed compliance as difficult.

StubHub, for example, has said it’s hard for the website to obey the legislation because there’s no way to confirm what buyers originally paid for tickets.

The company argues some tickets, like those purchased as a package for a season, don’t have prices on them, and also that receipts can easily be doctored by resellers wanting to list tickets for more than face value.

To confirm the prices and comply with the law, StubHub has said it would need data from the original platform a ticket was purchased from.

stories.title: B.C. NDP caucus meets to discuss potential early election after Findlay resignation
stories.summary: Conservative board of directors appointed MLA Lorne Doerkson as interim leader
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
The caucus of British Columbia’s governing NDP has met to discuss a potential early election after the resignation of Opposition B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Findlay quit Sunday, saying it was the right move for the party and province, and the Conservative board of directors appointed MLA Lorne Doerkson as interim leader hours later.

But the Conservative constitution prohibits an interim head from seeking the party’s leadership in a subsequent ballot, so if an election is called soon, the official Opposition candidate for premier would not immediately be clear.

Findlay’s resignation follows weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, with 13 defections or expulsions, including former leader John Rustad, who was ejected with two others on Friday.

Rustad is set to address reporters in Victoria today.

Gary Mason: The shocking implosion of B.C.’s Conservative Party

NDP MLAs met last night to discuss Findlay’s departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators on Sunday, instead of just those on the government benches.

“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the email obtained by The Canadian Press says.

It goes on to say the meeting was to “to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Premier David Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be “election ready.”

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo—Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the BC Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before crossing the floor to join the Conservatives and being reelected in 2024.

stories.title: Trump working on deal to buy potash from Belarus for lower price than Canada
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.
stories.author: Kayla Thompson
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.

“The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers,” he posted to Truth Social on Monday .

Canada is the leading exporter of potash, shipping about 22.9 million tonnes in 2024, accounting for over 39 per cent of global exports according to the Government of Canada.

The leading destination of Canadian exports of potash is the United States. The U.S. imports nearly 85 per cent of its potash from Canada.

Belarus ranks third in potash production behind Russia and Canada.

According to Belarusian media reports Monday , President Alexander Lukashenko said even if there was a desire to enter Western markets, there is nothing left to supply.

According to reporting from Reuters, potash from Belarus remains under EU sanctions , and the landlocked country has been barred from exporting via the Lithuanian port of Klaipeda since February 2022.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe, whose province provides the U.S. with more than 86 per cent of its potash supply from Canada, said Trump’s tentative deal is “wrong and it doesn’t make sense.”

“More than 40 countries - Canada and its allies - have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression” he posted to X Monday afternoon.

“Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan - right here in North America?”

More than 40 countries - Canada and its allies - have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression. It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense. All of that potash has to be… pic.twitter.com/Omat5YxNOq — Scott Moe (@PremierScottMoe) September 21, 2026

Potash leverage in U.S.-Canada trade war

In June, Trump told reporters that there is nothing the U.S. needs from Canada. However, U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said America needs a “tremendous amount of things” including Canadian potash, since there are “not lots of other places that you can get it.”

Canada’s premiers have been at odds about whether to leverage the critical mineral against the U.S. amid trade war tensions.

While Ontario Premier Doug Ford has previously pushed to retaliate against Trump’s tariffs by cutting U.S. access to electricity, oil and other minerals, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Moe said they were concerned about the long-term consequences for those industries.

Canada’s 10 active potash mines are located in Saskatchewan.

Moe has said the province would not support any kind of export taxes or withholding supply for the U.S., as losing its biggest customer would cause job losses, price hikes and a tremendous hit to the local economy.

“The United States of America, most assuredly, would switch to buying potash from other nations around the world. We would lose a long-term customer to some degree,” Moe said during trade talks.

Smith also echoed Moe in July, when she told reporters oil and potash being used as retaliatory measures is “not going to happen.”

Canadian potash has remained exempt from Trump’s tariffs amid the ongoing trade war. However, the U.S. looking to Belarus for potash supply signifies the latest escalation.

The move comes after Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the “ambition” to become the European Union’s first associate member, which Trump said he’ll retaliate against if he deems it to be a “hostile act.”

The U.S., Canada and EU have all imposed sanctions on Belarus for its crackdown on human rights and for allowing its territory to be used by Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

However, in December 2025, the U.S. agreed to lift sanctions on Belarusian potash, after Lukashenko freed 123 prisoners with the help of Trump’s envoy.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tiff 2026 exposed festival’s stellar cinematic taste, and worst institutional instincts
stories.summary: This year’s festival felt as if it was using a handful of exhilarating moments to paper over many, larger structural fissures and fault lines
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
Halfway into the new historical drama La Bola Negra , which follows three generations of gay Spanish men as they wrestle with devastation and desire, Penélope Cruz shows up for 10 minutes and brings the house down. Playing a 1930s showgirl who bewitches a troupe of soldiers during the Spanish Civil War, the actress delivers a quick but enduring jolt of energy to Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s feature – a movie that, while beautiful in its aesthetics and epic in its construction, mostly feels distended and reaching for a profundity just beyond its grasp.

It is that defining tension of La Bola Negra – a wannabe showstopper in which you can see its seams stretch and fray as it struggles to please its eager crowd – that was top of mind Sunday as the Toronto International Film Festival closed out its 51st edition by awarding Calvo and Ambrossi’s movie its coveted People’s Choice Award . Like the film that it was honouring, this year’s Tiff seemed, from a distance, to be a rather gorgeous, glamorous and highly ambitious affair. But upon closer inspection, Tiff 2026 also felt as if it was using a handful of exhilarating moments of Cruz-like potency to paper over many larger, structural fissures and fault lines .

We can start with La Bola Negra ’s own curious path from Cannes to the People’s Choice Award, a seeming moment of triumph that was offset by confusion when it was announced, just seconds before, that the British drama Elsinore had won the International People’s Choice Award.

Tiff 2026: The best (The Debut!), worst (smelly cinemas!) and weirdest (Trudeau?) film festival moments

Last year, Tiff organizers introduced a new “international” version of the PCA, in which audiences vote for the best festival film produced outside of Canada and the United States. Theoretically, this allows Tiff to spotlight foreign titles that might otherwise be overshadowed by the winner of the “real” PCA, which has long been considered an Oscars bellwether and has often gone to an English-language movie made in the Hollywood system.

But in practice, the new international award feels both confounding – unless you’ve read the fine print of the eligibility rules, you’d be rightly perplexed as to why the Spanish-language La Bola Negra won the “real” PCA, and the English-language Elsinore earned the international version – and nakedly opportunistic. Tiff is not spreading the wealth here for filmmakers, but for its own reputation as an Oscars kingmaker. Why settle for saying that your festival can cement the Academy Awards chances for one film when you can boast that you solidify the prospects for two?

Well, because almost everyone in the industry can see straight through the ploy. Just as all those players are taking an especially hard look at Tiff’s other big recent initiative, albeit one engineered and executed on a far grander scale: the launch of an official market .

The inaugural edition of Tiff: The Market, which ran parallel to the festival’s official screenings, gathered buyers, sellers and creators of film and TV under the roof of the Metro Toronto Convention Centre for seven days of meetings and potential deal-making. But if organizers hope that Tiff’s market will eventually match the reputation (and earned revenues) of Berlin’s European Film Market and the Marché du Film in Cannes, they’re going to need to embrace some sizable course corrections.

Not only did attendees highlight serious technical issues – hours-long waits to pick up badges, an app that felt designed in a hurry – but, to borrow the language of the industry’s coveted Gen Y demographic, the vibe was off.

Between a lack of foot traffic, a sizable portion of the convention floor being taken up by a sparsely populated food court, and too many stands occupied not by highly valued sales agencies, production companies or buyers but various countries’ national film bodies (Telefilm’s space was easily the busiest), the space often felt like a particularly sleepy version of a tourism conference. Sure, the high-profile Paris-based Goodfellas sales agency and production company had a large pavilion in the centre of the floor, but also a noticeable lack of on-site activity. Any producer hoping to score a connection from a walk-up there would likely need to keep on, well, walking.

Already, Tiff seems eager to crown the market an out-of-the-gate success – but in its rush to do so, organizers appear to have tripped over some key figures.

According to a press release sent Friday, market chief Charles Tremblay noted that 7,010 industry delegates were registered this year, a 40 per cent increase compared to Tiff’s “informal, previous offering, which typically drew 5,000 people to the city.” Yet according to Tiff’s own numbers from its 2025 edition, the festival attracted 6,000 industry delegates last year, making the actual jump in attendance just 16 per cent. At the same time, about 200 delegates, mostly international buyers who had either never attended Tiff or not been in several years, had their travel and accommodation subsidized. Will they return on their own dime?

Market organizers also boasted that the exhibition floor contained 238 exhibitors. But the official convention centre directory only listed about 100, depending on how you counted outfits that shared pavilion space and whether you included filmmakers participating in the “Innovation Hub” showcasing interactive media projects.

Meanwhile, higher-end companies, including AGC Studios, WME and StudioCanal, were holed up on floors inside the InterContinental and Ritz-Carlton hotels – spaces not quite as accessible and amenable to the kind of pop-in meetings that participation in the market intimated.

Then there were the market-only screenings, in which sellers paid Tiff to show films designed to spark buyer interest – presentations that represent a key revenue driver for the market and can act as a barometer of industry activity. Last year, Tiff said it would provide 650 market screening slots . But in the recently released figures, organizers said just 196 were booked, suggesting a lack of appetite compared to available inventory. (Even if that 650 figure included both private market-only screenings and the festival’s combined “press and market” screenings, for which every film in the official program receives at least one , then initial expectations were still not met.)

Finally, if the market was intended to spark a flurry of bidding wars that would prove Toronto to be an unmissable stop on the global industry calendar, then organizers can only so far point to the sale of a movie that was not technically up for sale at all: the horror movie River , which Universal paid US$10-million to acquire from IFC, which already had the film’s distribution rights coming into Tiff. (It is not unprecedented for a smaller distributor to give up a film to a larger company, but it is highly unusual; IFC must have figured that the deal was more than they’d be able to earn if they released the film on their own.)

The market was launched with significant support from the federal government, but Ottawa’s three-year $23-million commitment runs out this coming March . With or without Prime Minister Mark Carney’s help, Tiff will have to be flexible in vision if it hopes to keep the event going, let alone growing to a projected target of 12,000 delegates by 2030.

At Tiff, and in Washington, Quebec’s film industry finds itself in the hot seat

It is not even unreasonable to wonder, given where the industry winds appear to be blowing, whether Tiff should have accepted the federal cash in the first place and instead focused on sustaining its core asset, the festival. There is a pattern inside the organization, it feels, of introducing a new problem for itself instead of finding a solution to the challenges it already has.

Thankfully, one of Tiff’s longest continuing challenges – its programming – wasn’t as thorny this time around. Sure, Toronto missed out on a handful of titles that burnished the reputations of its festival-circuit rivals (Venice had the headline-making documentary Naza ; Telluride had the buzzy Nathan Fielder/Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything ; New York will soon debut the OpenAI docudrama Artificial ). But for the most part, nearly every prestige fall title available made its way onto Tiff screens.

Watching Mahershala Ali’s Muslim hitman destroy legions of racist henchmen in Bassam Tariq’s audacious Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother was a surreal delight. Peeling back the layers of class and contempt nestled inside Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love was a beguiling experience. Discovering an emerging Canadian director such as Toy Gun Bandit ’ s Rémi St-Michel was a real-time thrill. And seeing the 83-year-old Mike Leigh standing proud inside the Lightbox Cinema 1 after the premiere of his latest, and possibly final, drama Tender Loving Care was a singular privilege.

Of course, there was bloat – any festival with nearly 300 titles will do that – and there were a handful of selections that called into question the faculties of its programmers. Bring me the head of whoever approved Zack Snyder’s irredeemable The Last Photograph . And we’ve got to find out what is going on with the Gala slate, whose selections are instantly vaporized from memory.

But there were enough startling, pinch-me moments of cinematic joy to prove that Tiff is an institution worth fighting for. And that work needs to begin now – no matter how far La Bola Negra (or Elsinore) goes in the Oscar race.

Barry Hertz’s Top 10 Films of Tiff 2026

8. The Stunt Driver

5. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

4. Tender Loving Care

3. All of a Sudden

Discovering an emerging Canadian director such as Toy Gun Bandit ’ s Rémi St-Michel was a real-time thrill. And seeing the 83-year-old Mike Leigh standing proud inside the Lightbox Cinema 1 after the premiere of his latest, and possibly final, drama Tender Loving Care was a singular privilege.

But upon closer inspection, Tiff 2026 also felt as if it was using a handful of exhilarating moments of Cruz-like potency to paper over many larger, structural fissures and fault lines .

We can start with La Bola Negra ’s own curious path from Cannes to the People’s Choice Award, a seeming moment of triumph that was offset by confusion when it was announced, just seconds before, that the British drama Elsinore had won the International People’s Choice Award.
Tiff 2026: The best (The Debut!), worst (smelly cinemas!) and weirdest (Trudeau?) film festival moments

Last year, Tiff organizers introduced a new “international” version of the PCA, in which audiences vote for the best festival film produced outside of Canada and the United States. Theoretically, this allows Tiff to spotlight foreign titles that might otherwise be overshadowed by the winner of the “real” PCA, which has long been considered an Oscars bellwether and has often gone to an English-language movie made in the Hollywood system.

But in practice, the new international award feels both confounding – unless you’ve read the fine print of the eligibility rules, you’d be rightly perplexed as to why the Spanish-language La Bola Negra won the “real” PCA, and the English-language Elsinore earned the international version – and nakedly opportunistic. Tiff is not spreading the wealth here for filmmakers, but for its own reputation as an Oscars kingmaker. Why settle for saying that your festival can cement the Academy Awards chances for one film when you can boast that you solidify the prospects for two?

stories.title: 'Bang! Bang! Bang!': Witnesses recount confusion, gunshots during Belleville synagogue shooting
stories.summary: "I yelled for everyone to get on the floor, to crouch right down," said the synagogue's president.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
One resident told National Post he saw an officer on a stretcher being carried into the back of an ambulance

“Bang! Bang! Bang!”

Norman Weddum recalled the sound of bullets hitting the stained glass at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for the Jewish community.

Weddum, who has been the synagogue’s president for the past eight years, attended the Sunday-night service with around 25 congregants.

When he first arrived, he said he spoke briefly to the police officer who was stationed in front of the building. He said he thanked him for being there. “We (request an officer) when we have a lot of people in the building, just for safety concerns,” he told National Post.

The choice to proactively have an officer at Sons of Jacob comes after several targeted shootings at synagogues across Canada. One person at the scene, a security guard, told Belleville publication The Intelligencer that he believed it was that officer who intercepted the suspect.

By the time Weddum walked into the building, it was 6:45 p.m.

Congregants were ushered into the inner sanctuary of the synagogue around 7 p.m. for the prayer service to start.

“At that point, that’s when the first, ‘Bang! Bang! Bang!’ started, and we all kind of stopped in our tracks,” he said.

And then another round of shots.

A handful of congregants, including Weddum, went out into the main lobby to see what had occurred. Again, they heard the same noise. “And this time it was so loud and deafening … that there was no question that was shot being fired.”

They ran back into the area where the service was being held and shut the doors.

“I yelled for everyone to get on the floor, to crouch right down,” said Weddum. The shots were still being fired and they could hear it hitting the stained glass windows that decorated the outer part of the synagogue.

The shooting stopped eventually, after what felt like hours. “We waited and waited,” said Weddum.

He could see a heavy police presence outside.

“There were two officers who were tending to an injured officer that was sitting on the ground,” he said.

While Weddum said he never expected such an incident to occur in Belleville, another congregant and Belleville resident Doug Lobel told National Post he “almost predicted this was going to happen.”

Lobel was also at the synagogue on Sunday night, with his wife, Eva.

He was walking into the service when he heard loud noises. He said it was confusing because they heard “a lot of shots” but had no idea what was going on outside.

“Sitting there, we hear, ‘Pop! Pop! Pop!’ We don’t know if there’s only one shooter. For me the biggest concern was … are they going to get into the building?”

He said when the shooting stopped, police entered to do a sweep of the building. Congregants were taken by bus to the police station and then dropped off at home.

Lobel said he felt like an incident like this could happen because of past events held in Belleville where the hosts used antisemitic rhetoric. He expressed concern to Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis in an email.

“(The mayor’s) response was really tone deaf because he said if you don’t feel safe contact the Belleville police,” said Lobel.

In a statement to National Post, Ellis said that he could not comment on the details of an individual interaction, but the “concerns about safety and antisemitism are taken seriously.”

“The safety and security of everyone in our community is our highest priority,” the mayor’s statement continued. “The Belleville Police Service is responsible for public safety and for responding to incidents such as this, and I have the utmost confidence in their professionalism and their ability to keep our community safe.”

Lobel said he is especially grateful for the officer who was stationed in front of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue. He’s not sure what would have happened if he wasn’t there.

Belleville resident Justin Gannon told National Post that his daughter was walking home on Sunday night when she heard the gunshots. She texted him anxiously just after 7 p.m. He decided to go to the scene to see what was going on and arrived near the synagogue around 7:20 p.m. He saw officers with their guns drawn.

One yelled at him: “Get out of here! Get out of here! There’s an active shooter!”

Gannon said he could still see smoke in the air and smell gun powder. He saw an officer on a stretcher being carried into the back of an ambulance. The officer was awake but seemed like he was in pain, he said.

“We’ve never had anything like this. This is like a first for Belleville,” he said. “Small town. Everybody’s friendly here. We’ve had shootings before but nothing this major.”

On Monday, he said police continued to scour the area.

“It just seems like there’s so much hate out there right now in the world,” he said. “You can just sense it. If you go online, it’s everywhere.”

A woman identified by her first name, Jose, was at home nearby when she heard a total of 25 to 30 gunshots, she told The Intelligencer . She said it sounded like two different kinds of weapons, perhaps a shotgun and a handgun, exchanging fire.

“I stepped out on the porch to kind of see like where is it coming from … and I saw a truck driving off of the road onto the sidewalk,” she said.

She eventually called 911 after hearing more shots.

Another resident, identified by his first name, Sheldon, told the publication that he heard the shots at Meyers Pier. The pier is roughly 2.5 kilometres away from the synagogue. He went to the area where police lights were flashing to see what was happening. On two occasions, he said he saw people telling officers that their mothers were in the synagogue.

The synagogue remained closed Monday to the roughly 100 families who are members, Weddum said.

“We should have had all-day service and concluding tonight at sundown. But we can’t do that,” he said. “We’ll have services again. We will continue on. This is not going to stop us.”

On Monday, Belleville Police Service’s Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks identified the officer who was stationed outside the synagogue as Const. Jeff Smith. He is in critical but stable condition.

Because Smith and another officer discharged their weapons, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), Ontario’s police watchdog, is leading the investigation.

SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette said it is believed that the 29-year-old suspect drove to the area in a truck and opened fire on Smith with a shotgun. A second officer arrived at the scene, followed shortly after by multiple other officers.

The suspect remains in hospital in life-threatening condition.

Belleville police said it could not comment further on the criminal side of the investigation at this time.

This comes nearly a year after a deadly terror attack at a synagogue in Manchester, England, ON Yom Kippur. On Oct. 2, 2025, two people were stabbed to death and a third was killed by police after being caught in the crossfire.

Later that year, in December, members of the Jewish community were celebrating Hannukah, known as the Festival of Lights, at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia, when more than a dozen were shot to death .

Another resident, identified by his first name, Sheldon, told the publication that he heard the shots at Meyers Pier. The pier is roughly 2.5 kilometres away from the synagogue. He went to the area where police lights were flashing to see what was happening. On two occasions, he said he saw people telling officers that their mothers were in the synagogue.
The synagogue remained closed Monday to the roughly 100 families who are members, Weddum said.
“We should have had all-day service and concluding tonight at sundown. But we can’t do that,” he said. “We’ll have services again. We will continue on. This is not going to stop us.”
On Monday, Belleville Police Service’s Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks identified the officer who was stationed outside the synagogue as Const. Jeff Smith. He is in critical but stable condition.
Because Smith and another officer discharged their weapons, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), Ontario’s police watchdog, is leading the investigation.

SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette said it is believed that the 29-year-old suspect drove to the area in a truck and opened fire on Smith with a shotgun. A second officer arrived at the scene, followed shortly after by multiple other officers.
The suspect remains in hospital in life-threatening condition.
Belleville police said it could not comment further on the criminal side of the investigation at this time.

This comes nearly a year after a deadly terror attack at a synagogue in Manchester, England, ON Yom Kippur. On Oct. 2, 2025, two people were stabbed to death and a third was killed by police after being caught in the crossfire.

Later that year, in December, members of the Jewish community were celebrating Hannukah, known as the Festival of Lights, at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia, when more than a dozen were shot to death .

stories.title: Ontario to standardize entry-level truck driver training after auditor-general report
stories.summary: Scathing report showed the province was not effectively monitoring commercial truck driver training and licensing
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
The Ontario government says it will standardize commercial truck driver training in the wake of a scathing Auditor-General report that identified widespread issues with instruction and licensing in the province.

Ontario will work with industry stakeholders to develop a new curriculum aimed at strengthening road safety, Minister of Transportation Prabmeet Sarkaria said on Monday. But some representatives of the trucking industry say additional measures are required to address their concerns with training and oversight of commercial truck drivers.

The announcement follows a May report from provincial Auditor-General Shelley Spence, which found some private career colleges in Ontario were accrediting drivers without the minimum training requirements, and in some cases had altered student records to falsify their qualifications.

Currently, aspiring commercial truck drivers in Ontario must complete mandatory entry-level training, which consists of a minimum of 103.5 hours of instruction. Private career colleges must submit their curriculum details for approval to the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security to ensure they meet provincial standards.

The Transport Ministry said that under the new approach schools will be required to follow a standardized curriculum that will include “more than 103 hours of clear, robust and consistent training.” The plan is expected to be implemented by early 2027, after consultation with industry stakeholders.

While large trucks represent about 3 per cent of all vehicles on provincial roads, they accounted for 12 per cent of all fatal collisions between 2019 and 2023, Ms. Spence’s report noted. Truck driver violations in Ontario have also spiked in recent years. For example, between 2020 and 2024, the percentage of truck drivers found in violation of rules requiring them to keep daily vehicle inspection logs increased by 135 per cent.

It is not clear how the new curriculum proposals will differ from the province’s existing practices, but the province said it is considering additional training subjects such as fatigue management and rural driving.

Rolf VanderZwaag, one of the architects of Ontario’s mandatory entry-level training standards, which were implemented in 2017, said the essential driving skills program he helped develop is “effectively a standardized curriculum.”

“Most Ontario schools already use it,” said Mr. VanderZwaag, who is the CEO of Techni-Com Inc., which produces compliance and training products for the trucking industry.

Mike Millian, president of the Private Motor Truck Council of Canada, a national association representing companies with in-house commercial trucking fleets, said any improvement in training standards are welcome.

However, additional reforms are urgently needed to address industry’s concerns around training and oversight, he said.

“Having a standardized curriculum is not what our key issue is. Our key issue is people aren’t following the curriculums that they’re submitting,” he said.

Around one quarter of the 216 private colleges offering truck driver training in the province had never been inspected by the provincial colleges ministry, the report found – noting the ministry employed just eight inspectors to audit all 595 private colleges in Ontario.

As part of the research conducted for the May report, Ms. Spence’s office sent students undercover to five unnamed private colleges and found that some students were not taught the required elements of truck driving, including reverse parking and emergency stopping.

As previously reported by The Globe, industry groups have called on the province to overhaul training and licensing procedures, and for the Transport Ministry to take full carriage of the file from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities.

The Private Motor Truck Council of Canada has called for more inspections at private career colleges and heftier fines for those who fail to meet provincial training standards for truck drivers.

Currently, private career colleges face fines of between $250 and $1,000 for first offences, according to the Auditor-General report.

In its statement Monday, the Transport Ministry said it was introducing a dedicated integrity manager for truck driver testing across the province and weekly reviews of commercial driver training schools.

The Professional Truck Training Alliance of Canada (Pttac), which advocates for progress in education and training in the transportation sector, has also called for numerous reforms, including stricter screening of aspiring drivers’ criminal record and driver abstracts. The organization has also advocated for testing instructors to be equipped with body cameras as a fraud prevention tactic, and has called for dual-facing cameras to be required in training vehicles.

“We want to continue to see improvement, but at the end of the day, regulation and compliance without any enforcement falls on deaf ears,” said Kim Richardson, a senior adviser to Pttac.

The Private Motor Truck Council’s Mr. Millian said any improvements to the provincial curriculum must include more one-on-one training time for drivers.

“The key area that we see as an issue in the industry is people’s ability to back up the vehicle and operate the truck safely up and down the highway,” he said.

After completing entry-level training, aspiring drivers must take road exams at DriveTest centres. These are run by a third-party provider, Serco, for the Transport Ministry.

As previously reported by The Globe, five employees of driver-licensing centres in Ontario were also charged earlier this year with allegedly accepting bribes to manipulate the results of commercial truck-driving tests.

Mr. Millian says Serco’s Brampton, Ont. testing campus already employs two integrity officers to prevent cheating on road tests.

“We have seen some increases in enforcement, which is welcome,” he said. “But we need to go further.”
