stories.title: $1.5M gift to King’s University College funds classroom upgrades, student learning
stories.summary: King’s University College is set to receive a $1.5-million estate gift - the largest single donation in the institution’s history, to support classroom renewal projects and expand experiential learning opportunities for students.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
King’s University College is set to receive a $1.5-million estate gift from alumnus Frank Schlichtherle, the largest single donation in the institution’s history, to support classroom renewal projects and expand experiential learning opportunities for students.

The gift from Schlichtherle, a 1962 graduate of King’s, will fund modernization of learning spaces across campus, including a classroom that will be named in his honour. It will also establish an endowed experiential learning award to help a student access a global learning opportunity that might otherwise be financially out of reach.

King’s announced the donation as it continues efforts to upgrade teaching and learning spaces. A recently renovated classroom in Wemple Hall, funded through donor support, is among the projects already completed.

The college said Schlichtherle’s contribution will help advance broader renewal plans, including proposed upgrades to Wemple Hall’s east wing. Concept designs envision brighter classrooms with increased natural light, updated furnishings and new spaces for students to meet and collaborate.

“More than half a century after graduating, Frank Schlichtherle’s extraordinary gift will transform classrooms and gathering places into modern, accessible and inclusive spaces for students to learn and thrive,” King’s president Robert Ventresca said in a statement.

Ventresca said the donation will also help expand access to experiential learning opportunities for future students.

Schlichtherle graduated from King’s in 1962 and spent his career teaching history at Cayuga and Caledonia high schools before retiring in 1996. According to the college, he began supporting King’s in 1988 and remained a yearly donor for decades.

“For Frank, this is a crowning moment, a chance to give back to the place that helped shape who he became,” said Terra Ahrens, executive director of foundation, alumni and development at King’s. “More than 60 years after graduating, his connection to King’s continues through a gift that reflects both his lifelong commitment to education and his belief in the transformative power of the student experience.”

The college said the donation will create new capacity to update campus learning spaces while helping students participate in international and experiential learning programs.

The gift from Schlichtherle, a 1962 graduate of King’s, will fund modernization of learning spaces across campus, including a classroom that will be named in his honour. It will also establish an endowed experiential learning award to help a student access a global learning opportunity that might otherwise be financially out of reach.

King’s announced the donation as it continues efforts to upgrade teaching and learning spaces. A recently renovated classroom in Wemple Hall, funded through donor support, is among the projects already completed.

content_blocks.text: The college said Schlichtherle’s contribution will help advance broader renewal plans, including proposed upgrades to Wemple Hall’s east wing. Concept designs envision brighter classrooms with increased natural light, updated furnishings and new spaces for students to meet and collaborate.

“More than half a century after graduating, Frank Schlichtherle’s extraordinary gift will transform classrooms and gathering places into modern, accessible and inclusive spaces for students to learn and thrive,” King’s president Robert Ventresca said in a statement.
Ventresca said the donation will also help expand access to experiential learning opportunities for future students.

content_blocks.caption: Concept renderings of Wemple Hall’s East Wing, which illustrate how future classroom renewal could take shape. (Source: Kings University College)

content_blocks.text: Schlichtherle graduated from King’s in 1962 and spent his career teaching history at Cayuga and Caledonia high schools before retiring in 1996. According to the college, he began supporting King’s in 1988 and remained a yearly donor for decades.

“For Frank, this is a crowning moment, a chance to give back to the place that helped shape who he became,” said Terra Ahrens, executive director of foundation, alumni and development at King’s. “More than 60 years after graduating, his connection to King’s continues through a gift that reflects both his lifelong commitment to education and his belief in the transformative power of the student experience.”
The college said the donation will create new capacity to update campus learning spaces while helping students participate in international and experiential learning programs.

stories.title: Morning Update: Euro visions and Parliament’s return
stories.summary: Also in today’s edition: Okanagan’s summer lookback, and art for the season ahead
stories.author: Sierra Bein
stories.content:
Good morning. On the eve of Parliament’s return, Ottawa met once more with our close friends in Europe. More on that below, along with climate change in the Okanagan Valley and AI in the military.

Canada and France will start sharing space-launch systems and satellite data reception facilities, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced after a meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron on Saint-Pierre and Miquelon yesterday.

The big picture: Carney and Macron chose to meet on the archipelago of nearly 6,000 French citizens located 25 kilometres off Newfoundland’s Burin Peninsula as a show of solidarity and confirmation of sovereignty in the face of U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggression.

Up next: The two leaders are both headed to New York this week for United Nations General Assembly sessions.

Shannon Proudfoot : Canadian pride and rage in the face of tariff madness

Andrew Coyne : We May look back on this as the week Canada began to take its fate into its own hands

James Bradshaw : Carney’s investment summit attracted ‘all the right people.’ Will it bear fruit?

Paul Waldie : Carney, other Western leaders pleased with deal between U.S., Denmark and Greenland

Reading this online? Start your morning with context and insight on the day's biggest stories, in your inbox every weekday.

Investigations into a series of shootings in Toronto have been stymied because a key cellphone that was seized in connection with the case is running on a privacy-focused operating system and investigators have so far been unable to unlock the device, according to a police source.

The details: The phone operates on a little-known and highly secure operating system called GrapheneOS, reputed to be one of the most difficult systems to penetrate, the source said. It’s available for users to download and install for free, based on the Android Open Source Project. It was created by Toronto programmer Daniel Micay.

The federal government plans to kick off Monday’s return of parliamentary sittings with the introduction of major legislation targeting project approvals and Canada’s labour laws. The Canadian Labour Congress has already expressed concern with some of the proposals, which they say would limit bargaining power and encourage federal intervention to end strikes and lockouts.

What else: Another government bill that could be introduced will enable the extension of the federal gas tax break. MPs and senators will also debate several bills still making their way through Parliament, most notably the lawful access bill, C-22 .

Kerry-Lynne Findlay has resigned as leader of the Conservative Party of BC less than four months after taking the helm, ending a brief and tumultuous tenure beset by controversy, an exodus of MLAs and escalating internal opposition to her leadership.

The context: As of last night, 13 MLAs had departed since she became leader: 10 who quit, including Surrey-Serpentine River’s Linda Hepner, who left the party caucus earlier that day, and three whom Findlay removed. A 14th MLA, Reann Gasper, had given up her seat in Abbotsford-Mission to allow Findlay to run.

After a summer of fire in B.C.’s Okanagan Valley, weary locals are rethinking their way of life – or choosing to leave. The very climate that once made the the valley fruitful is now beginning to undermine both its bounty and its appeal. Devastating events once considered exceptional are now simply part of the region’s new reality.

What’s next: The defining season of the region is becoming harder to count on. The valley is gaining heat but losing water, gaining growing days but losing certainty about what crops will actually make it through to harvest. But it’s more than smoke and wildfires: Deep freezes have wiped out entire peach, nectarine and cherry crops, and, in some cases, entire vineyards.

Our arts team has collected all the best entertainment for the season. Forget about the trade war by settling in with these TV shows and documentaries , or venture outside for these intriguing new movies coming to the big screen near you. Take a friend to a show on the stage or to see visual art exhibitions across the country. For the listeners, there are new albums and many concerts to catch .

Catch up: The Globe and Mail’s Toronto International Film Festival team presents the highs, lows and all the moments in between from the 51st edition of the festival, which wrapped up yesterday.

Undeniably, China is ascendant in the world. Among all the factors behind it, the most underrated one, and therefore the one from which we gain the most by understanding, is the internal one. This idea of global China must be understood as reflective of domestic insecurities. — Ethan Lou, opinion editor in The Globe and Mail’s Report on Business

China’s scared, too: Behind every power, domestic insecurity lurks, Ethan Lou writes .

Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit the White House this week for the first time in a decade.

Kim Chow donated her kidney to a stranger , knowing it meant her older sister would receive one in exchange.

At home: A blood test that detects brain injury could soon help survivors of intimate partner violence.

Abroad: The main Kremlin party retained its majority in Russia’s parliament after a carefully orchestrated balloting that excluded most opposition candidates.

Middle East: Iran and the United States exchanged new threats as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi group escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Military: Canada is collaborating with domestic artificial-intelligence technologies to enhance military operations, as part of the MAIple Stack initiative launched last year.

Online: Here’s how to use The Globe’s Canadian digital brokerage ratings to suit your investments.

Offline: In the digital age, music listening parties offer opportunities for organic connection.

stories.title: Police investigate reports of missing election signs in Lambton County
stories.summary: Police say the unauthorized removal, damage or tampering of election signs could result in charges under the Criminal Code of Canada.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Lambton County OPP is reminding residents to respect election signs as municipalities across Ontario prepare for municipal elections on Oct. 26.

Police say the unauthorized removal, damage or tampering of election signs could result in charges under the Criminal Code of Canada.

The reminder comes after Lambton County OPP received complaints about election signs being removed without authorization in communities across the county.

OPP is asking anyone with information about the theft or damage of election signs to contact the Lambton County detachment at 1-888-310-1122.

Those wishing to remain anonymous can contact Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477) or submit a tip online through Sarnia-Lambton Crime Stoppers. Police note tipsters May be eligible for a cash reward of up to $2,000.

Municipal elections are scheduled to be held across Ontario on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Probes into Toronto’s shooter-for-hire network thwarted by impenetrable phone, police source says
stories.summary: Key cellphone seized in connection with the case runs on privacy-focused operating system, investigators so far unable to unlock it
stories.author: Joe Friesen, Robyn Doolittle
stories.content:
Investigations into a series of shootings in Toronto have been stymied because a key cellphone that was seized in connection with the case is running on a privacy-focused operating system and investigators have so far been unable to unlock the device, according to a police source.

Police believe the cellphone May contain communications and other data that could point to those responsible for ordering the shootings, including the March attack on the U.S. consulate, the source added.

In June, police launched a series of raids in response to the attack, as well as others on synagogues and local businesses in Toronto. An officer was killed in those operations and several suspects were arrested.

The phone operates on a little-known and highly secure operating system called GrapheneOS, reputed to be one of the most difficult to penetrate in the world, the source said. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source, who is not authorized to discuss the case.

GrapheneOS is available for users to download and install for free and is based on the Android Open Source Project, which allows developers to modify elements of the basic Android framework. GrapheneOS was created by Toronto programmer Daniel Micay .

Shooter-for-hire attacks linked to Toronto police constable’s licence plate searches, Project South documents allege

The police theory is that these shootings, which targeted buildings, businesses and other property, are the work of a loose network of mercenary gunmen unconnected to their targets, hired like gig workers via encrypted messages.

While GrapheneOS represents a uniquely difficult challenge for law enforcement, security features built into other technology also pose a serious problem. Newly released models of the iPhone, for example, can be complicated for investigators to crack, as are messaging apps such as Signal and WhatsApp, which offer users encryption and auto-delete functions.

The Toronto Police Service said that while it cannot comment on the status of a particular forensic examination, its officers are seeing encrypted technology used to plan a range of criminal activity.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw has publicly expressed his support for new federal legislation currently before Parliament, Bill C-22, that in his view would assist investigators who encounter encrypted information.

The controversial bill would force electronic service providers to facilitate the interception of data to help police and intelligence services with investigations. But it has been opposed by tech companies and advocates for civil liberties.

“As criminals increasingly use encrypted technology to facilitate serious criminal activity, law enforcement needs the appropriate lawful tools to keep pace,” said Stephanie Sayer, a Toronto police spokesperson.

Lawful-access bill could threaten encryption, deter investment, Chamber of Commerce warns

The GrapheneOS project said in a statement issued through its lawyers that, like any technology, it can be used for legitimate purposes or be misused by those involved in criminal activity. The project condemns all acts of violence, it said.

It also said it has not received any kind of request for assistance from a Canadian police force in recent months. If it were to receive such a request, the operating system is designed to make that type of assistance impossible, according to its statement.

“GrapheneOS is designed such that the project cannot bypass its own security protections. There are no backdoors, master keys, or remote access capabilities,” the statement said.

“This is a deliberate architectural choice: security that relies on the benevolence of the developer is not security at all.”

But GrapheneOS appears to be a different case.

It bills itself as a privacy- and security-focused operating system designed to protect against data theft, surveillance and security vulnerabilities. It has been praised by Edward Snowden, the former government contractor who revealed U.S. mass surveillance capabilities and was later charged with espionage.

Opinion: Shooters-for-hire network in Toronto shows a new front in the fight against terror financing

Mr. Micay, who declined an interview request but responded to questions through his lawyer, started work in this domain more than a decade ago when he was 20 years old.

He eventually co-founded a company called Copperhead along with two others that later dissolved in a legal dispute that’s still before Ontario’s Superior Court. But the project continues as GrapheneOS, which is a registered non-profit in Canada.

GrapheneOS has about 350,000 to 400,000 users, according to its website, compared with the billion or more people using Apple’s standard iPhone operating system.

It’s funded by donations, which it says have been substantial, according to a post on its website earlier this year connected to a Wired magazine article about the legal fight over Copperhead. The same post said that Mr. Micay’s income comes solely from sponsors on the GitHub platform, and that the GrapheneOS Foundation “is a non-profit and no one is getting rich from it.”

Mr. Micay said in court documents that he still contributes to the project but stepped down from the lead-developer role in 2023. The GrapheneOS Foundation lists Mr. Micay as a director, with a registered office address in Toronto.

Toronto police charge two suspects in U.S. consulate shooting

In its statement to The Globe, GrapheneOS said its system, like other operating systems, has protections against unauthorized access.

“In cases where individuals are attempting to access a device without the owner’s PIN or password, operating systems have no way of knowing whether an ‘unauthorized’ access attempt is valid,” the statement said. “The project does not distinguish between ‘good’ and ‘bad’ actors, because such distinctions are inherently subjective and subject to abuse.”

The tradeoff to using this kind of high-security operating system is that it’s less convenient, so few people do it, said David Lie, a professor of computer and electrical engineering at the University of Toronto. But Prof. Lie said there’s no legal prohibition against using a privacy-focused operating system, and in some cases, it May be essential for political dissidents, activists and journalists.

Last year, an American political activist who had GrapheneOS installed on his phone was stopped at a U.S. border entry point. He was asked to provide the code to unlock the device and instead provided what’s known as a duress PIN, which triggered a mechanism that wiped his phone clean. He has since been charged with destroying property to prevent seizure.

GrapheneOS issued a post on social media earlier this year defending the duress PIN, which it described as one relatively minor feature in its suite of defences.

“GrapheneOS is completely legal. We have no obligation to weaken any of the security protections it provides,” the post said. “Laws attempting to make it illegal or require weakening the security would be unconstitutional.”

Crown stays charges against man accused in GFL shootings case

Bill Budington, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, an organization that defends civil liberties in the digital sphere, said GrapheneOS’s effectiveness stems from the decision to treat any function that might compromise security as an opt-in choice for users.

“They’ve prioritized fixing areas of the operating system that will increase what’s called your attack surface, the places where an attacker can gain access to your device,” Mr. Budington said.

Mr. Budington said GrapheneOS is portrayed at times as a tool that appeals to bad actors, but that’s not accurate, in his view.

“There are a number of reasons why someone might want to use GrapheneOS rather than the base Android, and it has nothing at all to do with whether they’re committing crimes,” Mr. Budington said. “There are plenty of people using these operating systems because they don’t want [to give away] access to their devices.”

The technology’s appeal to criminal groups contributed to the breakdown of the Copperhead company in 2018, according to an affidavit filed by Mr. Micay.

He said his former business partner, James Donaldson, “decided to pursue business deals with criminal organizations.” The affidavit names a Canadian company called Phantom Secure, whose CEO was sentenced in the U.S. to nine years in prison for selling supposedly secure cellphones to transnational drug cartels.

Spate of police deaths sparks calls for action as officer mourned at Toronto funeral

Mr. Micay says in the court documents that he was uncomfortable with the proposals, which included making changes to the operating system’s security protocols and initiating remote updating systems that would allow third parties to have access to users’ phones.

He instead chose to delete part of the company’s technology to protect its users from interference from criminal organizations, the documents state. He subsequently ended his relationship with Mr. Donaldson, who is not connected to the GrapheneOS project.

Mr. Donaldson and Copperhead reject that version of events and said in their filings that they never pursued business deals with criminal organizations. They said the business relationship broke down because of Mr. Micay’s “belligerence and refusal to deal with Mr. Donaldson.”

Canadian authorities have long sought a law that would force electronic service providers to grant access to data in a timely manner, a provision some have compared to requiring an open electronic backdoor. Bill C-22, currently before Parliament, May finally grant law enforcement much of what they have been seeking. But how to strike a balance on privacy and security is the subject of intense debate.

Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto called the bill’s data-retention requirements, which would mandate electronic service providers keep detailed data of nearly every Canadian for a year, revealing their movements and who they contacted, “almost certainly unconstitutional.”

Major tech companies such as Signal, which provides secure messaging, and DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused search engine, have said they would withdraw from Canada if they were forced to reveal or retain user data that compromises users’ privacy.

Although it was once difficult for law enforcement to search locked cellphones, it’s now relatively routine, said Alain Filotto, a retired RCMP officer who now runs a digital-forensics company in B.C.

paragraphs: Investigations into a series of shootings in Toronto have been stymied because a key cellphone that was seized in connection with the case is running on a privacy-focused operating system and investigators have so far been unable to unlock the device, according to a police source.

Police believe the cellphone May contain communications and other data that could point to those responsible for ordering the shootings, including the March attack on the U.S. consulate, the source added.

In June, police launched a series of raids in response to the attack, as well as others on synagogues and local businesses in Toronto. An officer was killed in those operations and several suspects were arrested.

The phone operates on a little-known and highly secure operating system called GrapheneOS, reputed to be one of the most difficult to penetrate in the world, the source said. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source, who is not authorized to discuss the case.

GrapheneOS is available for users to download and install for free and is based on the Android Open Source Project, which allows developers to modify elements of the basic Android framework. GrapheneOS was created by Toronto programmer Daniel Micay .
Shooter-for-hire attacks linked to Toronto police constable’s licence plate searches, Project South documents allege

The police theory is that these shootings, which targeted buildings, businesses and other property, are the work of a loose network of mercenary gunmen unconnected to their targets, hired like gig workers via encrypted messages.

While GrapheneOS represents a uniquely difficult challenge for law enforcement, security features built into other technology also pose a serious problem. Newly released models of the iPhone, for example, can be complicated for investigators to crack, as are messaging apps such as Signal and WhatsApp, which offer users encryption and auto-delete functions.

The Toronto Police Service said that while it cannot comment on the status of a particular forensic examination, its officers are seeing encrypted technology used to plan a range of criminal activity.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw has publicly expressed his support for new federal legislation currently before Parliament, Bill C-22, that in his view would assist investigators who encounter encrypted information.

The controversial bill would force electronic service providers to facilitate the interception of data to help police and intelligence services with investigations. But it has been opposed by tech companies and advocates for civil liberties.

“As criminals increasingly use encrypted technology to facilitate serious criminal activity, law enforcement needs the appropriate lawful tools to keep pace,” said Stephanie Sayer, a Toronto police spokesperson.
Lawful-access bill could threaten encryption, deter investment, Chamber of Commerce warns

The GrapheneOS project said in a statement issued through its lawyers that, like any technology, it can be used for legitimate purposes or be misused by those involved in criminal activity. The project condemns all acts of violence, it said.

It also said it has not received any kind of request for assistance from a Canadian police force in recent months. If it were to receive such a request, the operating system is designed to make that type of assistance impossible, according to its statement.
“GrapheneOS is designed such that the project cannot bypass its own security protections. There are no backdoors, master keys, or remote access capabilities,” the statement said.
“This is a deliberate architectural choice: security that relies on the benevolence of the developer is not security at all.”
But GrapheneOS appears to be a different case.

It bills itself as a privacy- and security-focused operating system designed to protect against data theft, surveillance and security vulnerabilities. It has been praised by Edward Snowden, the former government contractor who revealed U.S. mass surveillance capabilities and was later charged with espionage.
Opinion: Shooters-for-hire network in Toronto shows a new front in the fight against terror financing
Mr. Micay, who declined an interview request but responded to questions through his lawyer, started work in this domain more than a decade ago when he was 20 years old.

He eventually co-founded a company called Copperhead along with two others that later dissolved in a legal dispute that’s still before Ontario’s Superior Court. But the project continues as GrapheneOS, which is a registered non-profit in Canada.
GrapheneOS has about 350,000 to 400,000 users, according to its website, compared with the billion or more people using Apple’s standard iPhone operating system.

It’s funded by donations, which it says have been substantial, according to a post on its website earlier this year connected to a Wired magazine article about the legal fight over Copperhead. The same post said that Mr. Micay’s income comes solely from sponsors on the GitHub platform, and that the GrapheneOS Foundation “is a non-profit and no one is getting rich from it.”

Mr. Micay said in court documents that he still contributes to the project but stepped down from the lead-developer role in 2023. The GrapheneOS Foundation lists Mr. Micay as a director, with a registered office address in Toronto.
Toronto police charge two suspects in U.S. consulate shooting
In its statement to The Globe, GrapheneOS said its system, like other operating systems, has protections against unauthorized access.

“In cases where individuals are attempting to access a device without the owner’s PIN or password, operating systems have no way of knowing whether an ‘unauthorized’ access attempt is valid,” the statement said. “The project does not distinguish between ‘good’ and ‘bad’ actors, because such distinctions are inherently subjective and subject to abuse.”

The tradeoff to using this kind of high-security operating system is that it’s less convenient, so few people do it, said David Lie, a professor of computer and electrical engineering at the University of Toronto. But Prof. Lie said there’s no legal prohibition against using a privacy-focused operating system, and in some cases, it May be essential for political dissidents, activists and journalists.

Last year, an American political activist who had GrapheneOS installed on his phone was stopped at a U.S. border entry point. He was asked to provide the code to unlock the device and instead provided what’s known as a duress PIN, which triggered a mechanism that wiped his phone clean. He has since been charged with destroying property to prevent seizure.
GrapheneOS issued a post on social media earlier this year defending the duress PIN, which it described as one relatively minor feature in its suite of defences.

“GrapheneOS is completely legal. We have no obligation to weaken any of the security protections it provides,” the post said. “Laws attempting to make it illegal or require weakening the security would be unconstitutional.”
Crown stays charges against man accused in GFL shootings case

Bill Budington, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, an organization that defends civil liberties in the digital sphere, said GrapheneOS’s effectiveness stems from the decision to treat any function that might compromise security as an opt-in choice for users.
“They’ve prioritized fixing areas of the operating system that will increase what’s called your attack surface, the places where an attacker can gain access to your device,” Mr. Budington said.
Mr. Budington said GrapheneOS is portrayed at times as a tool that appeals to bad actors, but that’s not accurate, in his view.

“There are a number of reasons why someone might want to use GrapheneOS rather than the base Android, and it has nothing at all to do with whether they’re committing crimes,” Mr. Budington said. “There are plenty of people using these operating systems because they don’t want [to give away] access to their devices.”
The technology’s appeal to criminal groups contributed to the breakdown of the Copperhead company in 2018, according to an affidavit filed by Mr. Micay.

He said his former business partner, James Donaldson, “decided to pursue business deals with criminal organizations.” The affidavit names a Canadian company called Phantom Secure, whose CEO was sentenced in the U.S. to nine years in prison for selling supposedly secure cellphones to transnational drug cartels.
Spate of police deaths sparks calls for action as officer mourned at Toronto funeral

Mr. Micay says in the court documents that he was uncomfortable with the proposals, which included making changes to the operating system’s security protocols and initiating remote updating systems that would allow third parties to have access to users’ phones.

He instead chose to delete part of the company’s technology to protect its users from interference from criminal organizations, the documents state. He subsequently ended his relationship with Mr. Donaldson, who is not connected to the GrapheneOS project.

He said there are two major software companies that supply digital-forensic solutions to police: Cellebrite, with headquarters in Virginia, and Magnet Forensics, based in Waterloo, Ont.
“They can pretty much unlock any phone,” Mr. Filotto said.
Neither Cellebrite nor Magnet Forensics would comment on whether it has ever succeeded in extracting digital data from a phone running GrapheneOS.
The RCMP and the FBI also declined to comment on that question.

stories.title: Here's how Buy Canadian scanner apps did on identifying food origins
stories.summary: Smartphone apps promising to help shoppers identify Canadian groceries have popped up since the onset of trade tensions with the United States last year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Smartphone apps promising to help shoppers identify Canadian groceries have popped up since the onset of trade tensions with the United States last year.

But how do these apps compare?

After reviewing more than a dozen options, The Canadian Press chose three apps to use on a variety of common grocery items.

Here are the results delivered by Buy Beaver, O SCANada and Maple Scan:

Pied-Mont Dora strawberry jam

Buy Beaver: The jam jar received a full score of 100 because it is manufactured in Quebec. The app didn’t provide information about the parent company or source of ingredients.

Buy Beaver rates items on a scale of zero to 100, which it says is based on the company’s manufacturing location, ingredient sources and the location of its parent company.

O SCANada: Dora was labelled as “Canadian-owned,” as it is a Canadian family-owned food manufacturer headquartered in Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Que. It didn’t specify the origin of ingredients used to make the jam, which it said was not publicly disclosed.

Maple Scan: Pied-Mont Dora was identified as a Quebec-based company, labelling it as both made and packaged in Canada. It also offers the company’s history, highlighting its Canadian roots.

Kraft peanut butter

Buy Beaver: It scored zero because Kraft Heinz Co. is headquartered in the U.S. The app didn’t recognize its Canadian manufacturing location or source of ingredients.

O SCANada: The app said the product is “not Canadian-owned,” but correctly identified its manufacturing location in Mont-Royal, Que. Meanwhile, ingredient origins aren’t specified. “Origin of peanuts is not publicly disclosed,” the scan found.

Maple Scan: The PB was labelled as both made and manufactured in Canada.

Redpath granulated sugar

Buy Beaver: The sugar scored 70 for being a subsidiary of American Sugar Refining Inc., which it has been since 2007. The app said its manufacturing location is in Canada and that most of its ingredients are Canadian.

Though refined and packaged by Redpath, the majority of sugar cane used in Canadian sugar production is imported in bulk from tropical regions in South and Central America, according to the Canadian Sugar Institute, since Canada’s climate is not suitable for growing sugar cane.

O SCANada: The app called the product “not Canadian-owned,” correctly noting Redpath is a subsidiary of the U.S.-based company. The country of origin for sugar cane was not disclosed. It called the product “not Canadian-owned.”

Maple Scan: The sugar was called a product of Canada, made in Canada and packaged domestically. The app said the manufacturer is based in Ontario and identified American Sugar Refining as its parent company.

French’s tomato ketchup

Buy Beaver: The ketchup earned a score of 70 out of 100, with the app identifying the U.S.-based McCormick & Co. as its owner (McCormick Canada brought its French’s ketchup production in-house in 2021). Manufacturing locations were listed as Canada and Baltimore, Md. It said the ingredients were “100 per cent Canadian.”

O SCANada: The product was labelled “not Canadian-owned,” but knew that its manufacturing plant is in London, Ont. and made with Canadian tomatoes sourced from Ontario growers.

Maple Scan: The app said it is not a product of Canada, but is made in Canada with 100 per cent Canadian tomatoes, and is bottled in Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Base Line Road East to close for underground servicing work
stories.summary: A signed detour will direct traffic along High Street, Emery Street East and Ridout Street South.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A stretch of Base Line Road East will be closed for several days beginning Monday as crews complete underground servicing work in the area.

The City of London says Base Line Road East will be closed between High Street and Ridout Street South from Sept. 21 until approximately Sept. 24. The work involves connecting water, storm sewer and sanitary sewer services to a nearby property.

A signed detour will direct traffic along High Street, Emery Street East and Ridout Street South.

The south sidewalk within the construction zone will also be closed. Access to nearby homes will be maintained throughout the project, according to the city.

Some London Transit Commission routes will be affected by the closure. Transit riders are encouraged to check the LTC website for updated route and schedule information.

The work is taking place near the Wellington Gateway Phase 2A and 2B construction area. Motorists should expect delays and changing traffic conditions and are advised to follow posted detour signs.

stories.summary: Called the MAIple Stack, the initiative was launched last year, but few details have been released publicly about what it entails
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
Canada is partnering with domestic artificial-intelligence technologies to enhance military operations, the Department of National Defence says, as the use of AI and data sovereignty become increasingly vital to national security and modern warfare.

Called the MAIple Stack, the initiative was launched last year, but few details have been released publicly about what it entails.

Through questions submitted to DND over the summer, The Globe and Mail has learned that MAIple Stack is bringing together a suite of sovereign AI technologies from Canadian companies for use in defence operations.

In a statement provided to The Globe, DND spokesperson Kened Sadiku said: “Ultimately, the initiative is intended to support [Canadian Armed Forces] personnel who operate in complex, data-rich environments, to improve situational awareness, and support faster, better-informed decision-making.”

He added that “Any companies that are involved with the MAIple Initiative at this time have been chosen through a lens of expanding Canada’s burgeoning sovereign AI ecosystem, ensuring partnerships with Canadian technology companies and alignment with the Defence Industrial Strategy.”

Ottawa awards first drone contracts worth up to $50-million through new marketplace

MAIple Stack represents a first step in assessing how the department, as well as the Forces, can implement future Canadian AI capabilities, he said.

AI is rapidly changing the way wars are fought. Militaries employing drones or sensors, for example, might use AI to help analyze and dissect the data collected by these devices. The technology is also being developed to speed up the pace of making decisions in military operations, as well as to create lifelike training simulations for soldiers away from the battlefield.

In recognition of this, the Armed Forces and DND released a 32-page AI Strategy in 2024 committing themselves to becoming “AI enabled” by 2030.

“The technology will not wait for us to act,” the strategy reads. “Falling behind now in our adoption of AI will risk the loss of our operational advantage.”

Despite the involvement of a handful of Canadian companies, Ottawa has offered little information about MAIple Stack’s function or importance. In response to a request for an interview about the initiative, the federal government initially agreed but later backed out, citing concerns over national security.

Opinion: In this new world, defence strategy is now economic strategy

Ottawa answered an initial list of questions sent by The Globe but did not respond to a second set asking for further details, such as funding or examples of use in operations.

In the 2026-27 DND departmental plan, with a $33.5-million “seed investment,” a “key initiative” around the use of sovereign AI technology is cited as being tested in military deployments.

The Globe reached out to a handful of Canadian companies working in AI and defence to ask about the initiative. However, they declined to speak about it and redirected questions to DND personnel such as Major Tyler Currie, an officer with the Canadian Armed Forces.

Maj. Currie did not respond to repeated requests for comment. However, when The Globe first reached out to him, it received an out-of-office reply redirecting queries on specific topics to various colleagues. This included inquiries about “MAIple Stack technologies,” that the reply listed as Canadian companies Cohere Inc., Anvil Intelligence Inc., H2 Analytics Inc., Larus Technologies Corporation and Tactiql Inc.

The use of AI by DND and the Armed Forces is not new. Many of the aforementioned companies have won contracts with Ottawa in recent years to help the country’s military with tasks such as collecting and analyzing data, or rapid decision-making.

Cibc commits $2-billion to help finance defence-related companies

It is unclear how the MAIple Stack initiative differs from or encompasses other work that these companies are already engaged in for the Forces.

The AI initiative is being introduced through a phased approach, which the federal government said includes experimentation, integration into its operations and “lessons learned.” Canadian defence tech companies have previously asked for more opportunities to test their products with the Forces and make changes based on feedback, rather than trying to fit a one-time set of criteria for procurements.

Over time, Mr. Sadiku said more technologies May be brought into MAIple Stack. He said that one of the goals of the program is to “explore complementary capabilities surrounding advanced analytics and data-management concepts.” He specified that it is not a “fixed, one-time project” and did not provide an end date when asked.

“The ecosystem is designed to evolve as the Canadian AI industry grows and diversifies its capabilities,” he wrote.

stories.title: Carney eyes UN reform in New York, unclear whether he’ll meet Trump at Unga
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s attempt to bring Canada closer to Europe and strengthen ties with countries around the world will continue this week in U.S. President Donald Trump’s hometown, as he attends the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (Unga) in New York City.
stories.author: Jeremie Charron, Mike Le Couteur
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney’s attempt to bring Canada closer to Europe and strengthen ties with countries around the world will continue this week in U.S. President Donald Trump’s hometown, as he attends the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (Unga) in New York City.

Senior government officials who briefed reporters ahead of the trip said Carney will meet with world leaders and business leaders, but it’s unclear if the prime minister and American president will meet on the sidelines of Unga.

As some world leaders, like Trump, move away from multilateralism, one of the things Carney will focus on is reform of the United Nations and selection of the organization’s next secretary-general. Antonio Guterres is in his second and final five-year term as head of the UN, which comes to a close at the end of this year.

“At a moment when the international order is being remade, Canada intends to help shape it,” Carney said in a statement ahead of the trip. “At the General Assembly, we will sit down with partners old and new, defend the rules that protect our sovereignty, and turn co-operation into real opportunity for Canadian workers and businesses.”

Senior government officials added that the prime minister will “call for concrete progress on UN reform efforts, so the organization remains relevant in this new context.” Officials noted that Carney wants to see reform that “helps the UN continue to be efficient and relevant in this period of significant global change.”

Part of that change has seen the Trump administration withdraw the U.S. from multiple UN agencies and organizations, like the World Health Organization and the cultural agency Unesco.

During a nearly one-hour speech at the General Assembly in 2025, during which the teleprompter stopped working, Trump railed against the UN and openly questioned the effectiveness of the organization, arguing it failed to serve U.S. interests.

“What is the purpose of the United Nations? The UN has such tremendous potential ... but it’s not even coming close to living up to that potential,” Trump said. Later, when meeting face-to-face with Guterres, Trump told the secretary-general, “our country is behind the United Nations 100 per cent.”

Advancing a two-state solution in the Middle East

On Tuesday, Carney is expected to co-host an event with France and the United Kingdom on the two-state solution, a year after the three countries recognized an independent Palestinian state at the General Assembly.

Last year, Canada recognized the state of Palestine as part of a co-ordinated international effort which Canadian officials said was to “preserve the viability of a two-state solution.”

That support came after the Palestinian Authority committed to advance governance reforms, pursue demilitarization and hold local elections.

Canadian officials told reporters these meetings will be an opportunity for nations to continue showing support for the two-state solution while looking at the implementation of key priorities and progress that has been made.

Face to Face with Trump

The Unga in New York will also mark the first time Prime Minister Carney and President Trump will be face-to-face since trade talks between the two countries fell apart.

After a caucus retreat on Parliament Hill Saturday, the prime minister was asked directly whether he has plans to meet with Trump in New York.

“We’ll meet with lots of leaders in New York,” said the prime minister, offering no definitive answer.

The question of a meeting in the Big Apple between the two leaders, or even with anyone from the U.S. administration, was also raised during a technical briefing with reporters ahead of Carney’s visit.

“Nothing is confirmed right now,” said a senior government official speaking on a not-for-attribution basis.

Meanwhile, Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said last week that her country is getting closer to a deal with Trump, and hopes to reach a deal soon.

Asked Saturday about what that could mean for Canada, the prime minister responded that “it means we’re a sovereign country.”

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives' Findlay resigns; interim leader named ahead of potential election
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia's political landscape continues to shift, with Kerry-Lynne Findlay stepping down as the leader of B-C's Conservatives Sunday, and the party's board of directors appointing MLA Lorne Doerkson as interim leader hours later.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - After weeks of defections, expulsions and ugly infighting that reduced the British Columbia Conservative caucus by more than a third, the official Opposition’s legislative ranks are growing again.

The party’s new interim leader, Lorne Doerkson — who was appointed Sunday after the resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay — has moved swiftly to restore five legislators to the caucus amid the prospect of an early election.

Former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford, and legislators Linda Hepner, Scott McInnis and Claire Rattée are all back in.

The party has been announcing the returns on social media on Monday under the slogan “Conservatives unite against the NDP.”

The appeal to unity comes after the tumultuous reign of Findlay, who had expelled Rustad, Halford and Rattée on Friday, with Hepner quitting early Sunday.

They were among 13 Conservatives who resigned or were evicted from the caucus since August, during upheaval centred on Findlay’s leadership and what some called “ideological purity tests.”

Findlay was narrowly chosen as leader in May, running on a platform of “faith, family and freedom.”

Rustad told a news conference at the legislature that there were “obviously lots of people” in B.C. who don’t know Doerkson, a Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but he called Doerkson a “quality individual” and said he would be happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wanted.

“I am returning to do the work, not to run the next chapter from the outside,” Rustad later said on social media.

“If the new leadership wants my help, they will have it. I will not force my old vision onto them.”

Rustad said talks between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party — which now houses eight former Conservative MLAs — should succeed and the province “cannot afford two opposition parties” with an election on the cards.

But while the theme of the day was unity, there were still some recriminations.

Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to “let politics go.”

He said Clark and Campbell were among the “players” trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that “their time is over.”

“That May mean time is over for me, too. I don’t know,” said Rustad, adding that “it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside.”

Clark swiftly clapped back.

“John! Pull yourself together man,” she said on social media.

Clark had earlier said in an interview that different factions on the right in B.C. needed to come together, to resolve this “chaotic” moment.

The former BC Liberal premier said she had been fielding calls all day on the way forward.

“I’m reminding them all, that we all used to work together, and we can all do that again,” she said, calling the prospect of an election call less than two years into Premier David Eby’s mandate “absolutely unheard of and it is a disgrace.”

She said she was not playing matchmaker between Opposition factions.

“I’m not deeply involved in negotiations or anything of that nature. I am just sitting by my phone...(we) absolutely cannot afford another four years of this absolutely terrible government.”

Rustad — who said his “time as leader is over” but not his service to the province — said “high level” unity talks underway between the Conservatives and CentreBC had a 95 per cent chance of success.

The legislature’s updated party standings are 47 for the NDP — giving them a one-seat majority — with 29 Conservatives, two Greens, two vacancies, and 15 Independents, including those joining CentreBC.

The developments come after the caucus of B.C.‘s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election in light of Findlay’s resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.

An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad said there was a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo—Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the BC Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before he crossed the floor to join the Conservatives. He was reelected in 2024.

Rustad also provided a timeline of the chaos that preceded his short-lived expulsion from the Conservatives on Friday.

He said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was “emotion and frustration around the table.”

The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.

But on Friday Rustad was told he was out.

Speculation about a snap election being called intensified Monday when the NDP announced that cabinet minister Lana Popham would not be running for a sixth term.

NDP MLAs had met the previous night to discuss Findlay’s departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.

“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the email obtained by The Canadian Press said.

It went on to say the meeting was to “to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

The Canadian Press briefly attended the meeting, along with at least two Conservative legislators, before being asked to leave.

Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be “election ready.”

McInnis, who represents Columbia River-Revelstoke, had quit the Conservative caucus on Sept. 2, saying he did not agree with the direction of Findlay’s leadership.

He said in a statement on Monday that the opportunity to return “home” came at a critical time for the province, and he rejected the need for “ideological purity tests.”

No party had ever defeated the B.C. NDP without being a “big tent party,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.
paragraphs: Victoria - After weeks of defections, expulsions and ugly infighting that reduced the British Columbia Conservative caucus by more than a third, the official Opposition’s legislative ranks are growing again.

The party’s new interim leader, Lorne Doerkson — who was appointed Sunday after the resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay — has moved swiftly to restore five legislators to the caucus amid the prospect of an early election.
Former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford, and legislators Linda Hepner, Scott McInnis and Claire Rattée are all back in.
The party has been announcing the returns on social media on Monday under the slogan “Conservatives unite against the NDP.”
The appeal to unity comes after the tumultuous reign of Findlay, who had expelled Rustad, Halford and Rattée on Friday, with Hepner quitting early Sunday.
They were among 13 Conservatives who resigned or were evicted from the caucus since August, during upheaval centred on Findlay’s leadership and what some called “ideological purity tests.”
Findlay was narrowly chosen as leader in May, running on a platform of “faith, family and freedom.”

Rustad told a news conference at the legislature that there were “obviously lots of people” in B.C. who don’t know Doerkson, a Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but he called Doerkson a “quality individual” and said he would be happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wanted.
“I am returning to do the work, not to run the next chapter from the outside,” Rustad later said on social media.
“If the new leadership wants my help, they will have it. I will not force my old vision onto them.”

Rustad said talks between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party — which now houses eight former Conservative MLAs — should succeed and the province “cannot afford two opposition parties” with an election on the cards.
But while the theme of the day was unity, there were still some recriminations.
Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to “let politics go.”
He said Clark and Campbell were among the “players” trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that “their time is over.”
“That May mean time is over for me, too. I don’t know,” said Rustad, adding that “it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside.”
Clark swiftly clapped back.
“John! Pull yourself together man,” she said on social media.
Clark had earlier said in an interview that different factions on the right in B.C. needed to come together, to resolve this “chaotic” moment.
The former BC Liberal premier said she had been fielding calls all day on the way forward.

“I’m reminding them all, that we all used to work together, and we can all do that again,” she said, calling the prospect of an election call less than two years into Premier David Eby’s mandate “absolutely unheard of and it is a disgrace.”
She said she was not playing matchmaker between Opposition factions.
“I’m not deeply involved in negotiations or anything of that nature. I am just sitting by my phone...(we) absolutely cannot afford another four years of this absolutely terrible government.”
Rustad — who said his “time as leader is over” but not his service to the province — said “high level” unity talks underway between the Conservatives and CentreBC had a 95 per cent chance of success.

The legislature’s updated party standings are 47 for the NDP — giving them a one-seat majority — with 29 Conservatives, two Greens, two vacancies, and 15 Independents, including those joining CentreBC.

The developments come after the caucus of B.C.‘s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election in light of Findlay’s resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.
An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad said there was a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo—Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the BC Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before he crossed the floor to join the Conservatives. He was reelected in 2024.
Rustad also provided a timeline of the chaos that preceded his short-lived expulsion from the Conservatives on Friday.
He said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was “emotion and frustration around the table.”
The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.
But on Friday Rustad was told he was out.
Speculation about a snap election being called intensified Monday when the NDP announced that cabinet minister Lana Popham would not be running for a sixth term.

NDP MLAs had met the previous night to discuss Findlay’s departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.
“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the email obtained by The Canadian Press said.

It went on to say the meeting was to “to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.
The Canadian Press briefly attended the meeting, along with at least two Conservative legislators, before being asked to leave.
Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be “election ready.”
McInnis, who represents Columbia River-Revelstoke, had quit the Conservative caucus on Sept. 2, saying he did not agree with the direction of Findlay’s leadership.
He said in a statement on Monday that the opportunity to return “home” came at a critical time for the province, and he rejected the need for “ideological purity tests.”
No party had ever defeated the B.C. NDP without being a “big tent party,” he said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

stories.title: NDP meets on election prospects as B.C. Conservatives name Doerkson interim leader
stories.summary: Victoria — The caucus of British Columbia's governing NDP has met to discuss a potential early election after the resignation of Opposition B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
B.C. Conservative leadership candidate Kerry-Lynne Findlay looks on during a debate at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference in Vancouver on Friday, April 24, 2026. Findlay went on to win the leadership contest but resigned on Sunday after weeks of upheaval in the caucus. THE Canadian Press/Chad Hipolito THE Canadian Press

By Wolfgang Depner, The Canadian Press

Posted September 21, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 21, 2026 10:42 am.

Victoria — The caucus of British Columbia’s governing NDP has met to discuss a potential early election after the resignation of Opposition B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Findlay quit Sunday, saying it was the right move for the party and province, and the Conservative board of directors appointed MLA Lorne Doerkson as interim leader hours later.

But the Conservative constitution prohibits an interim head from seeking the party’s leadership in a subsequent ballot, so if an election is called soon, the official Opposition candidate for premier would not immediately be clear.

Findlay’s resignation follows weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, with 13 defections or expulsions, including former leader John Rustad who was ejected with two others on Friday.

Rustad is set to address reporters in Victoria today.

NDP MLAs met last night to discuss Findlay’s departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators on Sunday, instead of just those on the government benches.

“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the email obtained by The Canadian Press says.

It goes on to say the meeting was to “to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Premier David Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be “election ready.”

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo—Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the BC Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before crossing the floor to join the Conservatives and being reelected in 2024.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

Wolfgang Depner, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Quebec election campaign enters 26th day
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec political leaders are entering their 26th day on the hustings, as the election campaign enters its final two-week stretch.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Leaders of Quebec’s political parties on Monday ruled out forming alliances with their opponents to govern, as polls point to a possible minority outcome with two weeks to go before the Oct. 5 provincial election.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said he’s not looking at forming an alliance with the Quebec Conservatives, or any other party, as opponents continued to try to paint his party and Éric Duhaime’s with the same brush.

stories.title: Montreal city council to debate bylaw banning insults against municipal employees
stories.summary: Montreal - Montreal city council is set to debate a proposed bylaw this week that could ban people from insulting municipal employees, including police officers.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.scrape_error: 429 Client Error: Too Many Requests for url: https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/quebec/montreal-city-council-to-debate-bylaw-banning-insults-against-municipal-employees/article_de999693-d7c2-52d0-aa05-999fc8d05597.html
paragraphs: Montreal - Montreal city council has adopted a bylaw to ban people from insulting police officers and other municipal employees.
The debate over the rule lasted over half an hour, with the official opposition saying the proposed bylaw was “half-baked.” It was adopted with 35 voting in favour and 25 opposed.
“We are being asked to vote now and consult later,” said Marie Plourde, leader of the official opposition.
Under the bylaw, residents who insult city staff would face fines between $300 and $1,000 for a first offence. Subsequent offences could result in fines up to $2,000.
City officials have not said when they will implement the bylaw.

Yves Francoeur, head of the police brotherhood, has said his union’s members have been pushing for such a bylaw for years. But lawyers and civil rights groups worry the bylaw could infringe on the constitutional right to freedom of expression.
Other municipalities in the province, including Quebec City, Laval, Longueuil and Sherbrooke, already have similar bylaws.
The Canadian Press reported in June that some of these municipalities have issued thousands of fines over the past six years.
“Giving the middle finger, it’s not what will give you a ticket,” the mayor said before the council meeting. “Let’s just be honest. There’s bigger issues in terms of the attitude of some citizens.”
The new Montreal bylaw would ban insults, harassment, threats, abuse and intimidation, as well as offensive and aggressive behaviour.
It also includes provisions saying city employees could refuse to provide services to someone who misbehaves. However, the bylaw doesn’t define what could be construed as an insult.
City councillor Carla Beauvais heavily criticized the administration for not providing clear definitions. She also questioned the lack of public consultations.

“A threat can be proven. An offensive word is felt. And how a person feels can vary from one person to another. So where does the offence begin? Where does permissible anger end? The text doesn’t say,” said Beauvais.
She cited various decisions from the Quebec City municipal court in which judges could not agree on what constitutes an insult, raising concerns that the rule will cause a backlog at the courthouse.

Opposition councillor Martine Musau Muele added that council was asked to vote on the rule without adequate information. She said the documents councillors received did not provide statistics and reports to support the need for the bylaw.
She also said the city did not conduct any risk assessment or prove that the measures under the Criminal Code are insufficient to deal with belligerent residents.

“Citizens are extremely concerned. People do not understand the reasoning of the administration. What led you to decide that today, with everything going on, that this is the most optimal move?” Muele said. “This is a draft, not a proposal.”

The two councillors also raised concerns around giving police more powers while public trust is fragile. In June, Montreal police disbanded a night patrol unit in the multicultural neighbourhood of Montréal-Nord over allegations of racism and misconduct.

During council, Martinez Ferrada acknowledged that “there will be more questions around this bylaw in the coming months” but insisted the administration “needed to act.” She said the administration would make reports publicly available.

She said she “understands the concerns,” and “shares some of them.” However, she said incidents of inappropriate behaviour have increased dramatically and are harming city employees, and making it more difficult to recruit new employees.

“We are simply saying that there is a line between challenging an institution and engaging in behaviour that is inappropriate toward the people who work for it,” said the mayor. “The thousands of women and men who work every day to serve Montreal have the right to protection from their employer, which is us.”
She noted that women are most often the target of disrespectful behaviour and listed misogynistic insults she said employees commonly receive.

The debate around banning insults in Montreal resurfaced in March, after videos of a man insulting a police officer with misogynistic comments went viral. The man was charged in July with defamatory libel under the Criminal Code and had pleaded not guilty.
However, critics have said the bylaw could hinder de-escalation efforts and harm those who are victims of racial profiling, in crisis, or experiencing homelessness.

Four community organizations sent the mayor a letter on Sept. 17 expressing their concerns. These organizations include rights and freedom advocacy groups, a legal clinic and an anti-racism group based in the borough of Montréal-Nord, where the police patrol unit was disbanded.

“The proposed regulation does not merely prohibit violent behaviour or conduct that threatens physical integrity, which is already prohibited by the Criminal Code,” the four organizations wrote in a joint letter. “It bans expressions that are not threatening simply because they are likely to cause discomfort, for example, ‘offensive’ behaviour.’”
They also argued the rules could be applied arbitrarily because it would be left to police officers’ discretion to issue fines.
Another lawyer, Sibel Ataogul, has proposed offering free legal help to citizens contesting the bylaw.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Vigil to mark one year since Nooran Rezayi shot and killed by police in Longueuil
stories.summary: Longueuil - An evening vigil is being held in Longueuil to mark one year since 15-year-old Nooran Rezayi was shot and killed by a local police officer.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Longueuil - It took about 20 minutes for a procession of mourners to walk from a police station in Longueuil, Que., to the location where 15-year-old Nooran Rezayi was killed.

CMU[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/quebec/vigil-to-mark-one-year-since-nooran-rezayi-shot-and-killed-by-police-in-longueuil/article_5764e30b-ce88-503c-961a-caff66a7a943.html)

By Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press

A year earlier, surveillance video released by his family’s lawyers appeared to show Rezayi was shot within seconds of police arriving at the scene.

When the group of about a dozen people reached the site Monday evening, Rezayi’s mother, Fahima Rezayi, clutched a small framed photograph of her son and screamed: “Justice for my son.”

Article continues below

Wheel It Studios: how a mobile recording studio is reshaping Toronto's music scene

The crowd then fell quiet for a minute of silence at the place where the teenager was killed on Sept. 21, 2025.

The vigil brought family, friends and supporters together on Montreal’s South Shore to mark a year without him — and a year spent waiting to learn whether the police officer who shot him will face criminal charges.

Many of those gathered outside the police station in Longueuil’s Saint-Hubert borough were dressed in black. Conversations were subdued, often little more than whispers, as the family stood together before beginning the walk.

Rezayi’s relatives occasionally embraced one another and wore white T-shirts bearing a photograph of the teenager smiling and giving a thumbs-up, alongside the words “Justice for Nooran.”

Nearby, several young people stood apart from the crowd wearing masks with messages calling for justice.

One person carried a sign reading “Nooran means light.” Another read “Forever 15.” Behind them, a large banner called for an end to police violence.

Rezayi’s sister, Frozan Rezayi, struggled through tears as she described her brother as “the light of our home, of our days,” and said he would remain the light of their hearts.

“He was a son, a brother, a cousin, a friend, a nephew, a child,” she told the crowd. “A child who brought joy everywhere he went.”

She remembered a teenager who liked making people laugh and smile, and who had dreams, plans and years of life still ahead of him.

“How has it already been a year since they took my brother’s life? And there are still no answers,” she said.

A year after Rezayi’s death, the central question for his family remains unresolved: whether the officer who shot him will face criminal charges.

Rezayi was killed after Longueuil police responded to a 911 call reporting a group of allegedly armed youths in a residential neighbourhood in Saint-Hubert.

Quebec’s police watchdog, the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes, later said the only firearm seized at the scene belonged to the officer who shot Rezayi. Investigators also seized a baseball bat, a backpack and ski masks.

The police watchdog completed its investigation in March and submitted its report to Quebec prosecutors, who must determine whether criminal charges should be laid.

Speaking at the vigil, family lawyer Fernando Belton said the lack of answers a year after the shooting has left Rezayi’s relatives living with uncertainty.

Belton told the crowd that the young people had been sitting on a sidewalk with their phones when police arrived and that Rezayi was shot within seconds. “Today, it is time to say: enough,” he said.

Belton said Rezayi’s death has also left other young people wondering about their own safety during encounters with police. “I think of every one of these young people who ask themselves, ‘Will I be next?’” he said.

He also spoke of parents fearing for their children when they leave home.

“I think of the mothers who have to send their child to school and who are forced to tell them, ‘Please, my boy, come back. Come back alive,’” Belton said.

He told Rezayi’s relatives their legal team would continue seeking answers. “We’re going to fight until the end to get justice for Nooran,” he said.

The shooting has led to several parallel proceedings. Six members of Rezayi’s family have filed a $2.2-million civil lawsuit against the City of Longueuil and its police force. The lawsuit alleges officers used unreasonable and disproportionate force. The allegations have not been tested in court.

The Quebec government has also launched an administrative investigation into the Longueuil police service over its actions following the shooting.

The police watchdog was notified of the shooting one hour and 36 minutes after it occurred. Documents released by Longueuil Mayor Catherine Fournier also indicated that Longueuil officers continued questioning witnesses at the scene.

Longueuil police have maintained their actions and the delay were justified under the circumstances.

Meanwhile, Montreal police conducted a separate criminal investigation into the alleged events preceding Rezayi’s death.

Eleven young people were charged in June, but prosecutors stayed the proceedings in August after obtaining new evidence that raised what they described as a complex legal issue. None of the charges involved possession of a firearm or harm to another person.

As the vigil returned to the place where her brother died, Frozan Rezayi urged those around her to keep saying his name.

“We are here to speak for Nooran, so that he is remembered,” she said. “So that his name continues to be heard.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

— with files from Erika Morris and Morgan Lowrie in Montreal
