Bell press release: Development would proceed in phases as customer commitments are secured and subject to commercial agreements, permits, approvals, and any relevant environmental assessments.
Government of Saskatchewan press release: If the project meets the threshold under Saskatchewan’s Environmental Assessment Act, it will go through the required assessment process.

Simon Enoch: On the original project when it was 300 megawatts, the environmental assessment that wasn’t done. Will that have to be redone given the expansion here? Or does the government consider the approval process already completed? I think there’s a lot of questions.

Anne Pasek: So far, the government’s approach to this seems to be to let that be decided by local bylaws, right, and the presumption is that building this kind of facility is the same as building any other kind of a facility, and the laws we have on the books are adequate to manage that. But, this expansion represents a real intensification of the scale of infrastructure that comes with commensurately large economic numbers, but it also comes with commensurately large environmental impacts. Things like noise. Things like how this is going to affect the hardscape or water implications on the site. Things like whether and how toxic chemicals are going to be stored on-site and how that’s going to be managed, diesel generators for backup and whether that will impact air pollution. How is that being monitored? I’d like to ask whether or not the overall climate impact of this facility has been considered in environmental assessments to date, or if it will be in the future. What does the Premier make of the fact that this facility is going to significantly put Saskatchewan behind in terms of meeting its climate commitments?

Government of Saskatchewan press release: Data centres do use a lot of electricity, which is why power planning is part of the work from the start. The project now includes a phased development of up to 900 MW of additional capacity through Saskatchewan’s Bring Your Own Power principle, creating a path to a 1.2 GW Canadian AI infrastructure hub in the province. Bell is responsible for bringing forward the power the expansion needs as it grows, and Saskatchewan families and businesses will not pay for that additional power.

Bell press release: The project aligns with the Government of Saskatchewan’s Data Centre Framework and reflects Bell’s commitments to Canadian control, data sovereignty, local jobs and investment, environmental stewardship and non-grid power. Together, these principles have created the conditions required for investment and development at this scale.

Brett Dolter: Moving from 300 megawatts to 1,200 megawatts, that’s a huge chunk of power. And if we think of the SaskPower system, the peak demand we’ve ever had in Saskatchewan was, back in 2021, it was 3,900 megawatts. And that was on a December night. It was cold, and so we had a lot of power demand, so 3,900 megawatts. If you stack another 1,200 megawatts on that, that’s a 30% increase in what we’d expect of our peak demand. So it’s a big increase in our peak demand. Also, that system is running all the time. SaskPower’s minimum load is more like 2,100 megawatts. And so you stack on another 1,200 megawatts on top of 2,100 megawatts, that’s a 57% increase in what our minimum would be. So we’re talking about a really big expansion of the electricity system. I think it’s really important how SaskPower deals with this new, very large customer. The rate review panel in their report was talking about creating a data centre rate class. And so we need to have a rate class just for data centres. And if they’re bringing their own power, I think that’s going to be a good thing for the rest of the province because anything new we’re building costs more than all the legacy assets, other legacy gas plants. So I think it’s wise to make sure that this stays in its own rate class and you don’t see a bit of a bleeding in of the impact of that new data centre on rates for other industrial customers. A 1,200 megawatt data centre is a huge increase in the amount of electricity generated and used in Saskatchewan. It’s important that it stays in its own rate class so it doesn’t have an effect of increasing the rates for everybody else in the province.

Bell’s press release includes the caveat that certain statements are based on current expectations and still depend on factors such as customer demand, agreements and regulatory approvals. THe company cautions those plans could change and the projected timelines, jobs and economic benefits are not guaranteed.

content_blocks.text: It’s a development that May constitute the largest single private-sector investment in the province’s history. And it has the potential to reshape the identity of Saskatchewan’s capital city.

Bell Canada and the provincial government announced a memorandum of understanding Monday at an investment summit hosted by Prime Minister Mark Carney in Toronto. The agreement would expand the controversial AI data centre near Regina from the original, still unfinished, 300-megawatt facility to a data centre hub with a total capacity of 1.2 gigawatts – quadrupling in scale.
It would also see Regina become the home of Bell AI Fabric’s headquarters.
The original press releases made many bold claims, but were sparse on details.
A day later, Saskatchewan’s NDP Leader of the Official Opposition, Carla Beck, called for a moratorium on new AI data centres until the province could provide more details.
Through conversations with three experts, Bell Canada and careful inspection of press releases, Global News seeks to bring you answers to the questions you May have.
Anne Pasek is the Canada Research Chair for Media, Culture and the Environment.
Simon Enoch is a senior researcher with the Canadian Centre for Alternative Policies and has been studying the rise of data centre backlash across North America.
Brett Dolter is an associate professor in the Faculty of Economics at the University of Regina with a focus on energy policy.
The answers provided by Bell came from its media relations department, or are quoted directly from its press release.
Global News has also quoted the Government of Saskatchewan press release, when relevant, for added context.
1: Where will this expansion be located?

Bell: It would not be possible to locate the full additional capacity within the current site footprint, given the setbacks and supporting power generation infrastructure required, so additional land will need to be purchased. Any future decision involving land acquisition, site selection or development will be made in close partnership with the local community, municipal council and provincial partners, with local input central to the process and subject to all applicable approvals. No site decisions have been made. Further details will be shared as customer commitments are secured and development plans advance.

No site decisions have been made. Further details will be shared as customer commitments are secured and development plans advance.

content_blocks.text: 2: How will the additional 900 MW of required power be produced?

Bell press release: The additional capacity would come from partner-developed power generation from natural gas. Bell: Consistent with Saskatchewan’s Data Centre Framework and its bring-your-own-power principle, the additional capacity will be supported by dedicated natural-gas generation located off the existing site, so it does not rely on Saskatchewan’s provincial electricity grid for load supply. Bell is working to identify an experienced third-party operating partner that will be responsible for the generation infrastructure.

Hopefully they’re also thinking about renewables because if you can integrate renewables with the gas, then you don’t have to run the gas plant as much and you’re not going to be polluting as much. Because at the same time as these new investments are expanding the grid, in Canada as a whole and Saskatchewan, the goal is to clean up our electricity system and get to zero emissions by 2050. So, 900 megawatts of gas, maybe that is right now the cheapest option, but let’s hopefully see it paired with wind and solar so we can actually bring down the pollution from that gas plant.

This would be the largest natural gas generating plant in Saskatchewan by a country mile. Currently, it’s the Queen Elizabeth power station in Saskatoon at 634 megawatts. This would be almost 300 megawatts more. So I think there’s a lot of questions for nearby residents who might not have signed up to live next to potentially the largest natural gas generating power plant in the province.

content_blocks.text: Anne Pasek: The part that stands out for me the most is the size of the gas plant that’s being plugged into this. The province has decided they want to prioritize clients that can bring their own power, that can build their own facilities to prevent grid operators from needing to shoulder all this burden, and that makes economic sense for ratepayers. But it’s really horrible math for the climate, right? Like we’re building a new city’s worth of emissions here. And that is glossed over, I think, in a lot of the discussion from the province. We could require renewable energy. It’s totally doable to go there in terms of the policy design. Australia, for example, nationally is requiring new data centres to have renewable power supply, some percentage that I think is going to be an escalating number over time. So the gas versus renewables issue is a choice the province is making and one that I think is fair for us to question.

content_blocks.text: 4: What about water consumption?

Bell press release: Consistent with all Bell AI Fabric projects, the proposed facilities will use closed-loop cooling technology that requires no municipal water. Bell: The sealed, closed-loop cooling system is filled at commissioning with a technical cooling fluid — a mixture of ultra-pure water, glycol and corrosion inhibitors — which then recirculates continuously to move heat away from the equipment. It is designed to operate continuously for more than 10 years without requiring the fluid to be changed, topped up or discharged during normal operation. When the fluid eventually requires replacement, it will be collected and transported offsite to an appropriate recycling facility for proper processing—not discharged into the municipal wastewater system. The system does not draw on municipal water for ongoing cooling operations.

It will eventually need to be discharged. That’s called backflow or the effluent of the system. That will need to be trucked usually off-site for water treatment. And we would definitely want there to be comprehensive environmental assessments to ensure that those chemicals don’t get released into the wild.

stories.title: Lawyer representing former Saskatoon Christian school principal questions witness credibility during closing arguments
stories.summary: Jurors heard from both the defense and prosecution Thursday as the two-week-long assault trial against a former Christian school principal in Saskatoon nears its end.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
The defence lawyer for a former principal of a private Christian school in Saskatoon told jurors Thursday that the five witnesses who testified during the assault trial were neither credible nor reliable.

Duff Arthur Friesen faces five counts of assault with a weapon for incidents between 1997 and 2007 during his time as an administrator of Christian Centre Academy , where he is accused of hitting students with a wooden paddle.

During the two-week-long trial, jurors heard from five former students, sharing testimonies on how they were paddled by the former Christian-school principal, some describing the paddles they were disciplined with.

Defence lawyer Daniel Mol told jurors Thursday that it is “unsafe” to convict his client based on the accounts of the five witnesses, saying some had their memories influenced by others not involved in the case, including that of a separate class-action lawsuit launched by former students against the school.

Earlier in the trial, Mol called into question the credibility of one witness , saying he gave testimony that differed from his 2021 statement to police.

Meanwhile, crown attorney Sheryl Fillo reminded the jury at the beginning of her closing arguments to consider each of the five counts separately, adding that an incident of paddling only had to take place once between the 20-year time span for it to be convictable.

Fillo also re-visited the testimonies of the five witnesses, recounting what one former student said about wearing multiple pairs of underwear to school to prepare for the paddling.

Fillo closed her arguments by asking jurors to use common sense when analyzing evidence and making a decision.

Judge Daryl Labach is expected to present the jury with legal instructions Friday morning before the deliberations begin.

Last year, Friesen was found guilty of one count of assault with a weapon and not guilty of three other counts in a separate trial.

Friesen received a six-month conditional sentence to be served in the community.

Christian Centre Academy was later renamed Legacy Christian Academy and is now known as Valour Academy.

stories.title: SubwayTakes coming to Canada? Kareem Rahma 100% agrees
stories.summary: A Toronto spinoff of the popular internet talk show is one of nine new Canadian-themed ‘creator shows’ announced at a YouTube Features event
stories.author: J. Kelly Nestruck
stories.content:
SubwayTakes is coming to Canada, bringing hot takes to the Toronto Transit Commission.

The popular YouTube talk show hosted by Egyptian-American comedian Kareem Rahma typically involves interviews with comedians and celebrities on the New York City subway – with occasional trips across the pond to ride the Tube in London.

But Rahma has been in Toronto riding the rocket this week – Line 1 Yonge-University to be specific – shooting an initial 14 episodes of subway-themed content while the cinematic spotlight has been on the Toronto International Film Festival .

“Toronto is one of the most diverse and exciting cities in the world, and there are so many interesting people here, from musicians to artists to chefs to comedians,” Rahma said in an interview with The Globe and Mail, adding he said he expected to now return regularly to the city.

SubwayTakes Canada was set to be officially announced at a YouTube Canada event on Thursday Rahma is hosting called YouTube Features – a rebranded version of the online video platform’s showcase for advertisers.

It is one of a slate of nine new “creator shows” made by Canadians or in Canada – and not just by those known primarily as social-media creators, but by Olympians, celebrity chefs and CBC stars.

Well-known Canadian athletes Sarah Nurse and Tessa Virtue are two set to launch new YouTube shows soon.

Nurse’s Sarah Tries it All will see the Vancouver Goldeneyes forward learn new skills working with professionals from chefs to fashion designers.

Virtue’s Virtuoso , meanwhile, is a new podcast series that will see the gold-medal-winning ice dancer sit down with artists, entrepreneurs and scientists at the top of their games.

In the culinary department, Matty Matheson’s Matty’s Farm will follow the Toronto chef and The Bear star as he sets up a farm in rural Ontario.

Is the future of Hollywood nestled inside the backrooms of YouTube?

Iron Chef Dad vs the Internet , meanwhile, will see chef Susur Lee and his son, Jet Bent-Lee, try out the latest viral recipes and food trends in their own kitchen.

The only scripted creator show being announced is Becky and Miranda, a new dark comedy created by Julie Nolke – recently named Creator of the Year at the Canadian Screen Awards – that she will star in alongside Nicole Power from Kim’s Convenience and its spinoff Strays .

“Creator shows” are a relatively new concept for YouTube – which does not produce its own content, but hosts it and splits advertising revenue with creators.

Users can upload episodic content under this designation and make their shows appear on YouTube more like what how you’d see a TV show be show on a streaming service such as Crave or Netflix, with videos organized into seasons and episodes.

“You finish one episode of SubwayTakes , and it’ll take you to the next episode of SubwayTakes , rather than bopping you back into the wide world of anything else on YouTube,” explains Nicole Bell, head of YouTube Canada.

For the top creator shows, YouTube will also help connect creators with brands that might want to come on board to sponsor them directly.

This is a way to entice more high-profile talent to the platform by helping them get money upfront to make content – and can also help established creators expand into a new market.

“So if you’re Kareem and you want to bring SubwayTakes up to Canada, we will try to match you with a brand that’s going to help fund that in a completely different way,” says Bell. “The creator makes that money, not YouTube. We’re just the matchmaker.”

Canadians, like audiences around the globe, are increasingly watching YouTube on their smart TVs rather than on their phones or laptops.

Rahma says 70 per cent of the viewers for his most recently episode of Keep the Meter Running – another show of his, where taxi drivers give him a tour of their favourites places in a city – were watching it on a television.

“I say I make independent television that’s distributed on YouTube,” he says. “The audience is totally getting in the habit of opening their TV and turning on YouTube.”

stories.title: Harvest delayed across the Prairies as farmers deal with waterlogged fields
stories.summary: Grain farmers on the Prairies are managing a challenging harvest this year, following a stormy summer across Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Many grain farmers are experiencing delayed harvests after a summer of heavy rainfall in the Prairie provinces.

Saskatchewan producers are furthest behind schedule when compared with their five-year average, but all three Prairie provinces are lagging.

Thirty-two per cent of the crop is in the bin in Saskatchewan – compared to the 71 per cent average, according to the provincial crop report for Sept. 8 through 14. The province cited “widespread rainfall across the province,” which forced farmers to pause work.

Rob Stone is a farmer in Davidson, Sask. He said it has been challenging to find crops that are dry enough to go through the combine.

“It kind of feels like we haven’t gotten anything done, but we’ve been harvesting since the third week of August, and we’re kind of settling into the latter part of September here now. It’s been interrupted by rain several times,” Stone said in an interview.

Stone said these conditions are atypical for farmers in his region.

“If we get a good stretch of weather for the next two weeks, a lot of crop is going to be harvested,” he continued, noting that some of those crops will still be wet or flattened and will require salvaging.

“The volume of precipitation that we’ve received in this last stretch, around eight inches since the end of August, is not unprecedented, but I would be hard pressed to find another year where we had quite that volume. So, we’re not used to that.”

As of Sept. 8 in Alberta, 21 per cent of all crops were harvested, compared with the province’s 43.5 per cent five-year average. The Alberta crop report said the rainy weekend continued to delay the harvest and baling.

“Weekend showers across the province continued to slow harvest progress and May decrease the quality of harvested grains. This joined with cool temperatures May keep some combines parked for several days,” Alberta’s report said.

“Compared with last season’s hot and dry weather through late summer and fall, this season’s conditions have slowed harvest progress to well behind the five- and 10-year averages.”

The south, central, northeast, northwest and Peace regions were all said to be behind in their harvests, with the northwest and northeastern regions experiencing the most drastic dip of 36 per cent when compared to 2025.

The Peace was 31 per cent behind last year’s level, it added.

Southern Alberta was the closest to average. The harvest was said to be 40 per cent complete, six per cent behind its 2025 pace.

Manitoba’s southwestern and northwestern regions were said to be below the 40 per cent average for all crops in the province, according to its Sept. 15 crop report. Officials reported the regions as being 27 per cent and 19 per cent complete respectively.

In contrast, the central region was 59 per cent harvested, while eastern Manitoba reported 62 per cent of the crop to be in the bin. Forty-seven per cent was taken from the fields of the Interlake fields.

“The (eastern) region saw rainfall last week ranging from five to 47 (millimetres). Producers are hoping for sunny and windy weather to dry things up quickly and resume harvest,” according to the provincial report. “Fall field work is ongoing as fields May be too wet to harvest.”

Jonothan Hodson, a cattle and grain farmer and board chair of the Manitoba Crop Alliance, told Global News heavy rainfall and windy weather at the onset of harvest season in August created subpar conditions for many farmers.

As a result, he said his farm is harvesting later than usual.

“It’s going to create a higher cost,” Hodson said, adding that “at some point (farmers have) got to dry that grain to be able to market it. Whether they’re paying the elevator and the dryers or their neighbour. So, it costs more.”

“I’ve farmed 40 years, and no two years ever seem to be the same. So, I don’t know what next year’s going to look like, maybe we’re going to appreciate the moisture we got right now. Maybe next year is going to be a really dry year and we’re going to be glad we got subsoil (moisture).”

Ranjan Sri Ranjan, a professor and acting head of the University of Manitoba’s department of biosystems engineering, said letting water sit on a field for extended periods can damage the crop.

“When there’s a lot of water sitting on the land, farmers, of course, try to put surface drainage but surface drainage is not the ideal thing to do, especially when you have machinery to cross over and you lose productive land,” he said.

Tile drainage could help farmers manage wetter-than-average summers, but they must be willing to pay the hefty $1,800 to $2,000 per acre price. Farmers would make their money back in the crops that the drainage would save, but it could take years depending on the amount of rainfall, the professor added.

Another issue farmers are facing with damp fields is soil compaction, which Sri Ranjan said can occur after “just a few passes” of heavy farming machinery when the ground is wet.

“If you keep driving on wet soils, you’re going to compact the soil, which is going to have (a) long-term impact on yield. So, it’s not only the day-to-day activity, but the long-term sustainability of soil is also affected by not having proper drainage,” he explained.

Looking ahead, he said constant “extremely high water levels will actually affect the yield.”

“This requires a comprehensive look at the changes in climate. And we need to have a big conversation because farmers alone cannot handle this.”

content_blocks.text: As of Sept. 8 in Alberta, 21 per cent of all crops were harvested, compared with the province’s 43.5 per cent five-year average. The Alberta crop report said the rainy weekend continued to delay the harvest and baling.

“Weekend showers across the province continued to slow harvest progress and May decrease the quality of harvested grains. This joined with cool temperatures May keep some combines parked for several days,” Alberta’s report said.
“Compared with last season’s hot and dry weather through late summer and fall, this season’s conditions have slowed harvest progress to well behind the five- and 10-year averages.”

The south, central, northeast, northwest and Peace regions were all said to be behind in their harvests, with the northwest and northeastern regions experiencing the most drastic dip of 36 per cent when compared to 2025.
The Peace was 31 per cent behind last year’s level, it added.
Southern Alberta was the closest to average. The harvest was said to be 40 per cent complete, six per cent behind its 2025 pace.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Central Alberta farmers suffering impact of extensive summer rain'

content_blocks.text: Manitoba’s southwestern and northwestern regions were said to be below the 40 per cent average for all crops in the province, according to its Sept. 15 crop report. Officials reported the regions as being 27 per cent and 19 per cent complete respectively.

In contrast, the central region was 59 per cent harvested, while eastern Manitoba reported 62 per cent of the crop to be in the bin. Forty-seven per cent was taken from the fields of the Interlake fields.

“The (eastern) region saw rainfall last week ranging from five to 47 (millimetres). Producers are hoping for sunny and windy weather to dry things up quickly and resume harvest,” according to the provincial report. “Fall field work is ongoing as fields May be too wet to harvest.”

Jonothan Hodson, a cattle and grain farmer and board chair of the Manitoba Crop Alliance, told Global News heavy rainfall and windy weather at the onset of harvest season in August created subpar conditions for many farmers.
As a result, he said his farm is harvesting later than usual.

“It’s going to create a higher cost,” Hodson said, adding that “at some point (farmers have) got to dry that grain to be able to market it. Whether they’re paying the elevator and the dryers or their neighbour. So, it costs more.”

“I’ve farmed 40 years, and no two years ever seem to be the same. So, I don’t know what next year’s going to look like, maybe we’re going to appreciate the moisture we got right now. Maybe next year is going to be a really dry year and we’re going to be glad we got subsoil (moisture).”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Manitoba farmers harvests crops reflecting on ‘volatile’ year'

content_blocks.text: Ranjan Sri Ranjan, a professor and acting head of the University of Manitoba’s department of biosystems engineering, said letting water sit on a field for extended periods can damage the crop.

“When there’s a lot of water sitting on the land, farmers, of course, try to put surface drainage but surface drainage is not the ideal thing to do, especially when you have machinery to cross over and you lose productive land,” he said.

Tile drainage could help farmers manage wetter-than-average summers, but they must be willing to pay the hefty $1,800 to $2,000 per acre price. Farmers would make their money back in the crops that the drainage would save, but it could take years depending on the amount of rainfall, the professor added.
Another issue farmers are facing with damp fields is soil compaction, which Sri Ranjan said can occur after “just a few passes” of heavy farming machinery when the ground is wet.

“If you keep driving on wet soils, you’re going to compact the soil, which is going to have (a) long-term impact on yield. So, it’s not only the day-to-day activity, but the long-term sustainability of soil is also affected by not having proper drainage,” he explained.
Looking ahead, he said constant “extremely high water levels will actually affect the yield.”
“This requires a comprehensive look at the changes in climate. And we need to have a big conversation because farmers alone cannot handle this.”

stories.title: Q+A: Retiring London Catholic school board trustee reflects on 40 years
stories.summary: The 84-year-old longtime trustee looks back on what changed and what he’ll miss after 40 years in office.
stories.author: Heather Rivers Davey
stories.content:
Known as a voice of reason on the London District Catholic school board, longtime trustee Bill Hall, 84, is calling it quits after four decades in office. His departure comes at one of the most tumultuous times for school trustees in Ontario. He spoke with The Free Press about his tenure.

Q. Forty years ago, why did you decide to become a trustee?

A. “My kids were in school. I had an interest in what was going on with their education. I thought, ‘Why don’t I just put my name in and run for the school board and see if I get elected?’”

Q. Why aren’t you running again?

A. “I figure after 40 years, I had a good run. I enjoyed it and I am happy with what I’ve done. There are a couple of people who have put their names in to run in Elgin County, and I thought maybe it’s time for some younger views on the board. After 40 years, it was time to pull the plug.”

Q. What are you most proud of during your career?

A. “We got a new high school built in St. Thomas, a replacement for St. Joseph’s. Now we have a new one being built, a second one in St. Thomas in the next couple of years. I was proud to have gotten St. Anne’s elementary school built in St. Thomas, as well as additions and upgrades to Monsignor Morrison in St. Thomas, Assumption elementary in Aylmer and St. Mary’s elementary school in West Lorne.

“For the last couple of years, the school board has been the fastest-growing board in Ontario. That’s because parents and students see value in Catholic education. Over the years, I have worked with 30 different trustees, seven directors and 26 student trustees. I am proud I got to visit all of our schools while I was on the school board.”

Q. What do you think of all the changes to the role of trustee made in the last year by Education Minister Paul Calandra?

A. “Our responsibilities have diminished quite a bit. When I was first elected, we used to be able to set the mill rate – that’s been taken away. We negotiated contracts with the unions. A trustee was even chair of the negotiating committee. That’s done by the province now.

“Transportation was something we used to be responsible for. That’s now in the hands of a consortium. Maybe even policies are going to be taken away from us now. The budget has been taken away. At our last meeting in June, the board voted against the budget that was being presented. It was unanimous except for two trustees who abstained. The director still submitted a budget, and it was accepted even though it had been rejected.

“We are not responsible for the things we used to be responsible for. It’s being put more and more in the hands of administration. That’s the way the government wants to go. It’s almost like a business venture now, not so much an educational venture. That’s the way they want it.”

Q. Anything else you want to say?

A. “I want to say thank you to the people who elected me over the years. It’s been a pleasure being on the board. I am going to miss it. I think we will still have a voice on the board; I just hope that our voices are heard.”

stories.title: Frank Stronach won't have to go to jail, judge says, after dramatic day of argument
stories.summary: Prosecutors argued the 94-year-old billionaire should go to jail for 6 months, give a sample of his DNA, and be registered as a sex offender.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Toronto — Frank Stronach will not go to jail for the crime of indecent assault, a judge said in surprise final comments at his sentencing hearing.

Judge Anne Molloy of the Ontario Superior Court said Stronach should return to hear his sentence in December. It will not be custodial but still could involve conditions on his freedom.

The news followed a dramatic day of argument Thursday in which the Crown argued the 94-year-old autoparts billionaire should go to jail for six months, surrender a sample of his DNA, and be listed on Canada’s sex offender registry for 10 years.

“Only a real deprivation of liberty will do,” said prosecutor Jelena Vlacic.

Stronach’s defence lawyer argued that he should be granted an absolute discharge, which means no conviction would be entered on the charge of indecent assault for which he was found guilty in June, and there would be no conditions on his release.

Stronach was originally charged with 12 offences involving seven women, but all other charges failed for various reasons.

The victim, now in her 70s, gave a short statement from the witness stand on Thursday, the only evidence called in the day-long hearing that was dominated by technical argument over precedent cases and the purposes of sentencing.

“I am 20 years younger than the defendant. I felt ambushed, I felt overpowered, I felt my physical privacy was violated without my consent. My body and my sense of security were instantly injured. My self reliance was wounded when by confidence in the defendants character was shattered.”

In her testimony earlier this year, the woman (whose identity is protected) testified that she knew Stronach socially and was with him at the Toronto bar he owned, Rooney’s. She accepted his invitation to a nearby apartment, where Stronach abruptly pushed her face down over the arm of a chair and pressed himself against her from behind while lifting her skirt. There was no direct contact with her skin and both remained clothed. She described it as “bizarre” and “pathetic.”

“I felt I deserved an apology, I was upset when none was forthcoming,” she said in her victim impact statement.

Both sides discussed comparable cases. There was argument over the Crown’s comparison of Stronach to Peter Nygard, 85, the fashion mogul who was sentenced in 2024 to 11 years in prison over historical sex assault charges.

Shemesh objected to this and other comparisons of Stronach to perpetrators of outrageous sexual crimes, such as home invasion sexual assaults and repeated predatory behaviour against vulnerable victims. Despite Stronach’s wealth and fame, the defence lawyer told the judge this case is not like Nygard, or Bill Cosby, or Harvey Weinstein.

But the Crown highlighted Nygard to emphasize the point that Stronach’s advanced age should not necessarily work in his favour. She quoted the judge in Nygard’s case: “Were I to punish him less harshly than his moral blameworthiness calls for because he is now an elderly man, it would, in effect, validate the immunity that wealth and power have given him. In my view, it would be contrary to public policy. It would significantly devalue the importance of denunciation and deterrence. It would send the message that if you are rich and powerful and your victims are vulnerable…, you can escape accountability if you can hold off the day of judgment long enough. That is exactly the wrong message for the court to send. Although age is a factor that I must consider, there is a limit to the amount of weight I will give it.”

Shemesh said she was unable to find any Canadian case of a 90-year-old person being sentenced at all, let alone sentenced to jail time. She said six months in jail would be “excessive” for a man who has “truly earned his place in Canadian history as a visionary” and has been “determined, over the course of his life, to really better society.”

Stronach is “quite a simple man,” she said, devoted to his children and his work, motivated by “goodness, kindness and charity.”

“He has learned to love simplicity,” she said.

Shemesh urged Molloy to find that Stronach has already been punished enough by the process of being charged and tried in the public glare. His name has been “dragged through the mud,” Shemesh said, and seen many of his lifetime honours revoked.

The Aurora Sports Hall of Fame removed his name, the Southlake Health Frank Stronach Cancer Centre removed his name, the City of Newmarket, Ont., renamed its Frank Stronach Park, as did a recreation centre in Aurora, Ont., and most “astonishing and shameful,” Shemesh said, was that the Automotive Hall of Fame had indicated it wants to revoke his induction.

Prosecutor Vlacic said this public reckoning should not minimize his sentence. “When you have a lot, you have a lot to lose,” Vlacic said.

It also emerged that, during his trial in March, Stronach was refused entry to the United States on his way to Tampa, Fla., ON the grounds of having outstanding charges against him.

“Whatever punishment the Ministry of the Attorney General was trying to garner, that punishment has already been meted out,” Shemesh said.

She said her client has engaged with this process with “hope and determination,” but the experience has “chipped away at him mentally” and “affected him cognitively” such that it was “difficult to watch.”

Stronach is also charged with other sexual offences involving six women, including as recently as 2024, in a separate matter that is not yet set for trial. That cannot be used against him here because he is presumed innocent, but it came up in the hearing.

“Can I make a positive finding that there’s been no repetition?” Molloy asked Shemesh, when she emphasized Stronach’s “unblemished” life since committing the indecent assault in 1977.

Shemesh said this court knows nothing of those other charges. “He comes before you with an unblemished record,” she said. “There’s no way for your honour to dispute the claim that he has lived an unblemished life.”

There was no direct contact with her skin and both remained clothed. She described it as “bizarre” and “pathetic.”
“I felt I deserved an apology, I was upset when none was forthcoming,” she said in her victim impact statement.

Both sides discussed comparable cases. There was argument over the Crown’s comparison of Stronach to Peter Nygard, 85, the fashion mogul who was sentenced in 2024 to 11 years in prison over historical sex assault charges.

Shemesh objected to this and other comparisons of Stronach to perpetrators of outrageous sexual crimes, such as home invasion sexual assaults and repeated predatory behaviour against vulnerable victims. Despite Stronach’s wealth and fame, the defence lawyer told the judge this case is not like Nygard, or Bill Cosby, or Harvey Weinstein.

But the Crown highlighted Nygard to emphasize the point that Stronach’s advanced age should not necessarily work in his favour. She quoted the judge in Nygard’s case: “Were I to punish him less harshly than his moral blameworthiness calls for because he is now an elderly man, it would, in effect, validate the immunity that wealth and power have given him. In my view, it would be contrary to public policy. It would significantly devalue the importance of denunciation and deterrence. It would send the message that if you are rich and powerful and your victims are vulnerable…, you can escape accountability if you can hold off the day of judgment long enough. That is exactly the wrong message for the court to send. Although age is a factor that I must consider, there is a limit to the amount of weight I will give it.”

Shemesh said she was unable to find any Canadian case of a 90-year-old person being sentenced at all, let alone sentenced to jail time. She said six months in jail would be “excessive” for a man who has “truly earned his place in Canadian history as a visionary” and has been “determined, over the course of his life, to really better society.”
Stronach is “quite a simple man,” she said, devoted to his children and his work, motivated by “goodness, kindness and charity.”
“He has learned to love simplicity,” she said.

Shemesh urged Molloy to find that Stronach has already been punished enough by the process of being charged and tried in the public glare. His name has been “dragged through the mud,” Shemesh said, and seen many of his lifetime honours revoked.

The Aurora Sports Hall of Fame removed his name, the Southlake Health Frank Stronach Cancer Centre removed his name, the City of Newmarket, Ont., renamed its Frank Stronach Park, as did a recreation centre in Aurora, Ont., and most “astonishing and shameful,” Shemesh said, was that the Automotive Hall of Fame had indicated it wants to revoke his induction.
Prosecutor Vlacic said this public reckoning should not minimize his sentence. “When you have a lot, you have a lot to lose,” Vlacic said.
It also emerged that, during his trial in March, Stronach was refused entry to the United States on his way to Tampa, Fla., ON the grounds of having outstanding charges against him.
“Whatever punishment the Ministry of the Attorney General was trying to garner, that punishment has already been meted out,” Shemesh said.

She said her client has engaged with this process with “hope and determination,” but the experience has “chipped away at him mentally” and “affected him cognitively” such that it was “difficult to watch.”

Stronach is also charged with other sexual offences involving six women, including as recently as 2024, in a separate matter that is not yet set for trial. That cannot be used against him here because he is presumed innocent, but it came up in the hearing.
“Can I make a positive finding that there’s been no repetition?” Molloy asked Shemesh, when she emphasized Stronach’s “unblemished” life since committing the indecent assault in 1977.

Shemesh said this court knows nothing of those other charges. “He comes before you with an unblemished record,” she said. “There’s no way for your honour to dispute the claim that he has lived an unblemished life.”

stories.title: Airline industry group opposes privatization of Canadian airports
stories.summary: Iata says consumers would ultimately pay the higher fees charged to airlines by for-profit companies
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
An executive at the International Air Transport Association, which represents 370 of the world’s airlines, has some advice for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he privatizes Canada’s biggest airports: Don’t do it.

Nick Careen, senior vice-president of operations at Iata, said the plan unveiled this week to transform airports in Montreal, Toronto, Calgary and Vancouver into for-profit companies would drive up fees paid by the airlines, which would be forced to pass on the higher costs to travellers.

“We’re against what they’re doing because it is primarily done to extract cash,” said Mr. Careen, whose members include Air Canada, WestJet and most other major carriers in the world. “We’ve got lots of examples of how that’s failed.”

Examples around the world show fees paid by airlines and passengers go up when investment funds seeking returns of 8 or 12 per cent become owners of airports, he said.

“Everybody wants a return on their investment. They’re not doing this for free,” Mr. Careen said in an interview.

“We’re only going to make it more expensive” to travel, he said. “It flies in the face of the argument that we’re trying to make travel in Canada less expensive. This is not going to do it.”

Carney details plans to open up Canada’s four largest airports to private investment

Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sept. 15 unveiled the government’s plan to sell operating concessions for Canada’s four largest airports. The government would retain ownership of the land and assets and take stakes in the companies through its sovereign wealth fund. The announcement was made at the government’s Canada Investment Summit, intended to showcase the country’s investment opportunities to global investors.

Details have not been decided upon but profits from the airport operations would go to the investors as well as toward upgrades at Canada’s other airports.

Mr. Carney said transforming the airports to for-profit operations is intended to “improve passenger services and find efficiencies.”

“The evidence shows travel costs go down over time,” Mr. Carney said.

Mr. Careen said the global examples, from Britain to Australia, show this is not the case.

Australia’s airports monitor found that the country’s airports, privatized beginning in the late 1990s, raised fees to airlines by 1.6-billion Australian dollars ($1.6-billion) over 10 years ending in 2016, based on the same passenger volumes.

What could airport privatization mean for travellers in Canada?

Shane Zhang, a professor of aviation at Australia’s Adelaide University, said the country’s airport privatization brought increased efficiencies, more incentives to invest in infrastructure and better cost controls.

But for passengers, the effects were mixed, Prof. Zhang said. While travelers enjoyed upgraded terminals, restaurants and other amenities, they also faced higher airfares as airports increased the fees they charge to airlines. Vehicle parking fees also rose, he said.

Iata’s Mr. Careen said Canada’s current airports regime is “okay” but needs better regulation over the fees charged to airlines and passengers, which the airports are allowed to raise at will. He said the federal government should be investing the hundreds of millions of dollars it collects in rent in the airports themselves, rather than adding it to the general coffers.

The government has collected $8.4-billion in rent from the airports since establishing the non-profit corporations beginning in the 1990s. Airports paid $556-million in rent to Ottawa in 2025, but received far less in return for infrastructure upgrades.

Editorial: Airport privatization is a flight path to accountability

Jean-Charles del Duchetto, a spokesman for Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec, said the fund manager has invested in airports around the world for 20 years. The Canadian privatizations are “an opportunity for La Caisse and we are open to looking at the options and using our expertise to the advantage of travelers and airlines.”

Air Canada spokesman Christophe Hennebelle said Canada’s largest airline is ready to participate in consultations with the government over the privatizations. Paramount for the airline is “ensuring that costs for passengers remain the same or lower, and reinvesting in aviation infrastructure, which is in dire need of it.”

“Air Canada and its customers pay a total of nearly $2-billion each year to Canadian airports, so this is an important issue for us,” Mr. Hennebelle said.

WestJet said in a statement any change to the airport system should have strong regulation and accountability to ensure affordability and competitiveness.

stories.title: Non-profit-led summit calls for clearer Great Lakes safety warnings
stories.summary: Officials from 11 Ontario communities gathered in St. Thomas to discuss more consistent messaging around rip currents and other water hazards.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
ST. Thomas – A non-profit organization promoting water safety in the Great Lakes is pushing for clearer, more consistent messaging about hazards such as rip currents across Ontario shoreline communities.

The Rip Current Information Project hosted the Great Lakes Drowning and Risk Communication Summit at Caso Station in downtown St. Thomas on Wednesday, drawing about 35 politicians, firefighters and police officers from 11 Ontario communities, including Elgin and Huron counties and as far away as Clarington, about 270 kilometres northeast of St. Thomas.

“The main message here is that currently, across Ontario, there is a fragmented approach to delivering this valuable life-saving information to residents and visitors to Ontario and to those beaches,” said Nathan MacIntyre, founder of the non-profit.

MacIntyre, a former Port Stanley lifeguard of 18 years, launched the organization in June 2025 after the death of 14-year-old Omar Buz in July 2024. Since then, he has advocated for more consistent public messaging about water hazards in shoreline communities.

His efforts are backed by Chris Houser, University of Waterloo’s dean of science, who has researched beach safety for 20 years and spoke at the summit.

Houser said events like Wednesday’s can save lives and called the turnout by officials “amazing.”

“This is the first time that we’ve had this great of representation from across Southwestern Ontario, and I hope this becomes an annual thing and it starts to expand,” Houser said. “It’s great to have these representatives here, but there’s still a lot of other spots that we need to bring into this conversation.”

Topics discussed during the four-hour presentation included beach safety information, recognizing local hazards, intervention and survival skills.

MacIntyre also encouraged communities to use accurate terminology when describing water hazards. He said undertow – water returning toward the lakebed beneath breaking waves – is commonly confused with rip currents, which can pose a greater danger because of their concentrated flow.

“(There’s a tendency to) paint all disasters and all tragedies and all incidents on the Great Lakes with the same brush of undertow,” he said. “Rip currents are one of them . . . and steep and fast wave periods (too).”

MacIntyre said the organization also wants to standardize public-safety messaging while allowing communities to tailor information to local conditions.

Elgin County Warden Dominique Giguere said the county wants to be proactive about water-safety awareness.

“This is an issue on all of the Great Lakes,” she said, noting Elgin County has about 100 kilometres of shoreline.

“We are blessed with that beautiful recreation (opportunity),” Giguere said. “We all enjoy it, but that beauty comes with risks. We have locally experienced our share of tragic, preventable drownings.”

An 80-year-old Cambridge man died after being pulled unresponsive from Lake Erie at Port Stanley in August 2025.

Bayham Mayor Ed Ketchabaw, who also attended the summit, said beach safety has been a topic of discussion in his municipality for several years.

He said there is interest in adopting more water-safety messaging in the mostly rural municipality of about 7,000 people, which includes Port Burwell.

“It’s really interesting because, you know, for years when I was a kid we were always taught stay away from that undertow . . . but it’s not (necessarily) the undertow,” Ketchabaw said. “So it’s been very eye-opening just to listen to this.”

The body of a 35-year-old Woodstock man was recovered from Lake Erie at Port Burwell in June 2025.

Earlier this month, police also reminded people about water safety after “several recent drownings” in Sarnia-Lambton. Lambton OPP have responded to 10 drowning incidents in Lambton and Huron counties in 2026, according to a Sept. 8 Sarnia Observer report .

stories.title: Bear River, N.S. residents raise concerns over planned aerial glyphosate spraying
stories.summary: Residents are sounding the alarm over planned aerial glyphosate spraying and alleging that regulations weren't followed when it came to notifying people.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
Residents of a small Nova Scotia community are sounding the alarm over planned aerial glyphosate spraying and alleging that regulations weren’t followed when it came to notifying people about the planned pesticide use.

Lenny Hornung is among the concerned residents of Bear River, N.S. who are trying to halt the province’s plans.

He says not enough notice was given, and points out he only learned about it after a neighbour went to pick berries and saw a sign announcing that spraying was planned in the area.

“If she hadn’t gone to pick berries there, we would never have known that (sign) was there,” he said.

The signs indicate spraying has been approved in the area, which is located in Annapolis and Digby counties, from Sept. 16 to 30.

According to documents shared with Global News by residents, a numbered company was approved for spraying along the Thomas, Guinea, and Victory roads on Aug. 19. Community members have filed a complaint with the province alleging violations of the mandatory 30-day notice requirement in Nova Scotia’s Pesticide Regulations.

They’re asking for the spraying to be put on pause until the investigation is concluded.

“The signs themselves are barely visible and then that warning is minuscule on the signs. So government and industry are not doing a good enough job warning the public of the dangers and keeping people safe,” said resident Robin Sturley.

Glyphosate is typically used in forestry to suppress vegetation that competes with commercially valuable trees.

However, there have been longstanding concerns about its health risks, which have prompted court cases and lawsuits .

There are also questions about how its use could affect wildfire risk.

In 2017, Health Canada re-approved glyphosate for sale in Canada until April 27, 2032, with the caveat that producers needed to have more details on labels.

The Assembly of Mi’kmaw Chiefs is also calling for a stop to spraying in the Bear River area — highlighting the significance of the area to the Bear River First Nation.

“This spraying threatens our ability to safely access and harvest the foods and medicines, and other resources that sustain us,” said Chief Carol Potter in a statement.

“These resources are part of who we are, our way of life, and how we connect with the land. This is about protecting our health as well as our lands.”

It’s a concern Phyllis Harlow, the local beekeeper for Bear River First Nation, shares. She started processing the honey from her hives early to avoid risking her bees coming into contact with glyphosate.

“It’s still warm out, so they’re still foraging. They’re still bringing in all the nectar from the flowers and whether it’s the goldenrod or the English asters, they’re bringing all that in,” Harlow said.

She adds for a community that relies heavily on hunting, fishing and foraging, blocking off certain areas from use isn’t feasible.

“We’re very in tune with what’s around us. And you can’t put up big fences and say, ‘This is our boundary and this one isn’t.’ Because it all flows together,” she added.

Environment and Climate Change Minister Timothy Halman says anyone with health and safety concerns about the pesticide should contact Health Canada.

He confirmed that the residents’ complaint is being investigated.

“So I can tell you process has been followed,” said Halman.

“We’re looking into the concerns that have been raised and I think that’s just good due diligence. We’re a responsive regulator.”

But ultimately, those who live in the area say they want to see glyphosate phased out entirely.

“With these practices and the failure to follow the regulations, we can’t safely do that. And that’s just a failure of the government to regulate the forestry industry,” said Sturley.

stories.title: New Brunswick mill laying off hundreds of workers, union says
stories.summary: Unifor says the closure of the AV Nackawic mill is a devastating decision that will put 228 people out of work and deliver a serious blow to the local economy.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
The union representing workers at a rural New Brunswick mill says hundreds of its members will be laid off in November.

Unifor says the closure of the AV Nackawic mill is a devastating decision that will put 228 people out of work and deliver a serious blow to the local economy.

Natural Resources Minister John Herron said the company will be temporarily idling its operations.

The mill, a subsidiary of the India-based Aditya Birla Group, is a key economic driver for the rural community of Nackawic-Millville.

The company’s website says the mill produces dissolving grade pulp used in the production of textiles.

Herron says the government is working on a response plan to support those who need it most.

Aditya Birla Group was not immediately available for comment.

stories.title: What can be done about intimate partner violence?
stories.summary: On September 15th, London Police arrived to a call where they found a woman suffering from life-threatening in...
stories.author: Kelly Nicol
stories.content:
On September 15th, London Police arrived to a call where they found a woman suffering from life-threatening injuries. Police arrested one individual at the scene, who was known to be in an intimate relationship with the victim.

Intimate partner violence continues to be an issue across the country. In 2025 the province of Ontario, including the city of London, declared intimate partner violence an epidemic. Detective Sergeant Micah Bordeau says women continue to represent the majority of victims in police-reported cases.

“We know many incidents go unreported. Addressing this issue requires a coordinated response, and we remain committed to working alongside our community partners … to better understand and respond to intimate partner violence and femicide.”

“It’s one of those times where it’s difficult to say if it’s on the rise,” said Jessie Rodger, Executive Director of Anova. The organization helps people struggling with intimate partner violence, an issue that Rodger says, comes from people’s lack of empathy.

“Bluntly, I don’t think we care enough about survivors of sexual assault, who are the majority of women and queer folk… Misogyny runs deep in our community, and in our country, and until we talk about prevention, how we use language, and socialize young people. It’s not a mystery, at least to me.”

Rodger went on to explain ways in which people can help those facing intimate partner violence. “The number one best thing that people can do is that when people tell you that they have been harmed, when they’ve been abused … the best thing to do is to believe them. Because that’s the scariest thing, is to tell someone that you trust, and they don’t believe you.”

While Anova deals with the victims of partner violence, other advocates tackle the source of that harm.

“I think it’s important to know that violence and abuse shows up in many different ways, and not everyone fully understands the behaviors that they are doing are harmful or abusive,” said Amiel Ostrander, Executive Director at Changing Ways, an organization that provides resources and services to people who have inflicted violence or abuse in relationships, both court mandated and voluntary.

Both organizations emphasized the importance of being proactive to prevent harm. “Whether it’s the person causing harm or the person being harmed, go in with curiosity and without judgement to have a deeper level of understanding if something is going on,” said Ostrander.

If you or a loved one are experiencing intimate partner violence, Anova’s crisis line can be reached at (519) 642-3000.

Changing Ways can be contacted at ( 519) 438-9869.

stories.title: A father’s crusade to fight drugs in Huron County
stories.summary: A bench with Joey Scrimgeour’s name on it sits along Goderich’s waterfront, a reminder of a life lost too young.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A bench with Joey Scrimgeour’s name on it sits along Goderich’s waterfront, a reminder of a life lost too young.

“It’d be three years ago, last Sunday, September 13th, my world turned upside down. I walked into my youngest son’s room, Joey, and found him deceased,” said Joey’s father, Brent Scrimgeour.

Scrimgeour was only 19. He died of an opioid overdose. Joey’s death sent his father into alcoholism, and suicidal thoughts. He’s on the other side of that struggle now eager to help parents avoid his family’s pain.

“What I walked into that morning, I would not wish that on my worst enemy. I see all these young kids, and everything around and the future that they can have, and I know how it destroyed my family. I don’t want others to go through that, and I truly mean that,” said Brent.

Scrimgeour has enlisted the help of Huron County native, and former RCMP undercover operative turned author, Garry Clement. Clement grew up in Hensall, and will be sharing his 34 years of policing experience, mostly fighting organized crime and the drug trade, with a crowd at South Huron District High School in Exeter today at 7:30 p.m.

“What people have to realize, even a line of cocaine, if you buy it, you’re supporting organized crime. Organized crime is human trafficking. It’s drug dealing. It’s credit card fraud. It’s all of that. And that’s a society that we’re supporting if we purchase any sort of these drugs,” said Clement.

He says many opioids are 10 times more potent than heroin, are killing thousands of Canadians, many of them young people each year. He doesn’t believe supervised drug consumption sites have worked, he has another idea.

“I really believe there’s only one solution. Mandatory treatment. And then society says ‘yeah, but look at what it’s going to cost us.’ And I go, okay, then you have to do two years in the military, it’ll give you structure and everything. Think of what it is costing our health care system,” said Clement.

Scrimgeour says he wants to see tougher sentences for drug dealers as well. One more tool, that might save a life.

“My son Joey made one bad decision that cost him his life, and I really don’t want to see more youth taken away too soon,” said Scrimgeour.

Clement’s direct talk about drugs will start at 7:30 p.m. tonight at South Huron District High School in Exeter.

stories.title: Discovery of baby in homeless camp highlights Quebec’s housing crisis ahead of election
stories.summary: Investigation under way after police find woman and child at encampment on Notre-Dame Street
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The discovery of a one-year-old child at a homeless encampment in Montreal has put the city’s worsening housing crisis in the spotlight of Quebec’s provincial election campaign.

Montreal police said an investigation is underway after officers located a woman and the child at an encampment on Notre-Dame Street in the city’s east end.

The discovery has prompted Quebec’s political leaders to weigh in on how to address homelessness, with opposition leaders criticizing the government’s response and Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette calling for governments and other partners to work together.

Montreal police said they received a call about the woman and child on Sept. 11 in the borough of Mercier—Hochelaga-Maisonneuve.

Five takeaways from the Quebec leaders’ debate

Police spokesperson Jean-Pierre Brabant said officers located them after conducting a search and noticed what they described as concerning elements.

Brabant said police were collaborating with Quebec’s youth protection agency on the investigation. He said the infant’s health and safety were not at risk.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada called the situation “heartbreaking” and a “wake-up call” in a social media post Wednesday night.

She said Montreal could no longer wait for the Quebec government to address what she described as a provincewide problem and said the city would take action at the Notre-Dame site.

Fréchette said she had spoken with the Montreal mayor and wanted the province and city to work together.

“It breaks my heart. I’m a mother first and foremost, and I can’t believe it,” Fréchette told reporters in Sainte-Julie, in the Montérégie region, east of Montreal.

She said governments, municipalities, the private sector and community organizations all have a role to play in addressing homelessness, adding her government is developing a provincewide plan.

Fréchette also said authorities need a clearer picture of who is living in encampments and whether other children are among them.

“Those children really have to be taken out of that environment,” she said, adding, “It’s not an environment for children at all.”

Québec solidaire Leader Ruba Ghazal said she was “extremely shocked” by the discovery.

“To think that this child ended up in an encampment with a family living in an unimaginably vulnerable situation, just talking about it gives me chills,” Ghazal told reporters in Sherbrooke.

“We’re in 2026, in a wealthy Quebec, and for things to have reached this point is completely unacceptable and shocking.”

Ghazal said tackling homelessness requires investment in housing and community organizations.

She also criticized the spending plan in Parti Québécois Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s platform, saying she found “zero dollars in infrastructure investment for housing” in the plan.

But St-Pierre Plamondon, who represents the riding where the Notre-Dame encampment is located, said homelessness would be his “social priority” if his party forms government.

The PQ leader said the situation was “embarrassing” for a wealthy society and accused the CAQ government of lacking political will on homelessness and other social issues.

“We shouldn’t accept this,” St-Pierre Plamondon told reporters in Longueuil, south of Montreal ”It’s a loss of control by the CAQ on this issue over the past few years, and it’s very sad.”

Quebec party leaders spar about referendum and sovereignty in second debate

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard also said he was concerned about the situation but stopped short of calling for the encampment to be dismantled.

Speaking in Lac-Mégantic, Milliard called on elected officials to intervene and said the City of Montreal has as important a role to play as the provincial government.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime also called it “totally unacceptable” for a child to be living in an encampment “in a society like ours.”

“Everyone is saddened. We have to have compassion for the people who live there and we have to find solutions, but an encampment is not a solution, it’s not alternative housing,” Duhaime told reporters in Saint-Pierre-de-la-Rivière-du-Sud, in Quebec’s Chaudière-Appalaches region.

He said governments should work to eliminate homeless encampments across the province as quickly as possible.

In a statement, Montreal’s official Opposition, Projet Montréal, called on the mayor to use 30 modular housing units it says are currently sitting unused and give priority to homeless parents and pregnant women.

Opposition Leader Ericka Alneus said the city acquired 90 modular units under the previous Projet Montréal administration, 30 of which have yet to be put into use.

“Finding a baby in an encampment is deeply upsetting. All of Quebec is shaken,” Alneus wrote.

“The modular units aren’t a perfect solution and will never replace real housing,” Alneus wrote, adding they could provide families with quicker access to services and help finding permanent housing.

stories.title: Record-high diesel prices in Canada drive up costs for lobster and seafood industries
stories.summary: Lobster is the top seafood export in the three Maritime provinces and according to fisherman Carl Allen, it’s an industry that runs on diesel. That means skyrocketing fuel prices are causing a lot of financial pain.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Eastern Passage, N.S. - Lobster is the top seafood export in the three Maritime provinces and according to fisherman Carl Allen, it’s an industry that runs on diesel. That means skyrocketing fuel prices are causing a lot of financial pain.

“Everybody should be worried about the fact that everything you interact with has been on one or several truck trailers that are powered by diesel fuel,” said Allen.

He has a boat with a fuel tank that holds 1,100 litres of diesel.

“That tank will last me three days, so I am looking at two fill-ups a week,” he said.

Lobster and other fishing boats using expensive fuel represent only a portion of the affordability issues facing people who work in the commercial fishing industry. Trucks that also use diesel are passing on their extra shipping costs with surcharges.

“Whoever is getting their products is going to have to say at some point they cannot eat that (cost) and then pass it on to the consumer,” said Allen, who works in the Northumberland Strait in the Lobster Fishing Area 25.

“And this is happening at a time when bait is more expensive than ever.”

As the cost to harvest, ship and deliver lobster and seafood to a store goes up, so do the prices customers pay.

“The correlation between diesel prices and food prices that you see at the grocery store is one of the highest of all factors,” said Dalhousie University professor and food researcher Sylvain Charlebois.

“And the other problem that lobster harvesters face is they do not set prices which means they are hit on both sides.”

The price of Seafood has gone up so much in recent weeks some people are taking it off their shopping lists.

“We used to buy a piece of haddock for $10 or $15,” said Bud Stevens as he finished shopping in Dartmouth, N.S. “Now it’s $25 or $30.”

Allen is worried that some in the fishing industry won’t be able to survive and stay in business. He said the size of their catch isn’t the problem, it’s high-priced diesel and overhead costs cutting into profits and crushing their bottom line.

“Biologically, these fisheries are sustainable,” said Allen. “But financially? That becomes a different conversation.”

According to Allen, many boat operators would like to get off diesel and switch to hybrid-electric motors to save money. However, he said that technology is still evolving for fishing vessels, and changing over from diesel engines could be expensive and come with a lot of upfront costs.

stories.title: What schools can learn from Ontario’s student cellphone ban
stories.summary: A new study of elementary and secondary students found a link between phone use and levels of depression and anxiety
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
When Ontario introduced restrictions on cellphones in schools that took effect in 2024, the goal was to help students focus and improve their well-being. Students in kindergarten to Grade 6 have to keep phones on silent and out of sight for the entire school day, while those in Grades 7 to 12 cannot use their phones during class time unless explicitly allowed by the teacher.

A new study of more than 600 kids and young adults ages six to 18 years published this month in the Canadian Journal of Psychiatry found that limiting access to cellphones and social media has had a clear effect on kids’ levels of depression and anxiety.

Provinces consider restricting cellphones and social media in schools as federal government weighs action

The Globe spoke to Dr. Daphne Korczak, a staff psychiatrist and senior scientist at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children and one of the authors of the study, about its findings and what schools could learn from the research.

Before you undertook this study, what did we know about cellphone restrictions at schools and their effects on mental health? By the sounds of it, we didn’t know very much.

That’s one of the reasons that we wanted to undertake the study in the first place. It’s a topic that I think, especially as a clinician, but also as a researcher, we had heard quite a lot about, anecdotally, from students and from parents and from educators. But it did seem to be mostly anecdotal, especially when it came to the Canadian and certainly the Ontario context. Our aim was really to try and add some data to the conversation.

How did you find the children and parents who participated in the study?

These were parents and children that have been participating in a longitudinal study that we have been running since the onset of the COVID pandemic. It’s a cohort that was assembled in the spring of 2020, and we’ve been following kids and parents since then to try and understand how the pandemic was impacting their lives and their health and their families and their school. But then over time as we’ve moved into recovery, we’ve realized that other issues have emerged, and screen time has been one of them.

Opinion: Test scores are falling, and the problem is staring us in the face

What did you find about schools sticking to the policy and what they meant for students’ mental health?

We found that the level of adherence to that policy varied quite a bit. So, greater adherence to the cellphone restrictions was associated with lower social media use and, in turn, lower symptoms of depression and anxiety.

How significant was the effect on on kids’ depression and anxiety?

Small to medium size. There are many contributors to depression and anxiety symptoms. If you apply even a small effect to a large population of kids you can still have quite a significant impact. Kids could be underneath the clinical threshold or at the threshold for clinically important symptoms. They could be at and just hovering around it. They could be above. They could be below. So, you know, a small effect, it really can be significant.

When you look at the study and its findings, what do you think the message is to schools?

This is really a finding about implementation. Adherence appears to be important for effectiveness with respect to children’s mental health outcomes. We need more collaborative conversations about implementation to learn what’s feasible, what’s effective, and learn from each other and understand what is contributing to that implementation variability.

What do you think kids make of the ban and its enforcement?

By and large, what I have heard in my own clinical practice is that children and adolescents say they actually would like it to be more consistent. They would like the adherence to be maybe a bit stricter and more consistent because they actually don’t like it when the teacher spends a lot of their time trying to deal with cellphones and somebody who’s not paying attention. They find it distracting, and they would like the teacher to spend the time teaching.

Based on my admittedly limited experience as the parent of two teenagers, the way this policy is enforced can differ very much even within the same school.

Implementation is the key. It’s not sufficient just to have the policies. We need to help educators with how to implement them in schools so they can be effective.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

These were parents and children that have been participating in a longitudinal study that we have been running since the onset of the COVID pandemic. It’s a cohort that was assembled in the spring of 2020, and we’ve been following kids and parents since then to try and understand how the pandemic was impacting their lives and their health and their families and their school. But then over time as we’ve moved into recovery, we’ve realized that other issues have emerged, and screen time has been one of them.
Opinion: Test scores are falling, and the problem is staring us in the face
What did you find about schools sticking to the policy and what they meant for students’ mental health?

We found that the level of adherence to that policy varied quite a bit. So, greater adherence to the cellphone restrictions was associated with lower social media use and, in turn, lower symptoms of depression and anxiety.
How significant was the effect on on kids’ depression and anxiety?

Small to medium size. There are many contributors to depression and anxiety symptoms. If you apply even a small effect to a large population of kids you can still have quite a significant impact. Kids could be underneath the clinical threshold or at the threshold for clinically important symptoms. They could be at and just hovering around it. They could be above. They could be below. So, you know, a small effect, it really can be significant.
When you look at the study and its findings, what do you think the message is to schools?

This is really a finding about implementation. Adherence appears to be important for effectiveness with respect to children’s mental health outcomes. We need more collaborative conversations about implementation to learn what’s feasible, what’s effective, and learn from each other and understand what is contributing to that implementation variability.
What do you think kids make of the ban and its enforcement?

By and large, what I have heard in my own clinical practice is that children and adolescents say they actually would like it to be more consistent. They would like the adherence to be maybe a bit stricter and more consistent because they actually don’t like it when the teacher spends a lot of their time trying to deal with cellphones and somebody who’s not paying attention. They find it distracting, and they would like the teacher to spend the time teaching.
Based on my admittedly limited experience as the parent of two teenagers, the way this policy is enforced can differ very much even within the same school.
Implementation is the key. It’s not sufficient just to have the policies. We need to help educators with how to implement them in schools so they can be effective.
This interview has been condensed and edited.

stories.title: Drowning summit urges common safety language and protocols across the Great Lakes
stories.summary: The inviting shores of southern Ontario beaches bring the sun-seekers and those attracted to the waves, but when a drowning takes place the impact goes far beyond the immediate devastation, according to Elgin County Warden Dominique Giguère.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
The inviting shores of southern Ontario beaches bring the sun-seekers and those attracted to the waves, but when a drowning takes place the impact goes far beyond the immediate devastation, according to Elgin County Warden Dominique Giguère.

“Just how people feel about the beach. Then there’s a risk of a love-hate relationship with this beautiful asset,” she said.

Sarnia Chief Fire Prevention Officer Pete Aalbers says it also puts pressure on those in the business of saving lives.

“A sense of urgency is real. We know it’s a short window of opportunity to be helpful,” he said.

Both Aalbers and Giguère were among those attending the first ever Great Lakes Drowning Risk Information Summit, which took place in St. Thomas Thursday, and attracted representatives from Great Lakes communities across southern Ontario.

The event, hosted by the Elgin County based RIP Current Information Project, follows an increasing number of drownings tied to rip currents- concentrated flows of water that move from the shoreline into deeper water. They are often associated with infrastructure, according to Nathan MacIntyre, of the RIP Current Information Project.

“It can happen in various places. We see it 100 per cent of the time near the structures on the Great Lakes. So, any time there’s a structure on a wavy day, you should stay away from the structure. It also happens in the middle of the beach between sandbars and deep areas between sandbars,” MacIntyre explained.

Municipalities are being asked to consider how they plan public areas around beaches. Chris Houser, a Dean of Science and Professor of Earth and Environmental Sciences at the University of Waterloo, says there’s much that can be done, in terms of layout.

“When they come onto a beach, they’re not paying attention to signs. They’re focused on where they’re going to sit on that beach. So the more you can have a design that forces them or moves them into a more safe area, keeps them close to a lifeguard, away from groins and jetties, away from where we know rip currents are forming, then you have that ability to reduce drownings, sometimes even more than just a warning sign or a flag,” Houser said.

Event organizers believe safety policies are far too inconsistent in beach communities across the province. Their goal is to have common safety standards to help prevent drownings, and that includes consistent Great Lakes water safety language.

“We can kind of work together in a cohesive way, and every beach can post the same language,” MacIntyre said.

“From today and moving forward, collectively work together, coordinate, standardize, make the information accessible and clear,” stressed Giguère.
