stories.title: First Nations youth continue fight over Carney’s major projects agenda, summit
stories.summary: Ottawa — As Canadian politicians were pitching their major projects plans to foreign investors at a first-of-its-kind summit in Toronto, First Nations youth in Ottawa were making a pitch to Canadians on why they should join the fight to stop them.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

Posted September 17, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 17, 2026 5:15 am.

Ottawa — As Canadian politicians were pitching their major projects plans to foreign investors at a first-of-its-kind summit in Toronto, First Nations youth in Ottawa were making a pitch to Canadians on why they should join the fight to stop them.

Jeronimo Kataquapit and his cousin Ramon had just returned from a weeks-long journey on the coast of James Bay, a body of water that straddles Quebec and Ontario at the southern tip of the Hudson Bay.

Jeronimo called it “hardcore camping,” where he, Ramon and his parents roughed it on the shorelines, spotting polar bears, flocks of geese and caribou along the way.

The trip wasn’t for rest and relaxation for the family from Attawapiskat First Nation. It was part of their ongoing efforts to leave physical traces of First Nations occupancy on the land and waters as the provincial and federal government work to develop the mineral-rich Ring of Fire — a so-called “major project” the Kataquapit family vehemently opposes.

“I didn’t want to wait around for our elected leaders to take action,” Jeronimo told attendees at an event held in St. Andrew’s Presbyterian Church on Tuesday evening, steps away from Parliament Hill.

“We needed to make our presence known on the river.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s tenure has, so far, been defined by his desire to build major projects in an effort to strengthen the Canadian economy in the face of increasing trade hostility from U.S. President Donald Trump.

The two-day summit in Toronto on Tuesday — a gathering of hundreds of domestic and global executives with trillions of dollars collectively in assets under management — sought to address both historic and fresh concerns about Canada’s investment climate.

Canadian officials and business leaders were trying to buck the country’s reputation as a tough place to earn a return and replace it with a message to the world that Canada is “open for business.”

The Kataquapits say it isn’t — or, at least, not in the way Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are making it out to be.

“They talk about the region as if it’s a statistic, as if it’s a number, as if it’s money to be made,” Jeronimo said, sitting in a wooden pew in the oldest Presbyterian Church in Ottawa, as the mostly non-Indigenous attendees funnelled out of the Together for Nature tour.

“But it’s people’s homes … We know what’s at stake. It’s our future that will be affected.”

The Together for Nature Tour, organized by Ontario Nature and Legal Advocates for Nature’s Defence, is seeking to build solidarity between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians to protect the environment and push back on Carney’s major projects agenda.

Carney’s government faced some loud opposition from Indigenous leaders last year when it pushed through legislation to speed up major projects. First Nations leaders warned his fast-track approach to development could infringe upon their rights, and accused Carney of sidelining their concerns in favour of investors.

The tone has changed since then from elected community leaders, but not for the youth who warn developments could irrevocably harm the landscapes and waterways they’ve known their entire lives, and that have sustained their ancestors for time immemorial.

It’s the message the Kataquapits are taking across the province this week, with stops in Ottawa, Toronto, Kitchener and London. And it’s the message they want attendees to share with their networks long after the events wrap.

“It’s all about the dollar (for Carney and investors). It’s about money and what they can gain in the short term,” Ramon said. “But when the long term comes to bite them and their children when they’re in the spirit world, they’ll wish that they would have done what was right.”

The summit was protested by Indigenous leaders, environmental groups and union leaders who said they rejected the idea of leaving Canada’s economic future in the hands of CEOs.

“Canada is getting very good at blackmailing the public,” Wet’suwet’en Hereditary Chief Na’Moks said at one such demonstration in Toronto, citing the prime minister’s argument that Canada needs to build more major projects to protect itself from predatory U.S. trade policy.

“That’s their story. Their story is false, the same way that they think that these projects will go on without your support, without our support.”

Youth on the other side of the country are making similar efforts to note their displeasure with the actions of their provincial and federal government.

Katisha Paul, founder and principal consultant of Nepenek and women’s representative for the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs, called the investment summit an “extraction pitch” and questioned whose “national interest” is being served by politicians and the business leaders they’re trying to court.

“Right now it’s not Canadian citizens. It’s a banker (Carney) sitting in front of a trillion dollars, deciding that their own national interest exists above any taxpayer. And he’s going to do anything that he can to further that.”

Paul worries about the salmon in her territories, the whales and the land.

More importantly, she’s worried about consent, saying the federal government is failing to adequately consult with First Nations title- and rights-holders who are often on the front line opposing developments.

“Everybody around the world loves the idea to stand up against somebody like Trump,” Paul said.

“But at the same time, what are we giving up? Who’s going to be hurting in the end?”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

— With files from Craig Lord

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tim Hortons ‘flight roast’ coming to WestJet flights, companies link loyalty programs
stories.summary: Toronto — Tim Hortons' coffee is cleared for takeoff.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

Posted September 17, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 17, 2026 5:15 am.

Toronto — Tim Hortons’ coffee is cleared for takeoff.

As Canadian brands increasingly search for ways to differentiate themselves in a crowded retail marketplace, the café giant is teaming up with WestJet.

Starting Nov. 30, a special in-flight brew from the café giant will be available on board the airline’s flights as part of a partnership between the two brands that will later include a loyalty program collaboration.

Dubbed the “flight roast,” Tim Hortons says the coffee features a unique blend specifically designed for passengers’ tastebuds at high altitudes. Hope Bagozzi, Tims’ chief marketing officer, called it distinct from the original and dark roast blends that customers are used to drinking at its restaurants.

“Our coffee teams sort of set to work saying, ‘OK, the first fundamental is we’re going to leverage the same 100 per cent premium arabica beans,’ so that’s a given. But the actual roast itself, we needed it to be a bit different because things taste different at high altitudes,” she said in an interview.

“Taste perceptions do change at altitudes, so we wanted to make sure that our roast suited that. So things like higher pressure, shorter brew times, a different temperature, all those matter.”

The second leg of the partnership is set to begin in 2027, when WestJet Rewards and Tims Rewards members will be able to link their accounts to earn points from both programs when they make eligible purchases at Tim Hortons.

The companies said account linking will also unlock exclusive offers and promotions. Additional details regarding the loyalty partnership and member benefits will be announced closer to the rollout, which is likely around a year away.

“It’s pretty simple in the sense that it’s pretty low friction, you link your account once, you go and every Timbit gets you closer to your next vacation,” said Steve McClelland, the airline’s vice-president of loyalty and strategic partnerships.

He called it a “natural partnership,” especially at a time when the buy Canadian trend is seeing a resurgence amid trade tensions with the United States. While the team-up with Tims is not a “response” to the geopolitical situation, McClelland said the “broader context of the world at large today certainly reinforces that fit.”

“There are only a few brands that are as Canadiana, as like deeply entrenched in the Canadian culture, as Tims,” he said.

“There’s only maybe a handful, if that, and we’re partnered with already quite a few of them.”

Tims has also been joining forces with other Canadian companies recently. Earlier this month, it announced a separate loyalty program collaboration with Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd.

Under that deal, customers who link their Triangle Rewards and Tims Rewards accounts can earn between two and five per cent in Canadian Tire money in addition to Tims points on select Tims purchases.

Canadian Tire money can be redeemed for savings on purchases at the retailer as well as its other banners, including SportChek, Mark’s and Party City. Tims points can be used to purchase food and beverages at the chain.

Canadian Tire has about 12 million Triangle Rewards members and 1,600 locations across its banners. Tims counts eight million loyalty program users and 4,000 restaurants in Canada.

Bagozzi said the moves are about being “realistic” that customers May prefer to save up for larger purchases such as flights or home goods rather than just coffee and doughnuts.

“We would have been having conversations even before any political changes, but having said that, even some of the celebrities that we partner with, hockey stars, we tend to gravitate to Canadian partners because we’re such a quintessential Canadian brand,” she said.

“It just kind of makes sense for us to do that.”

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: September 17, 2026
stories.summary: Travelling around London, I see a lot of rarely used bike lanes and poorly arranged bus rapid transit (BRT) lanes.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Travelling around London, I see a lot of rarely used bike lanes and poorly arranged bus rapid transit (BRT) lanes.

Why are BRT lanes on Wellington Road south and downtown in the middle of the road?

The bike path at Ridout Street and Commissioners Road is rarely used.

Go back to the old way: Sidewalks used by humans, their kids and bikes.

Roy Hanson, London

Last week, council’s planning and environment committee endorsed a proposed eight-storey apartment building on Sarnia Road, not far from the university. This replaces two once-posh homes in a beautiful family neighbourhood. NIMBY, yes, but sometimes offensive non-descript structures don’t fit.

But a few months ago, council rejected a proposed retirement home community development at 945 Bluegrass Dr. It was well planned and documented for a retirement home community. But neighbours killed the four-storey build in a clear case of NIMBY.

These two decisions show this city needs some consistent planning principles.

R. Webb, London

stories.title: Defying the odds: Renal patient celebrates 37 years on dialysis
stories.summary: September 17, 2026
stories.content:
September 17, 2026

Thirty-seven years ago, in 1989, music artists like Chicago, Paula Abdul, and Bette Midler were topping the charts (and future chart topper Taylor Swift was born). Movies such as Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, Back to the Future Part II, and The Little Mermaid were bringing in huge audiences to theatres and only about 1.5 per cent of the Canadian population had a cell phone.

Technology looked a lot different. You had an actual camera to take photos, a paper map for directions, and a Walkman to play music on-the-go.

What else happened thirty-seven years ago? Maria Medeiros started dialysis.

Maria was diagnosed with polycystic kidney disease (PKD) in the 1980s. PKD is an inherited disorder that causes fluid-filled cysts to grow in the kidneys.

"I was diagnosed with PKD a number of years before I started dialysis through blood work," Maria explains. "But it reached a point where my kidneys were not functioning properly anymore and I needed to start dialysis. I started my dialysis at the old Victoria Hospital in 1989 and went there for one year before going to Base Line Road when they had the dialysis centre. Now I go to Westmount as they transferred the program there."

Over the 37 years, Maria has also been the recipient of three kidney transplants, but unfortunately, they did not take. She became quite sick after her transplants and even ended up in intensive care.

"I am the only person in my family with polycystic kidney disease - none of my siblings have this. And when I started dialysis, I already had three children," shares Maria. "When my family was being tested as possible kidney donors, my siblings were not a match, but my daughter, who was 17 years old at the time, was. However, she was too young to donate, so I had to move forward with unrelated donors."

Maria notes the difficulties she experienced balancing raising three small children (the oldest was 10 years old when she started dialysis) and going to dialysis treatment in- centre three times a week. She shares that her social worker at that time helped her with balance when she was starting dialysis.

All of Maria's original care team members have left or retired, but she remains grateful for everyone's excellent care over the decades.

Maria says that "Dialysis has felt like a family where the team made it feel less medical. The staff have been great and always accommodate whatever I need. I like to make food, especially around Christmas, and bring it in for staff because I know they always do their best."

While having to go into the clinic three times a week for dialysis has been taxing in some ways, Maria is grateful for her care and hopes for many more years to spend with family.

"My children and I are close, and I have a granddaughter now. It's been a pleasure to see my children grow up and to meet my grandchild," Maria says.

"I've been a nurse practitioner for almost three decades," says JulieAnn Lawrence, Nurse Practitioner, Westmount Hemodialysis Unit, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC). "And while it's not frequent that I continue to care for patients from when I began, I've had about five of my patients approach the 30-year mark in their dialysis treatment."

Lawrence emphasizes the patient's strict adherence to the many lifestyle restrictions that come with kidney disease.

"Restrictions in diet, managing medications, keeping to dialysis schedules, attention to small deviations in their health status require an intense amount of energy, dedication, and resilience to incorporate in their everyday life," Lawrence explains. "That helps provide longevity, but people living with kidney disease have their own journey. Over the past decades there have been improvements to primary care support for the management of kidney disease, advancement in transplantation and immunosuppressive medication, as well as innovations and improvements in various dialysis modalities that not only extend life but enhance the quality of life."

Thanks to advancements and improvements in funding and the model of care, more recently, patients are treated holistically in the early stages of kidney disease to slow or reverse progression. Lawrence shares that this means that when patients end up needing dialysis, they will have support along the way as they participate in decisions around the treatment that suits their experience and care pathways that enhance patient outcomes.

Lawrence says, "There are still many kidney diseases that are related to autoimmune disorders and genetic conditions, such as Maria's polycystic kidney disease, and as more inheritable conditions are identified, there will hopefully be early surveillance and intervention opportunities in the future so those future generations May not need dialysis or transplantation."

A lot has changed in 37 years in dialysis, and Lawrence notes that improvements in access and the therapies themselves have helped give people more years to their life, and life to their years.

"Thankfully, now with regional hemodialysis programs, optimization of home therapies such as home hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis, as well as the introduction and improvements made to virtual care – more patients are able to access dialysis and enjoy a reasonable quality of life," Lawrence shares.

stories.title: Serious motor vehicle collision
stories.summary: London, ON (September 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section are investigating a serious motor vehicle collision involving a cyclist that took place in the downtown core yesterday afternoon.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (September 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section are investigating a serious motor vehicle collision involving a cyclist that took place in the downtown core yesterday afternoon.

On Wednesday, September 16, 2026, at approximately 4 p.m., emergency services responded to the intersection of Dundas and Maitland streets after a collision involving a motor vehicle and a cyclist.

An adult male cyclist was transported to hospital by paramedic services with life-threatening injuries. He remains in critical condition.

The driver of the involved vehicle remained at the scene.

The investigation has been reassigned to the LPS Road Safety Section and remains ongoing.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 3:45 p.m. and 4 p.m. on September 16, 2026, who may have dash-cam footage, or residential or business video surveillance, to contact police.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Base Line Road East will close for underground servicing work
stories.summary: Starting Monday, September 21, Base Line Road East will be closed between High Street and Ridout Street South until approximately September 2
stories.content:
Starting Monday, September 21, Base Line Road East will be closed between High Street and Ridout Street South until approximately September 24 while private underground servicing work connects water, storm sewers, and sanitary sewers to a property in the area.

A detour will be posted via High Street, Emery Street East, and Ridout Street South.

The south sidewalk will also be closed. Access to homes in the area will be maintained.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules.

This work is taking place near Wellington Gateway Phase 2A and 2B construction. Drivers should expect delays and changing traffic conditions in the area and follow posted signs and detours.

We recognize the amount of construction happening in this area and the added pressure it can put on nearby roads and neighbourhoods. The City reviews new work carefully and looks for opportunities to coordinate or defer projects when possible to avoid adding impacts to key routes. However, some work, including development servicing and utility connections, needs to proceed to support new development and essential infrastructure.

For this closure, the work is expected to take approximately three days, and crews will work to reopen the road as soon as it is complete.

Updated September 18, 2026.

stories.title: Rescue Rendezvous returns to The Catty Shack this Saturday
stories.summary: The City of London is inviting residents to The Catty Shack this Saturday, September 19, for
stories.content:
The City of London is inviting residents to The Catty Shack this Saturday, September 19, for Rescue Rendezvous , a family event that helps cats find loving homes.

Running from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at 756 Windermere Road, the event offers adoption discounts and opportunities to connect with local rescues. Visitors can spend time with cats waiting to become part of a new family.

“Rescue Rendezvous is more than an adoption event - it’s a chance for people to connect with the amazing cats at The Catty Shack and experience the joy of giving a cat a second chance,” says Michelle McBride, Animal Welfare Coordinator. “Every cat in our care is thoroughly assessed, loved, and ready to become a cherished member of a new family.”

Visitors will find The Catty Shack at the northwest corner of Adelaide Street North and Windermere Road. The adoption centre will be open throughout the event.

Event details can be found at London.CA/rescuerendezvous.

Can’t make it on September 19? Visit The Catty Shack during its regular hours:

Wednesday to Friday: 1 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Saturday and Sunday: 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The Catty Shack is the City of London’s cat adoption centre, providing a temporary home for healthy, friendly and vaccinated cats while they wait to be adopted. Its cozy, storefront-style house offers a welcoming space for Londoners to meet cats and find a new companion.

The Catty Shack does not accept animal intakes. Pet intakes for the City of London are handled by London Animal Care Centre at 121 Pine Valley Boulevard.

To learn more about the Catty Shack, visit London.CA/cattyshack

stories.title: TVDSB Technology Programs Benefit from Industry Donation Exceeding $50,000
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: - Sep
stories.content:
General News

All Notices and Updates

The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) is proud to recognize the outstanding generosity of John Warner and Great Lakes Copper , whose leadership and collaboration with community partners have resulted in a donation of more than $50,000 in copper pipe and personal protective equipment (PPE) for technology education programs across the board.

This significant contribution will provide valuable resources for students and educators in skilled trades and technology classrooms, helping to enhance hands-on learning experiences and support the development of future industry professionals.

TVDSB would also like to acknowledge the generosity of the following contributing organizations:

Cargill Canada

Tri HQ Inc.

Motion Canada

Inps Canada

Militex Canada

Liuna Local 1059

White Cap Supply Canada

Together, these industry partners have demonstrated an exceptional commitment to supporting student success, experiential learning, and workforce development.

About TVDSB Technology Education Programs

TVDSB secondary schools provide a wide variety of technology programming. The board also offers five Emphasis Technology schools, where students can delve deeper into their area of interest and achieve industry certifications (Clarke Road SS, College Avenue SS, Montcalm SS, Saunders SS and Strathroy DCI). Areas of study include communications technology, computer technology, design, construction, electrical, heating and cooling, sheet metal, green industries, hair and aesthetics, barbering, health care, hospitality and tourism, manufacturing, welding and machining, transportation and aviation. For more details, visit TVDSB’s Technology Emphasis webpage .

stories.title: Missing people -
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
Update- London, ON (September 18, 2026) - The previously reported missing persons have been located and are safe. We would like to thank the public for sharing the information. We kindly ask that all photographs of the missing persons be removed from publication.

London, ON (September 17, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating husband and wife - 57-year-old Hong Juan Fu and 56-year-old Bing Yue, of London.

Hong Juan Fu is described as Chinese, female, average build with short grey/brown hair. She was last seen wearing a bright pink and white jacket, light pink overcoat, black pants, and black running shoes with white soles.

Bing Yue is described as Chinese, male, average build, with short grey hair. He was last seen wearing a blue and grey plaid button-up shirt, beige coat, black pants, black running shoes, carrying a blue Walmart bag and white plastic bags.

The couple was reported missing on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, and were last seen on September 16, 2026, in the area of Dalmagarry Road and Fanshawe Park Road West. The couple are fluent in Mandarin and are known to frequent London, Toronto, and the Greater Toronto Area.

Police and family are concerned for their welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Vancouver Canucks return to Penticton for third straight training camp
stories.summary: The Vancouver Canucks are heading back to Penticton for training camp and the team's return is generating plenty of excitement in the South Okanagan.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
The Vancouver Canucks are heading back to Penticton for training camp and the team’s return is generating plenty of excitement in the South Okanagan.

The four-day pre-season camp gets underway Thursday at the South Okanagan Events Centre, marking the third consecutive year the Canucks have held their pre-season camp in Penticton.

“I’ve followed the Canucks for years, so to see them in person in your own rink and practice, it’s pretty amazing,” said Penticton resident Chris Hartt.

The camp includes practices and scrimmage games, all open to the public, giving local hockey fans an opportunity to watch NHL players up close.

“My husband is really excited about it,” said Penticton resident Katrina.

“He looks forward to it every year. He schedules all the times that he’s going to go with his friends and he goes.”

For Tom Scott, having the Canucks in Penticton is a natural fit for a community with a strong hockey culture.

“This is a hockey town, right? There’s lots of hockey schools and training here throughout the year, so it sort of makes sense,” Scott said.

For Penticton, however, hosting the Canucks is about more than the economic impact of bringing NHL hockey to town.

“It’s not about dollars. This is about status. This is about saying, yeah, the Canucks like Penticton. The Canucks like to come to Penticton,” said Penticton mayor Julius Bloomfield. “It’s a feather in our cap, that’s for sure, and it makes us feel good.”

The sentiment is shared by other fans who are proud to see the team continue to choose Penticton for its training camp.

“We think they know a good place when they see it,” said Penticton resident Joy Borkwood.

The Canucks’ training camp runs Thursday through Sunday at the South Okanagan Events Centre.

Tickets can be purchased online .

stories.title: Canadian goods banned from U.S. government purchases in escalating trade fight
stories.summary: Trump had said he would cut Canadian goods from U.S. government purchases “unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies”
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Canada

World

Earlier this month, Trump signalled he would cut Canadian goods from U.S. government purchases ‘unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies’

Author of the article:

Last updated 39 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/canadian-goods-banned-from-us-government-purchases#comments-area)

U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, ON September 16, 2026.Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

U.S. President Donald Trump directed agencies to remove Canadian goods from government contracts, executing an earlier threat as tensions between the two countries flare.

In a presidential memorandum, the White House criticized Canada for its barriers to U.S. companies seeking access to the Canadian government market through a “Buy Canadian” policy.

The order is the latest escalation by Trump in a trade fight that ramped up over the summer, as tit-for-tat tariff measures between the U.S. and Canada followed the last-minute collapse of a trade truce in August.

The procurement order comes after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered to make Canada an “associate member” during a speech on Wednesday. Trump criticized the proposal, calling it potentially a “hostile act” and threatened more tariffs on European goods or to “stop trading with Europe on many things.”

Trump signalled he would cut Canadian goods from U.S. government purchases in a social media post earlier this month, “unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies.”

At the time, Trump said the Canadian goods and services sold under the so-called Multiple Award Schedule are worth more than US$50 billion each year.

A senior administration official later clarified that although the White House calculates the U.S. procurement market at that amount, Canadian companies don’t always account for all of it.

stories.title: New ICE contracts for Quebec-based security firm involved with ‘Alligator Alcatraz’
stories.summary: ICE awarded two new contracts to the American branch of GardaWorld Security in late August.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has contracted a Montreal-based security firm again, this time to assist its efforts in Texas.

ICE awarded two new contracts to the American branch of GardaWorld Security in late August. Together, these contracts have a minimum value of close to US$118 million (C$165 million) and could reach a value of over US$1.3 billion (C$1.9 billion).

The first contract is for the renovation of a warehouse in San Antonio into a new detention centre and the operation of that centre. Its minimum value is around US$17.3 million and its maximum value is over US$1 billion.

The second contract is for armed ground transportation of people detained by ICE in Texas. The contract spans the period between Sept. 1, 2026, and Aug. 31, 2027, with a possible extension for three more years.

The minimum value of this contract is around US$100.5 million. Its value could reach around US$382.3 million.

On Sept. 10, days after the second contract was awarded, an American security contractor formally challenged Ice’s decision to award the contract to GardaWorld. ICE has suspended the contract due to this challenge.

GardaWorld is an international security firm headquartered in Montreal. In 2022, it received a $300-million investment from the government of Quebec “to support its global strategic vision,” according to a press release.

In March, ICE awarded a US$313-million contract to the American branch of GardaWorld to work on renovation and operation of another detention facility in Arizona.

GardaWorld previously worked on the so-called “Alligator Alcatraz,” a detention facility in the Florida Everglades. The facility closed this summer after months of protests, lawsuits and allegations of inhumane living conditions for detainees.

On Monday, a report by the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general outlined how detainees were held for up to two hours in small metal enclosures used as “calming areas,” a practice that “does not meet standards for humane treatment,” the report read.

The report listed a number of other concerns with the conditions in the facility, such as access to clean drinking water and to legal representation.

The Department of Homeland Security said in response to the report that any allegations of inhumane conditions are false.

“To our knowledge, the operations characterized as non-compliant in the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General report were not performed by GardaWorld Federal,” a spokesperson said.

Last week, Democratic U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, who represents a district that covers part of San Antonio, said he was “shocked” to hear the federal government had awarded another contract to GardaWorld, despite the allegations around “Alligator Alcatraz.”

Karen Hamilton, director of Above Ground, an organization pushing for accountability for Canadian companies working abroad, said the new contracts were “disappointing, but not surprising.”

Above Ground started following GardaWorld after the “Alligator Alcatraz” contract, she said, calling the company’s response to the outcry around the condition in the facility “dismissive.”

“There is just a general situation where you have a context of heightened human rights risk and serious concerns about whether GardaWorld had done proper due diligence, was taking proper steps to ensure that this Canadian company would not be involved in that abuse,” she said.

She said the new contracts fit into GardaWorld’s philosophy of expansion.

“It’s not surprising that it’s now going after other contracts. These are lucrative contracts,” she said.

Above Ground is lobbying for oversight and accountability for Canadian companies involved in potential human rights abuses abroad. Hamilton said the Canadian government has very few mechanisms to hold a company like GardaWorld to account for their actions abroad.

Both GardaWorld and ICE refused to comment on their latest contracts and GardaWorld did not comment further on the “Alligator Alcatraz” allegations.

The first contract is for the renovation of a warehouse in San Antonio into a new detention centre and the operation of that centre. Its minimum value is around US$17.3 million and its maximum value is over US$1 billion.

The second contract is for armed ground transportation of people detained by ICE in Texas. The contract spans the period between Sept. 1, 2026, and Aug. 31, 2027, with a possible extension for three more years.
The minimum value of this contract is around US$100.5 million. Its value could reach around US$382.3 million.

stories.title: Trump threatens to cut trade with EU if Canada association proposal is ‘at all a hostile act’
stories.summary: “If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility,” Trump said.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump threatened on Wednesday to cut trade with the European Union after the bloc proposed to make Canada its first ever associate member.

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen raised the prospect a day before Canada’s leader Mark Carney was due to address the European Parliament.

Her pitch comes as both Canada and the European Union seek to pivot away from an aggressive United States under Trump’s leadership.

“I think it’s laughable,” Trump told reporters when asked about the plan.

“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, ON many things.”

He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility.”

Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, who became the first non-European head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” speech.

The German told the European Parliament in Strasbourg that, as democracies face a “fracture in the international rules-based system,” Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.

“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen told the Canadian prime minister, drawing a standing ovation in the chamber.

Carney has been pursuing closer ties with the European Union as Canada gets drawn ever deeper into a trade war with the United States.

He is set to address the parliament on Thursday, with his visit meant to act as a catalyst ahead of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month.

Von der Leyen said it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and “bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said.

She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.

But both the EU and Canada have been buffeted by tariffs and territorial threats from the U.S. and competition from China.

“In a more dangerous and divided world, Canada is forging stronger relationships with trusted partners,” Carney’s office said in a statement.

While EU treaties do not envision the possibility of becoming an “associate member,” the idea was first floated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz this year for Ukraine.

Under that plan, which met a cold reception from a country pushing for full membership, Ukraine would have been allowed to attend the bloc’s summits and have a representative in the European Commission.

It would have also benefited from parts of the EU budget, but without full voting rights.

“We don’t really know yet what it means,” said Tobias Cremer, a centre-left European lawmaker from Germany and the main sponsor of a resolution urging stronger EU-Canada cooperation, after von der Leyen’s “associate membership” pitch.

Under EU rules, member states have to approve any form of partnership with a third country and it was unclear how much support von der Leyen’s proposal would receive from capitals.

Brussels and Ottawa already enjoy a considerable level of cooperation.

The Ceta free-trade agreement that abolished almost all tariffs has been credited with boosting trade in goods and services by more than 80 per cent since 2016.

And this year Canada became the first non-EU country to join a flagship defence loan program.

Carney later flew to Britain for his first meeting with new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

They attended a football match between Everton and Wolverhampton together before Carney’s return to Strasbourg for his Thursday speech.

stories.title: Trump says Canada-EU associate membership could be ‘hostile act’
stories.summary: Speaking to reporters in North Carolina, the president said if it's done with "bad intentions" he will "put very heavy tariffs on Europe."
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
After further escalating his trade war Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump said if Canada becomes the first associate member of the European Union it could be a “hostile act.”

Speaking to reporters in North Carolina, the president said if it’s done with “bad intentions” he will “put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

Trump also called Canada a “terrible trade partner” after earlier Wednesday signing a memorandum directing federal agencies overseeing government procurement in the United States to remove all products of Canadian origin.

“President Trump is taking action to hold Canada accountable for its continued unreasonable and discriminatory treatment of U.S. goods, which has burdened and disadvantaged hard-working Americans,” said a fact sheet from the White House.

A White House official, speaking on background, said that order was not related to the European Union forging closer ties with Canada.

Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney listened in the front row of the state of the European Union address as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen laid out the case for the closer relationship.

She said the two sides must “urgently reimagine” their partnership and move beyond a free-trade agreement to bring the relationship to the “highest level possible.”

Carney is set to address the European Parliament on Thursday. Officials have said the two sides are still talking about how to define an enhanced partnership.

Canada-U.S. relations were upended as Trump returned to the White House last year armed with ever-changing tariffs targeting America’s northern neighbour. But Trump’s trade war has ramped up in recent weeks after negotiations between the two countries broke down.

Carney has warned that Canada’s pivot away from the United States will come at a cost, but the alternative would be far worse.

To justify Trump’s latest move, the presidential order points to Ottawa’s “Buy Canadian” policy, which was launched, along with similar actions by some provinces, after the president hit Canada with tariffs and threats of annexation.

The order said Canada has “unreasonably imposed new barriers to United States companies seeking to access the Canadian government procurement market.”

“My administration will always act to combat such unreasonable or discriminatory practices,” the order said.

The order also said the United States Trade Representative will monitor for circumstances that May require the “need for further action.” It said the department will also inform the president if goods can be returned following “a change in policy by the Canadian government that would end the current treatment toward United States origin items.”

It was not immediately clear what would be affected by the procurement policy. Trump’s order said the move would affect access to goods the United States agreed to cover at the federal level under the World Trade Organization Agreement on Government Procurement, amounting to over $280 billion annually.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc’s office said they have taken note of the procurement restrictions. Spokesperson Gabriel Brunet said “we will review these measures with a focus on the best interest of Canadian businesses and workers.”

Trump first threatened to remove all Canadian-origin products from federal procurement in a post on social media last week.

“That is not reciprocity, it is a Canadian Trade Scam,” Trump’s post said of the Buy Canadian rules.

The Buy Canadian policy, implemented in December 2025, prioritizes Canadian companies in large federal purchases, requires the use of Canadian steel, aluminum and wood in major federal construction and defence projects, and restricts non-defence contracts to Canadian companies or international firms from countries which offer the same access to Canadian businesses.

The United States also has a “Buy America” policy that prioritizes domestic purchasing in key sectors. Former Democrat president Joe Biden implemented an array of protectionist procurement rules that Trump has since kept in place or expanded.

Trump initially hit Canada with economywide tariffs citing the flow of fentanyl last year. While those duties were squashed by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Trump administration replaced the tariff wall with a 10 per cent levy linked to forced labour in supply chains.

Those tariffs do not apply to goods compliant with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade.

Trump is also slamming Canada with separate sectoral tariffs on industries like steel, aluminum, automobiles and cabinetry.

Last month the Trump administration intensified the tariff spat by hitting an array of Canadian products, from hockey sticks to honey, with 50 per cent tariffs.

Ottawa’s retaliatory tariffs on specific American goods went into place Sept. 8. The same day, Trump signed executive orders to completely bar imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, some dairy products and alcoholic beverages, later this month.

The trade war between former close allies has caused major concerns for businesses in the deeply integrated North American market.

The Associated Equipment Distributors on Tuesday sent letters to U.S. governors from states with significant exposure to Canadian trade calling for a resolution.

“Our supply chains do not stop at state lines or national borders. Heavy machinery, agricultural equipment, industrial components, and service parts routinely cross the U.S.-Canada border multiple times during production and distribution,” President and CEO Brian P. McGuire wrote in the letter.

“The ongoing uncertainty created by trade disputes will disrupt significant multi-year capital investments, inflate equipment costs, and directly threaten local jobs.”

stories.title: Quebec party leaders meet for second TV debate ahead of election
stories.summary: Debate themes include the cost of living, finance and infrastructure, youth, health and protecting the French language
stories.content:
The prospect of a referendum on Quebec sovereignty took centre stage Wednesday as the heads of the main political parties squared off for a provincial election leaders’ debate in the shadow of an escalating trade war between Canada and the United States.

After opening the debate with a statement acknowledging her party was not perfect after eight years in government, Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette took aim at Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, challenging him on his promise to hold a referendum in the first four years of a PQ mandate.

“Is it really the time to add uncertainty with the referendum of Paul St-Pierre Plamondon? Me, I’ll work on your priorities. Him, he’ll work at planning a referendum,” she said in her opening statement.

St-Pierre Plamondon has pledged to spend over $130-million to organize a referendum on Quebec sovereignty if his party forms a government after the Oct. 5 election.

He has said, however, it would wait until U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029 before triggering a sovereignty vote.

Fréchette has not said how she would vote on a sovereignty referendum. She warned that St-Pierre Plamondon’s plans could destabilize Quebec and harm its economy.

Fréchette also brought up the issue as she faced off one-on-one against some of the other party leaders about unrelated issues, prompting Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard to remind her she was going off topic.

“Right now, you’re debating me,” Milliard said.

St-Pierre Plamondon, in a later segment, defended his referendum plans, saying that separation would give Quebec more control over its own future.

“I think that consulting people and reflecting on our future, in light of the fact that Quebec is in decline regarding the French language and its culture, are fundamental levers,” he said.

The themes of the 90-minute TV debate, hosted by Noovo, included the cost of living, finance and infrastructure, youth, health and protecting the French language.

Fréchette frequently came under attack over accusations she was part of a government that had wasted public money.

Duhaime pointed to her government’s decision to build a network of seniors’ homes “at $1-million per door,” as an example, counting her among Quebec politicians who “like to cut ribbons because it looks better than taking care of our dilapidated infrastructure.”

Fréchette fired back at Duhaime on his choice of candidates, saying he had “six or seven” who were pro-Trump.

The PQ and CAQ leaders were asked whether they supported cutting electricity exports to the United States in response to the escalating trade war.

Fréchette said she wouldn’t rule it out, although it wasn’t her first choice. St-Pierre Plamondon said he was “a bit surprised” to hear Fréchette was opening the door to escalate tensions with the United States.

“Me, I’m not in that school of thought,” he said.

The debate came hours after U.S. President Donald Trump signed a memorandum directing federal agencies overseeing government procurement in the United States to remove all products of Canadian origin. The move is the latest escalation of the trade war by the Trump administration after negotiations between Canada and the United States broke down last month.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal and Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime also debated strategies to address climate change. Duhaime suggested Quebec should exploit its natural gas resources through fracking to displace other fossil fuels.

Ghazal said Duhaime was proposing to pursue exactly what Trump wanted Quebec to do, and said the province should instead keep up with other jurisdictions that are growing their clean energy sectors.

Ghazal also said her party was the only one that wasn’t proposing to trim the size of government.

“When we’re in a crisis because of the tariff war, everyone including big businesses, who do they turn to? They turn to the state,” she said.

Later, a debate segment on protecting the French language led to a testy exchange between Milliard and Duhaime.

Duhaime highlighted his immigration plan to favour immigrants from democratic countries over others, and said Quebec children should have priority for daycare spots over the children of asylum seekers.

“I’m not going to try to win this election on the backs of children of asylum seekers,” Milliard said in response.

The candidates were also divided on the role that the private sector should play in the province’s struggling health-care network.

Both Duhaime and Fréchette said they were in favour of letting patients be treated in the private system without paying out of pocket when wait times grow too long, though Millard accused Fréchette of distancing herself from the public system.

Fréchette said the Coalition Avenir Québec government needed time to overcome budget cuts from the former Liberal government, which was last in power in 2018, prompting a rebuke from the Liberal leader.

“You attended about 150 cabinet meetings since you’ve been in politics,” Milliard said. “Stop blaming Pierre, Jean and his sister for all of the problems in health care.”

St-Pierre Plamondon also challenged Duhaime on his promotion of private care, suggesting doctors will simply “change address” from the public to the private system “while charging 35 per cent more.”

Wednesday’s debate was the second of three planned exchanges between the leaders of the five parties.

The final debate will air on Radio-Canada on Sept. 23.

Ghazal said Duhaime was proposing to pursue exactly what Trump wanted Quebec to do, and said the province should instead keep up with other jurisdictions that are growing their clean energy sectors.
Ghazal also said her party was the only one that wasn’t proposing to trim the size of government.
“When we’re in a crisis because of the tariff war, everyone including big businesses, who do they turn to? They turn to the state,” she said.
Later, a debate segment on protecting the French language led to a testy exchange between Milliard and Duhaime.

Duhaime highlighted his immigration plan to favour immigrants from democratic countries over others, and said Quebec children should have priority for daycare spots over the children of asylum seekers.
“I’m not going to try to win this election on the backs of children of asylum seekers,” Milliard said in response.
The candidates were also divided on the role that the private sector should play in the province’s struggling health-care network.

Both Duhaime and Fréchette said they were in favour of letting patients be treated in the private system without paying out of pocket when wait times grow too long, though Millard accused Fréchette of distancing herself from the public system.

Fréchette said the Coalition Avenir Québec government needed time to overcome budget cuts from the former Liberal government, which was last in power in 2018, prompting a rebuke from the Liberal leader.
“You attended about 150 cabinet meetings since you’ve been in politics,” Milliard said. “Stop blaming Pierre, Jean and his sister for all of the problems in health care.”
St-Pierre Plamondon also challenged Duhaime on his promotion of private care, suggesting doctors will simply “change address” from the public to the private system “while charging 35 per cent more.”
Wednesday’s debate was the second of three planned exchanges between the leaders of the five parties.
The final debate will air on Radio-Canada on Sept. 23.

stories.title: Cyclist, truck involved in serious collision near downtown London
stories.summary: A large stretch of Dundas Street was cordoned off as police investigated Wednesday evening.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
A large stretch of Dundas Street was cordoned off as police investigated Wednesday evening.

Last updated 22 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/cyclist-truck-involved-in-serious-collision-in-London#comments-area)

A major collision investigation vehicle is at the scene of a serious crash near Dundas and Maitland streets in London on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Brian Williams/The London Free Press)

An area near the city’s core was closed by police after a serious motor vehicle collision, London police say.

In a brief social media post at 4 p.m. Wednesday, police said emergency crews were at the scene of a serious collision in the area of Dundas and Maitland streets.

“Injuries are unknown at this time,” police said. “Please avoid the area.”

When The Free Press arrived at the Dundas and Maitland streets intersection shortly before 5:30 p.m., there was a heavy police presence, including about a dozen cruisers and unmarked vehicles and the major collision investigation truck.

A police officer at the scene said there had been a collision involving a truck and a cyclist.

A bicycle lies on its side near Dundas and Maitland streets in London on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Brian Williams/The London Free Press)

Caution tape cordoned off a sizeable area of Dundas Street east of Maitland Street, extending east to Beal Secondary School.

Inside the police tape, a bicycle was resting on its side in the bike lane on the south side of Dundas Street, with about nine green pylons placed nearby. A medium-duty commercial work vehicle was parked on Dundas Street facing east.

Mohit Dalwadi, 30, works at Markus Mini Mart at the southeast corner of Dundas and Maitland streets.

He said the cyclist was a regular customer who had been in the store “two or three minutes” before the collision.

“I was busy serving another customer, and suddenly I heard a loud noise,” Dalwadi said. “I went outside the store running, and then this guy got hit by a truck.”

The cyclist was in “really bad shape,” Dalwadi said.

“He’s a familiar face. I don’t know him personally, but I do see him almost every day. I sell him stuff from the store, so yeah, it’s sad.”

The cyclist’s condition remained unknown Wednesday evening. London police had not responded to The Free Press’s request for an update.

stories.title: Ford government says cities must not deviate from Buy Ontario rules
stories.summary: Minister threatens to cut funding to municipalities that don’t comply with province’s domestic procurement directives amid U.S. trade war
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford’s government is threatening to cut off funding to municipalities that don’t comply with new Buy Ontario rules, but cities say they are already choosing local products amid the trade war with the United States .

Meanwhile, Ontario’s Official Opposition accused Mr. Ford of ignoring his own procurement policies, and the group representing Ontario’s 444 municipalities said some of the new provincial directives come with added costs and complexities.

In a letter to municipal leaders released Wednesday, Ontario’s Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, Rob Flack, urged local leaders to closely review supply chains and coming purchases to “identify every opportunity to increase domestic procurement.”

The province last year passed a law requiring the public sector give preference to goods and services provided by companies based in Ontario or elsewhere in Canada, and added municipal requirements in April this year. That directive applies to purchases such as fleet vehicles, as well as capital infrastructure project procurements.

“Failure to comply with Buy Ontario requirements will force us to reconsider provincial funding made available to municipalities,” wrote Mr. Flack in the letter dated Sept. 15.

Sanofi inaugurates Toronto facility that will produce seasonal flu vaccines for Canadians

Asked Wednesday about the letter, Mr. Ford said he is reinforcing his expectation that municipalities prioritize domestic companies.

“It’s just reminding them that, buy Ontario first, buy anywhere else in Canada if you can’t buy it in Ontario. And it’s a shame that I even to have to put that out after you know saying it about 10 million times and you know – get with the program, buy Canadian,” Mr. Ford said at a press conference Wednesday at the opening of a new biomanufacturing facility in Toronto.

Riley Brockington, president of the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, said this is a period of “significant uncertainty” for the provincial economy. He said even before the new rules were in place, more than 98 per cent of municipal procurement for non-construction goods and services was from businesses with Canadian addresses.

The association said some of the new Buy Ontario rules are challenging for municipalities – including verifying domestic content and supply chains, and balancing domestic procurement requirements with value for money and project timelines.

“Municipalities now have several months of experience with the new requirements, and we are hearing from municipalities and industry that some of the rules are adding time, cost and complexity to procurement,” Mr. Brockington said in a statement.

“Working together to make the system clear, practical and workable will be critical to achieving our shared goal of strengthening Ontario’s economy.”

Opinion: Premiers now lead the charge in the trade war. Ottawa must recognize that

The effect of U.S. tariffs on municipalities has begun to dominate discussions at the local level, as cities are starting to look into how the trade war could blow holes in their budgets.

Many have already instituted their own buy local pledges, including Toronto Mayor Oliva Chow, who is running for re-election. Election day is Oct. 26.

Ms. Chow, appearing at the press conference Wednesday with Mr. Ford, said she is already prioritizing local purchases, noting all three levels of government came together earlier this year to announce new subway cars will be built in Thunder Bay.

“At this very uncertain, stressful time, in the global turbulence, disruptive trade conversation that’s happening, the Team Canada approach, working together united, we are stronger and we’re proving it right now,” she said.

Mr. Ford also talked up his working relationship with Ms. Chow, signalling support for the incumbent mayor he once predicted would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city.

“I just want to say the mayor and I have a phenomenal relationship,” he said. “We’re going to continue supporting the mayor. She’s doing an incredible job. So, read between the lines.”

Tariffs have already emerged as a key issue in the Mississauga mayor’s race, where incumbent Mayor Carolyn Parrish is taking on Bonnie Crombie, who previously held the city’s top job for three terms.

Ms. Crombie said Wednesday it shouldn’t take a letter from the province to spur the city to act.

“Mississauga should not need a warning from Queen’s Park to use its purchasing power to support Ontario workers. Yet Mayor Parrish has failed to put forward a tariff response plan while local businesses face real uncertainty,” she said in a statement.

Ms. Parrish, meanwhile, defended her response and said the city has had a local procurement policy in place since U.S. tariffs were first imposed, with exceptions for items that are part of the United States-Canada-Mexico Agreement and not affected by tariffs.

“We adhere to this strategy to the best of our abilities. When the provincial government encourages municipalities to support local businesses, we agree 100 per cent. This is a fundamental approach that helps us to continue building Canada and Mississauga strong,” she said in a statement.

Ontario’s Official Opposition NDP, however, accused the provincial government of trying to distract from its own failures to prioritize local companies.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the Premier has given American companies – such as Staples, which now runs the provincial school supplies portal – priority over Canadian ones.

“It’s a bit rich for this Premier to be lecturing municipalities when he should be cleaning up his own house first,” she said in an interview, adding that Mr. Ford should recall the legislature – which isn’t set to resume until Oct. 27 – to fix the procurement rules.

The provincial government refuted Ms. Stiles’ criticisms and accused her of playing political games. Giulia Paikin, a spokesperson for Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement Stephen Crawford, said Staples employs 11,000 people in more than 300 stores in Canada and was chosen through a competitive procurement.

stories.title: Charges dropped against 2 men accused in Toronto Pearson gold heist
stories.summary: Charges against Amit Jalota and Ali Raza, two men accused in connection with the $20-million Toronto Pearson gold heist, were dropped on consecutive days.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
Charges against two men accused in connection with the 2023 Toronto Pearson Airport gold heist have been dropped on consecutive days.

Amit Jalota, an Oakville man accused in connection with the theft, had his charges withdrawn in a Brampton court on Tuesday, his lawyer told Global News.

His lawyer, Leora Shemesh, confirmed the charges had been dropped and said Jalota was relieved by the decision after maintaining his innocence throughout the case.

“Mr. Jalota is certainly delighted that the Crown finally chose to withdraw the charges against him,” Shemesh said in a statement to Global News.

“However, he has been punitively and unreasonably punished for the last three years as he was forced to navigate the criminal justice system and the fall out of these allegations that were publicly broadcasted both nationally and internationally.”

Shemesh said Jalota had been denied the right to bank at Ontario financial institutions and faced restrictions on where he could work after his name and photograph were widely circulated.

“He was at all times entirely innocent of these allegations,” she said.

A day later, the charge against Ali Raza, another man accused in connection with the heist, was also withdrawn.

Raza appeared in a Brampton courtroom Wednesday, where the charge against him was dropped.

“I am happy,” Raza said when asked how he felt walking out of court.

His lawyer, Brij Mohan, said Raza had maintained his innocence from the beginning.

“These weak allegations have ruined this man’s life,” Mohan said.

“He is standing in front of you with his head high today and I hope it gives him a chance to regain his integrity in his community.”

Mohan said the allegations had “deeply affected his business, reputation and family.”

The lawyers for both Jalota and Raza say their families are now left to move forward from the case.

Raza and Jalota were among nine people charged in connection with the April 17, 2023, theft of about $20 million worth of gold bars from an Air Canada cargo facility at Toronto Pearson International Airport.

Police alleged the shipment arrived on an Air Canada flight from Zurich, Switzerland, before one suspect used a fraudulent airway bill to obtain the cargo.

Arsalan Chaudhary, 44, pleaded guilty earlier this year for his role as the mastermind of the massive theft that made international headlines. He was sentenced to four years in prison and ordered to refund $22 million to Brinks Canada.

Court records show the remaining accused are scheduled to stand trial beginning Sept. 28.

stories.title: Woman dead, one arrested in femicide investigation
stories.summary: A woman has died and a man has been charged with second degree murder in a femicide investigation.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
A woman has died and a man has been charged with second degree murder in a femicide investigation.

“Uniform officers were called to an address on Shelton Road last night around 6:30 p.m. in response to a violent incident,” said Micah Bourdeau with London Police Services.

Bourdeau said they located an adult female with life threatening injuries; she was transported to hospital where she later died.

41-year-old Mandeep Singh of London was arrested on scene.

“We now know that those two parties were involved in an intimate relationship,” said Bourdeau.

According to police, this is the fifth homicide in London this year but the first to show signs of a “possible femicide”.

“There are some indications that it could meet the threshold of a femicide,” said Bourdeau.

“That’s not clear yet and we need to investigate much more to determine that.”

Jennifer Dunn with the London Abused Women’s Centre (Lawc) said she was heartbroken when she heard the news.

“One is too many,” said Dunn.

“There shouldn’t be any men killing women in our city or anywhere.”

Dunn said this comes amid ongoing concern regarding intimate partner violence in our community.

“In 2023, there were four femicides that were well known here in the community,” said Dunn.

“We have not stopped talking about them ever since and it really varies year over year in the city of London.”

Dunn said if deemed a femicide, this will be the first case in London since Bill C16 was passed.

“BC16 received royal assent,” said Dunn.

“As part of this bill femicide is now recognized in the criminal code.”

Bourdeau explained this would mean an automatic first-degree murder charge.

“A conviction for a first-degree murder charge comes with an automatic 25-year sentence,” said Bourdeau.

According to police, Chelton road was closed for a duration of the day Thursday but has since reopened.

The investigation remains on going.

Anyone with information is asked to call the LPS at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 or online .

A list of resources and contact information for those experiencing intimate partner violence can be found on the LPS’ website .

stories.title: 'Canadians are out of money': Facing big challenges, Poilievre promises big cuts
stories.summary: Canadian businesses and consumers can’t afford the wasteful spending, Poilievre told his party’s MPs.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

Canadian businesses and consumers can’t afford the wasteful spending, Poilievre told his party’s MPs

Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre gestures while speaking during a press conference at Hotel Saskatchewan in Regina, ON Monday, September 7, 2026.Photo by Heywood Yu /Regina Leader-Post

Penticton, B.C. — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre rallied his caucus on Wednesday in the Okanagan Valley by vowing to take a big cut out of government spending.

Poilievre’s own climb up the political mountain is looking steeper than ever and, with a new parliamentary session opening next week, he told the majority of his caucus MPs during a speech in Penticton, B.C. that he’s found $150-billion in savings from government spending. He said the money could be used to lower federal debt, cut taxes and reduce inflation.

Repeating his recent emphasis on saving Canadians’ money, Poilievre said the cuts would come largely from reducing the federal bureaucracy, foreign aid, corporate welfare, fake asylum claims and “boondoggles” like the government’s high-speed rail plan.

“They’re out of touch,” he said of the governing Liberals, “and Canadians are out of money.”

The Conservative leader also tried to create space between himself and Prime Minister Mark Carney by saying that Canada doesn’t need to match American tariffs with counter-tariffs.

“We must outcompete the Americans, not out-tax them.”

And in response to reports that Carney May be moving Canada towards a closer relationship with the European Union, Poilievre told his caucus that Conservatives support free trade but not European taxes, laws and open borders. Canadian policy decisions can’t be made in Washington, Beijing or Brussels, he added.

“Canadians are not pawns on a global chess board,” he said.

Poilievre, facing reports of dissension within his caucus as Carney and his government soar in recent opinion polls, did not address his party’s struggles during his 20-minute speech.

But MP Melissa Lantsman,the party’s deputy leader, acknowledged earlier in the day to reporters that “this is not the position we want to be in at this juncture,” she said when asked about caucus morale. “There’s no question about this.”

Lantsman also said that MPs were gathering to discuss their tactics and strategies for the upcoming parliamentary session, which would be shared once MPs return to Ottawa.

The Conservatives are in a difficult place. Carney and the Liberals are attracting widespread support among Canadians, according to opinion polls, as they attempt to tackle the country’s economic challenges, particularly the Trump trade tariffs.

Recent opinion polls show the Conservatives’ challenges. The Liberals have been in power for more than a decade and some Conservative MPs are beginning to question if they see a light at the end of the tunnel.

An Abacus Data poll from earlier this month found that 54 per cent of Canadians have a positive impression of Carney, with just 27 per cent of respondents saying they have a negative view of the prime minister. And 59 per cent said they approve of the government’s performance.

The Liberals also lead the Conservative in most recent polls by at least a dozen percentage points, raising questions about the Tories’ strategies and leader.

The Conservatives have also been hit with internal squabbles and four caucus defections to the Liberals over the last year. In a recent byelection in Quebec that following the appointment of MP Richard Martel to the Senate, the Conservatives finished third.

And in response to reports that Carney May be moving Canada towards a closer relationship with the European Union, Poilievre told his caucus that Conservatives support free trade but not European taxes, laws and open borders. Canadian policy decisions can’t be made in Washington, Beijing or Brussels, he added.
“Canadians are not pawns on a global chess board,” he said.
Poilievre, facing reports of dissension within his caucus as Carney and his government soar in recent opinion polls, did not address his party’s struggles during his 20-minute speech.

But MP Melissa Lantsman,the party’s deputy leader, acknowledged earlier in the day to reporters that “this is not the position we want to be in at this juncture,” she said when asked about caucus morale. “There’s no question about this.”
Lantsman also said that MPs were gathering to discuss their tactics and strategies for the upcoming parliamentary session, which would be shared once MPs return to Ottawa.

The Conservatives are in a difficult place. Carney and the Liberals are attracting widespread support among Canadians, according to opinion polls, as they attempt to tackle the country’s economic challenges, particularly the Trump trade tariffs.

Recent opinion polls show the Conservatives’ challenges. The Liberals have been in power for more than a decade and some Conservative MPs are beginning to question if they see a light at the end of the tunnel.

An Abacus Data poll from earlier this month found that 54 per cent of Canadians have a positive impression of Carney, with just 27 per cent of respondents saying they have a negative view of the prime minister. And 59 per cent said they approve of the government’s performance.
The Liberals also lead the Conservative in most recent polls by at least a dozen percentage points, raising questions about the Tories’ strategies and leader.

The Conservatives have also been hit with internal squabbles and four caucus defections to the Liberals over the last year. In a recent byelection in Quebec that following the appointment of MP Richard Martel to the Senate, the Conservatives finished third.

stories.title: Alberta drivers face another jump at the pump after Illinois refinery outage
stories.summary: This latest price jump isn't the first this year, as the ongoing war in Iran and blockage of the Strait of Hormuz are causing costs to soar.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Gas prices have increased in Alberta, but while disruptions around the world have kept costs high this summer, that’s not the cause of the recent spike.

When pumps rolled over, the prices jumped by as much as $0.30 in some locations.

In Edmonton, some gas stations were seeing a $1.81 cost per litre, while Calgary sat at $1.84.

This latest price jump isn’t the first this year, as the ongoing war in Iran and blockage of the Strait of Hormuz are causing costs to soar. The cost for gas has ranged between $1.80 in the spring to $1.50 in July.

But Dan McTeague, president of Canadians for Affordable Energy, told Global News this latest jump isn’t due to global pressures but a recent power failure at a refinery in Illinois.

“We’re seeing the effects of what amounts to net $0.18 for gasoline and about roughly $0.24 to $0.25 for diesel,” McTeague said.

The Exxon Mobil Joliet refinery in Channahon, Ill., lost power on Sunday and as of Tuesday afternoon had not yet come back online.

The jump May be short-lived as the plant is slowly brought back online, but even if it sees prices drop, McTeague added the focus should centre around the price of diesel.

According to McTeague, diesel is already double what it was at this time last year and could make things more expensive and less affordable in the weeks to come.

“Think of trucks, transportation, construction, municipal vehicles,” he said. “Think of trains, think of jets.”

He warned another spike in gas prices could come sooner rather than later, though he did not specify how soon.

— with files from Global News’ Gates Guarin

stories.title: Amazon raises warehouse wages by $1 an hour across Canada amid union dispute
stories.summary: The company has for years been trying to fend off unionization attempts by workers in multiple jurisdictions across the U.S. and Canada
stories.author: Vanmala Subramaniam
stories.content:
Amazon Amzn-Q is raising hourly wages for thousands of Canadian warehouse workers by $1, amid a labour dispute with a Vancouver union pushing for a historic first collective agreement.

The tech behemoth announced Wednesday that it would boost the average hourly base wage for “operations employees” in Canada from $25.27 an hour to $26.27 an hour, effectively a 4-per-cent year-over-year increase in pay.

Amazon is also giving all its employees, including corporate staff, 10 per cent off online grocery purchases on Amazon.CA starting Oct. 1. In a statement, the company said that the pay increase and grocery discount builds on an existing workplace benefits package, which includes health, vision and dental benefits.

Group of B.C. Amazon workers tries to decertify union on verge of securing historic agreement

The company periodically boosts wages and benefits for warehouse employees, usually ahead of Prime Days in the fall and the holiday season.

Amazon has for years been trying to fend off unionization attempts by workers in multiple jurisdictions across the U.S. and Canada. Poor workplace conditions have been the impetus for union drives, but while Amazon workers in New York and Vancouver have successfully formed unions, no union has managed to secure an official collective agreement.

Unifor, one of the largest private-sector unions in Canada, unionized warehouse workers in Vancouver last July. It said in a statement on Wednesday that Amazon’s wage increase coincides closely with the B.C. labour relations board’s decision last month to force both sides into binding arbitration for a first contract.

“It’s about time Amazon recognizes that if they want to operate in Canada, they will do it while respecting the rights of the very workers they employ. We’re going to keep the pressure on to see workers across Canada benefit from the gains made through collective bargaining,” Unifor national president Lana Payne said.

According to a 2025 report from Amazon, the company employs 46,000 people in Canada, including 8,000 corporate employees. It has 70 operations and logistics sites across the country.

“Every day, our associates across Canada go the extra mile to prepare packages for customer deliveries, and we’re grateful for their dedication,” said Jasmin Begagic, director of Amazon Logistics Canada.

The Seattle tech giant has faced scrutiny over its track record on worker safety and working conditions. In 2023, Amazon was one of 21 employers penalized by Ontario’s Workplace Safety and Insurance Board for workers’ compensation violations. Specifically, the company failed to file an injury claim involving a worker at one of its Brampton, Ont., fulfillment centres.

Amazon refused to provide wage proposals to B.C. union, resulting in bargaining impasse, mediator says

In October, 2025, Unifor began discussions with Amazon about terms of a collective agreement for the 800 Vancouver warehouse workers, but the process has been fraught with complications. The union alleged that Amazon had “slow walked” the negotiating process by not tabling essential wage proposals in a timely manner .

Then in June, 2026, a mediator appointed by the BC Labour Relations Board sided with the union, saying in a report that the tech giant’s approach to bargaining was effectively “unreasonable” and hindered the process of agreeing to a new collective agreement.

Last month, the provincial labour board ordered binding arbitration to force Amazon into agreeing to terms of a first contract. The company has since appealed that decision.

Amazon workers at YVR2, the unionized warehouse in the Vancouver area, get paid between $18 and $25 per hour, according to Gavin McGarrigle, Unifor’s Western regional director. Mr. McGarrigle said that the union proposed wage increases of 4 per cent in 2026, 3.5 per cent in 2027 and 3.5 per cent in 2028 in the first collective agreement, but that Amazon countered with wage increases of 2.5 per cent, 2 per cent and 0 per cent.

The core issue of contention between both sides is the pace of work and injury rates. The union wants to establish clear rules for workload and productivity, but Amazon told the labour board’s mediator in June that it would not negotiate on how hard and fast workers are required to work.

In Wednesday’s statement, Amazon said that the pay boost will bring the annual salary for full-time warehouse workers, working 40 hours a week, to an average of $54,000.
