stories.title: London’s annual residence satisfaction survey is underway
stories.summary: has begun. 500 Londoners will be randomly selected for a phone c...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
has begun. 500 Londoners will be randomly selected for a phone call to ask about what they like and don’t like about London.

“ I would expect relative consistency in terms of the issues and level of satisfaction.” said the Director of Strategy, Innovation and Economic Development with the City of London, Trevor Fowler. “The trend line for the past three or four years has been fairly consistent. B ased on past trends, things have been relatively stable the past few years.”

Fowler said that the survey will involve questions revolving around how the person views the quality of life in London, as well as how satisfied they are with the city services, how connected they feel to the London community, and more.

The survey also allows the City of London to discover what people want improved in the City of London.

“ 2025, the top issues were in the areas of housing and homelessness, traffic and mental health and drug addiction.” said Fowler.

Well into 2026, it seems that there are some new issues at the forefront of peoples minds.

“Downtown for sure.” Said Nazar Vuyiv. “They need to make it prettier and safer, especially for people at nighttime.”

“Something I want to see improved in London is the construction.” Said Elizabeth Miller. “It’s like they set up these construction zones everywhere and block them off, and only work at them one at a time.”

stories.title: CTV News in the Arctic: Aurora borealis stretches across northern sky
stories.summary: Even in the Arctic, when the northern lights appear, you drop everything and look up. That’s what happened Tuesday night for our three-person CTV News crew, embedded with the Canadian Coast Guard aboard their icebreaker, the Des Groseilliers.
stories.author: Graham Richardson
stories.content:
On Thursday, CTV News will share an exclusive look at how Canada is boosting Arctic security aboard the Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker, the Des Groseilliers.

Above THE Arctic Circle — Even in the Arctic, when the northern lights appear, you drop everything and look up.

That’s what happened Tuesday night for our three-person CTV News crew, embedded with the Canadian Coast Guard aboard their icebreaker, the Des Groseilliers.

Most of the ship’s crew was asleep while we worked through a late-night edit when CTV News photographer Marley Parker stepped onto the deck for some fresh air.

He came back almost immediately.

“The northern lights are out.”

We rushed into the Arctic night. The wind had eased, the sea was calmer and the sky had cleared.

Above us, the aurora borealis seemed to paint a ribbon of green and yellow across the darkness, wrapping the ship in light.

Parker set up a time-lapse camera on the bow and left it running for an hour.

These are the results.

It wasn’t a walrus, a polar bear or an orca sighting. But it May have been the next best thing: a brief September display stretching across the sky above the Northwest Passage.

stories.title: New Brunswick’s nuclear power plant expected to be off-line for weeks, official says
stories.summary: A representative for New Brunswick's nuclear power plant says it's expected to remain off-line for a few weeks as they make a repair.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
By Eli Ridder The Canadian Press

Posted September 16, 2026 6:06 pm

A representative for New Brunswick’s nuclear power plant says it’s expected to remain off-line for a few weeks as they make a repair.

The station’s community manager Kathleen Duguay says plant workers have located a heavy-water leak from a broken pipe known as an instrumentation line.

She says workers weren’t able to access the broken line until the plant cooled down — and even then they still needed to use special equipment such as a scissor lift.

With the problem identified, Duguay says crews are working out a plan to fix the line at the Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station.

The station was first taken off-line Sept. 11, the third shutdown this year.

NB Power, the public utility that operates the plant, says there is no risk to the public, employees or the environment.

While the 43-year-old plant’s nuclear core was largely rebuilt some 14 years ago, many of its auxiliary components such as the instrumentation lines have been in place since it opened in the 1980s.

Earlier this year, the nuclear power facility was off-line from April to August for scheduled system checks and other maintenance.

Then, it was off-line for several days in early September for turbine system repairs.

stories.title: Poilievre urges Conservatives to put national interest first in caucus address
stories.summary: Conservative Leader paints picture of a country in precarious times, says party must fight for those struggling
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre kicked off his address to his caucus Thursday with a promise that the Official Opposition will unite behind the national interest and urged his MPs to be a voice for Canadians in the House of Commons.

“Our duty is country before party, now and always. As Canadian patriots, we must reflect on the job we have as loyal Opposition in these challenging times,” he said at a caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C.

Poilievre painted a picture of a country in precarious times: “People can’t afford their bills, are losing their jobs, the economy is flat, crime is worsening, and our economy is facing unfair tariffs,” he said.

He said his party has a duty to fight for people who are struggling.

“Should we shut up about their stories until Donald Trump goes away? No,” he said to applause from gathered members of the caucus.

Poilievre also warned against conflating criticism of the government with criticism of the country itself, arguing it is not disloyal to hold the Liberals to account.

Robyn Urback: Pierre Poilievre should oppose the government – but he can support it, too

The Conservatives have taken aim at Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberals this week over the news Canada is being invited into discussions about becoming the first “associate member” of the European Union.

Carney is set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, this week, a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced she was opening the door to Canada becoming an EU associate member – a title that currently does not exist.

It’s not clear what that would entail. Carney has suggested tighter alliances are being discussed on a number of fronts, including energy and security.

In his speech on Wednesday, Poilievre accused Carney of “secretly negotiating” with the EU and said decisions for Canada “must not be made in Washington, Beijing or Brussels, but by Canadians here at home.”

“While we support free trade and continued Nato co-operation with our European allies, Conservatives say no EU taxes, no EU laws and no EU open border rules on immigration in Canada,” he said.

The Conservatives are meeting after a tumultuous few months that saw them lose a fifth House of Commons seat to the government benches.

The trade war with the U.S. has dominated the news cycle and the Tories are polling well behind Carney’s Liberals.

Inside conservative circles, public infighting about the direction of the federal party has drawn in some members of Parliament.

That’s led a number of Conservative strategists to publicly question Poilievre’s control of caucus and the discipline in the ranks.

Political science professor Lori Turnbull said there are real differences of opinion among Conservatives over what the party ought to do going forward, and it’s not clear that Poilievre can regain the control he had before last year’s election.

“It doesn’t matter how disciplined they are, they’re not going to beat Carney now,” said Turnbull, a professor at the Dalhousie University faculty of management.

“There’s no election in the offing. The (majority) government is secure.”

As for Poilievre’s efforts to lead the Official Opposition through this moment, Turnbull said “he’s totally screwed.”

“He’s got to hold the government to account, that’s his job in a formal sense, but he’s also got to figure out how to get the party more rallied around him,” she said.

When the Conservatives were preparing to return to the House of Commons a year ago, the party had 144 MPs and vowed to bring strong opposition to the House of Commons.

At the time, Poilievre had just returned to the role of Opposition leader in the House, having spent the summer campaigning in a by-election after losing his longtime Ontario seat in April’s national vote.

Since then, MPs Chris d’Entremont, Michael Ma, Matt Jeneroux and Marilyn Gladu have defected to the Liberal benches. The popular Quebec MP Richard Martel accepted a seat in the Senate this summer, and the Conservative party posted a disappointing third-place result in the by-election to replace him last month.

Cathay Wagantall has stepped aside, leaving her eastern Saskatchewan seat vacant, and her Conservative colleague Larry Brock is set to resign his seat this week. By-election dates haven’t been set in those ridings yet.

Poilievre is set to hold a campaign-style rally on the weekend in Brantford, Ont., in Brock’s riding.

That will mark the first time the Tory leader has stepped onto a rally stage since the April 2025 election. Those rally events were a key part of the campaign and contributed to Poilievre’s rise in the polls between 2022 and 2024.

stories.title: Canada seeks full membership in U.K.-led military coalition
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada has formally applied to join the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force as a full-time member, a bid that London is supporting.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Liverpool — Prime Minister Mark Carney met for the first time face-to-face with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday, bonding over common values, a love of sports and a shared loss of their fathers to Alzheimer’s disease.

When they had their first call in July, a readout from 10 Downing said Burnham told Carney he “hoped to be able to roll out the blue carpet” for him in the future — a reference to Everton’s colours and the invitation to the game.

The two men sported the blue and yellow brooch of the Alzheimer Society on Wednesday, in recognition of Burham’s father who just recently died of the disease. In his own remarks, Carney noted that he too had lost his father to Alzheimer’s.

Burnham called Carney a “great progressive leader” and spoke about the shared values between U.K. and Canada, and where the two have a shared opportunity on defence co-operation, trade and AI.

“There’s been positive developments in that direction recently between the U.K. and Canada,” said Burnham, who took office after Keir Starmer resigned over the summer. “And it’s just so good for me to think that I will have somebody to talk to and commiserate about Everton at a G7 meeting.”

Canada has formally applied to join the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force as a full-time member, a bid that London is supporting, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said in a media statement Wednesday.

The joint force is a military coalition made up of 10 allied countries focused on Nato’s northern flank. It was assembled in 2014 to create a rapid-response force.

Canada’s military has worked with the force in multinational drills but has not been a permanent member of the group.

In their official meeting, the two leaders talked about defence, trade and the development of artificial intelligence, according to a readout from the Prime Minister’s Office in Ottawa.

It did not say whether the two leaders discussed U.S. President Donald Trump. Burnham is expected to meet Trump for the first time next week in New York.

Carney’s PMO noted that the two countries are working on a “new permanent arrangement” to modernize British Army Training Unit Suffield.

CFB Suffield’s 2,700-kilometre square training area in Alberta is being used by the British military for exercises and the testing of drones and other equipment.

London plans to spend some $18.7 million on British Army Training Unit Suffield through to 2031.

Canadian officials said London and Ottawa are also in active talks on merging their proposed defence financing initiatives to amplify their effects.

A senior Canadian government official who briefed reporters on background said Ottawa is very confident they’ll reach an agreement on bringing the two proposals together to form a joint institution.

Carney has championed the creation of a global Defence, Security and Resilience Bank to supply allies with low-cost borrowing for defence.

He’s enlisted support for that venture from eight countries, including Latvia, Luxembourg, Greece, Belgium and Ukraine. But no G7 country other than Canada has joined.

The United Kingdom’s separate effort, called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism, is designed as a financing vehicle for joint purchases of military equipment and has won support from the Netherlands, Finland and Poland.

British media first reported this week that Burnham’s finance minister, John Healey, is considering joining the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank.

Canada and the U.K. issued a joint statement at the annual Nato summit in Ankara, Turkey, this summer on how the two financial institutions could work together.

The statement said the two countries want to ensure their “respective initiatives develop in a coherent and mutually supportive way” and will “seek opportunities to co-operate closely and ensure complementarity.”

Money put into the defence bank counts toward the Nato target of having alliance members spend the equivalent of five per cent of their GDP on defence by 2035.

The head of Canada’s Business Development Bank, Isabelle Hudon, is working as the lead negotiator for the defence bank.

The U.K. is allocating $749 million toward the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and aims to stand it up in 2027.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

With files from Kyle Duggan in Ottawa

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

“There’s been positive developments in that direction recently between the U.K. and Canada,” said Burnham, who took office after Keir Starmer resigned over the summer. “And it’s just so good for me to think that I will have somebody to talk to and commiserate about Everton at a G7 meeting.”

Canada has formally applied to join the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force as a full-time member, a bid that London is supporting, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said in a media statement Wednesday.
The joint force is a military coalition made up of 10 allied countries focused on Nato’s northern flank. It was assembled in 2014 to create a rapid-response force.
Canada’s military has worked with the force in multinational drills but has not been a permanent member of the group.
In their official meeting, the two leaders talked about defence, trade and the development of artificial intelligence, according to a readout from the Prime Minister’s Office in Ottawa.
It did not say whether the two leaders discussed U.S. President Donald Trump. Burnham is expected to meet Trump for the first time next week in New York.
Carney’s PMO noted that the two countries are working on a “new permanent arrangement” to modernize British Army Training Unit Suffield.
CFB Suffield’s 2,700-kilometre square training area in Alberta is being used by the British military for exercises and the testing of drones and other equipment.
London plans to spend some $18.7 million on British Army Training Unit Suffield through to 2031.
Canadian officials said London and Ottawa are also in active talks on merging their proposed defence financing initiatives to amplify their effects.
A senior Canadian government official who briefed reporters on background said Ottawa is very confident they’ll reach an agreement on bringing the two proposals together to form a joint institution.
Carney has championed the creation of a global Defence, Security and Resilience Bank to supply allies with low-cost borrowing for defence.
He’s enlisted support for that venture from eight countries, including Latvia, Luxembourg, Greece, Belgium and Ukraine. But no G7 country other than Canada has joined.

The United Kingdom’s separate effort, called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism, is designed as a financing vehicle for joint purchases of military equipment and has won support from the Netherlands, Finland and Poland.
British media first reported this week that Burnham’s finance minister, John Healey, is considering joining the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank.
Canada and the U.K. issued a joint statement at the annual Nato summit in Ankara, Turkey, this summer on how the two financial institutions could work together.

The statement said the two countries want to ensure their “respective initiatives develop in a coherent and mutually supportive way” and will “seek opportunities to co-operate closely and ensure complementarity.”
Money put into the defence bank counts toward the Nato target of having alliance members spend the equivalent of five per cent of their GDP on defence by 2035.
The head of Canada’s Business Development Bank, Isabelle Hudon, is working as the lead negotiator for the defence bank.
The U.K. is allocating $749 million toward the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and aims to stand it up in 2027.

stories.title: Free retro game night brings Fanshawe community together
stories.summary: Fanshawe College students are getting a chance to connect through a shared hobby today as the college hosts a ...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
Fanshawe College students are getting a chance to connect through a shared hobby today as the college hosts a Retro Game Night.

The event, hosted by Fuel Esports, happens from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. in the Forwell Hall. Students can play classic video games while socializing with the Fanshawe community.

Not only is this event great for meeting new people, but admission is also free.

Photo by: Torey Joseph Legarrie

Fuel Esports is located at Fanshawe College in room J2018. It’s operated by the Fanshawe Student Union, and provides students with a quiet space with free access to gaming computers and consoles.

For students adapting to the new school year, events like these provide an opportunity to relax from the stress of school, with people who share similar interests.

This event could make it easier to socialize.” And it does make it easier to socialize with an event like this.” said Takumi Nicholls who is a student at Fanshawe College.

Photo by: Torey Joseph Legarrie, Takumi Nicholls, electrical engineering technology, year 1

Retro games offer something different from newer games because they’re often simpler and more familiar. Adam Boyce, Fuel esports media lead believes that classic games are more appealing since they’re more familiar. “People like playing games that they played in their childhood. So being able to bring that back and let people have fun with it, we’ve got it.”

Photo by: Torey Joseph Legarrie, Adam Boyce, esports media lead

Some games included at the event are Wii with B-Sports, Mario Kart, Game Cubes, Super Smash Bros, as well as a rock band kit on stage.

Dozens of people were coming in as the event began, and students starting competing against their friends. The event even included retro tv’s to make it feel even more old-school.

This event is an easy way to make new friends. For anybody who is wanting a stress-free evening, pick up a controller and enjoy the event.

Here is the interview with Takumi Nicholls, and Adam Boyce:

stories.title: Former co-worker testifies to corporal discipline in Friesen jury trial
stories.summary: A former administrator of the Saskatoon Christian school at the centre of a jury trial took the stand confirming previous victim claims of a policy of physical punishment.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
A former administrator of the Saskatoon Christian school at the centre of a jury trial took the stand confirming previous victim claims of a policy of physical punishment.

Louis Brunelle, a former administrative assistant at Christian Centre Academy, was the first witness brought forward by defense counsel.

Brunelle testified to being responsible for disciplining students up to Grade 4.

Brunelle identified himself in a piece of evidence, a 1997 edition of Maclean’s magazine article, where he is photographed with a paddle victims have testified was likely used on them.

The article quotes Brunelle saying, “the child is given three swats on the bum with a witness present.”

Brunelle also testified to being named as a defendant in a lawsuit for systemic abuse involving the school and associated church, Mile Two.

Defense counsel finished bringing forward witnesses Monday. The trial will continue with closing arguments Thursday.

The 2022 lawsuit is continuing this year following a Saskatchewan Court of Appeal decision overturning an abuse of process ruling from the Court of King’s Bench Court in Saskatoon.

A King’s Bench judge halted the case last year after the plaintiffs failed to promptly disclose settlement agreements with three former defendants.

While the court of appeal agreed they should have been disclosed sooner, it ruled there was no abuse of process.

The plaintiffs intend to move forward with the case now the stay has been lifted.

stories.title: Fredericton’s tap water named best in North America in taste test
stories.summary: The New Brunswick capital was voted the best of 32 regional winners by a team of "professionally trained flavour profilers," according to the city.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
A panel of expert judges has determined that Fredericton tops municipalities across North America for the “taste, aroma, and consistency” — not of their wine, or fine cuisine — but drinking water.

“We’ve always thought we had a good product. This just confirms that what we thought was right,” said Trent Brewer, manager of H2O Fredericton, the city’s water and sewer division.

“It’s years and years of us and city council that are making the right decisions on investing into our water and sewer systems.”

Fredericton was bestowed the honour by the American Water Works Association at its annual conference in June. The non-profit association aims to improve water quality and supply.

The New Brunswick capital was voted the best of 32 regional winners by a team of “professionally trained flavour profilers,” according to the city.

About 20-million litres of water move through the city’s system every day — drawn from 11 production wells tapping an aquifer beneath downtown.

And Brewer says he believes the city has an advantage when it comes to producing excellent tasting water.

“It’s the quality of water we’re getting. We’re a groundwater source, so all of our water comes from wells, which are naturally filtered through the downtown aquifer from the St. John River down to our wells,” said Brewer.

Kerry MacQuarrie, a civil engineering professor at UNB Fredericton and researcher with the Canadian Rivers Institute, says that groundwater gives the city an edge over the other competitors.

“It’s mainly the mineral content. What’s dissolved in the water would give it its taste. So in the case of the Fredericton water, which is sourced from groundwater, it would be mainly mineral content, dissolved mineral content that would give the taste,” MacQuarrie said.

The water in Fredericton is treated at one of two treatment plants. While the water is drinkable coming out of the ground, chlorine is added to remove manganese and disinfect the water. Meanwhile, lime is used to adjust the pH and help remove other solids.

“Once it goes through the treatment, it goes into reaction vessels where it sort of mixes around. It goes through filters. That’s where all the solids are sort of pulled out,” said Bennett Moss, a water treatment plant operator.

“After that, it leaves the plant and heads on out into our distribution system.”

From there, it travels through 440 km of water main to about 18,500 customers.

And taste is only one test.

The city says water sampled every week at about 50 locations is sent to an independent lab to make sure it meets Canadian drinking water guidelines.

MacQuarrie, who calls the award “a real feather in the cap of the City of Fredericton,” says the award shows the municipality is doing something right.

“It does, I think, show that the water treatment is effective, the water source is reliable and safe,” MacQuarrie said.

“So I do think that taste, although it’s a subjective thing — it’s not sort of a scientific measure of the water quality — I think taste does reflect the water quality and safety.”

The city says it spends roughly $30 million a year on operating and capital work and is planning two more production wells as Fredericton grows.

stories.title: Trump signs order to remove Canadian goods from federal procurement
stories.summary: Trump signed an order directing federal agencies overseeing government procurement in the U.S. to remove all products of Canadian origin.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Washington — U.S. President Donald Trump signed an memorandum Wednesday directing federal agencies overseeing government procurement in the United States to remove all products of Canadian origin.

The move is the latest escalation of the trade war by the Trump administration after negotiations between Canada and the United States broke down last month.

The presidential order points to Ottawa’s “Buy Canadian” policy, which was launched, along with similar actions by some provinces, after the president targeted Canada with tariffs and threats of annexation.

It said Canada has “unreasonably imposed new barriers to United States companies seeking to access the Canadian government procurement market.”

“My Administration will always act to combat such unreasonable or discriminatory practices,” the order said.

stories.title: Ottawa urged to fund intensive housing for homeless Canadians with cognitive impairments
stories.summary: The proposed model would be secure or semi-secure units with 24-7 staff, including nurses and health care aides, similar to a dementia unit
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Ottawa should invest in intensive housing for Canadians with severe cognitive impairment, a small but uniquely visible and costly subgroup in the homeless population that no current housing model is designed to serve, a leading organization on homelessness argues.

The Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness, a national charity, has submitted a proposal on the issue to the federal government ahead of its coming budget.

Advocates, housing agencies and front-line clinicians say intensive housing could be the missing piece in Canada’s housing system for this medically complex and underserved segment of society.

Opinion: Older Canadians are the largest, fastest-growing homeless population. It’s a collective shame upon our country

In a policy proposal sent to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government and provided to The Globe and Mail, the Caeh is lobbying Ottawa for a $2-billion investment to build 6,250 intensive units across the country catered to people who are chronically homeless with severe, permanent cognitive impairment.

The proposed model for intensive housing would be secure or semi-secure units with 24-7 staff, including nurses and health care aides, similar to a dementia unit.

Monty Ghosh, an inner-city physician in Alberta, said he often treats this highly vulnerable group of unhoused people who are living with severe, permanent cognitive impairment as a result of traumatic brain injuries, fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, trauma and substance use.

He said the cognitive impairment is so severe that they are unable to manage their own housing or safety but there is nowhere for them to go. They are stuck in a revolving door between hospitals, shelters and the criminal-justice system.

Dr. Ghosh, who worked with the Caeh on its proposal, estimates that between 20 and 30 per cent of the homeless population fits into this category.

Tim Richter, president of the organization, said intervening to house this medically complex population will not only support people in dire need of help but would reduce public-safety incidents – a lightning-rod issue for governments of all stripes.

“It’s unsettling if you see someone in the throes of this kind of disability on the train into work or unconscious on the side of the road,” said Mr. Richter. “We just need to make sure that there is a humane, effective and appropriate housing solution for them – and that’s not a jail.”

He said intensive housing for this population is an alternative to involuntary addictions treatment, which is gaining political traction across Canada and set to soon come into practice in Saskatchewan and Alberta. Just last month, Ontario’s Big City Mayors group asked the province to review existing mental health laws with the goal of expanding involuntary treatment.

Alexandra Flynn: Homelessness must be solved by every level of government

But Mr. Richter stressed that this population with irreversible cognitive impairment will not recover after involuntary intervention and would benefit from lifelong housing rather than a short stint in an involuntary treatment centre. He said these individuals should not be in a prison-like setting.

Intensive housing sites would also have on-site occupational therapy, physiotherapy and cognitive rehabilitation, in addition to addiction and mental-health supports when needed, according to the proposal. The model is mirrored after long-term care “not on psychiatric institutionalization” and its core goals are rehabilitation, stability and dignity.

It would not be appropriate for all Canadians experiencing homelessness, but for those who have not been able to stabilize in shelters or through other forms of housing and have no capacity for individual decision-making, it states.

Dr. Ghosh said he often has to send these patients back onto the streets.

“I discharge patients with dementia, Alzheimer’s, traumatic brain injury from motor-vehicle accidents to these long-term care facilities for lifetime support and yet I can’t discharge these individuals to those facilities,” said Dr. Ghosh.

He explained that it is also difficult to find these patients’ families, which leads to a lengthy public guardianship process.

The Carney Liberals have made housing a key commitment, recently announcing a $2.7 billion investment for 18 projects across Toronto. The Liberals have also created a federal Crown corporation, Build Canada Homes, to accelerate the construction of affordable housing across Canada.

Arianna Durgerian, press secretary to Canada’s Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Gregor Robertson, declined to comment on the intensive housing proposal.

She said the federal government is focused on building up the supply of affordable and supportive housing and is working with other levels of government to do so.

Rising cost of low-end rental units driving increase in homelessness, report shows

Mr. Richter said building intensive housing would be expensive but is cheaper than ignoring the problem.

The proposal notes that people in this subgroup visit EDs and are admitted to hospital frequently, costing between $1,000 and $3,000 per emergency department visit and between $1,500 and $2,500 daily for a hospital admission.

“The downstream savings from stabilizing this population in appropriate residential care are substantial and accrue directly to provincial health, justice and social-service budgets,” the document states, before outlining an ethical obligation.

“Leaving people with the functional cognitive capacity of a young child to navigate street homelessness unprotected is an abdication of care.”

Sandra Clarkson, chief executive of the Calgary Drop-In Centre, one of the largest emergency shelters in North America, said the shelter system was never designed to serve this complex population but is the only place for these individuals to go.

She said intensive housing is badly needed and could help hundreds of people currently seeking shelter at the Drop-In.

“This is not a homelessness issue alone. It’s a health care, cognitive disability issue that is showing up in homelessness.”

stories.title: Sanofi inaugurates Toronto facility that will produce seasonal flu vaccines for Canadians
stories.summary: French pharmaceutical maker’s site is also designed to provide new capacity for vaccine production in event of another pandemic
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
French pharmaceutical maker Sanofi SA says its Toronto facility will soon be ready to start producing seasonal flu vaccines for Canadian patients, a project that started during the height of the pandemic and is now opening during another surge in interest in domestic drug manufacturing.

The shots will be produced at the Charles Best Building, which was officially inaugurated Wednesday at a news conference with company representatives and federal, provincial and municipal politicians, including federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

The facility, which broke ground in 2021, was built thanks to a $925-million investment, which included $415-million from the federal government and $55-million from the province.

Sanofi plans to begin manufacturing the Fluzone High-Dose influenza vaccine for seniors in Canada starting early in 2027, with doses ready to begin shipping around next August, in advance of the 2027-28 flu season.

The facility is also designed to provide new capacity for vaccine production in the event of another pandemic.

Ms. Joly said the COVID-19 pandemic exposed key vulnerabilities in the domestic supply chain, including production of vaccines and medical supplies.

More recently, the pharmaceutical sector in Canada and other countries has come under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump. The Trump administration has put pressure on drug companies to move their manufacturing to the United States and raise prices in other jurisdictions.

Ms. Joly said the recent “weaponization of trade” has shown the continued importance of investing in local production, such as the Sanofi plant.

“We know very much that life sciences is a sector that is being targeted in the context of trade negotiations, obviously with many jurisdictions from the EU and us, and we want to make sure that we support our companies and we attract more investments,” she said.

Quebec will not administer free flu shots this fall

André Picard: All Canadians should be eligible for a free shingles vaccine

Kate Winchester, Sanofi’s vice-president, head of manufacturing and supply Canada, said the Toronto site’s main focus is on producing vaccines for the domestic market, but it will have capacity to supply other global markets if needed.

She said the entire end-to-end production of the vaccine will happen in the Sanofi campus, from producing the influenza antigens to filling the syringes.

Ms. Winchester said that while interest in some vaccines can ebb and flow, demand for influenza vaccines is relatively consistent because of how widely the virus can spread and how much pressure it can put on the public health care system.

“There’s add-on beneficial effects associated with seniors taking this flu vaccine,” she said. “It helps to prevent 15,000 hospitalizations every year.”

Ms. Joly said the recent “weaponization of trade” has shown the continued importance of investing in local production, such as the Sanofi plant.

“We know very much that life sciences is a sector that is being targeted in the context of trade negotiations, obviously with many jurisdictions from the EU and us, and we want to make sure that we support our companies and we attract more investments,” she said.

André Picard: All Canadians should be eligible for a free shingles vaccine

Kate Winchester, Sanofi’s vice-president, head of manufacturing and supply Canada, said the Toronto site’s main focus is on producing vaccines for the domestic market, but it will have capacity to supply other global markets if needed.
She said the entire end-to-end production of the vaccine will happen in the Sanofi campus, from producing the influenza antigens to filling the syringes.

Ms. Winchester said that while interest in some vaccines can ebb and flow, demand for influenza vaccines is relatively consistent because of how widely the virus can spread and how much pressure it can put on the public health care system.
“There’s add-on beneficial effects associated with seniors taking this flu vaccine,” she said. “It helps to prevent 15,000 hospitalizations every year.”

The shots will be produced at the Charles Best Building, which was officially inaugurated Wednesday at a news conference with company representatives and federal, provincial and municipal politicians, including federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Ontario Premier Doug Ford.
The facility, which broke ground in 2021, was built thanks to a $925-million investment, which included $415-million from the federal government and $55-million from the province.

Sanofi plans to begin manufacturing the Fluzone High-Dose influenza vaccine for seniors in Canada starting early in 2027, with doses ready to begin shipping around next August, in advance of the 2027-28 flu season.
The facility is also designed to provide new capacity for vaccine production in the event of another pandemic.

stories.title: She risked $55K to start a Christian women's event in London. Her faith paid off
stories.summary: Women's Christian conference She Will Rise returns to London on Sept. 19, with organizers expecting 1,000 attendees.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
Women's Christian conference She Will Rise returns to London on Saturday, with organizers expecting 1,000 attendees.

Last updated 17 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/she-risked-55k-to-start-a-christian-womens-event-in-London-her-faith-paid-off#comments-area)

Madison Keener was photographed in London on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

Madison Keener had faith.

She also had $55,000 on her personal credit cards to bankroll her dream event, a women’s Christian conference in London, and a list of ticket-buyers that wasn’t even half-way to the 700 needed to break even.

“I was quite literally having panic attacks three weeks before, thinking we need to cancel the keynote speaker, we need to back out, we can’t do this,” Keener, 32, recalled of organizing the first She Will Rise event, in 2023.

Keener, a Strathroy resident who says her family lives paycheque-to-paycheque, wanted the event to be “big.” But it was drawing relatively little interest. Still, she recalls, she pushed ahead.

“I would go to church and it’s like the pastor was talking straight to me. It would be some sort of message that was, ‘You have to keep going,’” Keener said.

In the final three weeks leading up to the debut conference, Keener thought her phone was glitching as ticket sales went from 300 to 709 “in the blink of an eye” – more than enough to break even.

“If I was able to do it all on my own, then God wouldn’t get the glory,” she said. “He had to make it look impossible for me and my team, so that when people saw how incredible the event was and how we ended up having 700 women, they didn’t say that it wasn’t hard. They say the only possible way that could have happened is because of God’s grace.”

The fourth She Will Rise event is set to be held on Saturday, with 1,000 women expected to attend. It has moved to downtown’s Centennial Hall from Forest City Community Church to accommodate its growth.

Keener said she was inspired by similar large-scale conferences she attended in the United States and South Africa, where thousands of women gathered. Her event, she says, gives women a place to connect in-person, with dedicated time for worship, local and international speakers and vendors.

She is hoping 1,000 women will attend on Saturday, with 35 vendors and several guest speakers scheduled throughout the day. Tickets cost $120. Keener notes the event is not only open to Christian women.

“I want women to know that there are other women that care about them, and that they have a community that will welcome them. I don’t want women to feel that if they don’t believe in Jesus or they were born into a different religion, that they’re not welcome in this space,” Keener said.

“I just want women to leave the event feeling better than when they walked in.”

stories.title: Diver hospitalized after great white shark attack in Quebec, Coast Guard say
stories.summary: Canadian Shark Attack Registry says this type of incident in Canadian waters is exceptionally rare
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
The Canadian Coast Guard says a diver was taken to hospital after being bitten by a shark off Percé, Que., ON the eastern tip of the Gaspé Peninsula.

The Coast Guard says it was alerted to the incident at about 10:27 a.m. and paramedics met the vessel when it arrived in Percé.

Local diving centre Plongée Percé says the person received first aid before being transported to hospital for further evaluation.

The company says all of its diving activities have been suspended for the rest of the season as a precaution.

The Canadian Shark Attack Registry says this type of incident in Canadian waters is exceptionally rare.

The registry is maintained by the independent non-profit St. Lawrence Shark Observatory and contains 30 reported incidents dating back more than three centuries, only 15 of which are considered confirmed.

The observatory says great white shark sightings and detections have become increasingly common in Atlantic Canada in recent years.

stories.title: Apartment construction continues to fuel London’s building trend
stories.summary: New statistics from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (Cmhc) show the region is bucking a national downward trend when it comes to housing starts.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
the London area’s building trend. New statistics from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (Cmhc) show the region is bucking a national downward trend when it comes to housing starts.

In August, there were 213 new home starts in the London Census Metro Area, which includes parts of Middlesex and St. Thomas-Elgin. Year to date new home starts reached 2,862, exceeding the region’s January to August ten year benchmark of 2,133.

“You’ve had a very strong year. You’re well above what we typically build in London,” said Anthony Passarelli, Cmhc Lead Economist (Southern Ontario). “It’s heavily skewed toward the rental sector, particularly, there’s rental apartments that has really dominated construction activity.

Not so much in that townhome, single-detached segment of the market yet. But it’s still been a very strong year,” he said. The city of London, itself, recorded 2,490 new home starts from January to August- well above its ten year benchmark of 1,589 home starts for that period.

London Home Builders Association CEO Jared Zaifman says homebuyers continue to take advantage of this year’s HST cut on new homes, but we won’t necessarily see shovels in the ground right away. “Because of the HST rebate, enhanced rebate, so that’s very positive to see.

But at the same time, there’s been a lot of deals signed for new purchases, but a lot of those won’t get constructed until Spring, 2027,” Zaifman said. Currently, London has 1,899 permit-approved housing units awaiting construction.

Passarelli says given that large number, near term housing starts are expected to remain strong, with continued activity in apartment construction. “There’s still a fair amount of permitted rental apartments that are probably going to break ground soon.

So that trend will continue going forward in the short term,” he said.

stories.title: Key issues in London school board trustee elections overlooked, but important, says observer
stories.summary: Amid the campaign signs for mayor and city council dotted across the city of London stand the school board tru...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
Amid the campaign signs for mayor and city council dotted across the city of London stand the school board trustees, competing at the same time and in the same election for trustee positions in the London District Catholic and Thames Valley District school boards. Despite the visibility of their own signs, as well as the past visibility of London’s school board trustees in the public eye, the issues facing the trustees can seem overlooked.

“They get occluded by the ward races,” says Mike Donachie, the editor-in-chief of the London Ontario Online News ( The Loon ). “I would really like to see the trustee races or some… form of that become a better conversation in this community.”

The trustee races within the city come at a turning point within Ontario school boards. The election represents the first one held since the

Medway High School. The issues surrounding the trustee election for London school boards come at a transition point for the Thames Valley District School Board. Source: XFM News

Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) was placed under supervision by the provincial government. It is also the first election to be held since Bill 101 was passed, restricting the power of trustees in Ontario school boards.

Donachie believes these have contributed to the trustee races being overlooked, and that they speak to flaws within the trustee system.

“That then undermines people’s sense of agency around using their vote there,” he says.

His beliefs are not unanimously shared, however. Joanne Andrews, a candiate in Wards 11, 12, and 13 in the London District Catholic School Board (LDCSB) believes that while “there can always be more attention placed upon [the elections],” the notion of it being overlooked is one she disagrees with.

“It’s up to us as candidates to bring that attention,” she says.

Andrews says that the voting public within her ward has been paying attention as well. She says that during her campaign, she has heard concerns about a wide range of issues, including student success, classroom size, and school and transportation safety.

Likewise, in a statement provided to XFM News by Andrews’ fellow LDCSB Wards 11, 12, and 13 candidate Dr. Swapna Simon, issues cited as being important to voters also included accessibility to opportunities for students, namely the International Baccalaureate program.

“For me, this raises a simple but important question: If a student qualifies for a specialized program but cannot realistically get to it, is that opportunity truly accessible?” writes Dr. Simon.

There are concerns with with the restriction of trustee powers as well. “It’s definitely a limiting factor,” says Andrews, but adding that she doesn’t consider it insurmountable.

“There’s ways we can work together… use teamwork, use collaboration, use consensus-building to get to the point we need to get to.”

Overall, both Andrews and Dr. Simon agree that the experience of the students within the school boards is the most important issue in the trustee elections.

“It’s about making sure the students… maximize their potential, reach their potential, even go beyond if possible,” Andrews says. “When you boil it all down, that’s what it comes down to.”

Source: XFM News

content_blocks.text: Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) was placed under supervision by the provincial government. It is also the first election to be held since Bill 101 was passed, restricting the power of trustees in Ontario school boards.
Donachie believes these have contributed to the trustee races being overlooked, and that they speak to flaws within the trustee system.
“That then undermines people’s sense of agency around using their vote there,” he says.

His beliefs are not unanimously shared, however. Joanne Andrews, a candiate in Wards 11, 12, and 13 in the London District Catholic School Board (LDCSB) believes that while “there can always be more attention placed upon [the elections],” the notion of it being overlooked is one she disagrees with.
“It’s up to us as candidates to bring that attention,” she says.

Andrews says that the voting public within her ward has been paying attention as well. She says that during her campaign, she has heard concerns about a wide range of issues, including student success, classroom size, and school and transportation safety.

Likewise, in a statement provided to XFM News by Andrews’ fellow LDCSB Wards 11, 12, and 13 candidate Dr. Swapna Simon, issues cited as being important to voters also included accessibility to opportunities for students, namely the International Baccalaureate program.
“For me, this raises a simple but important question: If a student qualifies for a specialized program but cannot realistically get to it, is that opportunity truly accessible?” writes Dr. Simon.
There are concerns with with the restriction of trustee powers as well. “It’s definitely a limiting factor,” says Andrews, but adding that she doesn’t consider it insurmountable.
“There’s ways we can work together… use teamwork, use collaboration, use consensus-building to get to the point we need to get to.”
Overall, both Andrews and Dr. Simon agree that the experience of the students within the school boards is the most important issue in the trustee elections.
“It’s about making sure the students… maximize their potential, reach their potential, even go beyond if possible,” Andrews says. “When you boil it all down, that’s what it comes down to.”

stories.title: How Canada-EU ‘associate member’ proposal raises questions with few answers
stories.summary: Usula von der Leyen’s suggestion that Canada could become an associate member of the European Union is raising concerns over costs, sovereignty.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The challenge with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s suggestion that Canada could become a European Union “associate member” is that nobody seems precisely sure what that means.

That confusion is already creating fertile ground for critics of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push to diversify Canada’s trade and political partnerships away from the U.S. under President Donald Trump.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has already asserted — without evidence, since there’s no clear information from Carney or von der Leyen so far about the proposal — that such a partnership could include Canadians contributing tax dollars to the EU budget, accepting regulations drafted by bureaucrats in Brussels, or ceding control over immigration levels.

Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador to the EU and a former cabinet minister, did not appear fully comfortable with the term “associate member” Wednesday — telling reporters the important thing isn’t the name for the relationship, but the results deeper cooperation could bring.

“We are not looking to be a member of the European Union, because that is a sovereignty issue and people give up certain portions of their sovereignty (to be part of the bloc),” Wilkinson told reporters.

“At the end of the day, what we are looking to do is get as close as we possibly can in a manner that’s going to actually strengthen all of our respective countries without giving up significant chunks of sovereignty.”

In a speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, Wednesday, von der Leyen told Carney that she wants to work with him to “open the door” to Canada being the political and trading bloc’s first “associate member.”

More concretely, von der Leyen said she wants to move from the Canada-European Trade Agreement (Ceta) to what she calls an “Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space.”

“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project. We will work on energy, critical minerals and batteries. On AI, quantum (computing), cyber and economic security,” von der Leyen’s prepared remarks read.

“In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

Those are all things Canada and Europe have been working on since at least June 2025, when Carney and von der Leyen began a process to “deepen ties.” They will all likely factor in to Carney’s address to European leaders on Thursday, and be topics for discussion when Canada-EU talks continue in Montreal next month.

There is currently no legal meaning for “associate membership” in the European Union, although the designation has been floated in the past — most recently, for Ukraine, which has for years been working toward full EU membership before Russia’s invasion.

In Ukraine’s case, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested the country be granted temporary associate status as it worked toward full ascension into the bloc. It would’ve given Ukraine a presence at EU summits and meetings, but no voting rights.

It would not have given the country access to the $27 trillion European Single Market, or to EU funds. Merz’s idea would grant Ukraine a measure of security guarantees that Canada already enjoys through membership in the North American Treaty Organization (Nato).

Officials with the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) told reporters traveling with Carney that Canada was not seeking formal membership of any kind with the EU.

“We welcome President von der Leyen’s proposal that Canada and the European Union move beyond the Ceta to an Alliance for the Future,” PMO said in a statement.

“This is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on our shared values.”

Polling released by Abacus Data this week suggested an overwhelming majority — 80 per cent — of Canadians support stronger economic, defence and political ties between Ottawa and Europe.

That support cuts across Canada’s regions and partisan differences. Opposition was strongest among Conservative voters, but 69 per cent of that cohort still backed deepening ties with Europe.

Of course, that support could change if Canada were asked to pay into Europe’s collective budget, or change domestic policies around issues like immigration to more closely align with the continent.

In a press conference Tuesday, Poilievre raised similar questions.

“What more is Mr. Carney proposing? Because what Conservatives do not support is forcing waitresses who are struggling to pay their rent or welders who are worried about losing their homes to pay higher taxes to a government in Europe, or to follow law made by European bureaucrats that don’t even know where the Lower Mainland of B.C. is,” Poilievre said.

“Or to have European immigration policies that will further overwhelm our housing, health care and job market. We want Canada to have free trade with Europe, cooperation with Europe, but we never surrender our independence and sovereignty over our laws, our tax money, and our immigration policies.”

stories.title: Diver hospitalized after apparent white shark encounter in Quebec
stories.summary: Montreal — The Canadian Coast Guard says a diver was taken to hospital after being bitten by a shark off Percé, Que., ON the eastern tip of the Gaspé Peninsula.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Montreal — The Canadian Coast Guard says a diver was taken to hospital after being bitten by a shark off Percé, Que., ON the eastern tip of the Gaspé Peninsula.

The Coast Guard says it was alerted to the incident at about 10:27 a.m. and paramedics met the vessel when it arrived in Percé.

Local diving centre Plongée Percé says the person received first aid before being transported to hospital for further evaluation.

The company says all of its diving activities have been suspended for the rest of the season as a precaution.

The Canadian Shark Attack Registry says this type of incident in Canadian waters is exceptionally rare.

The registry is maintained by the independent non-profit St. Lawrence Shark Observatory and contains 30 reported incidents dating back more than three centuries, only 15 of which are considered confirmed.

The observatory says white shark sightings and detections have become increasingly common in Atlantic Canada in recent years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

Charlotte Glorieux, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Students hesitant to comment on Ed Sheeran-Macklemore controversy
stories.summary: As more artists announced they were leaving Ed Sheeran's U.S. Loop Tour to support musicians using their platf...
stories.author: Kelly Nicol
stories.content:
A photo posted by Macklemore on Instagram

As more artists announced they were leaving Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour to support musicians using their platforms to speak out on issues, many people flooded online forums with strong opinions on the topic. But in the halls of Fanshawe College, students were often hesitant to speak their minds.

The controversy erupted Sunday, when rapper Macklemore announced he was dropped from Sheeran’s tour after voicing support for “Free Palestine” on a New Jersey stage.

Since then, all Sheeran’s other supporting acts have dropped out of the tour, reports said Tuesday .

“He shouldn’t have been kicked out just for saying that,” said London Barrett, one of a few students willing to state their opinion on the topic to an XFM News reporter.

While some other students agreed artists should be allowed to use their platforms to speak on political issues, many did not want to give their full names.

Macklemore, an outspoken advocate for Palestinian rights, has repeatedly used his platform to call for a U.S. arms embargo against Israel, including creating two singles about the student protests in the spring of 2024.

“One of the reasons I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up here on stages and stadiums across America, and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” Macklemore said on the New Jersey stage Sept. 4 .

While he has insisted his comments were not antisemitic, some Israeli advocacy groups disagreed and called for his removal.

In a statement Sunday, Macklemore announced Sheeran and his team removed him from the Loop tour.

“I am not a victim,” Macklemore wrote. “Ed Sheeran is not a victim.”

Ed Sheeran responded to the controversy on Tuesday. “After Macklemore’s performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting… I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge… I was also involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all,” he said.

stories.title: B.C. skyrunner’s family believe she fell to her death on Italy’s Matterhorn
stories.summary: Kalie McCrystal, 38, was last seen on Sept. 1 while training to break the record for the fastest ascent and descent of the nearly 4,500-metre mountain.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
The family of a B.C. woman who disappeared while running on the Matterhorn in Italy has issued a statement saying they believe she fell to her death.

Kalie McCrystal, 38, was last seen on Sept. 1, 2026, while training to break the record for the fastest ascent and descent of the nearly 4,500-metre mountain.

Her disappearance prompted an extensive search by the Guardia di Finanza rescue team, but they could not locate her.

McCrystal, from Squamish, was a skilled climber, according to her family and had previous experience climbing the Matterhorn.

“Kalie was an incredibly special person,” her mom and sister wrote in the statement issued on Sept. 15.

“She moved through life with equal parts determination and fun. Her absence will undoubtedly leave a huge hole in the communities she was so invested in, across Skyrunning, Squamish and beyond.”

Mountain trail runner Hillary Gerardi told The Canadian Press that she and another friend were set to help McCrystal attempt to break a running record in early September, but when they realized no one had heard from her, they alerted authorities.

Gerardi told Outside Online that McCrystal was scouting the mountain ahead of an attempt to become the fastest woman to run it.

She told the magazine that she planned to support McCrystal’s attempt to break the fastest known time for ascending the peak.

McCrystal’s mom and sister said that their family will never be the same.

“While we desperately wish we could have found her, we find peace in knowing that she was doing what made her feel most alive until her very last moments, and that she remains among the mountains where she felt most at home.”

McCrystal was one of Canada’s top skyrunners, according to skyrunnerworldseries.com .

Skyrunning is described as reaching the highest mountain peak in the shortest amount of time from a town or village.

It is defined by the International Skyrunning Federation that was formed to govern the sport in 2008, as “running in the mountains above 2,000m altitude where the climbing difficulty does not exceed II° grade and the incline is over 30%,” according to skyrunning.com .

stories.title: Diver hospitalized after great white shark attack off Quebec’s Gaspé coast
stories.summary: The Canadian Coast Guard confirmed the incident to Global News.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
A diver was sent to hospital after being bitten by a great white shark off the Gaspé coast on Wednesday morning, prompting a local diving operator to suspend all activities for the remainder of the season.

In a statement, scuba diving centre Plongée Percé said the incident occurred during a diving activity.

The company did not provide details about the diver’s injuries or the circumstances surrounding the encounter, citing privacy concerns.

“Out of respect for the privacy of the person concerned, no additional details will be communicated on this matter,” the statement said.

Plongée Percé said emergency response measures were activated immediately after the incident. The diver received first aid at the scene before being taken to hospital for further assessment.

Plongée Percé said it has received confirmation that the person’s life is not in danger.

The Canadian Coast Guard confirmed the incident to Global News.

“This morning, at approximately 10:27 EDT on September 16, 2026, the Maritime Joint Rescue Coordination Centre (Québec) was alerted that a diver from the Yoda—a private vessel which is also part of the Canadian Coast Guard Auxiliary—had been bitten by a shark,” media relations officer Craig Macartney said.

“Ambulance services were dispatched to tend the victim when the vessel arrived in Percé, Québec.”

As a precaution, Plongée Percé announced all diving activities have been suspended for the rest of the season.

The shark bite occurred in waters near Percé, a popular tourist destination on Quebec’s Gaspé Peninsula known for its marine wildlife and diving opportunities.

The encounter comes as more great white shark sightings have been reported in the Gulf of St. Lawrence in recent years, including in waters off Quebec’s Gaspé Peninsula, the Magdalen Islands and Atlantic Canada.

Four of these sharks are being tracked by Ocearch, a global non-profit research organization.

An 8-foot, 10-inch long, 456 lbs. juvenile female great white shark named Brookes was last pinged by researchers on Aug. 18 at 8:03 a.m., swimming in the river north of Sainte-Anne-des-Monts and west of Anticosti Island.

She was first tagged in September of 2025 off the Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia and has traveled the length of the Eastern Seaboard and into the Gulf of Mexico.

Goodall, a 13-foot-long adult female great white shark weighing in at 1,393 lbs., was last pinged on Aug. 11, at 6:01 p.m. in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. She was also tagged off Mahone Bay in September of 2025.

In August, the recent shark sightings off Nova Scotia beaches caused enough concern among beach-goers that some were calling for new monitoring measures as officials stressed existing safety precautions.

Several Nova Scotia beaches temporarily closed following shark sightings in recent years. Martinique Beach was shut down for several hours in July after a reported sighting, while Queensland Beach was closed for a period last summer for the same reason.

The sightings prompted discussion about whether Atlantic Canada should adopt other technology used in other jurisdictions to monitor for sharks.

While shark bites on humans are very rare, a 2020 study at the University of Technology in Auckland noted an increase in trends such as the ‘wildlife selfie,’ which it says requires close proximity to unpredictable animal species and has been gaining popularity in a way that May “contribute to wildlife harassment” or provoke animal behaviour that could “pose a hazard for people.”

There is no information that would suggest the diver in Quebec was shark diving or taking an underwater selfie.

In July, fishing influencer Henry Gibbs was creating content in Fiji and almost lost his leg after being bitten by a reef shark. Similarly, in February last year, a Canadian tourist in Turks and Caicos lost both her hands while trying to get a photograph of a bull shark.

In April of 2025, the remains of a snorkeler in Israel who was reportedly swimming with a selfie stick were found after being killed by sharks while trying to snap photos, the BBC reported.

The New Zealand study also found influencers and photographers were most likely to ignore safety instructions during shark-diving expeditions, though shark attacks are still extremely uncommon.

The University of Florida’s International Shark Attack File (Isaf) reports the odds of being bitten by a shark are incredibly low. Isaf recommends ocean swimmers stay close to shore, avoid swimming at dawn or dusk and avoid excessive splashing.

The Isaf investigated 105 alleged shark-human interactions worldwide in 2025, with five total cases coming from the Bahamas.

Isaf confirmed 65 unprovoked shark bites on humans and 29 provoked bites, which occur when a human initiates interaction with a shark in some way.

The 2025 worldwide total of 65 confirmed unprovoked cases is in line with the most recent five-year (2020 to 2024) average of 61 incidents annually, according to the Isaf.

–with files from Rachel Goodman

While shark bites on humans are very rare, a 2020 study at the University of Technology in Auckland noted an increase in trends such as the ‘wildlife selfie,’ which it says requires close proximity to unpredictable animal species and has been gaining popularity in a way that May “contribute to wildlife harassment” or provoke animal behaviour that could “pose a hazard for people.”
There is no information that would suggest the diver in Quebec was shark diving or taking an underwater selfie.

In July, fishing influencer Henry Gibbs was creating content in Fiji and almost lost his leg after being bitten by a reef shark. Similarly, in February last year, a Canadian tourist in Turks and Caicos lost both her hands while trying to get a photograph of a bull shark.
In April of 2025, the remains of a snorkeler in Israel who was reportedly swimming with a selfie stick were found after being killed by sharks while trying to snap photos, the BBC reported.
The New Zealand study also found influencers and photographers were most likely to ignore safety instructions during shark-diving expeditions, though shark attacks are still extremely uncommon.

The University of Florida’s International Shark Attack File (Isaf) reports the odds of being bitten by a shark are incredibly low. Isaf recommends ocean swimmers stay close to shore, avoid swimming at dawn or dusk and avoid excessive splashing.
The Isaf investigated 105 alleged shark-human interactions worldwide in 2025, with five total cases coming from the Bahamas.
Isaf confirmed 65 unprovoked shark bites on humans and 29 provoked bites, which occur when a human initiates interaction with a shark in some way.
The 2025 worldwide total of 65 confirmed unprovoked cases is in line with the most recent five-year (2020 to 2024) average of 61 incidents annually, according to the Isaf.

stories.title: Group blames speed camera removal for 560% increase in speeding on Toronto road
stories.summary: New figures recorded from light-up speed signs around the city show the number of people speeding on Parkside Drive has increased significantly since speed cameras were banned.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
A local group says that new data from the City of Toronto proves a moratorium on automated speed enforcement cameras could be leading to a massive spike in the number of drivers breaking the limit on a key road.

New figures recorded from light-up speed signs around the city show the number of people speeding on Parkside Drive has increased significantly since speed cameras were banned.

In July, a total of 3,675 vehicles went 60 km/h or above on Parkside Drive, where the limit is 40 km/h. That’s an increase of 560 per cent over July 2025, when the number was 556.

Safe Parkside, a local anti-speeding advocacy group, put the increase down to the province’s decision to ban automated speed cameras in legislation that was rushed through last fall.

“The consequences of Doug Ford’s ill-advised speed safety camera ban are being felt across Toronto,” the group wrote in a statement.

“Thirty-nine people were killed in traffic-related collisions in Toronto in 2025, the fewest in a decade. Toronto has already reached 29 traffic-related deaths in just the first seven months of 2026, putting Toronto on pace for 49 traffic-related deaths, an increase that reflects the sharp increase in speeding on our streets.”

Asked about the data, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Parkside Drive should be redesigned to make it harder to speed.

“Put roundabouts and speed bumps, that guarantees to slow people down,” he said at an unrelated event on Wednesday.

“Have you ever went through Forest Hill or Rosedale? You can’t get from one stop sign to the other without hitting a speed bump or a raised crosswalk. There’s no speeding in Forest Hill, I guarantee you.”

A spokesperson for Minister of Transportation Prabmeet Sarkaria said the City of Toronto hadn’t yet applied for the second round of funding offered by Queen’s Park to pay for design changes.

“Toronto has received over $10 million through our government’s $210 million Road Safety Initiative Fund to put tangible measures in place, like speed bumps and roundabouts, to slow down drivers down,” they said.

“They have not submitted their application to unlock further funding through the Rsif which would enable them to put additional traffic calming measures in place to protect children and families.”

They said the 70,000 tickets issued by the Parkside Drive camera when it was in operation were evidence it did not slow drivers down.

Before the Ford government banned automated speed cameras — calling them a cash grab — Parkside Drive was the centre of the debate over their effectiveness.

The camera on Parkside Drive was vandalized and chopped down repeatedly — a road which was also the scene of a number of dangerous crashes in recent years

Several years ago, a suspended driver hit more than 100 km/h on the road, rear-ending another vehicle and killing two people inside .

stories.title: Human remains found in Strathroy Conservation Area
stories.summary: Human remains have been found in the Strathroy Conservation Area, confirmed by police.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Human remains have been found in the Strathroy Conservation Area, confirmed by police.

On Sept. 11, the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service received a report of the human remains in the conservation area, to the east of Riverview Drive.

Officers confirmed there was a dead man. An investigation is ongoing, alongside the Ontario Coroner’s Service.

Strathroy police say there is no concern to public safety in connection to the death.

stories.title: Father walks to Queen’s Park, demanding Ohip cover daughter’s crucial out-of-province surgery
stories.summary: A determined London father has completed his walk to Queen’s Park, bringing his plea for provincial funding for his daughter’s life-saving surgery directly to the steps of the Ontario legislature.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
A determined London father has completed his walk to Queen’s Park, bringing his plea for provincial funding for his daughter’s life-saving surgery directly to the steps of the Ontario legislature.

Joe Gesualdi, embarking on his ‘Miles4aMiracle’ journey from his London home on Aug. 4, arrived at Queen’s Park on Wednesday, pushing an empty wheelchair to represent his daughter Sydney’s ongoing battle with a rare condition and the urgent need for Ohip coverage of her out-of-province treatment.

Sydney Gesualdi, then 24, suffered a catastrophic neck injury in July 2023 when her vehicle was struck from behind while stopped at a red light on Wharncliffe Road South in London.

The severe trauma resulted in Cranial Cervical Instability (CCI), a condition where her neck can no longer adequately support her head, a diagnosis compounded by tethered cord syndrome.

The Gesualdi family faced a devastating blow when Ohip denied funding for the surgery, despite recommendations from Canadian neurosurgeons. The procedure is available in New York but carries a steep price tag of approximately $493,600.

“Ohip now behaves like an American insurance company denying care, fighting patients instead of collaborating and opening pathways to treatment,” Joe Gesualdi stated, criticizing the provincial health system’s approach.

He added that the family had been rejected by 10 neurosurgeons in London and the GTA, leaving them with no viable treatment options within Canada.

Gesualdi’s walk, which traversed through a number of communities in southwestern Ontario, was designed to amplify public awareness and generate crucial funds. The ‘Miles4aMiracle’ campaign has so far raised $231,626 towards the total cost of Sydney’s surgery. Donations continue to be accepted via their website and GoFundMe page.

Upon his arrival, Gesualdi stood alongside his daughter Sydney and London-Fanshawe NDP MPP Teresa Armstrong at a news conference held at Queen’s Park.

Sydney Gesualdi spoke poignantly about the personal impact of the protracted wait.

“While these arguments take place on paper, I am the person who has to keep living inside the body everybody is arguing about,” she said.

“My life doesn’t stop while I wait for a decision. My condition doesn’t stop progressing because there is an appeal. And I can measure that time and pieces of my life, and pieces of myself that are gone.”

The family is actively pursuing an appeal of the Ohip decision, hoping their persistent advocacy and the community’s support will secure the necessary treatment for Sydney.

The ‘Miles4aMiracle’ campaign has so far raised $231,626 towards the total cost of Sydney’s surgery. Donations continue to be accepted via their website and GoFundMe page.
Upon his arrival, Gesualdi stood alongside his daughter Sydney and London-Fanshawe NDP MPP Teresa Armstrong at a news conference held at Queen’s Park.
Sydney Gesualdi spoke poignantly about the personal impact of the protracted wait.
“While these arguments take place on paper, I am the person who has to keep living inside the body everybody is arguing about,” she said.

“My life doesn’t stop while I wait for a decision. My condition doesn’t stop progressing because there is an appeal. And I can measure that time and pieces of my life, and pieces of myself that are gone.”
The family is actively pursuing an appeal of the Ohip decision, hoping their persistent advocacy and the community’s support will secure the necessary treatment for Sydney.

stories.title: London Knights still navigating roster fluctuations ahead of season opener Friday
stories.summary: The London Knights started with 80 players in training camp and still have about 30 players as their roster remains in flux.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The London Knights started with 80 players in training camp and still have about 30 players as their roster remains in flux. The club still has multiple players away at NHL camps and even two days ahead of their season opener are unsure about whether any of them will suit up Friday. “It’s definitely still a work in progress without knowing who’s coming back and when they’re coming back from NHL camps,” said Rob Simpson, Knights associate general manager.

Thomas of the Gohl. In exchange for Wassilyn, they acquired centre Carson Harmer from Saginaw in time for the game against Windsor Friday. “I’m excited, it’s going to be a fun night Friday because I have a lot of family and friends coming,” said Harmer who is from nearby Mitchell, Ont. The Knights wanted to add the veteran because he can help down the middle of the ice.

“We felt at centre we needed to get a little bit older at that position,” said Simpson. “I think he did a good need for us down through the middle to kind of slot everybody into positions where hopefully they can be a little bit more successful Friday night”. Harmer describes himself as a “200-foot player”.

“I like to contribute offensively but being good defensively too,” said Harmer who has 41 goals and 94 points over the past two years. “I played in the league for two years now, so adding more experience too will help”. When they take the ice Friday, this roster will be far from complete. Veteran Caleb Mitchell will be one familiar name to fans.

“I’m really excited to play in front of the fans again,” said Mitchell, a Knights defenceman. “There’s a lot of younger guys who are experiencing the first OHL games, so it’s going to be exciting for them as well. There’s never really a rebuild year here because it’s a great coaching and a great staff.
