stories.title: Redblacks, Stampeders are both in need of victory
stories.summary: McLeod Bethel-Thompson and the Ottawa Redblacks won't be the only ones in dire need of a win this week.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
McLeod Bethel-Thompson and the Ottawa Redblacks won’t be the only ones in dire need of a win this week.

Bethel-Thompson will make his first start of the season when Ottawa (0-12) visits the Calgary Stampeders (5-8) on Saturday night. The Redblacks have dropped 18 straight games dating back to 2025, a CFL modern-era record for consecutive defeats.

But Calgary also desperately needs a victory. The Stampeders are coming off consecutive losses to the Edmonton Elks and stand fifth in the West Division, four points behind the third-place Winnipeg Blue Bombers (7-6) and B.C. Lions (7-6).

Right now, Winnipeg, B.C. and Calgary have more wins than the Hamilton Tiger-Cats (4-9), who are third in the East Division. The Stamps can make the playoffs by finishing third in the West or by finishing fourth with more points than the East’s third-place team.

This game starts an important stretch for Calgary. After completing a home-and-home with Ottawa on Sept. 26, the Stampeders will finish their regular season visiting Saskatchewan (Oct. 2) and Winnipeg (Oct. 10) before hosting B.C. (Oct. 17).

Calgary lost its first meeting this season with Saskatchewan in overtime and is 1-1 versus both Winnipeg and B.C.

Bethel-Thompson replaced starter Jake Maier in the second quarter of Ottawa’s 26-23 road loss to Toronto last week. Bethel-Thompson provided a definite spark, completing 16-of-23 passes for 192 yards and a TD, but the Redblacks couldn’t take full advantage of two late opportunities that allowed the Argonauts to earn their second win in five days.

Ottawa had to settle for a Brett Lauther field goal following Kalil Pimpleton’s 88-yard punt return to the Argos’ 17-yard line that made it 23-23 at 10:09 of the fourth quarter. After a Toronto two-and-out, the Redblacks took over at the home team’s 53-yard line, but Ralph Holley’s second-down sack of Bethel-Thompson knocked the visitors out of field-goal range.

Lirim Hajrullahu’s game-ending 29-yard field goal capped a stellar 12-play, 74-yard March by Toronto (7-6), which took possession at its 14-yard line with 2:25 remaining.

The Redblacks were eliminated from playoff contention with last week’s loss. So now, their primary focus is earning a victory.

Calgary’s Labour Day finale versus Edmonton last week was one to forget. Starter Vernon Adams Jr. threw two first-half interceptions while the Elks recovered a blocked punt in the end zone for a touchdown en route to a 53-16 victory.

Calgary defensive lineman Clarence Hicks did register two sacks, giving him a CFL-high 11 this season. And veteran receiver Reggie Begelton returned for his first game since suffering a knee injury versus Toronto on June 18, 2025.

Begelton was targeted five times and finished the contest with two catches for 25 yards.

Montreal Alouettes vs Hamilton Tiger-Cats (Friday night)

At Hamilton, the Ticats come off the bye having suffered three straight losses. Canadian Tre Ford (head) resumed practising this week after being forced from the Labour Day clash with Toronto but will back up Harrison Frost, who’ll make his third start of the season. Frost completed 16-of-28 passes for 218 yards with two TDs and an interception in the 37-22 home loss to the Argos. Montreal (10-3) has dropped two of its last three games, including last week’s 48-29 road decision to B.C. Lions quarterback Nathan Rourke threw for 317 yards and a TD and ran for 77 yards and a touchdown on five carries. However, the Alouettes are 6-0 within the East Division.

Edmonton Elks vs Toronto Argonauts (Saturday afternoon)

At Toronto, Edmonton (10-3) has won four straight and clinched its first playoff berth since 2019. Cody Fajardo threw three TD passes in last week’s home victory over the Stampeders, two going to Joe Robustelli. Joshua Cephus had six catches for 119 yards and a touchdown while Tyrell Ford recorded his league-high sixth pick. The Argos (7-6) can clinch a home playoff game with a third straight win and a Hamilton loss Friday night. Chad Kelly leads the CFL in passing (4,404 yards), TDs (29) and interceptions (20). The Double Blue is 3-0 since returning to BMO Field but 3-4 versus the West and 0-1 against the Elks.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa won't say if people misused a now-defunct refugee residency sponsorship policy
stories.summary: The Immigration Department refuses to say whether any applicants actually misused a refugee permanent resident sponsorship policy which the government let expire last week, citing “potential integrity concerns.”
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Immigration Department refuses to say whether any applicants actually misused a refugee permanent resident sponsorship policy the government allowed to expire last week, citing “potential integrity concerns.”

The policy offered exemptions to allow certain refugees to sponsor a family member for permanent residency who was not listed on their initial application.

Without this exemption, applicants are permanently barred from sponsoring family members for permanent residency if they were not declared on their original application.

Advocates and academics who pushed for the policy said it was most commonly used to sponsor children — including some who had not been born when an application was first made — and LGBTQ2S+ partners in countries where those relationships are criminalized.

Nir Gepner, an Ontario immigration lawyer with the legal aid clinic Willowdale Community Legal Services, said the best way to uphold the “integrity” of the system is to respect the objectives of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, which include facilitating refugee family reunification.

“I don’t know what the integrity of the system means to the minister. I think it’s a general term that is extremely vague,” he said.

“What is the lifetime ban for? For not declaring somebody because they were just born? For not declaring someone because you would be in danger if you declared them? For not declaring somebody because you were in a rush to get to Canada to save yourself?”

He said the number of these binding federal immigration policies — which can be cancelled without consultation — spiked under the government of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.

Jenny Kwan, the Ndp’s immigration critic, said refugees trying to come to Canada should not be punished for circumstances beyond their control. She said the government has offered “no credible explanation” for the policy’s termination.

“They quietly shut it down, and now it is going to have, I have no doubt, significant implications for refugee families in that reunification,” Kwan said.

“So they’re not broadcasting it, it means that they’re not proud of it.”

The policy took effect in 2019 and expired on Sept. 10. Refugee advocacy groups were only informed on Sept. 9 that the government did not plan to renew the policy.

A 2023 memo prepared for then-immigration minister Marc Miller said most people who did not list a family member did so innocently and the exemption posed a “minimal” risk to program integrity. Miller recommended extending the policy for three years.

That same memo said an applicant might not declare a family member for any one of several reasons — including a child’s birth or a marriage taking place after an application was filed, custody challenges, faulty immigration advice or the stigma associated with a child being born out of wedlock.

Undeclared family members eligible for sponsorship under the former policy included spouses, common-law partners, dependent children and grandchildren.

Gepner said he has represented refugees whose families grew after they submitted permanent residency applications. He said they face an impossible choice: file a new application and face further delays, bring the child to Canada and deal with the consequences, or leave the new baby behind.

“I’ve had multiple cases where because of delays … family members are left abroad and you see mothers with their kids in a different country for years, and you see fathers without their families for years and you see shells of people,” Gepner said.

The Canadian Press first asked the Immigration Department on Monday if anyone had misused the policy.

In an email sent late Tuesday, the department again cited “potential integrity concerns” and said it will consider exemptions case-by-case on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. The spokesperson added the government continues to “examine longer-term options” but offered no specifics.

The Canadian Press asked again Wednesday if anyone had actually misused the seven-year old policy.

“We have nothing further to add,” a department spokesperson said.

“It’s fair to say that Canadians expect immigration programs to be applied as intended. And we take seriously our responsibility to put in place policies that people can trust and that serve them well.”

Kwan said ending this policy will have serious consequences for refugee families.

“I have met refugee families who did not know that their young child, as an example, was still alive. They came to Canada and the young child was not part of that application because they thought that they had lost their child. They thought that the child was dead,” Kwan said.

“These things happen because people are displaced. They’re in sometimes a war environment in conflict, they get separated from their loved ones, they don’t even know that possibly their loved ones could still be alive .”

Advocates have criticized the government for saying that exemptions might still be considered on humanitarian or compassionate grounds. They point out that those applications face waiting periods of more than 10 years, according to the government’s own website.

Kwan said the minister should know that ending the undeclared family policy means moving these applications to a “severely backlogged process” that will delay family reunification for years.

The Canadian Council for Refugees sent a letter to Immigration Minister Lena Diab last week demanding that she restore the policy. The council said the decision to revert to what it called “the cruelty of the previous situation” was “inexplicable.”

The department has said the best way prevent lengthy or permanent family separation is for all permanent resident applicants to list all family at the time of application.

Government data shows about 2,000 people used the policy between September 2019 and July 2023, with a 90 per cent approval rate. The department said it would take upwards of 10 days to pull more recent application data.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

“What is the lifetime ban for? For not declaring somebody because they were just born? For not declaring someone because you would be in danger if you declared them? For not declaring somebody because you were in a rush to get to Canada to save yourself?”
He said the number of these binding federal immigration policies — which can be cancelled without consultation — spiked under the government of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.

Jenny Kwan, the Ndp’s immigration critic, said refugees trying to come to Canada should not be punished for circumstances beyond their control. She said the government has offered “no credible explanation” for the policy’s termination.
“They quietly shut it down, and now it is going to have, I have no doubt, significant implications for refugee families in that reunification,” Kwan said.
“So they’re not broadcasting it, it means that they’re not proud of it.”
The policy took effect in 2019 and expired on Sept. 10. Refugee advocacy groups were only informed on Sept. 9 that the government did not plan to renew the policy.

A 2023 memo prepared for then-immigration minister Marc Miller said most people who did not list a family member did so innocently and the exemption posed a “minimal” risk to program integrity. Miller recommended extending the policy for three years.

That same memo said an applicant might not declare a family member for any one of several reasons — including a child’s birth or a marriage taking place after an application was filed, custody challenges, faulty immigration advice or the stigma associated with a child being born out of wedlock.
Undeclared family members eligible for sponsorship under the former policy included spouses, common-law partners, dependent children and grandchildren.

Gepner said he has represented refugees whose families grew after they submitted permanent residency applications. He said they face an impossible choice: file a new application and face further delays, bring the child to Canada and deal with the consequences, or leave the new baby behind.

“I’ve had multiple cases where because of delays … family members are left abroad and you see mothers with their kids in a different country for years, and you see fathers without their families for years and you see shells of people,” Gepner said.
The Canadian Press first asked the Immigration Department on Monday if anyone had misused the policy.

In an email sent late Tuesday, the department again cited “potential integrity concerns” and said it will consider exemptions case-by-case on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. The spokesperson added the government continues to “examine longer-term options” but offered no specifics.
The Canadian Press asked again Wednesday if anyone had actually misused the seven-year old policy.
“We have nothing further to add,” a department spokesperson said.

“It’s fair to say that Canadians expect immigration programs to be applied as intended. And we take seriously our responsibility to put in place policies that people can trust and that serve them well.”
Kwan said ending this policy will have serious consequences for refugee families.

“I have met refugee families who did not know that their young child, as an example, was still alive. They came to Canada and the young child was not part of that application because they thought that they had lost their child. They thought that the child was dead,” Kwan said.

“These things happen because people are displaced. They’re in sometimes a war environment in conflict, they get separated from their loved ones, they don’t even know that possibly their loved ones could still be alive .”

Advocates have criticized the government for saying that exemptions might still be considered on humanitarian or compassionate grounds. They point out that those applications face waiting periods of more than 10 years, according to the government’s own website.
Kwan said the minister should know that ending the undeclared family policy means moving these applications to a “severely backlogged process” that will delay family reunification for years.

The Canadian Council for Refugees sent a letter to Immigration Minister Lena Diab last week demanding that she restore the policy. The council said the decision to revert to what it called “the cruelty of the previous situation” was “inexplicable.”
The department has said the best way prevent lengthy or permanent family separation is for all permanent resident applicants to list all family at the time of application.

Government data shows about 2,000 people used the policy between September 2019 and July 2023, with a 90 per cent approval rate. The department said it would take upwards of 10 days to pull more recent application data.

stories.title: Sports notes: Hhof brings exhibits to London, Knights assign Kesler to Stars, field renovations at CCH
stories.summary: A travelling exhibit by the Hockey Hall of Fame (Hhof) has arrived in London.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
A travelling exhibit by the Hockey Hall of Fame (Hhof) has arrived in London.

Setup began Wednesday morning as members of the hall unloaded historical treasures from its collection.

Running Thursday to Saturday on the main pad at Western Fair Sports Centre, the display will be included with fair admission.

“It is the biggest setup we take on the road,” said Izak Westgate, direct of community for the Hhof.

“We have all of our traveling components, we have two different display systems, we have an Art of Hockey exhibit, we have a travelling theatre, and we also have a bunch of the NHL trophies and interactive games.”

Because many people can’t travel to Toronto to see the Hhof, they try to bring some memorabilia with local ties on the road.

“We always work with the local organizers to make sure we’re telling the story they want to see,” added Westgate.

St. Thomas stars get Ryker Kesler from London Knights

Off to a perfect 2-0 start in the Gohl, the St. Thomas Stars roster just got stronger.

Tuesday, the London Knights assigned second round pick Ryker Kesler to the Stars.

“I played against Ryan [Kesler, Ryker’s dad] in the NHL, and I’ve had a relationship with him a little bit doing some Red Wing alumni stuff that he helped out with, so it’s great to have him here,” said Stars head coach Jason Williams.

“I think he’s going to be a big factor for us, and I’m excited to see what he can bring. We’ve got two of their 16-year-olds right now and one local guy with Graham Littlejohn. I’m excited to see what this season is going to bring for us.”

The Knights selected Kesler 27th overall out of the Detroit Little Caesars program.

“When you’re getting a high pick like that, they have some special talent,” added Williams.

“He’s shown that he can put the puck in the net and put some numbers up and we hope that we can continue to his development.”

Kennedy Field gets much needed upgrade prior to football season

For years, the Catholic Central Crusaders have dominated home games on their small field east of the high school.

When their opponents step onto Kennedy Field this fall, they’ll notice something different.

This summer the London District Catholic School Board approved renovations to the field.

“Now our field is actually the width of a full Canadian football field,” said Alex Kurowski, Crusaders head football coach.

“Our side practice area where we used to call “the pit”, which was all grass, dirt and gravel has been totally renovated with brand new sod being watered as we speak.”

Anyone who has attended games over the years noticed the smaller dimensions. The LDCSB has ripped out two lanes of the track on the south side and added about 3 metres on each side of the field.

“Often, opponents from other schools would come and they’d say it’s unfair because it was it was a narrower football field and a 10-yard end zone,” said Kurowski.

“Now, we actually have the regulation of a full football field, which is which is great.”

Ranked number one in the province by multiple prognosticators, the Crusaders will play an exhibition game against Westmount Secondary School from Hamilton this week.

Their first game at Kennedy Field will be Oct. 9.

stories.title: Ruck 2 Remember “rucking” across region to combat veteran homelessness
stories.summary: If you see 7 people carrying “ruck sacks” on the side of the road through Midwestern Ontario this week, it’s likely members of a Ruck 2 Remember, raising money and awareness to combat homelessness amongst Canadian veterans.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
If you see 7 people carrying “ruck sacks” on the side of the road through Midwestern Ontario this week, it’s likely members of a Ruck 2 Remember, raising money and awareness to combat homelessness amongst Canadian veterans.

“It represents what these guys would have carried when they were working. And, to a certain extent, the load that they carry when they get back. So you do the things, the hard things, that these guys had to do to make people think about who it is that we’re supporting,” says Lino di Julio, founder of Ruck 2 Remember.

Di Julio was denied the ability to serve in Canada’s military because he is epileptic. Twelve years ago, he found another way to serve his country, by starting Ruck 2 Remember, a non-profit organization that raises money, along with the Royal Canadian Legion, to help veterans who find themselves without a home.

“We have 388 branches who support this program, and it helps to take homeless veterans off the streets, get them into housing, get them into apartments, and get them a start-up kit to get them going, and get their life back in order again.

Since this program began back about 13 years ago, there has been over 1400 veterans that we’ve assisted in this program,” says Royal Canadian Legion Ontario Provincial Command President, Lynn Mclellan. The seven “ruckers” left the Wingham Legion at 8 a.m. this morning, bound for Listowel.

They’ll make stops in Mount Forest, Elora, and Guelph over their 4 day ruck March, which will encompass 142 kilometres. Two kilometres for every veteran or first responder, they know of, that passed away in 2025. “From my perspective, this is a really good way to connect with other veterans.

I’ve done this for about four years now, and I’ve seen the way it reaches people in the local communities,” says Yarden Caplan, who has served in Canada’s military for the past eight years. This week’s ruck March is the organization’s largest fundraiser.

In the winter, they also do, in person outreach, looking for homeless vets on the streets of major cities. “We have found veterans on the street just by walking around. So, I just like being part of the process,” says Caplan.

The Ruck 2 Remember will wrap up on Saturday in Guelph. Of the roughly 610,000 Canadian veterans, Statistics Canada says approximately, 2,000 are unhoused. “It’s like, okay, it could be like a run for any number of worthy causes.

But, you know, you see some guys with Canadian flags and with rucksacks, people are like, oh, this is a military thing, right. And it gets them keyed in right away on what it is that we’re trying to do and represent,” says di Julio, Ruck 2 Remember Founder.

“It certainly helps to have people out there, as opposed to just selling raffle tickets and raising money. It’s an actual visual presentation to have these folks out on the road with their flags, and their backpacks, and their rucksacks.

It’s quite a visual presence,” says Legion Commander, Mclellan.

stories.title: Stevenson pledges tax increases under one per cent through 2028 and below inflation following two years, Morgan fires back
stories.summary: Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson is making a bold financial commitment to London voters ahead of next month’s election, but incumbent Josh Morgan warns her pledge would come back to bite taxpayers.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson is making a bold financial commitment to London voters ahead of next month’s election, but incumbent Josh Morgan warns her pledge would come back to bite taxpayers.

“Under one per cent in 2027 and 2028, with zero as the goal. Inflation or less in 2029 and 2030,” Stevenson pledged during a news conference inside her campaign office on Wednesday morning.

Stevenson calculates the cumulative property tax rate increase over the last four years to be 22.5 per cent, “To have a couple of years at under one per cent, or zero, especially when I brought forward motions for 2026 that could have brought this year to close to zero, I’m not uninformed in this space.”

The current multi-year budget projects a property tax increase of 4.7 per cent in 2027.

Lowering the rate by one percentage point requires finding approximately $9.25 million in savings, new revenue, or one-time dollars.

Stevenson is confident that, if elected, she could find the necessary $34.3 million within the budget.

“I’ll give the example of the Enwave $10 million capital cost that was funded through a budget contingency line that we had no idea even existed. That’s over and above the other contingency reserves and reserve funds that we have,” Stevenson said.

“How many other things do we have like that where in a pinch we are able to go for $10 million? So, I just need a couple of $10 million things to meet the goals that I have set. And I have no doubt that I can find them.”

Incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan quickly fired back in an interview with CTV News, “Tax promises with absolutely no plan on how to get there, it only pushes the can down the road. It only comes back to bite taxpayers in the butt.”

“She’s been on council for four years, and everybody knows there’s an operating budget contingency reserve. Every budget has a contingency reserve because when you plan a four-year budget, you’ve got to have some cushion in that budget to actually deal with things that come up, like the Enwave situation,” Morgan added.

Stevenson says during her time as councillor, she hasn’t been provided the detailed departmental budgets needed to find greater savings.

As mayor, that would change.

Stevenson acknowledges that she was one of the councillors on the Strategic Opportunities Review Working Group (Sorwg) at city hall that was disbanded after failing to find significant long-term savings.

“We randomly brought things forward, but we didn’t actually get to look at any of the departments and where the pressures were and where there were potential savings,” she explained.

“I have to be clear; we have not seen a line-by-line actuals-to-budget during this term of council. So, without seeing that, how are we supposed to find [savings]?”

Details of potential budget savings from 2027-2030 would come after she is elected.

“The objective is always permanent savings, but we May need to find one-time savings in order to just carry us through. But the commitment is to find savings. And I don’t think Londoners are going to find it hard to believe that we could find some wasteful or duplicative programs or services in the city’s $1.5 billion budget,” she added.

Morgan points out that Stevenson currently sits on the Audit Committee at city hall, “We’re very clear on the way we do things. There’s only one member of council who can’t seem to find the budget information that she needs to make decisions. All other members of council have done this for four years in a row.”

“We’ve seen this before. It doesn’t work. It’s not sustainable,” Morgan said, alluding to the budget pressures experienced at city hall following Mayor Joe Fontana’s tax freeze pledge from 2010 to 2014.

“This is not a transparent promise. This is not something that is sustainable.”

“For someone who asks a lot of questions at council, I think Londoners should be asking a lot of questions about what are you going to cut?” he asserted.

“This is a leadership issue,” said Stevenson, referencing the mayor’s responsibility to draft the municipal budget each year.

“Families need room in their budgets, city hall needs to make room in its own.”

Stevenson also pledged to expand the property tax deferral program for qualifying low-income seniors and people with disabilities.

Her commitment also includes greater scrutiny of municipal finances.

“It’s essential that we provide the oversight and accountability that we’re mandated to do under the Municipal Act. Londoners are watching and seeing. They know we need a Waste and Fraud Hotline. They know that there’s cost overruns on these projects that aren’t being reviewed by their elected officials, and they’re frustrated about it, and they want us to do our job,” she said.

stories.title: Two men charged in the Toronto Pearson Airport gold heist have their charges dropped
stories.summary: Ali Raza and Amit Jalota were accused in the Toronto Pearson Airport gold heist but have had all charges against them dropped.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Two men charged in the spectacular Toronto Pearson Airport gold heist have had all charges against them dropped.

Both men, Ali Raza and Amit Jalota, were accused of helping to move and melt the stolen gold after the heist in which a shipping crate containing $22 million in gold and cash was stolen from an Air Canada cargo warehouse.

Raza, 39, of Toronto, pegged as “the jeweller” in the heist plot, appeared in a Brampton, Ont., courtroom Wednesday afternoon dressed in a suit and tie, where he heard the news as he sat with his lawyers.

He had been accused of melting stolen gold in the basement workshop of his jewellery store and was charged with possession of property obtained by crime.

Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic told Ontario Superior Court Justice Nancy Dennison that the prosecution’s case “rested upon circumstantial evidence and the inferences available from that evidence.”

As the investigation and prosecution evolved, prosecutors heard additional evidence and new details of the heist, leading the Crown to conclude there was no longer a reasonable prospect of conviction, Vlacic said. The changing landscape of the evidence impacted the prosecution of both Raza and Jalota.

The specific details of the evidence cannot be published under a court order because of a pending jury trial against those still accused in the gold heist, which is scheduled to begin next month.

On Tuesday, a similar hearing before the same judge with the same result unfolded for Jalota, 42, of Oakville.

Jalota was originally accused of bringing stolen gold to Raza for melting and redistribution. Jalota was charged with possession of property obtained by crime, theft over $5,000, and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence, but all charges were dropped on Tuesday.

Raza and Jalota were among the first to be arrested a year after the bewildering and internationally high-profile gold heist in 2023.

Ringleader of $22M Toronto airport gold heist gets four years in prison for his spectacularly simple plan

Gold heist ringleader pleads guilty to theft of $22M in gold and cash from Toronto's Pearson airport

Raza is one of the proprietors of Mashallah Jewellers, according to his lawyer, Brij Mohan.

The storefront is less than 600 metres along Airport Road from the airport’s property line in a low-rise strip plaza, part of a retail hub catering primarily to South Asian and Middle Eastern interest in gold and gold jewellery. Another six gold jewellers are tenants in the plaza, with three more in the plaza to its right and still more in the plaza to its left.

“Buy, sell, trade, custom orders,” reads a sign outside. Its website projects a more luxurious experience: “Purity in every karat” it says over a video of an elegant woman wearing multiple intricate gold designs.

The shipping container at the heart of the case was filled with almost-pure gold bars, weighing 400.19 kilograms, and stolen from an Air Canada cargo facility shortly after arriving on an Air Canada flight from Zurich, Switzerland, ON April 17, 2023.

Even though the cargo was valued at more than $22 million, a driver walked into the warehouse alone and presented an Air Canada waybill for a shipment of seafood that had already been picked up; bizarrely a warehouse employee loaded the gold shipment onto the man’s truck with a forklift.

The theft was so smooth it wasn’t noticed until three hours later when Brink’s security arrived to collect the container and nobody could find it.

On the first anniversary of the brazen theft, Peel Regional Police announced nine arrest warrants issued as part of their gold heist investigation, codenamed Project 24K.

Five of the accused were arrested in Canada and four more were listed as fugitives, although one, the driver of the truck that carted the gold out of the airport, is in custody in the United States, where he was arrested after police stopped a car in Pennsylvania and found 65 handguns in the trunk being smuggled to Canada. He has pleaded guilty to firearms charges. Authorities said a portion of proceeds from the stolen gold was used to fund a cross-border gun-running plot.

A small portion of gold from the heist was recovered, police said. It had been forged into six crudely made gold bracelets but with the purity of the gold they were worth about $90,000.

Arsalan Chaudhary, a 43-year-old man formerly of Mississauga, Ont., was found to be the mastermind, or, as Vlacic called him Wednesday, “the principal organizer and benefactor of the heist.” He was given a four-year sentence in April, along with an order to pay $22 million in restitution to Brink’s, which was moving the cargo on behalf of two clients, the TD Bank in Toronto and a foreign exchange in Vancouver.

Raza maintained his innocence. Instead of going into hiding, he agreed to an on-camera interview with CBC and gave a tour of the workshop under his store, saying his equipment is only capable of melting small amounts, a gold ring but not a gold bar.

“Mr. Raza was an innocent man — today he gets his life back,” Raza’s lawyer, Mohan, said outside of court. “Mr. Raza himself was fully cooperative with police and even reached out to the police himself.

“His business and life were destroyed by these allegations, and he can now move forward with his life,” Mohan said. “It is too early for Mr. Raza to be considering any type of legal action; he just wants his life to go back to normal.” Raza thanked his family and supporters and lawyers for believing in him.

Jalota’s lawyer, Leora Shemesh, said that despite having charges dropped, her client continues to suffer from the arrest.

“He has at all times professed his innocence and has painfully endured three years navigating the justice system. He was fortunate to have been released on bail and had the ability to continue to care for his young family, however, he was punitively punished by the national and international coverage of this case.

“His photo was printed and posted everywhere and every financial institution in Ontario refused to do business with him and his extended family — including his parents who were hard-working, honest Canadians,” Shemesh said.

“People like Mr. Jalota don’t ever receive an apology or a public retraction. There is no commentary from the police publicly that they had gotten it wrong. Instead, Mr. Jalota is forced to simply move on and pick up the pieces for himself and his family.”

stories.title: Woman dead, man in custody as London police launch femicide investigation
stories.summary: A woman is dead and a man in police custody after an incident in London's southeast on Tuesday.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A woman is dead and a man in police custody after an incident in London's southeast on Tuesday.
· Posted: Sep 16, 2026 1:33 PM EDT | Last Updated: 20 minutes ago
A woman is dead and a man in police custody after an incident in London's southeast on Tuesday, and police have launched a femicide investigation.
Emergency crews were called to a home on Chelton Road in Summerside, near Highbury and Commissioners roads, at around 6:30 p.m.
When officers arrived, they found a woman suffering from life-threatening injuries, police said. The woman was taken to hospital by paramedics and has since succumbed to her injuries.
A man, identified as Mandeep Singh, 41, of London, has been arrested and charged with second-degree murder.
The accused remains in custody and was scheduled to appear in London court on Wednesday.
The man and woman were in an intimate relationship, police said.
Other family members were home at the time of the incident, but no additional injuries were reported, police said.
The investigation is in its early stages.
Alongside their announcement of the investigation, police issued a statement on the impacts of intimate partner violence.

"Intimate partner violence remains a significant public safety and community wellbeing concern,” said LPS Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau. “Women continue to represent the majority of victims in police-reported cases and we know many incidents go unreported."

Police said they are committed to addressing the issue, "working alongside our community partners to strengthen prevention efforts ... and support ongoing efforts to better understand and respond to intimate partner violence and femicide.”
This is London's fourth homicide, and first femicide of 2026.

"Finding out about this was incredibly heartbreaking. We're in the month of September. We've thought, maybe something like this wouldn't happen this year, and here we are," said Jennifer Dunn, the executive director of the London Abused Women's Centre (LAWC).
"It shows us, and we know this based on the work that we do every single day, that intimate partner violence and violence against women and girls is still very significant in our community."
LAWC offers advocacy, counselling and support for women and girls subjected to intimate partner violence, sexual assault, sexual exploitation, trafficking and non-state torture, its website says.
Dunn said the agency has continued to see a steady flow of people coming to them for support over the last several years.
"Women require true wraparound support and real choices and real options for whatever their journey to justice looks like, so to speak. We remain, honestly, as busy as ever," Dunn said.
"We obviously had a shift around the pandemic, just like everybody else did, and we're seeing how that plays out in the level of trauma and violence that women are subjected to."

On Jan 12, police responded to a multiple calls about a stabbing in the 700-block of Dundas Street. They found an unresponsive man in the hallway of an apartment building. Brandon Christopher Jamieson Nichols, 45, was identified as the man who died. Robert Mitchell Cornelius, 38 , was charged with second degree murder.

On Jan. 25, police were called to the same block of Dundas Street after reports of multiple gunshots. They found two men and took both to hospital. One of the men found, Ramone Thomas, 26, of Toronto, died of his injuries. Londoner Matthew Yousufy, 26, was charged with second-degree murder and a number of drug and firearm offences.

On Aug. 22, an elderly woman was woken up by a loud noise and found a man in her home on Raywood Avenue, near Wellington and Baseline roads. The 73-year-old was assaulted and stabbed and died of her injuries days later. Property records show the home was owned by Lillian Anne Leonard. Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, was charged with second degree murder.

Police said they are committed to addressing the issue, "working alongside our community partners to strengthen prevention efforts ... and support ongoing efforts to better understand and respond to intimate partner violence and femicide.”

This is London's fourth homicide, and first femicide of 2026.

"Finding out about this was incredibly heartbreaking. We're in the month of September. We've thought, maybe something like this wouldn't happen this year, and here we are," said Jennifer Dunn, the executive director of the London Abused Women's Centre (LAWC).

"It shows us, and we know this based on the work that we do every single day, that intimate partner violence and violence against women and girls is still very significant in our community."

LAWC offers advocacy, counselling and support for women and girls subjected to intimate partner violence, sexual assault, sexual exploitation, trafficking and non-state torture, its website says.

Dunn said the agency has continued to see a steady flow of people coming to them for support over the last several years.

"Women require true wraparound support and real choices and real options for whatever their journey to justice looks like, so to speak. We remain, honestly, as busy as ever," Dunn said.

"We obviously had a shift around the pandemic, just like everybody else did, and we're seeing how that plays out in the level of trauma and violence that women are subjected to."

On Jan 12, police responded to a multiple calls about a stabbing in the 700-block of Dundas Street. They found an unresponsive man in the hallway of an apartment building. Brandon Christopher Jamieson Nichols, 45, was identified as the man who died. Robert Mitchell Cornelius, 38 , was charged with second degree murder.

On Jan. 25, police were called to the same block of Dundas Street after reports of multiple gunshots. They found two men and took both to hospital. One of the men found, Ramone Thomas, 26, of Toronto, died of his injuries. Londoner Matthew Yousufy, 26, was charged with second-degree murder and a number of drug and firearm offences.

On Aug. 22, an elderly woman was woken up by a loud noise and found a man in her home on Raywood Avenue, near Wellington and Baseline roads. The 73-year-old was assaulted and stabbed and died of her injuries days later. Property records show the home was owned by Lillian Anne Leonard. Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, was charged with second degree murder.

stories.title: Air Canada removes in-flight director from service after antisemitic posts
stories.summary: The airline says it is doing a full investigation and "denounces hate speech and promotion of violence in all forms."
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Air Canada says they are investigating after antisemitic comments were made by an in-flight service director on social media.

Airline spokesperson Sean Davidson confirmed to National Post in a written statement on Wednesday that the individual was “removed from service” and there is a “full investigation underway.”

A Facebook account with the same name as the in-flight service director had dozens of posts about the conflict in Gaza. “This is a Holocaust created by Jews against people who refuse to allow them to steal their land,” he wrote on Aug. 6. He compared Zionism to Nazism, saying the former was “every bit as evil.”

He also referred to an antisemitic trope and conspiracy theory about Jewish people owning the media in one post from late August. “This is why we never hear the truth about Israel,” he wrote.

Many times he referred to the situation in Gaza as a genocide, perpetrated by Israel.

“The people who pull the Holocaust card or the antisemitism card, their eternal ‘victim’ card, at every opportunity, are now executing people based on them not being Jewish,” he wrote in a post in April.

On Jan. 27, 2025, which is International Holocaust Remembrance Day, he wrote that he no longer thinks of or respects this day “through the same lens as I did in the past because of Israel’s actions the past 15 months.”

“The fact that they are still playing the victim card in the face of genocide is revolting. I hope that some day their actions match their words,” he said.

When reached for comment by National Post, the service director said he could not provide a statement at this time.

A spokesperson for the Air Canada Component of Cupe told National Post that the union is aware of the situation and “is in contact with the member, and will fulfill its legal obligations of representation during the investigation.”

Air Canada said in its statement that it “denounces hate speech and promotion of violence in all forms.” It did not clarify if the service director was removed with or without pay.

Jeffrey Herf: 'Nakba' exhibit is a direct assault on historical truths

Yoni Goldstein: Macklemore’s cancellation is no victory for the pro-Israel crowd

On Tuesday, Air Canada announced its flights to Israel would resume on Nov. 30 after being suspended since March. The airline said the suspension was due to the “military situation in the Middle East.”

In 2023, the airline fired a pilot after social media posts surfaced of him attending an anti-Israel protest in Montreal, CTV News reported . Air Canada said at the time that the posts were “unacceptable.” The pilot reportedly appeared at the protest wearing his uniform and holding a sign that referenced Nazi leader Adolf Hitler.

stories.title: Squirrel, system failure blamed for London outage that hit 15,000
stories.summary: The outage should have affected 2,500 customers but a protection system failed to operate as expected, the utility says.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The outage should have affected 2,500 customers but a protection system failed to operate as expected, the utility says.

Last updated 25 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/squirrel-system-failure-blamed-for-London-outage-that-hit-15000#comments-area)

A London Hydro employee working on Friday, Sept. 26, 2025. (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press)

A squirrel triggered a large-scale power outage in London that was made worse when a protection system didn’t work as expected, an official with the utility provider says.

The squirrel caused a short circuit at a Hydro One transformer station – one of seven that Ontario’s largest electricity provider supplies to London Hydro – on Tuesday, said Allan Van Damme, London Hydro’s vice-president of engineering and construction.

“Outages caused by animals are difficult to totally eliminate, as animals are unpredictable,” Van Damme said. “However, we do install insulated covers and guards on many of our devices to prevent such animal-related short circuits.”

We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try again

Crews found a dead squirrel at the base of a utility pole on Oxford Street near Laurel Street, west of Wonderland Road, Van Damme said.

The outage should have affected 2,500 customers, but Hydro One’s systems didn’t operate as expected, leaving a total of 15,000 customers without power for 90 minutes, Van Damme said. An electrical engineer by trade, he has spent nearly three decades at London Hydro.

“This is not a common occurrence. We are working productively with Hydro One to determine why their system operated in this way,” he said, adding the two utilities are prioritizing work on equipment related to the station where the short circuit happened.

Damage to London Hydro equipment is shown after animal contact caused an equipment failure and power outages in northwest London on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (London Hydro/X)

London Hydro used its remote-controlled high-voltage switches to restore power to all affected customers within 90 minutes, Van Damme said.

The remote system, known as distribution automation, allows London Hydro to restore power without sending crews to the scene, a process that can take time when power outages disrupt traffic lights and cause gridlock on streets.

Tuesday’s outage affected customers in the Carling, Oakridge and Medway areas.

“We understand that outages of this nature are frustrating and inconvenient and I want our customers to know that we are working with Hydro One to try and resolve this issue.”

stories.title: London man charged with second-degree murder in partner’s death
stories.summary: Police characterize the woman’s death as a femicide; the accused was arrested at the scene.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
Police characterize the woman’s death as a femicide; the accused was arrested at the scene.

Last updated 3 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/London-man-charged-with-second-degree-murder-in-partners-death#comments-area)

A London police forensic investigator photographs evidence outside a home at 695 Chelton Rd. on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. ( Dale Carruthers/ The London Free Press)

A London man is charged with second-degree murder in the death of a woman who suffered life-threatening injuries at a southeast London home and later died, London police say

Officers responded at about 6:25 p.m. Tuesday to a home on Chelton Road, southeast of Commissioners Road and Highbury Avenue, where they found the injured woman, police said.

The woman, whose name wasn’t released, was taken to hospital and later died of her injuries, police said.

A man was arrested at the scene, police said. He and the woman were known to each other and involved in an intimate relationship, police said.

“There were additional family members at the residence at the time . . ., none of whom were injured,” police said.

Mandeep Singh, 41, of London is charged with second-degree murder. He was scheduled to appear in court Wednesday.

Investigators characterized the death as a femicide, the gender-based killing of women and girls, but did not release a cause of death.

Several municipalities across Ontario, including London, have declared intimate-partner violence an epidemic.

“Intimate partner violence remains a significant public safety and community wellbeing concern,” Det.-Sgt. Micah Bourdeau of the major crime section said.

“Women continue to represent the majority of victims in police-reported cases and we know many incidents go unreported,” Bourdeau said in a statement.

“Addressing this issue requires a co-ordinated response, and we remain committed to working alongside our community partners to strengthen prevention efforts, enhance education and awareness, improve intervention strategies, and support ongoing efforts to better understand and respond to intimate-partner violence and femicide.”

This is the city’s fourth homicide of the year and second killing in less than a month.

Lillian Leonard, 73, died in hospital from stab wounds she received during a break-in at her Raywood Avenue home, north of the intersection of Wellington and Base Line roads, ON Aug. 22.

Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of no fixed address, is charged with second-degree murder.

stories.title: Warm temperatures hold Wednesday with breaks of sunshine, cooling into overnight
stories.summary: A warm and humid day in London is set to start cooling off heading into the overnight as a cold front moves through southern Ontario.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
A warm and humid day in London is set to start cooling off heading into the overnight as a cold front moves through southern Ontario. Wednesday began with some rainfall, but only a small chance of rain at 30 per cent into the evening.

“Still feeling like 32 C in London, but look to the north. So, that’s where the northernly flow is starting to dry things out,” said CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison. “The cold front that’s making the move through will be stalling south of the Great Lakes and that could be a bit problematic for our Thursday morning.

The reason, we’ll see a little wave of low pressure develop along that front as that wave comes in, it’ll bring the chance for some showers.” Atchison added a chance of light rain will clear out by Thursday afternoon. Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast Wednesday night: Mainly cloudy with a 30 per cent chance of showers.

A few showers beginning before morning. Low 16 C. Thursday: A few showers ending in the afternoon, then clearing. High 23 C, humidex 28 C. Friday: Sunny. High 23 C. Saturday: Cloudy with 60 per cent chance of showers. High 17 C.

Sunday: Cloudy with a 70 per cent chance of showers. High 20 C.

stories.title: 10/3 podcast: B.C. Conservatives rocked by defections. What happens next?
stories.summary: B.C.'s Conservative Party has been rocked with defections in recent weeks, mere months after Kerry-Lynne Findlay was elected leader.
stories.author: Shawn Knox
stories.content:
B.C.’s Conservative Party has been rocked with defections in recent weeks, mere months after Kerry-Lynne Findlay was elected leader.

The events are the latest in a couple of years of turmoil in right-of-centre politics in B.C. as the Conservative Party has grown as the main opposition to the governing NDP.

Vancouver Sun columnist Vaughn Palmer joins host Dave Breakenridge to discuss what led to Findlay’s ascension as Conservative leader, why some MLAs have jumped ship, and whether it means NDP Premier David Eby could call a snap election.

stories.title: CPP Investments and Brookfield just launched a $50B Maple Fund. What is it?
stories.summary: The Canada Pension Plan Investments Board (Cppib) and Brookfield on Tuesday launched a $50 billion "Maple Fund" that they say will funnel capital towards major national projects.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The Canada Pension Plan Investments Board (Cppib) and Brookfield on Tuesday launched a $50 billion “Maple Fund” that they say will funnel capital towards critical infrastructure and strategic industries across Canada.

The announcement from the Cppib, which manages the investments in the Canada Pension Plan, and investment management firm Brookfield was one of the main funding projects that came out from a recent two-day investment summit hosted by Carney and the premiers.

With the Canada Pension Plan playing a central role in many Canadians’ retirement planning, many May be wondering what this decision means for their retirements.

The Maple Fund will operate as an investing framework to provide funding for specific projects, and will include up to $25 billion each from the Cppib and Brookfield over a five-year timespan.

The fund is focused on complex large-scale projects that each require significant upfront resources and development capabilities, and a minimum of $5 billion in capital funding, according to a press release.

Each project must also be individually approved by both partners in the fund, and the framework allows for either firm to bring in additional investors to partner on specific approved projects within the fund.

Although both Cppib and Brookfield are providing an equal amount of long-term cash, or capital, the release says Cppib will be involved in the fund’s operations by providing investing expertise, while Brookfield will also provide the development and management of the projects being funded.

The release did not mention specific projects or investments, but that those will be announced once they are finalized.

Connor Teskey, CEO of Brookfield Asset Management, in the release said, “we believe the Maple Fund can help drive a generational investment program to invest in critical infrastructure, industries and businesses that will support the growth of globally competitive Canadian businesses.”

The president and CEO of the Cppib, John Graham, said in a release that these opportunities “offer compelling value.”

“CPP Investments has the capital, long-term investment horizon and expertise to pursue these opportunities, and the Maple Fund brings together our strengths with Brookfield’s strong origination and development capabilities to help move ambitious projects from opportunity to investment,” said Graham.

“The Maple Fund positions us well to meet this moment and move with speed on opportunities of unusual scale and complexity when they offer compelling value for the CPP Fund.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has been working since last year to pivot Canada’s economy away from relying on the United States amid tariffs and trade war uncertainty .

It’s been doing this mainly by proposing or starting new major projects of national interest with the aim of making Canada more attractive to a diverse and growing list of new international trading partners.

Most working Canadians’ are now indirect stakeholders in these projects by way of paying into the CPP Fund through regular work contributions for their retirements. The Cppib then allocates that money towards investing opportunities to grow the fund, similar to a retirement savings portfolio.

Global News sent a request to CPP Investments asking about why the fund specifically offers value for average Canadians. A spokesperson deferred to Graham’s statement but did not provide further comment.

Andrew DiCapua, principal economist at the Canadian Chamber of Commerce says the idea of the Maple Fund is promising on a national level, but questions remain including how success is measured.

“The more Canadian assets that we can keep Canadian-owned is a great opportunity to advance sovereignty in the country and ensure that we benefit from that as Canadians, because, of course, pension funds are to the benefit of all Canadians and we maintain that sovereignty,” says DiCapua.

“How are we going to measure success and how are we going to actually execute and ensure that both business and government are working well together? And that remains to be seen because of course the work still needs to be done. “

Canadians who are employed or self-employed must make regular CPP contributions, which are usually deducted automatically from pay cheques.

The goal is to grow that money over the long term with strategic investments made by the Cppib, and Canadians can withdraw their CPP earnings when it comes time to retire.

Most investments are long-term strategies, which means the total returns or growth on this $50 billion investment, and more specifically the $25 billion share from CPP, May not be seen for some time.

“The CPP exists for one reason and one reason only: it’s to maximize the return for whatever tolerable level of risk they’re willing to take on,” says economics professor Moshe Lander of Concordia University.

“The entire objective is: you make sure that there is the biggest pot of money available for us when we retire — that’s it. So, if they’re saying that ‘there’s compelling value here,’ is that just political phraseology to say that maybe we’re not pursuing the path of greatest return for a given level of risk?”

Like with any investment, there is a level of risk that these projects May not pay off or May not generate as much of a return as hoped, but the release states “each potential investment will be independently assessed and approved by CPP Investments and Brookfield against their respective requirements and through their established investment and governance processes.”

“CPP Investments May not be looking for the highest growth opportunities, but they are looking for predictable returns and where government and where industry can open the aperture and present those opportunities to the pension fund,” says DiCapua.

“The commitment to capital by the pension funds, including CPP investments, seems to signal that they see some opportunities that they can participate in, which is encouraging.”

According to the release, the Cppib operates “at arm’s length from governments,” and as of June 30, 2026, the total value of its fund was C$863.6 billion. It adds that it manages the fund “in the best interest of the more than 22 million contributors and beneficiaries.”

stories.title: Woman dead, one arrested in femicide investigation: LPS
stories.summary: A woman has died and a man has been arrested in a femicide investigation.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
A woman has died and a man has been charged with second degree murder in a femicide investigation.

“Uniform officers were called to an address on Shelton Road last night around 6:30 p.m. in response to a violent incident,” said Micah Bourdeau with London Police Services.

Bourdeau said they located an adult female with life threatening injuries; she was transported to hospital where she later died.

41-year-old Mandeep Singh of London was arrested on scene.

“We now know that those two parties were involved in an intimate relationship,” said Bourdeau.

According to police, this is the fifth homicide in London this year but the first to show signs of a “possible femicide”.

“There are some indications that it could meet the threshold of a femicide,” said Bourdeau.

“That’s not clear yet and we need to investigate much more to determine that.”

Jennifer Dunn with the London Abused Women’s Centre (Lawc) said she was heartbroken when she heard the news.

“One is too many,” said Dunn.

“There shouldn’t be any men killing women in our city or anywhere.”

Dunn said this comes amid ongoing concern regarding intimate partner violence in our community.

“In 2023, there were four femicides that were well known here in the community,” said Dunn.

“We have not stopped talking about them ever since and it really varies year over year in the city of London.”

Dunn said if deemed a femicide, this will be the first case in London since Bill C16 was passed.

“BC16 received royal assent,” said Dunn.

“As part of this bill femicide is now recognized in the criminal code.”

Bourdeau explained this would mean an automatic first-degree murder charge.

“A conviction for a first-degree murder charge comes with an automatic 25-year sentence,” said Bourdeau.

According to police, Chelton road was closed for a duration of the day Thursday but has since reopened.

The investigation remains on going.

Anyone with information is asked to call the LPS at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 or online .

A list of resources and contact information for those experiencing intimate partner violence can be found on the LPS’ website .

stories.title: Woman dead, man charged with murder in London femicide investigation
stories.summary: A woman is dead, and a man is in police custody after an incident at a home in southeast London on Tuesday.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A woman is dead, and a man is in police custody after an incident at a home in southeast London on Tuesday.
· Posted: Sep 16, 2026 1:33 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
A woman is dead, and a man is in police custody after an incident at a home in southeast London on Tuesday, in what London police are investigating as a femicide.
Emergency crews were called to a home on Chelton Road in the Summerside neighbourhood, near Highbury and Commissioners roads, at around 6:30 p.m.
When officers arrived, they found a woman suffering from life-threatening injuries, police said. She was taken to hospital by paramedics, where she later died.
Police have charged Mandeep Singh, 41, of London, with second-degree murder.
Singh remains in custody and was scheduled to appear in London court on Wednesday.
The man and woman were in an intimate relationship, police said.
Other family members were home at the time of the incident, but no additional injuries were reported, police said.
Several neighbours told CBC News the man and women lived at 685 Chelton Road. They said the pair were married with two young children, and lived with the woman's mother.
Some said they saw the children and their grandmother frantically exit the home before police arrived Tuesday night.
"We saw an old lady coming out shouting and hitting herself, with two [children]," said Sam Awdi, who lives across the street.
"I feel bad. I've been in this city 40 years but never saw something like that, honestly," he said.
Awdi said several police cars remained at the house overnight.
By Wednesday afternoon, two police cars and a forensic identification van remained at the home. Three forensic investigators were seen going in and out of the house and taking photographs.
Police tape blocked off the house and front yard, as well as a wide area of the sidewalk on both sides.
"We've never seen this kind of activity in this neighbourhood," said nearby neighbour Anto Vibin Charles.
Many residents describe Chelton Road as a quiet, family-oriented neighbourhood.
"Even at that house, those kids are usually playing outside," Vibin Charles said, adding that he watched the grandmother teach the children how to ride a bike over the summer.
Multiple neighbours told CBC News the family was generally quiet and kept to themselves.
Vibin Charles said he had never heard fighting at the home. Awdi said he had occasionally heard shouting, although he could not say whether it came from the house.
"We hear, from time to time, shouting and all, but I don't know if it's in the same house," Awdi said.
Alongside their announcement of the investigation, police issued a statement on the impacts of intimate partner violence.

"Intimate partner violence remains a significant public safety and community wellbeing concern,” said LPS Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau. “Women continue to represent the majority of victims in police-reported cases and we know many incidents go unreported."

Police said they are committed to addressing the issue, "working alongside our community partners to strengthen prevention efforts ... and support ongoing efforts to better understand and respond to intimate partner violence and femicide.”
Police are investigating the death as London's first femicide of 2026. It is the city's fourth homicide this year.

"Finding out about this was incredibly heartbreaking. We're in the month of September. We've thought, maybe something like this wouldn't happen this year, and here we are," said Jennifer Dunn, the executive director of the London Abused Women's Centre (LAWC).
"It shows us, and we know this based on the work that we do every single day, that intimate partner violence and violence against women and girls is still very significant in our community."
LAWC offers advocacy, counselling and support for women and girls subjected to intimate partner violence, sexual assault, sexual exploitation, trafficking and non-state torture, its website says.
Dunn said the agency has continued to see a steady flow of people coming to them for support over the last several years.
"Women require true wraparound support and real choices and real options for whatever their journey to justice looks like, so to speak. We remain, honestly, as busy as ever," Dunn said.
"We obviously had a shift around the pandemic, just like everybody else did, and we're seeing how that plays out in the level of trauma and violence that women are subjected to."

On Jan 12, police responded to a multiple calls about a stabbing in the 700-block of Dundas Street. They found an unresponsive man in the hallway of an apartment building. Brandon Christopher Jamieson Nichols, 45, was identified as the man who died. Robert Mitchell Cornelius, 38 , was charged with second degree murder.

On Jan. 25, police were called to the same block of Dundas Street after reports of multiple gunshots. They found two men and took both to hospital. One of the men found, Ramone Thomas, 26, of Toronto, died of his injuries. Londoner Matthew Yousufy, 26, was charged with second-degree murder and a number of drug and firearm offences.

On Aug. 22, an elderly woman was woken up by a loud noise and found a man in her home on Raywood Avenue, near Wellington and Baseline roads. The 73-year-old was assaulted and stabbed and died of her injuries days later. Property records show the home was owned by Lillian Anne Leonard. Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, was charged with second degree murder.

A woman is dead, and a man is in police custody after an incident at a home in southeast London on Tuesday.

· Posted: Sep 16, 2026 1:33 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

A woman is dead, and a man is in police custody after an incident at a home in southeast London on Tuesday, in what London police are investigating as a femicide.

Emergency crews were called to a home on Chelton Road in the Summerside neighbourhood, near Highbury and Commissioners roads, at around 6:30 p.m.

When officers arrived, they found a woman suffering from life-threatening injuries, police said. She was taken to hospital by paramedics, where she later died.

Police have charged Mandeep Singh, 41, of London, with second-degree murder.

Singh remains in custody and was scheduled to appear in London court on Wednesday.

The man and woman were in an intimate relationship, police said.

Other family members were home at the time of the incident, but no additional injuries were reported, police said.

Several neighbours told CBC News the man and women lived at 685 Chelton Road. They said the pair were married with two young children, and lived with the woman's mother.

Some said they saw the children and their grandmother frantically exit the home before police arrived Tuesday night.

"We saw an old lady coming out shouting and hitting herself, with two [children]," said Sam Awdi, who lives across the street.

"I feel bad. I've been in this city 40 years but never saw something like that, honestly," he said.

Awdi said several police cars remained at the house overnight.

By Wednesday afternoon, two police cars and a forensic identification van remained at the home. Three forensic investigators were seen going in and out of the house and taking photographs.

Police tape blocked off the house and front yard, as well as a wide area of the sidewalk on both sides.

"We've never seen this kind of activity in this neighbourhood," said nearby neighbour Anto Vibin Charles.

Many residents describe Chelton Road as a quiet, family-oriented neighbourhood.

"Even at that house, those kids are usually playing outside," Vibin Charles said, adding that he watched the grandmother teach the children how to ride a bike over the summer.

Multiple neighbours told CBC News the family was generally quiet and kept to themselves.

Vibin Charles said he had never heard fighting at the home. Awdi said he had occasionally heard shouting, although he could not say whether it came from the house.

"We hear, from time to time, shouting and all, but I don't know if it's in the same house," Awdi said.

Alongside their announcement of the investigation, police issued a statement on the impacts of intimate partner violence.

"Intimate partner violence remains a significant public safety and community wellbeing concern,” said LPS Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau. “Women continue to represent the majority of victims in police-reported cases and we know many incidents go unreported."

Police said they are committed to addressing the issue, "working alongside our community partners to strengthen prevention efforts ... and support ongoing efforts to better understand and respond to intimate partner violence and femicide.”

Police are investigating the death as London's first femicide of 2026. It is the city's fourth homicide this year.

"Finding out about this was incredibly heartbreaking. We're in the month of September. We've thought, maybe something like this wouldn't happen this year, and here we are," said Jennifer Dunn, the executive director of the London Abused Women's Centre (LAWC).

"It shows us, and we know this based on the work that we do every single day, that intimate partner violence and violence against women and girls is still very significant in our community."

LAWC offers advocacy, counselling and support for women and girls subjected to intimate partner violence, sexual assault, sexual exploitation, trafficking and non-state torture, its website says.

Dunn said the agency has continued to see a steady flow of people coming to them for support over the last several years.

"Women require true wraparound support and real choices and real options for whatever their journey to justice looks like, so to speak. We remain, honestly, as busy as ever," Dunn said.

"We obviously had a shift around the pandemic, just like everybody else did, and we're seeing how that plays out in the level of trauma and violence that women are subjected to."

Brandon Christopher Jamieson Nichols, 45, was identified as the man who died. Robert Mitchell Cornelius, 38 , was charged with second degree murder.

The 73-year-old was assaulted and stabbed and died of her injuries days later. Property records show the home was owned by Lillian Anne Leonard. stories.title: No livestreams, fewer public meetings at supervised Thames Valley board
stories.summary: Trustees say reduced access to meetings is raising concerns about transparency and public accountability.
stories.author: Heather Rivers Davey
stories.content:
Trustees say reduced access to meetings is raising concerns about transparency and public accountability.

The Thames Valley District school board building in London. (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press)

More than a year after the Thames Valley District school board was placed under provincial supervision, some meetings continue to be held behind closed doors while public meetings are no longer livestreamed.

“What we have seen under supervision is quite troubling, and that’s a problem for anybody that cares about the issue of parents’ involvement in schools and special education as well,” said Marianne Larsen, a Thames Valley trustee and scholar specializing in education policy. “My sense is they are doing the absolute minimum.”

In October 2025, the public school board’s trustees learned special education and parent committee meetings would no longer be available for viewing online and participants would have to register to attend in person.

For buyers, sellers, renters and dreamers — London's complex, fascinating real estate market is brought into focus and into context with this newsletter.

By signing up, you consent to receive the above newsletter from Postmedia Network Inc.

A welcome email is on its way. If you don't see it, please check your junk folder.

The next issue of Homes in London will soon be in your inbox.

We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try again

“There are committees that school boards by law must have through legislation and regulation,” said Larsen, who is not running again for trustee in the fall election.

“My understanding is they need to be publicly accessible as well,” she said. “I personally find it very troubling. Since the supervision in April 2025, we are seeing fewer and fewer of those meetings and we are seeing more restrictions. They are not being livestreamed.”

She added: “I think that’s a problem in terms of accountability and transparency in terms of decisions that are made.”

The school board was placed under provincial supervision in April 2025 by the Ministry of Education in the wake of a costly three-day retreat to Toronto by top officials in the summer of 2024.

An audit by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP found “indications of potential financial mismanagement,” the province said.

Following the supervision order, the school board cancelled almost all of its public committee meetings except for special education and parent advisory committee meetings. Audit committee meetings are considered public, but almost all of the work is conducted in closed sessions.

“I made this decision to maintain meetings that are productive, professional, and focused on improving student success and achievement, rather than serving as a forum for political commentary,” Education Minister Paul Calandra said in an email in October 2025.

London-area trustee Lori-Ann Pizzolato was on the special education advisory committee for six years before she and the board’s other trustees lost their roles under the supervision order.

“The lack of streaming is frustrating and disappointing,” she said. “This shows a lack of transparency. The public has a right to know what is going on and why the budget is the way it is.”

When asked earlier this year about the lack of livestreaming, the board’s new chief executive officer, Kevin Auckland, said he would discuss it with board supervisor Paul Boniferro this fall.

“At that time, we will discuss what the state of how things will be,” he said. “Some of the decisions are not necessarily going to be my decision, but we will know more as I walk into the position.”

The chair of the London District Catholic school board said all of its meetings, including its special education advisory committee meetings, are open to the public in person and streamed through a link provided by the board upon request.

“Families can attend, participate, and see decisions made firsthand,” Gabe Pizzuti said.

Officials at the Thames Valley District school board directed The Free Press to the Ministry of Education for more information about why meetings were still not being livestreamed.

The ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
