stories.title: London mayor hopeful Susan Stevenson takes aim at tax hikes with new pledge
stories.summary: "Those increases stay on the bill, families keep paying for them long after budget day is over."
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
London mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson speaks during the launch of her campaign in London on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Geoff Robins/The London Free Press

London mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson on Wednesday unveiled her campaign pledge on property taxes while assailing the tax hikes Londoners have faced over the past four years.

Speaking to reporters Wednesday at her downtown campaign office, Stevenson promised that if elected she would hold property tax increases under one per cent in her first two years in office, while committing to the rate of inflation or less in the final two years.

She specifically called out London’s 8.7 and 7.3 per cent tax hikes in 2024 and 2025, respectively, saying they far exceeded the rate of inflation over the same period.

For buyers, sellers, renters and dreamers — London's complex, fascinating real estate market is brought into focus and into context with this newsletter.

By signing up, you consent to receive the above newsletter from Postmedia Network Inc.

A welcome email is on its way. If you don't see it, please check your junk folder.

The next issue of Homes in London will soon be in your inbox.

We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try again

“Those increases stay on the bill, families keep paying for them long after budget day is over,” she said. “Today, I am setting the commitment and standard of accountability. The detailed work will identify the savings. Each annual budget will show the choices and what they mean for the years ahead.”

More specifically, Stevenson, who has been the Ward 4 councillor this term, is pledging to review the city’s reserve funds, department budgets, and expand the property tax deferral program to more low-income households – the latter of which was narrowly defeated by council previously.

Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson was photographed during an announcement at her campaign headquarters in downtown London on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Jack Moulton/The London Free Press)

In the 2010 mayoral race, Joe Fontana successfully ran on a promise of property tax freezes during the term. He was only able to deliver freezes for two of four years, while later politicians derided the freezes as merely delaying tax hikes.

Wednesday, Stevenson did not suggest any concrete ideas for where the savings could come from, but said a more detailed budget could help find savings, both in one-time funding or permanent savings.

“I don’t think Londoners are going to find it hard to believe that we could find some wasteful or duplicative programs or services in the city’s $1.5-billion budget,” she said.

City hall already conducts an annual service review of its operations, often yielding several million dollars in savings. This term’s council also convened a working group to find savings in the budget and barely came up with anything.

Many of the proposed savings brought to council included cuts to things like road and park maintenance, street lights, and closing the city’s wading pools – something politicians mostly shied away from.

On the goal of that working group, Stevenson said she was disappointed at the lack of detail brought forward.

Stevenson said she “won’t touch” services Londoners depend on, such as garbage pickup or traffic calming – instead emphasizing that savings can be found through more detailed financial reporting while singling out the cost of items like the bus rapid transit shelters, the housing collaborative initiative, and the special constables feasibility study.

“In fact, we need improvements in those basic services. So, where is the $1.5 billion going? Where are the leaks?” she said. “As a councillor, we’ve looked at resident requests, they would like an extra garbage can at the park, they would like some traffic calming on their street. Oftentimes, the answer is there’s no room in the budget.”

For police spending, which was responsible for a significant portion of the higher tax hikes in 2024 and 2025, she said it’s one of the city’s budget priorities, and the rest of the city’s spending should be based around it.

Stevenson, 59, is running to beat Mayor Josh Morgan, who is seeking a second term as the city’s top politician. During his campaign launch event, the 48-year-old Morgan pledged to keep tax hikes “within the three per cent range” over the term if re-elected.

In addition to Morgan and Stevenson, the other 10 registered mayoral candidates are John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Kirsten Krose, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam and Mustafa Zeboon. Voters go to the polls on Oct. 26.

stories.title: What does it mean for Canada to become EU’s first associate member
stories.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen says the two sides would create a ‘common prosperity and economic space’
stories.author: Julia Payne
stories.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the European Union’s first “associate member.”

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney – who was in Strasbourg to listen to von der Leyen’s annual State of the Union address – said Canada was seeking a “unique alliance” with the EU but not membership.

There is currently no such status as “associate member” set out in the European Union’s treaties – though various versions of an associate-type of membership have been floated in the bloc over the years.

Most recently, Germany suggested Ukraine be an associate member as an interim stage to full accession, though the proposal failed to gain traction as some EU capitals pushed back.

EU chief calls for Canada to become bloc’s first associate member

Carney is seeking new alliances amid repeated threats by U.S. President Donald Trump against Canada’s sovereignty.

Both sides want to forge deeper co-operation to counter U.S. and Chinese economic dominance as well as preserve democracy and the rules-based international order, which they see as under threat.

In her speech, von der Leyen said the two sides would create a “common prosperity and economic space.” This would include joint work on manufacturing, a tech alliance, integration of defence industrial bases, the Arctic, AI, energy and critical minerals.

Canada and the European Union are working on what Prime Minister Mark Carney, has called a 'unique alliance'. Here's more on what that means and why the two powers have drawn closer together.

Implementing such an ’associate’ status would be unprecedented and May be legally complex.

Von der Leyen was speaking in her capacity as President of the European Commission, the bloc’s executive arm. It would fall on the EU member states to decide whether the idea flies.

There is no suggestion von der Leyen is proposing enshrining the status of ’associate member’ in EU treaties. That would require unanimity among all 27 capitals and ratification by all domestically.

Canada and the EU already have a trade agreement, called Ceta. More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it.

Opinion: If Canada joins the European Union show, it will only be from the upper balcony

If Canada wishes to become locked into the EU’s Single Market, Ottawa would need to reconcile Canada’s norms and regulations to match EU law.

Canada would become a rule-taker with no say on policy if it entered the Single Market without full membership like Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein who are members of the European Economic Area.

Canada’s rules have historically been geared toward its biggest trade partner, the United States.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen opened a path for Canada to become the first associate member of the European Union as part of a new 'alliance for the future.'

European Commission

The quest for a deeper alliance between Canada and the EU will not impact the path to accession for European candidate states – but it May serve as an irritant if Canada is perceived to be getting special treatment.

Accession negotiations and aligning with EU norms is a long process that often requires candidate nations to push through politically sensitive reform.

Full membership can only be granted to European states and provides access to the bloc’s €18-trillion Single Market, voting and representation, EU funding and legal recourse to the European Court of Justice.

Ukraine saw Germany’s proposal for “associate membership” as “unfair” as Kyiv would participate but with no voting rights.

The EU has said it could admit new members as soon as 2030. Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova are the most advanced among candidate countries.

stories.title: What is an 'associate member' of the EU? Nobody in Europe seems to have a clue
stories.summary: European journalists, political staffers and MEPs were left scratching their heads about what it actually meant.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Strasbourg, France — What does it mean for Canada to become an “associate member” of the European Union? At the European parliament, no one seems to have a clue.

And while some members of the continental parliament seem excited at the prospect, the move has blindsided European governments, who were never asked to sign off on the announcement and are struggling to understand what it means , according to media reports.

On Wednesday morning, EU President Ursula von der Leyen officially extended an invitation for Canada to become an “associate member” of the 27-state block. The result of that invitation — and ongoing negotiations between both parties — is expected to be announced at a Canada-EU summit in Montreal in late October.

The announcement by the EU head was cheered by most of the hundreds of members of European parliament (MEP) in the room for her State of the European Union speech. In their replies to von der Leyen’s speech, many Parliamentary leaders celebrated the news.

But after the fact, European journalists, political staffers and MEPs were left scratching their heads about what it actually meant for Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU — a status that does not exist.

“It is a new category,” summarized Teresa Ribera, the European Commissioner for Competitiveness and a key figure in von der Leyen’s Commission. “What being an associated member today could mean will need to be developed and detailed in the time to come.”

She, like a half-dozen other MEPs interviewed by National Post after von der Leyen’s speech, was elated at the push between the EU and Canada to deepen their relationship unlike any other non-European country.

But as to what that actually looks like, no one seems to have a clue beyond Carney and von der Leyen.

As confusion reigned on both sides of the Atlantic, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote on social media that Carney “can’t seem to get his story straight about the ‘associate membership,’ ‘unique alliance,’ or whatever else he is negotiating with the EU.”

“But no EU taxes, no EU laws, and no EU open-border immigration policies should be imposed on Canadians. Canada must be independent and sovereign. Period,” wrote Poilievre.

Tobias Cremer, a centre-left German MEP who sponsored a spring resolution urging closer Canada-EU ties, said no one knows what “associate member” means, but it’s “provocative” — and he likes that.

“The signal should really be that we want as close in lines with Canada as possible. But I also think it might it will be interesting how it will be spelled out… It’s the first time that we are doing these things with non-geographically European countries.”

Speaking to reporters Wednesday afternoon, Canada’s incoming ambassador to the EU Jonathan Wilkinson explained that “associate member” was a name chosen by the Europeans to define the new deepening alliance.

After the Wall Street Journal reported last week that Carney and the EU were working towards an “associate membership” for Canada, the prime minister came out firmly denying that he was seeking any kind of formal membership within the European bloc.

“I think we’re still a ways away from actually landing on what we think is the best way to describe it,” Wilkinson said while avoiding to use the terms “associate member”.

A key concern with any form of membership in the EU would be submitting Canada to the union’s legendarily heavy regulatory regime in a wide swath of sectors.

Wilkinson said that there was a chance Canada would be bound by at least some of the EU’s regulations.

“It depends on the sector. We are focused on the things that we think we can make a lot of progress in the short term. Of course, there aren’t a lot of sectors in which we’d need to change regulations… But we can make progress without a lot of change to regulations,” Wilkinson said.

But what the final deal looks like is still up in the air, with both Canada and the EU submitting proposals as to how they could further collaborate short of fully integrating Canada into the union, the incoming ambassador said.

Dutch Labour politician Thijs Reuten said that he expects the new deal in the works with Canada will probably be extended to other interested non-EU countries eventually as well.

The important thing is that the countries share the same fundamental values.

“However, we need to see what is in the details of this, and surely how it also links to the most important topic, in my opinion: our collective defence and security,” Reuten said.

Virginijus Sinkevicius, an MEP from Lithuania, said the potential of a new class of EU member could be an opportunity to rethink the EU project.

A new, deeper relationship with Canada could lead to more labour and academic mobility between countries.

“But I think we start with the free movement of goods,” Sinkevicius said.

Could other non-EU countries, such as Ukraine or the U.K., eventually achieve associate member status?

“Who knows? Potentially. Who knows? It May be the case,” said Teresa Ribera, the first executive vice-president of the European Commission for a Clean, Just, and Competitive Transition and the European Commissioner for Competitiveness.

stories.title: $1.4B of federal grants spent on research about Justin Trudeau's speeches, Canadian dancefloors, and low-carbon videogames: CTF
stories.summary: The federal government will spend $1.4 billion this year on research funding for studies on ancient temple brewers and low-carbon videogames.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
And an analysis of federal grant data by the Canadian Taxpayers Federation (CTF) reveals this money is being spent on ancient temple brewers, Arctic climate comics, low-carbon videogames and Justin Trudeau’s speeches, to name a few of the research topics the government is funding.

The Sshrc is a federal agency that promotes and supports research in the humanities and social sciences through its funding opportunities, and the government says Sshrc-funded research provides “insights on the issues that matter most to Canadians.”

However, CTF questions how many of the funded topics resonate with Canadians. “Studies about climate comics and the state of Canadian dancefloors don’t sound like studies that matter most to Canadians like the government claims,” said Franco Terrazzano, CTF federal director.

“A government that can find $30,987 for temple brewers in ancient Mesopotamia can find savings for Canadian taxpayers,” he adds.

Terrazzano is referring to a study on “struggling temple brewers in sixth century BCE Mesopotamia” by a researcher at University of Toronto and was awarded the sum by the federal government in a February 2026 competition .

Among the other projects mentioned are a Quebec-based study on the “state of the dancefloor in Canada” that was awarded $78,623 in funding, and University of Calgary research on Arctic climate comics that was granted $88,591.

Elsewhere, Sshrc gave a University of Ottawa professor $43,693 to study the “contested meaning” of former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s speeches. The research will analyze 326 Trudeau speeches, tracking how he used terms including “feminist,” “reconciliation,” “protest” and “freedom.”

Taxpayer group calls for Carney to cut the cord on CBC, Senate, past GGs

'Wasteful' government spending on 'corporate welfare' could be replaced by business tax relief: study

Meanwhile, a Concordia University professor who had previously published work imagining water had constitutional rights has been awarded $99,850 for a new study titled “A Liquid Frontier: Water Governance through Choral Storytelling,” and an Alberta-based professor who previously built a solar-powered server on her apartment balcony to host “low-carbon videogames” was given $37,275.

CTF also questions how relevant the government-funded research is for Canadians, given that at least 50 research projects awarded funding in 2026 focused on topics in other countries. These grants cost taxpayers nearly $3.9 million, CTF says.

The projects include $93,467 to create a digital edition of a 1908 book about Sri Lankan art and $65,833 to study Western-style sweets in “modern Japan and beyond.”

“The Sshrc is little more than a subsidy for academics to work on their pet projects that nobody else will read,” Terrazzano said in a scathing assessment.

Referring to $105,000 in funding awarded to a Simon Fraser University study in 2018 , he added: “Just because nobody will voluntarily pay to study the birth, life and death of a grocery cart, that doesn’t mean taxpayers should be forced to.”

Meanwhile, CTF points out that Sshrc’s $1.4 billion is on top of the $17.9 billion the federal government expects to send to the provinces through the Canada Social Transfer in 2026/27. The CST is intended to support post-secondary education, as well as social assistance and social services, and early childhood development, early learning and childcare.

This CTF analysis comes after the taxpayers’ watchdog submitted its pre-budget recommendations to the federal government, which call for around $60-billion in annual spending cuts.

It also calls for slashing the costs of the federal bureaucracy and Parliament itself to reduce the costs of the fast-growing federal debt, with measures including returning salaries and benefits for federal politicians to 2020 levels and reducing the governor general’s salary to that of cabinet ministers ($264,000).

“The massive accumulation of debt is due to a government spending problem, not a revenue problem,” the Ctf’s submission states.

The Carney government’s second budget is expected to be released within the next couple of months.

stories.title: At Massey Hall, Sara Bareilles walked audiences through her grief – and shepherded them through their own
stories.summary: Bareilles, best known for the affable pop music that made her famous in the late 2000s, offered an intimate concert rooted in loss
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
We should have known what we were in for. At Sara Bareilles’s intimate concert at Toronto’s Massey Hall on Tuesday night, free packets of Bareilles-branded tissues were available for the taking at stations around the venue. You’re going to cry , the stacked Kleenex seemed to warn. Best take one of us before you do.

On the whole, Bareilles is not known for being sad. Her piano-heavy back catalogue deals jointly in affable doo-wop pop and musical theatre; her fashion choices, Tuesday night’s Charlie Chaplin-adjacent bowler hat included, tend toward twee.

But in August, Bareilles released Good Grief , an album that explores the specific pain of loss in all its shades. The record’s themes are as tough as you’d expect – feelings about death and dying intertwine with longing for a pre-Donald Trump United States – but the bluesy humour for which Bareilles became famous in the late 2000s sparkles across the album. (Could any other artist pull off a smiley, jazz-tinged croon about a nervous breakdown? I’d wager not.)

Sara Bareilles grieves both a friend and the U.S. on her new album

On Tuesday, her first concert in Toronto since 2013, Bareilles sang through most of Good Grief and a few longstanding hits, welcoming us to join her on the road to inner peace. Loss, she explained, is best managed in community with others, an idea investigated at length on her latest album: “Tell me your story, I’ll tell you mine,” she implores on Home, the record’s opening track and the first song on its accompanying tour’s setlist.

It’s not that Tuesday’s tour stop was uniformly tearful. In fact, for much of its two-hour-plus runtime, the gig felt surprisingly airy, a dual showcase of Bareilles’s satiny voice and sharp wit. A jaunty Whitney Houston cover – you can guess of what song – saw Massey Hall transform into a 2,500-person dance party, creating a brightly-lit partition between Bareilles’s new record and the assortment of past chart-toppers at the end of her set. Playful jokes from the audience, too, were answered rather than ignored.

Even Good Grief ’s saddest songs, lush with complex instrumentation, betrayed a striking sort of weightlessness: Still Crying saw Bareilles repeatedly hit a high B-flat, seemingly without even blinking. (“That song is sponsored by high notes,” she quipped between long sips of water while the audience roared.)

But Bareilles, 46, has spent the last decade working through real pain. She’s lost friends; she’s struggled with infertility; she’s seen her country devolve into a strange facsimile of its past ideals. “I want to be able to love my country,” she said between songs, vaguely condemning Trump without ever saying his name. Of the types of grief she claims as hers, “grief of country” is among the most cutting, she said.

Celine Dion makes emotional return to stage after six years

Where the night got weepy was in pretaped recordings submitted by fans and played over the venue’s speakers between songs: “Remember answering machines?” cracked Bareilles as she introduced the project. In each recording, an anonymous stranger – a widower in his 80s, a parent-to-be at the finish line of a gruelling IVF journey – unleashed their experiences of loss.

Some of the voicemails suggested acceptance; others conveyed feelings of rage, denial, depression. Carefully curated to complement the themes of Bareilles’s new album – Ladies in a Line ’s fed-up account of trying to conceive, Just a Kid ’s requiem for a friend who died far too young from cancer – the voice memos felt like vital supplementary material for the record, never cheesy or extractive in their emotional wallop.

When Bareilles closed her eyes to listen, undoubtedly for the dozenth or so time, there was no doubt she was hearing each story with fresh ears – that some new detail had connected with her as free tissue packets crinkled in the otherwise silent audience.

Even a more cynical critic would struggle to find evidence that Bareilles is not as warm offstage as she is when she sings. Her first words on Tuesday night – “Hello, Toronto!” excluded – were effusive thanks for the crew who managed to fit a set designed for larger spaces on Massey’s cozy stage. When an audience member loudly requested a song Bareilles had no intention of playing – You Matter to Me , a duet from her musical Waitress – she sweetly declined before leading the venue in a short, a cappella singalong of the ballad’s chorus.

In a time of profound suffering – on personal, political and global levels – there’s something to be said in favour of a big cry and kindness for kindness’ sake. Deeply sentimental and unexpectedly funny, Bareilles’s Toronto tour stop offered fans a community to trade stories of heartache, both with each other and with Bareilles herself. Never before has grief felt so good.

stories.title: Cost of Alberta separation could be up to $170B: report
stories.summary: The report looks at two scenarios involving how separation would occur, but in both cases the short-term costs of leaving Confederation would be high.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
An independent report into the possible separation of Alberta presents multiple outcomes, but ultimately determines the cost to leave Canada could cost up to $170 billion.

The report by the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy was commissioned by the Alberta government and released Wednesday.

It found Albertans would face high costs in the short term with uncertain benefits in the long run, and whether talks with Canada are “smooth” or “difficult” would impact that future.

“If you’re kind of a very optimistic person — you think everyone will go well — there’s a scenario where that happens,” said Tim Sargent with the University of Calgary School of Public Policy.

“But there’s also a very big risk that thing could not go well and Alberta could pay a very big price.”

Two hypothetical scenarios are given to provide Albertans a look into the costs that come with separation.

A “smooth” scenario would see a quick, comprehensive and favourable deal with Canada that gives an orderly transition of the province to become a separate country.

The “difficult” path would see Canada and other countries be hostile and could result in a deal taking a much longer time if one is reached at all.

“It all depends on a lot of events that are outside the control of Alberta,” Sargent said.

1:46 Alberta Business Council urges residents to choose Canada ahead of referendum

In either situation, the report said establishing a new country could range from $50 billion up to $170 billion in the first five years of separation, in addition to the impacts on economic growth and the province’s own fiscal position.

If Alberta experiences the “difficult” scenario though, the report paints a stark picture.

The GDP would see a loss within five years of 10.1 per cent, employment could drop by 10 per cent, a typical worker could earn almost $5,500 less than if the province had not separated, and the tax each person pays could increase up to $5,500 annually.

Get expert insights, Q&A on markets, housing, inflation, and personal finance information delivered to you every Saturday.

After 20 years, the report suggests while unemployment would decline, many people would depart the workforce, leaving the unemployment rate at 4.7 per cent.

Annual wages for a typical worker could be almost $12,000 below what they could have been without separation and taxes per person would rise by $6,600. The province’s GDP would also fall by 16.2 per cent.

The government’s debt would hit $442.3 billion in this scenario, which includes its preexisting share of the federal debt plus the deficits that come with transition costs.

2:01 Alberta NDP upsets UCP stronghold in byelection

Under the “smooth” path, the report could see the province maintain access to major trade markets, expand its resource development, and provide government services more efficiently.

But it also finds Alberta’s gross domestic product (GDP) could be lower by about 2.2 per cent within five years, with employment 0.7 per cent lower than it currently is, take-home pay could see a dip of more than $1,200 annually and each taxpayer would pay about $800 more.

After about 20 years, the report estimated the GDP would increase by 3.4 per cent, employment would go up by 0.7 per cent and the taxes Albertans pay would decrease by $1,100. Take-home pay for workers could also rise by more than $1,800 annually compared to what they would have been.

Even with these apparent benefits, Alberta’s debt would soar to $324.1 billion.

Independence supporter Keith Wilson say the report is inaccurate, adding Alberta’s resources give it leverage in any discussions with other provinces and nations.

“The overall theme of the report is to make worst-case assumptions about workers, about the buildings the federal government has, about how negotiations would go,” Wilson said.

Jeffrey Rath, one of the driving forces behind the separatism movement, said supporters of independence are already improving conditions for Alberta to become its own nation.

“That’s why we were flying to the United States to meet with the U.S. State Department in Washington,” Rath said. “I’m still in contact with them on a regular basis.

“The simple fact is, the United States would welcome a robust trading relationship with Alberta.”

2:01 Foreign interference intensifies ahead of Alberta separation vote

Those who worked on the report aren’t so sure.

“”Nobody can confidently say that they will know what will happen,” Sargent said.

An expert advisory panel was appointed to review the report and prepare an independent assessment.

“The panel concurs that separation results in short run economic costs for Alberta for uncertain net benefits in the longer run. However, we also stress that Canadians should be aware that Alberta’s separation will undoubtedly harm Canada as well,” said Jack Mintz, chair of the advisory panel.

Alberta assuming responsibility for federal programs, determining its monetary policy, building international trade relationships, and holding negotiations around Canadian debt were among the issues analyzed by the report.

According to the report, setting up a new country would also require “significant” transition costs, the purchase of office buildings, new IT systems and an added 70,000 public servants.

“The uncertainties do look significant, the risks look significant and the potential benefit is far from certain,” said Mount Royal University political scientist Lori Williams.

“Alberta is going to be worse-off for the short-term — however long that lasts — and more importantly, there’s no guarantee Alberta will be better off.”

2:29 Immigrant groups say racism increasing in Alberta, is linked to independence referendum

Treasury Board President and Finance Minister Jason Nixon said in a statement following the release of the report that it gives “important considerations” for Albertans as they prepare to vote in the upcoming Oct. 19 referendum.

He also said the advisory panel’s own insights will help Albertans interpret the report.

“The panel’s assessment emphasizes that both the scenarios outlined in the report highlight how costly it would be for Alberta to separate from Canada in the short term and also highlight the substantial amount of uncertainty Alberta would face in the long term,” Nixon said.

Albertans are set to vote in the Oct. 19 referendum, in which one question asks voters whether Alberta should stay in Canada or hold a second binding referendum to quit Confederation.

— with files from The Canadian Press and Karen Bartko, Global News

stories.title: First batch of B.C. law students takes course over bar exam as Ontario mulls switch
stories.summary: B.C. is the sixth province to scrap the bar exam in favour of a four-phase program meant to assess legal knowledge, advocacy, ethics, practice management and other skills.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
While the jury’s still out on a proposal to replace the Ontario bar exam with a skills-based course, law schools in British Columbia have made the switch, with the first batch of students set to experience the new system this fall.

B.C. is the sixth province to scrap the bar exam in favour of a four-phase program meant to assess legal knowledge, advocacy, ethics, practice management and other skills, following in the footsteps of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and Nunavut.

The province’s law society announced the change last October, saying training for the bar needed to be brought up to date as the needs of students — and the skills required to practise law — had evolved.

The news came about a month after its Ontario counterpart floated a similar shift as a better alternative to revamping the bar exam, which consists of two tests on separate days.

The proposal divided Ontario’s legal profession at the time, with some arguing the multiple-choice, open-book exam evaluates reading speed rather than legal know-how, while others argued it represents an objective assessment of students’ knowledge of the law regardless of its shortcomings.

Consultations on the proposed switch wrapped in January, and the Law Society of Ontario said last month it had not reached a decision, nor did it have a time frame to make the call.

In B.C., where the new program also replaces a full-time, 10-week course, some recent graduates said that while there are pros and cons to both systems, it would be best if the assessment process was consistent across Canada.

“I honestly think it would be better to have a standardized kind of style of testing — either everyone’s doing a bar exam or everyone’s doing a skills-based course. I think that would make things more cohesive and just easier for people as they transition across provinces,” said Sydney Dahrouge, who went to law school in Alberta before completing the bar training and exam as well as articling in B.C.

The current patchwork of assessments “makes things confusing,” Dahrouge said in a recent interview.

Though the program now offers more flexibility, some of her law school friends in Alberta struggled to get through the skills-based course while completing their articling, a mandatory job placement for graduates to learn the ropes from experienced lawyers, she said.

“They found it really challenging to have it integrated while they were working … 10- to 12-hour days at work, having to go home and study, do these assessments or assignments,” she said.

In the last few years, law students in Alberta have had the option to take an accelerated, full-time version of the course before starting their articling term, a development that came after students reported challenges juggling both sets of demands.

Students in B.C. also have the same choice. The first full-time program was scheduled to start this month, with the next cycle set for February, while the part-time version is planned for May.

Richard Jiang, who was in the same articling cohort as Dahrouge, said his work experience has made him believe a more practical approach might be more helpful than the traditional exam, especially given the increasing use of artificial intelligence in law firms.

Passing the bar exam depended on navigating an index quickly, a skill that’s now obsolete when AI “can scan an entire legal database and pull a set of relevant cases or the precise rule in a few seconds,” Jiang, who attended the University of British Columbia’s Peter A. Allard School of Law, said in an email.

“AI handles the retrieval; the role of the junior (lawyer) is shifting more and more towards judgment, drafting, and other aspects of practice that traditionally came later,” he said.

Focusing on practical assignments can likely better gauge a student’s thought process, communication, presentation and ethics, among other measures, he said.

While there’s a risk of inconsistencies in marking compared to a multiple-choice, black-and-white exam, Jiang said he believes “the shift away from exam-based assessment isn’t a lowering of standards, it’s a realignment of standards with the actual demands of modern practice.”

Still, both Jiang and Dahrouge said the transition from one system to the other might prove bumpy for the first cohort. In a profession that relies heavily on mentorship, no one will be able to tell students what to expect or how to prepare, they said.

“They’re kind of the first test subjects of like, how is this going to go? How are things going to work?” Dahrouge said. “But I think if you just do the work, you do what they are telling you to do, you do your studying … I’m sure everyone will do great.”

Students in B.C. also have the same choice. The first full-time program was scheduled to start this month, with the next cycle set for February, while the part-time version is planned for May.

Richard Jiang, who was in the same articling cohort as Dahrouge, said his work experience has made him believe a more practical approach might be more helpful than the traditional exam, especially given the increasing use of artificial intelligence in law firms.

Passing the bar exam depended on navigating an index quickly, a skill that’s now obsolete when AI “can scan an entire legal database and pull a set of relevant cases or the precise rule in a few seconds,” Jiang, who attended the University of British Columbia’s Peter A. Allard School of Law, said in an email.
“AI handles the retrieval; the role of the junior (lawyer) is shifting more and more towards judgment, drafting, and other aspects of practice that traditionally came later,” he said.
Focusing on practical assignments can likely better gauge a student’s thought process, communication, presentation and ethics, among other measures, he said.

While there’s a risk of inconsistencies in marking compared to a multiple-choice, black-and-white exam, Jiang said he believes “the shift away from exam-based assessment isn’t a lowering of standards, it’s a realignment of standards with the actual demands of modern practice.”

Still, both Jiang and Dahrouge said the transition from one system to the other might prove bumpy for the first cohort. In a profession that relies heavily on mentorship, no one will be able to tell students what to expect or how to prepare, they said.

“They’re kind of the first test subjects of like, how is this going to go? How are things going to work?” Dahrouge said. “But I think if you just do the work, you do what they are telling you to do, you do your studying … I’m sure everyone will do great.”

stories.title: Federal government invests $76 million in national basketball centre in Toronto
stories.summary: The facility will be the future home of Canada Basketball, with six gymnasiums for provincial, national and international basketball.
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
Jamaica’s Tyran De Lattibeaudiere (23) defends against Canada’s Dillon Brooks (24) during Fiba world cup qualification action in Hamilton, Monday, July 6, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Nick Iwanyshyn The Canadian Press

By The Canadian Press

Posted September 16, 2026 12:21 pm.

The federal government is investing $76 million into a new national basketball centre at Humber Polytechnic’s North Campus in Toronto.

It will be the future home of Canada Basketball, with six gymnasiums for provincial, national and international basketball.

The facility will include a high-performance training centre, a domed playing field and other spaces for community, academic and athletic uses.

The money for the project comes from the federal government’s Build Communities Strong Fund, which provides $51 billion over the next 10 years and $3 billion per year after that, to build and renew public infrastructure.

Humber previously provided temporary training space for the national basketball teams.

Canada Basketball president and chief executive officer Michael Bartlett said in a statement that a permanent home can help Canada become the best in the world in the sport.

stories.title: ‘The PM’s on fire’: Ford praises Pearson privatization, wants same approach for Toronto’s Billy Bishop airport
stories.summary: Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport has been at the centre of political debate with past disputes over runway expansion and development.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Ontario Doug Ford said he's on board with the federal government's plan to allow private investment to operate four of Canada's largest airports, saying Toronto's Billy Bishop should be next.

By Lucas Casaletto

Posted September 16, 2026 12:18 pm.

Premier Doug Ford says he is fully supportive of the federal government’s move toward privatizing major Canadian airports, signaling he intends to push Ottawa to extend the same approach to Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport.

Ford made the comments at an unrelated press conference in Toronto on Wednesday, responding to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s proposal to maintain ownership but allow for private investment and operations at four of Canada’s largest airports, including Toronto Pearson International Airport.

“I have to give credit where credit is due: the PM is on fire,” Ford said.

Carney wants private investors to run Canada’s four largest airports

Federal government rejects Ford’s Billy Bishop airport expansion plan

Construction to begin on Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport runway safety buffer zones

“He’s moving. He’s lowering taxes like we have done for years. He’s privatizing airports, which should have been done years ago, but there’s one airport that has to be privatized and that’s Billy Bishop.”

On Tuesday, Carney said Canada must rethink how airports are funded and operated. He stated his government is examining ways to bring private capital into airport operations to help fund expansions, improve passenger experience, and reduce bottlenecks.

“We will reinvest the tens of billions of dollars of capital that we raise into infrastructure that Canada needs for the next generation,” Carney said in his speech, noting new funding would support more regional airports in the country.

The federal plan includes exploring private‑sector involvement at Toronto Pearson International Airport, Vancouver International Airport, Montréal‑Trudeau International Airport, and Calgary International Airport.

Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport has been at the centre of political debate for more than a decade with past disputes involving runway expansion, waterfront development, and noise concerns.

“It’s shovel ready,” Ford said on Wednesday.

“$5 to $7 billion of private investment, not costing the taxpayers anything, creating thousands and thousands of jobs, so I look forward to sitting down with [Carney] when he gets back.”

Ford also expressed his confidence in “more effective, more efficient airports.”

“That was the prime minister’s decision that I support 1,000 per cent,” the premier continued.

“Hopefully, at lower cost. I always believe the market dictates. The people will determine. There’s nothing better than competition.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford speaks at an event at Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport on Monday March 23, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Frank Gunn

Premier Doug Ford says he is fully supportive of the federal government’s move toward privatizing major Canadian airports, signaling he intends to push Ottawa to extend the same approach to Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport.

Ford made the comments at an unrelated press conference in Toronto on Wednesday, responding to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s proposal to maintain ownership but allow for private investment and operations at four of Canada’s largest airports, including Toronto Pearson International Airport.
“I have to give credit where credit is due: the PM is on fire,” Ford said.

items: Carney wants private investors to run Canada’s four largest airports
Federal government rejects Ford’s Billy Bishop airport expansion plan
Construction to begin on Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport runway safety buffer zones

content_blocks.text: “He’s moving. He’s lowering taxes like we have done for years. He’s privatizing airports, which should have been done years ago, but there’s one airport that has to be privatized and that’s Billy Bishop.”

On Tuesday, Carney said Canada must rethink how airports are funded and operated. He stated his government is examining ways to bring private capital into airport operations to help fund expansions, improve passenger experience, and reduce bottlenecks.

“We will reinvest the tens of billions of dollars of capital that we raise into infrastructure that Canada needs for the next generation,” Carney said in his speech, noting new funding would support more regional airports in the country.
Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport: A long‑running political flashpoint

The federal plan includes exploring private‑sector involvement at Toronto Pearson International Airport, Vancouver International Airport, Montréal‑Trudeau International Airport, and Calgary International Airport.
Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport has been at the centre of political debate for more than a decade with past disputes involving runway expansion, waterfront development, and noise concerns.
“It’s shovel ready,” Ford said on Wednesday.
“$5 to $7 billion of private investment, not costing the taxpayers anything, creating thousands and thousands of jobs, so I look forward to sitting down with [Carney] when he gets back.”
Ford also expressed his confidence in “more effective, more efficient airports.”
“That was the prime minister’s decision that I support 1,000 per cent,” the premier continued.
“Hopefully, at lower cost. I always believe the market dictates. The people will determine. There’s nothing better than competition.”

stories.title: Alberta separation could cost up to $170-billion over first five years, report estimates
stories.summary: University of Calgary authors present two scenarios for secession – ‘smooth’ and ‘difficult’ paths – in report commissioned by province
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Abandoning Confederation and setting up a sovereign country would cost Alberta up to $170-billion over the first five years of independence and would devastate the economy of a shrunken Canada, a report commissioned by the provincial government estimates.

And even in the best-case scenario, the report says secession would provide only minimal economic gains for Alberta. In a more painful separation, wages would plummet, GDP would decline precipitously and government debt would balloon.

The province on Wednesday published the report, which was produced by an independent panel of experts at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy.

The report provides a wide range of estimated costs to separation, painting one relatively rosy scenario in which Ottawa co-operates in negotiations and gives the province a favourable deal, and another in which Alberta and Canada enter hostile, prolonged talks that bring the country’s economy to a standstill.

Alberta is currently in the midst of a heated campaign over provincial separation, with voters preparing to decide on Oct. 19 whether to remain in Canada or lay the legal groundwork for a second, binding referendum.

Support for separation in Alberta, estimated to be between 25 and 30 per cent, has remained steady for years. The referendum arrives at a time of heightened concerns over national unity and threats to Canadian sovereignty in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation rhetoric.

Quebec voters, meanwhile, are roughly three weeks from a provincial election. The sovereigntist Parti Québécois has led in the polls for the better part of three years but currently seems unlikely to form a majority government. In June, the party published its 524-page Livre bleu – its latest blueprint for independence.

Martha Hall Findlay, director of the UofC’s School of Public Policy, wrote in the Alberta report that the document is non-partisan. It “neither advocates for, nor opposes, separation,” she wrote.

Tim Sargent, the report’s lead author, said in an interview that one of the biggest challenges during the exercise was finding real-world scenarios that could accurately inform the outcomes of a possible Alberta divorce from Canada.

Over the past year, numerous groups and voices in Alberta’s separatism debate have jockeyed to pin down the consequences of secession; the report is the first comprehensive analysis published by an academic institution.

“You’re really staring in the crystal ball,” Mr. Sargent said.

The report says that establishing a separate Alberta could cost between $50-billion and $170-billion in the first five years. It also says Alberta’s debt would hit roughly $324-billion in the best-case scenario and $442-billion if negotiations between the province and Canada aren’t friendly.

The rest of Canada, meanwhile, would be economically devastated by Alberta’s departure. The authors predict that Canada’s global economic standing would fall, its currency would weaken and that there would be major challenges to interprovincial and international trade routes.

The panel said its findings underline two key points: that separation would involve significant short-term costs, and that the long-term economic and fiscal consequences would be highly uncertain.

Alberta Finance Minister Jason Nixon pointed to that uncertainty in a Wednesday statement responding to the report.

“The panel’s assessment emphasizes that both the scenarios outlined in the report highlight how costly it would be for Alberta to separate from Canada in the short term and also highlight the substantial amount of uncertainty Alberta would face in the long term,” he wrote.

NDP finance critic Court Ellingson said in a statement that the report demonstrates that separatism is a “terrible idea for Alberta’s economy and families” and shows that the Oct. 19 referendum is a “waste of money.”

Alberta’s path to secession would largely rest on Ottawa’s reaction and its negotiation strategy, the report says. A “smooth” departure would require the Canadian government – in this case, motivated by providing certainty and limiting the economic damage – to quickly conclude negotiations with Alberta.

The “difficult” scenario, meanwhile, would likely see Ottawa limit its concessions to Alberta to discourage other provinces from leaving, which the authors say motivated the European Union’s approach when Britain voted to leave the bloc.

Prolonged negotiations would weigh on investment, interest rates and the exchange rate because investors would be hesitant to put money into Alberta and Canada until they had a clear picture of the future, the report says.

The vast range of potential outcomes is reflected in some of the estimates.

Under the “smooth” scenario, the authors expect that the Alberta government’s surplus over a 20-year horizon would be around $7.8-billion, while GDP would increase by about three per cent more than if Alberta had stayed in the country. The “difficult” scenario estimates that the province’s deficit would grow to $31-billion and GDP would contract by 16 per cent.

The report also ponders Alberta’s relationship with the U.S., things the new country would not need to spend money on – such as a Coast Guard – and how it would set up a military.

Alberta wouldn’t inherit assets such as fighter jets, which would “need to be acquired quickly,” the report says, and as a new country it would need to spend about $10-billion to meet Nato’s requirement that members spend 2 per cent of gross domestic product on defence. That would increase to $25-billion as Nato countries last year committed to investing 5 per cent of GDP annually on defence by 2035.

Keith Wilson, leader of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, said he feels that the report is “unrealistically pessimistic” because it ignores the province’s leverage in negotiations with the rest of Canada. Even the best-case scenario dismisses the province’s economic levers, he said.

“Canada does not have that economic strength. Alberta holds the cards here,” said Mr. Wilson, who recently published his own economic projections under what he called the Alberta Transition Council.

The relatively minor benefits outlined in the “smooth” scenario are highly unlikely and underline the limited upside of separation, Adam Legge, president of the Business Council of Alberta, said in an interview.

“The highest probability is that we would be landing somewhere in negative economic territory,” said Mr. Legge, a member of the report’s advisory panel.

Mr. Legge added that the best-case scenario was included to “insulate” the report from criticism that it only looked at the negative consequences of separation.

“It was really about ensuring that we enabled the report to stand the test of a challenge and not being a predetermined conclusion.”

The Toronto Maple Leafs medical staff had a busy off-season.

General manager John Chayka announced Wednesday that Max Domi failed his physical and will be out indefinitely.

Chayka added that the 31-year-old would address the situation publicly “at the right time in the near future.”

Domi underwent a procedure to deal with an injury that hampered him throughout the 2025-26 campaign. The team did not reveal the nature of the injury or surgery.

Domi has two years remaining on his contract with a $3.75-million cap hit.

In positive news for Leafs fans, veteran defenceman Chris Tanev has been given the green light from the medical staff to be on the ice to start training camp.

Tanev had core muscle surgery in March that forced him to miss the rest of the season. He struggled with injuries, which limited him to 11 games and 17:58 average ice time, the lowest since the 2012-13 season.

stories.title: Trump criticizes Canada over drugs but leaves it off list of drug-producing countries
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is again accusing Canada of not doing enough to clamp down on drugs but did not include it in a list of major drug-producing countries released today.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington — U.S. President Donald Trump is again accusing Canada of not doing enough to clamp down on drugs but did not include it in a list of major drug-producing countries released today.

The list, which is published each year, cites Afghanistan, China, Colombia, Guatemala, Haiti, Mexico and other nations deemed major drug producers.

In a declaration submitted to Congress, Trump praised the efforts of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum’s administration to stop the flow of drugs and shut down labs but said Mexico and Canada still need to do more.

Trump alleged that fentanyl is being made in clandestine Canadian labs and transported south into the United States, and claimed Chinese gangs are operating along the border.

U.S. government data shows a minuscule volume of drugs is seized at the northern border compared to the boundary with Mexico.

Trump used fentanyl as a reason to hit Canada with tariffs last year before the U.S. Supreme Court struck down those duties.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta separation could cost $170 billion in first 5 years: report
stories.summary: A report on Alberta’s separation from Canada finds establishing a new country would cost several tens of billions of dollars and as much as $170 billion in the first five years. However, the report also shows some long term benefits for Albertans. In addressing the report, the province says in a news release “the short-term […]
stories.author: Darren Rathwell
stories.content:
Posted September 16, 2026 12:03 pm.

A report on Alberta’s separation from Canada finds establishing a new country would cost several tens of billions of dollars and as much as $170 billion in the first five years.

However, the report also shows some long term benefits for Albertans. In addressing the report, the province says in a news release “the short-term impacts of potential separation would result in significant economic disruption and costs for Albertans.”

They add the report was commissioned by the Danielle Smith government to “provide Albertans with reliable, transparent information ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum”, and examine potential the potential economic impact of separation.

The University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy report says the cost of establishing a new country could range from $50 billion to $170 billion in the first five years following separation, and would be in addition to the impact on economic growth and Alberta’s fiscal position.

The report outlines a pair of scenarios for separation, a “smooth” and “difficult” transition, both of which are expected to be economically troublesome.

In the difficult case, the report anticipates limits on trade and market access that could create lasting economic challenges for both Alberta and Canada.

“Even after 20 years, employment could be nearly five per cent lower and Alberta’s economy more than 16 per cent smaller than if the province remained in Canada. Despite higher taxes, the government could face an ongoing annual budget deficit of more than $30 billion.”

A smoother transition could see Alberta possibly keeping access to major trade markets, as well as expand resource development depending on a positive climate. But long term benefits could be seen by Albertans with higher income and less taxes.

The report studied factors such as the costs of administering programs under federal jurisdiction, monetary policy, labour mobility and international trade relationships.

The province is also revealing the results of an advisory panel appointed to review the new report and prepare an independent assessment.

“The panel concurs that separation results in short run economic costs for Alberta for uncertain net benefits in the longer run. However, we also stress that Canadians should be aware that Alberta’s separation will undoubtedly harm Canada as well.” says the panel’s chair Dr. Jack Mintz in a statement.

The report can be read online.

stories.title: Teen in critical condition after e-scooter collides with SUV in Winnipeg
stories.summary: A teenager was taken to hospital in critical condition after a collision between an e-scooter and an SUV at Waverley Street and Lake Crest Road.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A teenager is suffering from life-threatening injuries after being struck by an SUV while riding an e-scooter in Winnipeg, police said.

The teen was crossing Waverley Stret at Lake Crest Road with their e-scooter Monday, when a 2010 Honda CRV heading southbound struck them, the Winnipeg Police Service (WPS) said in a news release. Officers responded to the reported collision around 9:30 p.m.

The e-scooter operator was taken to hospital in critical condition, where they remain as of Wednesday morning, WPS continued. The driver of the CRV, a person in their late teens, remained on the scene and spoke with investigators.

Anyone with dashcam or cell phone video is being asked to contact Winnipeg police’s traffic division.

stories.title: Montreal AI research institute denounces violence after office vandalized
stories.summary: Montreal — Hours after the office of a Quebec artificial intelligence institute was vandalized Tuesday night, the founder of the organization warned that violence would not resolve public concerns about the rapidly evolving technology.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Posted September 16, 2026 11:48 am.

Last Updated September 16, 2026 3:35 pm.

Montreal — Hours after the office of a Quebec artificial intelligence institute was vandalized Tuesday night, the founder of the organization warned that violence would not resolve public concerns about the rapidly evolving technology.

Mila’s Yoshua Bengio made the comments Wednesday morning at the opening of All In, a major artificial intelligence conference in Montreal, where he and federal Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon were set to announce new funding for research into the potential dangers of AI systems.

“Violence is not an answer to these risks and fears, which I can understand,” Bengio said at the AI and tech summit.

Montreal police say a group of about 10 people targeted the building at the corner of Saint-Urbain and Saint-Zotique streets at around 11:45 p.m. on Tuesday, smashing several windows and spray-painting graffiti on its walls.

A 25-year-old woman was arrested near the scene. Johany Charland, a spokesperson for Montreal police, said the woman was released Wednesday afternoon after being interviewed by investigators. Charland would not say if the woman was still considered a suspect in the investigation.

Mila says its central mission is to develop ethical and safe artificial intelligence that serves the public interest. It also says it focuses its mission on core research areas such as health, environment and climate change and that it carries out research using an open science approach to promote collaboration and foster the transfer of knowledge.

At the conference, Bengio said he has spent years examining the responsibilities of researchers, companies and governments as increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems raise ethical and safety questions.

“How can we make sure that ethics are at the centre of our decisions?” Bengio said, adding that doing so isn’t necessarily easy amid market competition and geopolitical pressures.

He said raising public awareness can lead to democratic debate about the choices society wants to make — “certainly not through violence.”

Solomon also condemned the vandalism, calling it unacceptable in a democracy and saying researchers and students have the right to work in peace and safety.

“There are real questions about technology, and we welcome them in our democracy,” Solomon said. He added that people should be able to ask questions and protest peacefully.

Mila separately condemned what it described as acts of vandalism and intimidation targeting its premises.

“While we respect the fundamental right to express differing opinions and social criticism, we strongly condemn any use of violence, property damage and tactics aimed at intimidating our staff and researchers,” the research institute wrote in a statement Wednesday.

Montreal police said investigators were reviewing surveillance footage and gathering evidence in an effort to identify other suspects. ”The investigation is ongoing,” said Charland.

Montreal police also said their presence at the city’s main convention centre, where the conference is taking place, had not been increased in response to the vandalism. Police said deployments had already been planned and no additional officers were assigned as a result of the overnight incident.

The comments from Bengio and Solomon came as the federal minister announced $150 million in funding for LawZero,a non-profit AI safety research organization founded by Bengio and incubated at Mila.

German federal Minister for Digital Transformation and Government Modernization Karsten Wildberger also announced plans to provide up to 100 million euros for the project, subject to approval by the European Commission.

Bengio said the money will help researchers demonstrate how artificial intelligence can be trained with safety guarantees.

Bengio also said some of the most serious risks posed by advanced AI are difficult to predict, but that doesn’t mean they should be ignored.

“The more powerful it is, the more beneficial it can be — and also the more dangerous,” Bengio said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

Charlotte Glorieux, The Canadian Press

stories.title: A list of Ontario cities that are weighing restrictions on AI data centres
stories.summary: Mississauga city council is set to vote Wednesday on a one-year data centre moratorium
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The boom in artificial intelligence has put Ontario municipalities on the front lines of a major debate over how to regulate a new wave of large, energy-hungry data centres.

Several municipalities have voted in recent months on temporary data centre moratoriums while they study possible guardrails, and at least one has amended its bylaws to specifically permit them on industrial lands.

Under pressure from local lawmakers, the Ontario government released a draft framework last month to deal with an influx of proposals that are causing some municipalities to consider temporary bans on constructing these facilities.

Here’s a brief look at what some Ontario municipalities have done, and plan to do.

Council directed staff last month to draft a moratorium on data centres with energy demands over 50 megawatts. A vote on that moratorium is expected on Sept. 21.

Council directed staff in July to review the city’s planning policies around data centres and pressed the province to come up with an Ontario-wide framework. Staff were also told to alert city councillors about any large data centre applications.

City council directed staff last month to study and develop an assessment framework for data centres, including possible amendments to city policy. stories.title: Ottawa gets it on tax policy, gamechanger ‘mega deduction’ shows
stories.summary: Initiative will address Canada’s lagging productivity by reducing the after-tax cost of investment
stories.author: Steve Suarez
stories.content:
Steve Suarez is a partner in the Toronto office of BLG, and the co-chair of the Taxation and Economics Committee of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s announcement Tuesday of the “ productivity mega deduction ” is one of the most consequential Canadian tax policy initiatives of the 21st century. At a stroke, the Canadian government has signalled to the business community “we get it.”

In simple terms (and simplicity is one of this measure’s virtues), this new “immediate expensing” deduction is a timing measure: It allows businesses to deduct for tax purposes the cost of eligible expenditures much sooner than would be the case under existing rules. The taxpayer doesn’t get a bigger deduction or more tax savings: just the same tax savings faster.

This is because while current rules require these business expenditures to be deducted for tax purposes over a period of years even if paid for up front, the productivity mega deduction allows the taxpayer to deduct the entire expenditure in the year in which the property in question becomes “available for use” (basically installed and capable of operation). Generally this means that taxpayers are much less likely to pay tax on profits before recovering their costs, which is eminently fair.

What is truly remarkable is the breadth of what qualifies. Most new investments in capital property acquired on or after Sept. 15 are eligible. Taken together with a 2025 federal budget measure for other property, the government estimates that some two-thirds of business investments in capital assets are now eligible for immediate expensing, with the Prime Minister’s Office describing the expanded scope as including “fibre-optic cable, mining property, oil and gas pipelines, software, research and development, computer equipment, aircraft and vehicles, patents, rail track, bridges, and roads.”

Opinion: Mark Carney’s investment moment

This initiative is vitally important to Canada’s economy for many reasons. Most importantly, it directly addresses Canada’s dreadful productivity record over the past 25 years. In March, 2026, Statistics Canada estimated that our labour productivity relative to the U.S. has fallen 26 per cent since the late 1990s, much of which occurred in the past five years.

Immediate expensing on this scale moves the needle on this problem by reducing the after-tax cost of badly needed investment. Measured by marginal effective tax rate (tax imposed on an additional dollar of business investment), the government estimates that Canada’s Metr on eligible investment will be reduced to 6.4 per cent, well below the comparable U.S. rate of 16.9 per cent. Making investments in productive assets cheaper in this way and on this scale was the Canadian Chamber of Commerce’s first recommendation in its 2026 prebudget submission to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne this summer, prompting president and CEO Candace Laing to describe this measure as “a launchpad to make Canada globally tax competitive.”

While this measure is not limited to any particular industry, Pierre Gratton, president and CEO of the Mining Association of Canada, described it as “transformative” in the resource sector. Building new mines is a high-risk, capital-intensive exercise often stretching over several years. Under current rules, only 30 per cent of most mine development costs can be deducted in the year incurred. Under immediate expensing, they would be 100-per-cent deductible when incurred: a huge difference.

Also critical is the fact that broad-based immediate expensing responds to a wave of 2025 U.S. business-friendly tax changes. Lisa Baiton, president and CEO of the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers, acknowledged this on Tuesday, observing that “Canada’s largest competitor for upstream oil and natural gas investment is the United States, and the productivity mega deduction closes a significant competitive gap between the two countries in terms of capital cost expensing.” Canadian business deserves a level playing field to compete on.

Broad-based immediate expensing hopefully signals a larger and long-overdue shift in Canada’s tax policy toward actively investing in our economy and its tax base, which is needed to fund the social programs that are part of what makes us Canada. Tuesday’s Department of Finance release described immediate expensing as representing “a sea-change in how Canada intends to stimulate business investment decisions,” which is exactly what our tax policy should be doing in these circumstances: actively supporting our larger economic strategy.

Reduced tax revenue today will generate much more tax revenue later, based on the estimated increased economic activity of 1.4 to three times the government’s cost of these measures and long-term employment increases of up to 80,000 jobs annually 10 years from now. Apart from these businesses, the workers building these investments today and those using them in the future are themselves taxpayers, who will add to our tax base.

The productivity mega deduction is a powerful and welcome statement of the federal government’s intention to make the cost of doing business in Canada much cheaper (hopefully the provinces follow suit). Canada just became a much more interesting place for Canadians and foreigners alike to invest in.

stories.title: Élections Québec ordered to mail bilingual voter information by Quebec judge
stories.summary: The judge said there is serious concern that a large number of English-speaking seniors could be unable to exercise their right to vote due to a lack of understandable information.
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
A Quebec Superior Court judge has ordered Élections Québec to mail voting reminder cards in both French and English.

This was the first year the elections authority sent out voter guides in French only, to comply with new provincial language legislation. The guides included a QR code to access information in English online.

Groups representing anglophones in the province heavily criticized the move, saying it infringes on the right to vote.

Justice Sylvain Lussier wrote in his 23-page decision that there was concern of serious and irreparable prejudice against Quebecers who do not understand French.

Geoffrey Chambers, a Westmount resident and the former president of an anglophone rights group, was the lead plaintiff in the case.

He had asked the judge to grant an emergency order to get the elections agency to provide English copies of the provincial election guide, a notice sent to electors, and a reminder card.

He argued that the QR code isn’t an adequate substitute because many people can’t access them, including some seniors and people without cellphones or reliable internet.

“The proof raises concerns that a large number of English-speaking seniors could be unable to exercise their right to vote due to a lack of understandable information,” Lussier wrote.

According to Lussier, there is also concern that election results could be invalidated if the right to vote is infringed on.

He pointed to the result of the 2025 federal byelection in Terrebonne, which was invalidated because of a clerical error on the return address for some mail-in ballots.

A recount handed the win to Liberal Tatiana Auguste by a single vote.

The one-vote result triggered a challenge after a Bloc voter’s mail-in ballot was returned because of an incorrect postal code on an Elections Canada return envelope

“It is clear that the loss of the right to vote in an election is permanent,” wrote Lussier. “The loss of a single vote was enough to invalidate the federal election in Terrebonne.”

However, lawyers representing the elections authority said it was impossible to reprint all documents to include English information given the time and budgetary constraints, which Lussier acknowledged in his decision.

He nonetheless asked Élections Québec to send the voter reminder card in both official languages. The list of candidates on the cards is finalized at 2 p.m. on Sept. 17, and the agency had already planned to print out reminder cards to mail out after that deadline.

Lussier’s ruling suspends provisions of the Charter of the French Language for 10 days to allow the printing of bilingual reminder cards.

Élections Québec had asked the government to be exempt from provisions forcing government institutions to issue public communications in French only as early as 2023. It raised concerns that it could not fulfil its mission to make elections accessible to all Quebecers as a result of the law.

Quebec voters go to the polls on Oct. 5.

stories.title: Cohere, Aleph Alpha combine to target enterprise AI market
stories.summary: Merged company will operate as Cohere, have headquarters in Toronto and Berlin
stories.author: Leo Marchandon
stories.content:
Canada’s Cohere and Germany’s Aleph Alpha signed a definitive merger agreement on Wednesday, the AI companies said.

The combined business will operate as Cohere, with dual headquarters in Toronto and Berlin, while Aleph Alpha’s Heidelberg office will focus on research. Aleph Alpha co-chief Ilhan Scheer will become chief operating officer of Cohere.

The merger brings together a Canadian AI model developer and a German company that has increasingly focused on helping governments and businesses deploy artificial intelligence. The companies said demand was growing for AI systems that can operate within a customer’s own infrastructure and comply with local regulatory requirements.

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez said the tie-up aimed to meet demand for AI “powerful enough to compete, but secure and governable enough to trust.”

Cohere, Open Text to pitch Canadian-made AI agent tools to enterprises

The plan was first disclosed in April, a combination valued at about US$20-billion at the time. Lidl-owner Schwarz Group is investing €500-million (US572-million) in the new entity. The companies did not disclose updated financial terms and said the transaction remained subject to regulatory approvals.

The deal comes as European AI companies attract fresh investment. Mistral, Europe’s lead model maker, last week raised €3-billion (US$3.46-billion) at a valuation of more than €21-billion (US$24.2-billion).

Cohere develops Command, a family of open source AI models designed to run inside a customer’s own computing environment, positioning the company to serve businesses, governments and public administrations rather than consumers.

Aleph Alpha, once touted as Germany’s AI champion, stepped back from developing frontier AI models and refocused on AI integration software. Co-founder Jonas Andrulis left the company earlier this year after relinquishing the chief executive role in 2025.

Cohere reported US$240-million in annual recurring revenue last year, while Aleph Alpha reported revenue of less than €1-million (US$1.15-million) in 2023, according to its latest public accounts.

The companies said Schwarz Group would provide computing capacity through its cloud arm StackIT. The retailer is investing between €11-billion (US$1.15-million) and €13-billion (US$15-billion) in a German data-centre campus expected to house up to 100,000 AI chips.

stories.title: Danny Boyle defends use of AI in new film ‘Ink’ at Tiff screening
stories.summary: Toronto — Danny Boyle says he tried to be responsible with the small amount of artificial intelligence used in the making of his new film “Ink.”
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Danny Boyle says he tried to be responsible with the small amount of artificial intelligence used in the making of his new film “Ink.”

At a Tuesday screening of the movie at the Toronto International Film Festival, the British director said he was careful to think about potential job losses when deciding to use the technology for about 30 seconds in the movie.

His remarks were met with jeers by some in the audience.

“We try to be very responsible and make sure that no actors were out of work because of it,” he explained during a panel after the screening, when an audience member asked about his use of AI. “We would always employ actors if we were going to use a bit of it.”

AI helped Boyle animate old photographs used in a montage and add mice to another scene in the movie about the sensationalism of U.K. tabloid the Sun under owner Rupert Murdoch.

Boyle didn’t explain why he felt it necessary to rely on the technology but said it’s an issue both the industry and humanity need to explore in the future.

“The wider question of It and its place in our society, of course, including our profession is a huge and complicated one, which I don’t think we could probably go into here,” he said. “But we will need to go into it more.”

As he wrapped up answering the question, an audience member shouted that he should never use AI in his film again. A Tiff employee who was moderating the panel with Boyle and stars Guy Pearce and Jack O’Connell then ended the question session.

Boyle is best known for “Slumdog Millionaire,” a rags to riches film that won Tiff’s People’s Choice Award in 2008 and then an Academy Award for best picture.

“Ink” screened at Tiff about a week after its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Annual pace of housing starts dips in August, Cmhc says
stories.summary: Modest gains in Quebec and Alberta only partially offset decline in other provinces
stories.content:
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. reports the annual pace of housing starts for August edged lower compared with July.

The national housing agency says the seasonally adjusted annual rate of housing starts came in at 229,046 units for August, down from 229,360 in July.

The result came as actual monthly housing starts in centres with a population of 10,000 or more totalled 17,691 in August, down from 18,112 units in August 2025.

The annual pace of rural starts was estimated at 11,224 units.

The six-month moving average of the seasonally adjusted annual rate of total housing starts for all areas in Canada was 244,149 in August, down 1.3 per cent from July.

Cmhc deputy chief economist Kevin Hughes says housing starts continued to trend slightly down in August, as modest gains in Quebec and Alberta only partially offset the decline in other provinces, most notably, Ontario.
